subjects.name: Old Testament Studies
subjects.description: Prophets and Prophecy in Israel: the prophetic institution, Deuteronomy and the Former Prophets, ninth-century prophetism, the Book of Amos and the Book of Malachi.

blocks.text: In Part One of the Local Preacher's syllabus, we looked at the General Introduction to the Old Testament. In Part Two, the studies will concentrate on the Prophets and Prophecy in Israel.
By the end of the study;
(i) 	Local Preachers should be able to explain who prophets are and their role in the religion and life of Israel.
(ii) 	Candidates should also be able to classify and name the books of the Old Testament that are designated as Prophetic Books.

(iii) 	There will be a brief look at Deuteronomy and the Former Prophets. Candidates should then be able to explain why the Books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are referred to as the Former Prophets and be able to apply them in their teaching and preaching.
(iv) 	Another area that is covered is Prophetism in Israel in the 9th Century B.C. using the traditions of Elijah and Elisha.

(v) 		An in-depth study of the Book of Amos has been carried out to demonstrate the extent to which the Prophets were concerned with the Religious, Political and the Social life of Israel in the 8th Century B.C.
(vi) 	Finally, the syllabus takes a look at the Book of Malachi and the religious atmosphere during the 5th Century B.C.

chapters.title: INTRODUCTION TO PROPHETS AND PROPHECY IN ISRAEL

blocks.text:
The phenomena of Prophets and Prophecy is not confined to Israel. Prophecy has been a 
feature of almost every religion throughout all cultures. We find many prophets in the Ancient 
Near East. Archaeology has helped us to discover the phenomena of prophets, prophecy and 
prophetism. The Old Testament tells us that there were prophets in other religions, e.g. the 
prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). The word used for the prophets of Baal is exactly the same as 
that for the prophets of Israel (Nabi).

reference.subject: Old Testament Studies
reference.chapter: I. INTRODUCTION TO PROPHETS AND PROPHECY IN ISRAEL
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — INTRODUCTION TO PROPHETS AND PROPHECY IN ISRAEL — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶25)

blocks.text:
In the Old Testament, three Hebrew words are normally used to designate the Prophets. 
These are Nāvi, rõ'eh and hõzeh. Rõ'eh and hõzeh are properly rendered as "seer", and are 
practically synonymous in meaning. Nāvi on the other hand is difficult to explain 
etymologically (that is, when you try to use the root word or the origin and history of the word 
to explain it). We can only work out what it means by looking at how it is used.

Each of the three words designates one who is a spokesman for God. An example of how Ntivi 
is used is found in Exodus 4:15-16 ("and you shall speak unto him and put words in his mouth... 
and he shall be your spokesman (Niivi] unto the people. . ."). Exodus 7:1 (And the Lord said to 
Moses, see I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet," 
spokesman, nāvi). In these passages it is explained that Moses stood in relation to  
Pharaoh as God and between them was Aaron who was to speak to Pharaoh on behalf of 
Moses (Aaron was a Nõvi). The man who can be designated a "Ntivi", then is one who speaks 
forth for God. "Rõ'eh" and "hõzeh" primarily refer to the fact that the person so designated, 
sees the message God gives him/her, (seer). This seeing may mean that the message first 
comes through a vision and in some instances it did. The use of these two words may refer to 
sight, but they usually refer to insight.

Thus the words rõeh and hõzeh designate one who, whether by vision or otherwise, is given 
insight into the mind of God, and who declares what has been "seen" as a message to the 
people. A prophet in the Old Testament then is a person who receives a message from God 
and utters the actual words that God has given to him, without any modification or 
interpretation on his part. An example of this is given in Deut. 18:18 "l will put my words in 
his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him." In the Old Testament the prophets 
are given various names which include man of God, seer, soothsayer, fortune-teller etc.

topics.title: The Establishment of the Prophetic Institution

blocks.text:
The Prophetic Institution became necessary during the settlement of the Nation of Israel in 
the Promised Land. When Israel entered Canaan they had the Law as a precious possession. 
This Law, revealed by God at Mount Sinai, laid the broad basis on which the life of the people 
of God was to be built and guided. The Ten Commandments was seen as the basis on which 
the principles of ethics and morality are founded, while other rules for particular situations 
are expressed in the other laws. On the basis of this the life of the people of God (Israel) was 
to be conducted.

The Law, however, was not adequate to meet all the situations that would arise when they 
settled in the Promised Land. This inadequacy was not due to any inherent weakness in the 
Law itself, but simply to the fact that the Law did not speak in detail on every possible 
situation that would arise in Israel's life. There would be occasions when a specific revelation 
of God would be needed in order to show the nation the course it should pursue. The needed 
revelation, God would give to the people through his servants, the prophets.

Again, when Israel entered Canaan, it was find that the people of that land sought to learn 
about the future and the will of the gods by various means that the Bible calls "abominations" 
or "detestable ways" (Deut. 18:9). There was the danger that the Israelites would be 
influenced by the Canaanites on whose land they lived and (the Israelites) might learn to do 
same. To avoid this danger, the Lord declared that He would raise up the prophets and that 
the Israelites were to listen to the prophets and to obey them (Duet. 18: 15).

The prophets whom the Lord would raise were to be like Moses; just as Moses was a mediator between God and the nation, so would the prophets serve as mediators between God and the Nation. Just as the priests represented the people before God, so the prophets represented God to the people.

In ancient Greece we have the god, the oracle, the prophet and the people, and we have the 
same for the Mesopotamian countries. In Israel, however, there was only one intermediary 
between God and the people. This arrangement was truly unique. One who heard the words 
of the prophet heard the very words of God himself (Thus says the Lord) and these words 
required implicit obedience.
According to the testimony of the Bible, the prophetic institution of Israel was of divine origin, God Himself set up this institution (Deut. 18:15-18).

After the people had entered the Promised Land, there came a time when "everyone did as he 
saw fit" (Judges 21:25). There was the danger not only from the idolatry of Canaan but also 
from the incursion of the Philistines. There was, therefore, the need for encouragement and 
the spiritual welfare of the nation. For this reason bands (hevel) of prophets were raised up. 
It is believed that Samuel was the founder of such groups. Following the death of Samuel, 
these prophetical bodies seem to have disbanded. We do not hear of them until the times of 
Elijah and Elisha. During the days of these men, groups of prophets appeared again. During 
Elijah's day these bands of prophets appeared only in the Northern Kingdom. The kingdom 
had become divided because of the rebellion of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. There was now 
need for support against the worship of the Tyrian Baal as well as the Calf worship at Dan and 
Bethel. Both Elijah and Elisha exercised a vigorous ministry in the North, but were strongly 
opposed by the government. Elijah and Elisha therefore needed assistance and this was 
found in the companies who bore the designation "sons of the prophets". The phrase reveals 
the close and intimate association in which these men stood to the great prophets Elijah and 
Elisha. After this period, however, they seem to die out and we hear no more of them.

topics.title: Forms of Prophets and Prophetic Groups in Israel

blocks.text:
In the Old Testament there are very varied forms and groups of prophets and prophecy, but 
broadly speaking the Old Testament prophecy falls into three main forms: The Company of 
Prophets, the Royal Cults or Court Prophets and Individual Prophets.

Company of Prophets: These are called by various names e.g. sons or bands or congregation of prophets. They are especially associated with Samuel, (1 Sam. 10:5 ff; 19:20) and Elijah 
(1Kings 18:4 & 22; 2Kings 2:1-8). These sons or bands of prophets appear to have lived 
together in communities and seem to have been associated with sanctuaries and used music 
as part of the method or technique of prophesying. They also gave oracles, (1 Sam. 
10:5 ff). For example, Saul sought Samuel on the loss of his father's asses, (I Samuel 9:3-10). 
Samuel appears to have been one of the leaders of this group.

Royal Prophets / Cult Prophets or Court Prophets: These prophets were associated with the 
Royal Sanctuaries, e.g. Jerusalem. They had special responsibility for guiding the King. There 
were differences in the way these prophets approached their work. For example, Nathan, who 
gave advice to David and Solomon, was honest and straight. But there were other prophets 
who told the Kings what they wanted to hear rather than the truth.

Prophets like Jeremiah condemned the royal prophets who proclaimed; "Peace, Peace" while 
there was no peace. These prophets are sometimes called "shalom" prophets, but, it was 
these prophets who went to war with the king's army and cursed the enemy.

Individual Prophets: These prophets stand alone as individuals. They sometimes belonged to 
a group or stood as individuals on the staff of the sanctuary - e.g. Elijah, Jeremiah, Hosea, 
Isaiah. In Israel, the job of the priest seemed to be largely concerned with sacrifice and 
counselling with regard to ritual matters, while the general preaching of morality was the 
work of the prophets.

blocks.text: 1.4.1 	The Role of the Prophets in Israel
The prophets played a variety of roles in the life of Israel. These included.
i) 	Giving of oracles which was generally consultative.
ii) 	Preaching and teaching during worship.

iii) 	Interceding on behalf of the people, e.g. Amos prays that the judgment of God should 
not come upon his people. They also spoke of the needs of the people to God.
iv)	Declaring the will and the purpose of God even when this was not requested and in other contexts than the cultic services.

Prophetic ministry in Israel was unpredictable. The prophet was free to act as and when the Spirit of God directed. They were feared in society. They were free to speak whatever came to 
them. The prophets were free from all constraints; for example, Jeremiah would have been 
persecuted as a traitor immediately after his first utterance, had he not been a prophet. They 
had the sovereign freedom to say things, when, where and to whom they were directed to 
declare the will of God, (e.g. Nathan and David, 2Sam 12: 1-12).
1.4.2 	The Prophetic Word

In ancient Israel, the WORD was something very important. A man's spoken word had great 
significance. The written word for the Israelites was not as important as the spoken word, 
since there were only a few people who could read and write at that time. It was your spoken 
word that testified against you when you were sent to the court, (e.g. "the blessing is a 
powerful word" - Jacob steals the blessing, yet since the word had been given it could not be taken back, that is why when Esau asked "what is left for me?", the father said, "nothing", all 
that he wanted to say had been said.

The word had an independent power. It was an instrument of effective power. That is why 
the word of the Prophet was very important. Again the Prophetic word was the very word of 
God, the same word was to be proclaimed by the prophet. It was not the prophet's own 
words, but the word of God.
1.4.3 	The Prophetic Action

The prophets do not only speak but act, this is what is termed the prophetic action or 
prophetic symbolism. The prophetic action is itself creative of what it depicts. For example, 
Ezekiel builds a city on sand with mud and makes a toy soldier (Ezekiel 4) etc. By this Ezekiel 
meant he was helping to bring about the siege and the destruction of Jerusalem.

These actions were not just illustrations but depicted what was likely to happen. The 
performing of the action was in itself a contribution to bring about what was being conveyed. 
The prophetic actions were believed to contain power to shape the future.
1.4.4 	Prophecy and the Future
What does the word prophecy mean?

A commonly held meaning of the word is: To Predict the Future. Although this understanding 
is popular these days, it is not the proper meaning of the word. In the Old Testament the word means To Speak the Word of God. Therefore prophecy takes many forms and has many 
aspects. Sometimes prophecy is an explanation of past events, sometimes it is a warning, an 
admonition or appeal, a piece of advice or exhortation in the present, and sometimes it is 
directed to the future. Prophecy, in the Old Testament therefore, has past reference 
occasionally, a future reference occasionally and the present most often. The prophets were 
primarily religious commentators on the life they saw around them, and that included the 
social, economic and political life of the day.

Very often the future reference was to the immediate future, and again the future reference 
was conditional, ". . .if you do not repent then. . ." Very often the prophets pointed out what 
will happen if the people did not repent.

Generally, the words of the writing prophets had reference to their own times, but as 
indicated earlier, they foretold the certainty of the future plans of God for humankind. 
Occasionally their words made reference to the future coming of Christ (Isa. 7:14; 9:6; 
11:1 ff, cf. Luke 1:31 ff; Isa. 53; Micah 5:2, cf. Matt. 2:5 & 6).
1.4.5 	True and False Prophets

In every religion there are true and false prophets. Israel's true religion had always been 
plagued by imitators alongside the faithful and true prophets of the Lord. There were other 
men who had not received a revelation from God. Jeremiah refused to have anything to do 
with these men. They were regarded as false prophets. They were men who deceived. 
Sometimes they claimed to have received messages from God, when they had not received 
such messages. Probably the best illustration of false prophecy can be seen in 1 Kings 13 
where one prophet lied to another prophet.

The distinction between the true and the false prophet is very clear in 1 Kings 22 where 400 
false prophets encouraged King Ahab of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah to fight against 
the Syrians at Ramoth-Gilead. Only the prophet Micaiah son of Imlah, tried to discourage 
them from going to battle. Ahab told King Jehoshaphat that he hated Micaiah because he 
always prophesied evil against him. In the end Micaiah's words proved true and Ahab died in 
battle which was, as Deut. 18:20-22 had said, the test of a true prophet.

In the Old Testament, there were three tests which the people could use to discern between 
true and false prophets.

The Theological test (Deut.13): Through Moses there had been a revelation of the Lord who brought his people out of Egypt. Therefore, even if the prophet performed some signs to give validation to what he was saying, if his message contradicted Mosaic theology - the truth known about the Lord who brought his people out of Egypt - the prophet was false.

The Practical Test (Deut. 18:20ff): The prophecy that is not fulfilled has not come from the Lord. It must be noted that, this is a negative test. It does not say that fulfillment is proof that the Lord has spoken, since that might in fact be used as evidence offered by a false prophet to validate his word. What is not fulfilled is not from the Lord.

The Moral Test (Jer. 23:9ff): This is a test first to be applied to the lives of the prophets themselves (Jer. 23:13-14) and then to the tendency of the message they preached. Do they in fact strengthen the hands of evildoers, assuring them that they need not fear judgement to come (Jer. 23:17)? This is a sure sign that they have not stood before the Lord to hear his word (Jer. 23:18-19). The prophet who comes fresh from the Lord's presence has a message turning people from evil (Jer. 23:22).

Often the false prophets were greater in number than the true prophets. For example, in 1 
Kings 22, there were 400 false prophets and Micaiah was the only true prophet. The false 
prophets were also popular. They told the people, or the King, what they wanted to hear. 
They made no moral demands upon the people to obey God.

The God they worshipped was an easy-going God. This was why Ahab hated Micaiah. Micaiah always prophesied "evil" things against the King, i.e. the judgment of God. But Micaiah knew that a true prophet must only prophesy what God speaks to him. Nothing more, nothing less (1 Kings 22:14).

This was Jeremiah's experience as well. He discovered that his colleagues were prophesying lies, they were immoral (Jer. 23:24); they filled the people with vain hopes of peace instead of the woes of God's judgment (Jer. 23:14); they prophesied lying dreams (Jer. 23:32) and used 
,lthe phrase "the burden of the Lord" in an hypocritical fashion (vv. 33-40). Above all, the false 
prophets had not "stood in the council of the Lord" (23:18-22). This was why they 
prophesied lies. They did not know God personally, nor did they understand His ways.

By contrast the true prophet could receive messages from God because he did stand in the 
council of the Lord. But a true prophet would always face opposition from two directions, as 
Micaiah did. This was the stubbornness of the people they prophesied to, including the 
leaders (Jer. 13:8-11) and the lies of their own fellow prophets who were "false" (Jer. 14:13- 
16).

blocks.text:
The books of the Hebrew Old Testament are arranged in three parts - the Law, the Prophets 
and the Writings. In this section we shall be looking at the Books that Constitute the 
PROPHETS and attention will be focused primarily on the FORMER PROPHETS.

reference.subject: Old Testament Studies
reference.chapter: II. DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶119)

topics.title: The Books of the Old Testament that Constitute the Prophets

blocks.text:
The "Prophets" is further divided into two parts - THE FORMER and the LATTER PROPHETS 
with each containing four scrolls.
The Former Prophets: The books are: Joshua, Judges, I & II Samuel and I & II Kings

These books are anonymous, their authors are not known. They are classified as "former 
prophets" because the history they contain conform to the biblical definition of prophecy as a 
declaration of the wonderful works of God (Acts 2:11, 18). This does not mean they are less 
than true history, but that what was selected for recording was to demonstrate the moral 
principles of divine providence worked out over the centuries. It is against this background 
of interpretative history that we are to understand the work of the great prophets. The 
former prophets cover the period from Israel's entrance into the Promised Land until the 
destruction of the theocracy under Nebuchadnezzar.
The Latter Prophets: These are also called the writing prophets. Under this group we have:
Major Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel
Minor Prophets: The Twelve - Hosea to Malachi

These prophets exercised a great ministry in Israel. The use of the term "Latter" does not 
necessarily have reference to historical chronology or order, but is simply a term used to 
show that they follow the "former" prophets in the Hebrew arrangement of the Old 
Testament.

The "Latter" or "Writing" prophets were not anonymous. They were entrusted by God with 
the task and responsibility of addressing prophetic messages not only to the people of their 
own day but also to posterity. They are prophets whose identities, names, places and time of 
prophecy are known. It must be noted, however that there were some prophets whose 
names are not known.

The writing prophets uttered messages that are more relevant to us (e.g. the coming of the 
Messiah) and so we have to be assured that those who gave such messages were truly 
accredited spokesmen of the Lord. Both the former and the latter prophets complemented 
one another. The former prophets set forth the history of a particular period in the life of 
Israel and the latter or writing prophets interpreted particular phases of that history. The 
one is necessary for the proper understanding of the other.

reference.subject: Old Testament Studies
reference.chapter: II. DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS
reference.topic: 2.1 The Books of the Old Testament that Constitute the Prophets
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — The Books of the Old Testament that Constitute the Prophets (syllabus ¶122)

blocks.text:
In this section we shall briefly look at the "Deuteronomic" or "Prophetic" view of History, and 
why the Historical Books are called former prophets.

When we read the story of the call of Moses in Exodus 4:14-17 we note that Aaron was to be 
Moses' Nabi, that is, Aaron was to speak on behalf of Moses. In short a prophet speaks on behalf of another person or a deity. As far as the Old Testament is concerned, especially when 
we read the Book of Deuteronomy, there are several passages depicting Moses speaking on 
behalf of God to the people of Israel and again Moses speaking on behalf of the people to God. 
In these passages Moses reveals to the people, the character of God, the results of obedience 
or disobedience to God's commandment, and how God acts in the life and history of His 
people. (Read Deut. 28:1-35 to enable you understand.) In several places in Deuteronomy, Moses warned the people that if they obeyed God, He would greatly bless them, but if they disobeyed Him, He would certainly punish them. (Read Deut. 5:32- 6:3; 6:10- 15; 7:12-15; 8:11-20; 11:8-17, 26-28.)

In these passages Moses acted as a prophet of God revealing to the people of Israel His true 
character. God's blessing would come to the whole nation and be seen in its life and history if 
it obeyed God. The nation would be strong and would defeat its enemies. On the other hand, 
if the nation disobeyed God His punishment for sin would come upon the nation and be seen 
in its history. If the nation grew weak and was invaded, then God was punishing it. It is this 
way of presenting the Old Testament history that is seen in the books collectively referred to 
as "former prophets". The style or interpretation of history is a reflection of what Moses said 
in the Book of Deuteronomy, hence what is referred to as "Deuteronomic" view of history. 
These facts are clearly illustrated in the books of the former prophets' section of the Hebrew 
OT, where the prophetic teachings of Moses about blessing and punishment are recorded. For 
example, in the Book of Judges there is the record of the cycle of events: the people sin, God is 
angry and sells them into the hands of oppressors; during the oppression they cry to God for 
deliverance; God sends a judge - a warrior - and saves them and the land enjoys peace again. 
At the death of the judge, the people fall into sin again and the cycle continues. (Read Judges 
Chapters 1 to 12 to illustrate the point.)

reference.subject: Old Testament Studies
reference.chapter: II. DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — Deuteronomy and the Former Prophets (syllabus ¶138)

topics.title: Why the Prophetic Books are referred to as Former Prophets

blocks.text: Firstly, the prophetic books (Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings) continue to teach the Deuteronomic philosophy of history. They emphasize Moses' prophetic teaching that obedience brings blessing in national life, while disobedience to God brings disaster. (These have been discussed in the preceding section.)

Secondly, they were the first books written to describe the activities of the early prophets of 
Israel like Samuel, Elijah and Elisha.

The Story of Samuel is recorded in the Book of Samuel, while the Books of Kings deal with the 
stories and activities of Elijah and Elisha.

reference.chapter: II. DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS
reference.topic: 2.3 Why the Prophetic Books are referred to as Former Prophets
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — DEUTERONOMY AND THE FORMER PROPHETS — Why the Prophetic Books are referred to as Former Prophets (syllabus ¶145)

topics.title: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets

blocks.text: 2.4.1 	Joshua

The book of Joshua deals with the history of Israel after the death of Moses (Deut. 34). It deals with the conquest and settlement in the Promised Land. At every step, Joshua was successful. (Invasion of the land - Chapters 1-5; the fall of Jericho - Chapter 6; Conquest of the south - chapter 10; Conquest of the North-chapters 11-12; division of the land, appointment of cities of refuge, chapters 13-22; and the farewell address and death of Joshua, 23-24.) The crossing of the River Jordan, the capture of Jericho, the quick military operations against the 
important cities of Canaan, all come to illustrate the successes of Joshua. His one failure was 
at Ai. The reason for this defeat was because Achan coveted some of the spoils from Jericho 
and kept them for himself instead of letting it all be offered to God. He and his family suffered

a very severe punishment in being totally destroyed. Here we see a grim illustration of the 
prophetic interpretation of history where disobedience brings disaster - chapter 7.

According to Keith B. Anderson (The Theology of the Bible) God applied this principle to the 
people of Canaan and demanded that none of them should be left alive. Otherwise they would 
infect the Israelites with their evil ways (Deut. 7:1-6; Joshua 8:21-29; 11:14ff). This prophecy 
of racial destruction may seem immoral to us today, but it must be noted that the religion of 
Canaan was a "fertility religion". This religion is centered on sex with many sexual symbols 
and organized religious prostitution at every "high place" of worship. For the faith of Yahweh, 
the God of Israel to survive, this kind of religion will have to be destroyed completely. The 
one occasion when Joshua entered into a covenant with the people of Gibeon was described 
as a mistake because Israel "did not ask direction from the Lord" (Joshua 9:14-27).

The second half of the book tells how the land was divided up among the twelve tribes of 
Israel, and ends with the rededication of the people and just before his death, Joshua renews 
the covenant with Israel at Shechem. They cried out to Joshua "The Lord our God we will 
serve, and His voice we will obey" (Joshua 24:24). But their spiritual enthusiasm did not last 
long as it is portrayed in the book of Judges.
2.4.2 	Judges

Judges covers the period in Israel's history between Joshua's death and the rise of Samuel - 
roughly 1220 to 1050 B.C. It was a time of transition where the only thing that held the 
scattered tribes together was their common faith. Loyalty to God meant a strong united 
nation. Turning to gods around brought weakness and division.

The story in Judges Chapter 1 gives the impression that Israel under Joshua could not drive 
out the Canaanites as portrayed in the book of Joshua. This failure leads on to a story of 
increasing chaos and confusion. One thing which comes out clearly in the book of Judges is 
that history continually repeated itself through the period. This pattern of failure is repeated 
in the books of Samuel and Kings.

Analysis of the Book: The prophetic interpretation of this pattern of history is described 
carefully in Judges 2:11-23, and here we have five stages:

The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the Lord; they forsook the Lord 
and served Balls, the gods of the Canaanites.
The Lord's anger came upon Israel and He gave them up into the hands of foreign powers, the Moabites, Midianites, Ammorites, and Philistines etc.

Then they cried to the Lord and He had pity on His people's sufferings and He raised 
up Judges to deliver them. Some of the Judges were Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, 
Abimelech, Tola, Jair, Jephthah etc.
The Judges were given military victory and success by God against their enemies.

When the judges died, the people returned to their old sinful and idolatrous ways; and so the pattern of failure started all over again. The book ends with an appendix to illustrate more clearly the moral and religious decline of those times (chapter 17-21). The people committed falsehood, murder, homosexuality, rape, civil war and mass abduction as they went their way instead of God's way.

In Judges 17:6 and 21:25, the explanation given for this state of affairs is that, "There was no 
King in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes".
2.4.3 	1 & 2 Samuel

I & II Samuel were originally one volume, or one book as contained in the Hebrew Old 
Testament. It was the Septuagint (LXX) that divided it into two. These two books provide us 
with the history of Israel from the end of the period of the Judges to the last years of David, 
the nation's second King who is also considered as the greatest of their Kings. The period 
covers about 100 years, from 1075 to 975 B.C. It is indeed a religious history, which 
concentrates on three main personalities - Samuel, Saul and David. It is the story of God and 
his dealings with his people Israel, especially its leaders.

The name Samuel is given to the books not because he is the writer, but because he is 
the dominating figure. He is seen in the book as the King maker - he anointed both Saul and 
David as Kings.

Analysis of the Books: In brief, the books may be divided into the following main themes or 
sections:

i. 	Shiloh and Samuel (1 Samuel 1:1-7:1) 
ii. 	Samuel and Saul (1 Samuel 7:2 - 15:35)

iii. 	Saul and David (1 Samuel 16:5-31:35; 2 Samuel 1) 
iv. 	David as King of Judah (2 Samuel 2-4)
v. 	David as King of all Israel (2 Samuel 5-24)

The book begins with Hannah's distress because of her bareness, her prayer to God and 
the answer - the birth of Samuel. Hannah's song shows a relationship to both the 
Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55) and the prophecy of Zachariah (1:68-79). The book records 
that Samuel's childhood was spent at Shiloh, where God spoke and revealed to him the 
future of the priestly line of Eli. Israel's battle with the Philistines resulted in a Philistine 
victory, the capture of the Ark of God and the death of the sons of Eli, Hophni and 
Phinehas. This resulted in what we now refer to as the "Philistine menace", which went 
on until the ark was sent back to Israel.

When the people requested for a King, Samuel disagreed with them but God directed 
him to grant their request and Saul was secretly anointed as King. This selection was 
later confirmed by casting of lot at an assembly of all Israel at Mizpah. Saul's first 
impressive act, the rescue of Jabesh-Gilead from the besieging Ammonites, led to his 
confirmation as king at Gilead. Samuel then retired from active public life (1 Samuel 12)

though he continued to serve as adviser to the King. Saul's disobedience brought about 
his rejection from the kingship.

David was then designated as the successor and Samuel secretly anointed him. David 
killed Goliath in a single combat to save the nation, Israel. Saul then inquired concerning 
David's family, so that Jesse too could be honoured (1 Sam. 17:55:58). Later David 
became a close friend of Jonathan, Saul's son, but Saul was now both jealous and afraid 
of David. Saul was openly hostile to David and made several attempts to kill him. David 
was forced to flee, and Saul pursued him until the Philistines defeated the Israelites on 
Mt. Gilboa where Saul and his son Jonathan perished. David mourned their passing 
away in an eloquent eulogy.
David reigned as King of Judah in Hebron for seven and half years, and made every effort to unite all Israel under his leadership.

David succeeded in his effort and wisely took Jerusalem as the new Capital. David 
continued to build the kingdom and the Lord announced to him the continuity of his 
dynasty (2 Sam.7). Though David conquered his enemies and was gracious to Jonathan's 
son, he was overcome by temptation in idleness and his affair with Bathsheba led to 
bitter heartache even though there was sincere repentance on the part of the King.

Circumstances in the royal family brought the rebellion of Absalom, which again saw 
David in flight for his life. The killing of Absalom ended the revolt but increased David's 
sorrow. He was restored to Jerusalem, but had to deal promptly with the short-lived 
revolt of Sheba. 2 Samuel ends with a summary of battles with the Philistines, David's 
praise of the Lord (2 Sam. 22, 23:2-7); the listing of his mighty men, and the catastrophe 
of the census.

The books present the history of Israel for that period (Romans 15:4; 2 Cor. 10:11) and 
serve as warning, instruction and encouragement. More specifically, the books of Samuel 
present the establishment of the kingship in Israel. In preserving the account of Samuel 
the judge, and prophet, the books mark the transition from the rule of the judges to 
monarchy since he filled the prophetic office and administered the induction into office 
of Israel's first two kings.

Like Samuel, l & 2 Kings were originally written as one volume but was divided into two 
at the time of the LXX (Septuagint). The two books cover four centuries (400 years) of 
Israel's history from the close of David's reign (930 B.C) through the golden age of 
Solomon, and the rift between Israel and Judah, to the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and the 
destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BC, and ends with the release of Jehoiachin (in Babylon, 
after 561 BC).

In the original Hebrew canon (The Law, Prophets and Writings) Kings preceded Isaiah 
as the concluding volume of the former prophets: (Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings). 
Even though they are listed among the Historical books in the current English Bible, the 
four books possess an essentially prophetic character (contrast the priestly volumes of 
Chronicles). They record the events of past history and conclude with a statement 
showing whether the king obeyed or did not obey the word of God (2 Kings 8:22).

In the book of Kings, more emphasis is placed on the 40 years of Solomon's reign (eleven chapters) than on the 200 years period from his death in BC 930 until the fall of Samaria in BC 722 (28 chapters: 1 Kings 12 - 2Kings 17). The great interest in Solomon is to be expected since he was as great as his father David, although in different ways.

The other great interest of Kings is the prophetic ministry of Elijah and Elisha. They 
represented the great northern "resistance" movement against the corrupting influence 
of King Ahab and the Baal religion of his wife Jezebel. Their revolt was characterized by 
power to work miracles, which had not been seen in the life of Israel since the Exodus (1 
Kings 17 - 2 Kings 13). The last eight chapters from 2 Kings 18 complete the history of 
Judah up to the time of the exile.

chapters.title: PROPHETISM IN ISRAEL IN THE 9TH CENTURY

topics.title: Background - The Conflict between Yahwism and Baalism during the Settlement in the land of Canaan

blocks.text:
The accounts in 1Kings chapters 17 to 19 and 2Kings show that the Prophet Elijah, who came 
from Tishbe in Gilead prophesied during the reign of Ahab (c. 873 -851 B.C.), while Elisha's 
ministry was from the period of Ahab through to the reign of Jehoahaz (c. 815 -800 B.c.).

The traditions of Elijah and Elisha are basically concerned with the issue of YAHWISM and 
BAALISM, that is, the Israelite religion ofYahwism and the Canaanite religion ofBaalism. The problem is this: The people who came from the desert with Moses came with their 
religion - Yahwism. The people in the land of Canaan had a religion - Baalism, and the 
question was, what was to be the relationship between the two religions?

Yahwism, the Israelite religion, has a theological position of monolatry or henotheism, (i.e. 
worship was to be given exclusively to Yahweh). It abhors visual representation of any kind. 
The worship of Yahweh was very plain, no statues and or pictorial representation of any kind was allowed. Yahwism laid no stress on sanctuaries or sacred places. Yahweh is not a god, therefore, of a particular place. This religion is characterized by laying strong emphasis on morality and the keeping of the commandment given on Mt. Sinai. To worship Yahweh was primarily to keep his commandments.

Baalism, by contrast, was a religion tied to the land, a religion of times and seasons. It was 
purely an agricultural religion that laid great emphasis on local shrines, sanctuaries, and high places. As an agricultural religion, Baalism was intimately connected with the fertility of the land. It was a polytheistic religion and laid no stress at all on morality. To worship Baal was to celebrate rites and festivals designed to procure the fertility of the land.

As far as the Israelites were concerned, there was a conflict between the two religions and 
this related to their settlement in the land of Canaan. The problem here was, how could the 
people of Israel occupy the land without also taking over their religion. The Israelites were 
shepherds without very good ideas about food crop farming, which was also the predominant occupation of the Canaanites. Since the Israelite was to sow crop, it became necessary to adopt the religion of Baalism, which had conflicting ideas with the worship ofYahwism.

The Canaanite neighbours told them that unless they adopt the worship of Baalism, 
agricultural practices would be impossible. This was the problem that the Israelites had to
face.

Another feature of Baalism was its festivals with its cultic practices including - the orgies, 
feasting, drinking, eating and sex. Therefore from a purely sensory point of view, Baalism was an attractive religion. This was opposed to Yahwism. Unfortunately, The Conquest of the land by Joshua did not lead to the complete extermination of Baalism. What then was to be the relationship between these two religions?

Generally, the relationship between the two religions, as far as the Israelites were concerned, 
was one of compromise. Israel took over some of the practices and theology of Baalism. It did 
so by accepting that Yahweh was able to do all that Baal was able to do, and many of the 
words that applied to Baal were also applied to Yahweh.

However, certain words could not be applied to Yahweh. There was no way of thinking of 
Yahweh as dying and rising, or as one who approved of any kind of sexual expression in his 
worship.

topics.title: The Traditions of Elijah and Elisha

blocks.text:
With the above background, it can be seen that the traditions of Elijah were basically 
concerned with the clash between Yahwism and Baalism - Elijah's prediction of drought,      (1 Kings 17:1-5) the Mt Carmel contest (1 Kings 18) the denunciation of crime against Naboth (1 Kings 21) and his oracles against Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:1ff) are all examples of his handling of the conflict.

Elisha's traditions, however, do not show the same tension between Yahwism and Baalisrn, 
but that of the performance of Signs and Wonders both at personal and national levels (2 
Kings Chapters 2 - 8).
The Traditions of Elijah and Elisha are, therefore, of vital importance for the understanding of the nature of Prophetism in Israel in the 9th Century 8.c.

The Elijah tradition, especially the Mount Carmel contest, illustrates the variety of Prophetism in the 9th century B.C. Though Elijah had connections with the prophetic communities, he was pre-eminently solitary. He travelled alone and sometimes vanished mysteriously and then reappeared unheralded, a tradition which is of peculiar importance. Elisha's performance of signs and wonders were meant to demonstrate the power of Yahweh and a call to serve Him alone in the 9th Century B.C. These show that we had individual prophets as well as Prophetic groups in the 9th Century Be.

blocks.text:
Amos is one of the courageous prophets who had well-founded convictions, and stood up for 
what he believed. He was always willing, no matter the cost even at the peril of his life, to 
speak that which was true, though it may not be popular with the people. Amos was a man 
who had a keen sense of justice and even in the face of serious opposition, he was willing to 
stand up for the rights of the powerless and the poor. Amos is seen as a true servant of God.

He was a dynamic person who exploded onto the public scene at a time when Society, 
Religion and Government were totally corrupt. He is regarded as the first of the classical 
prophets and ranks as the greatest of the Minor Prophets.
The Name Amos: Amos means "burden-bearer." He is the only man in the Old Testament with this name. The name should not be confused with Amoz who was the father of the prophet Isaiah.

Hometown: Amos was from a town called Tekoa, a small mountain-top town in Judah, (Amos 
1: 1; 7: 12). Tekoa was about twelve (12) miles from Jerusalem, the capital of the Southern 
Kingdom and about six (6) miles south east of Bethlehem. This town was believed to be the 
center of a large sheep-farming district, and Amos states that when he was called to the office 
of a prophet, he was taking care of his flock.

Occupation: Two terms are used to describe Amos (in Amos 7:14) a Shepherd and a 
dresser of sycamore fig-trees. The actual social status of Amos is difficult to determine, but gathering of sycamore fruit, which was a seasonal occupation was among the lowest of 
occupations in Palestine. This gives an idea of Amos' poor economic condition. But in Chapter 
1:1, another term nõqĕd which is translated as shepherd is used of Amos. The term nõqĕd 
was used to describe the keeper of a particular kind of desert sheep that were highly priced 
on account of the excellence of their wool. The word is unusual, occurring only at 2 Kings 3:4 
in respect of Mesha, King of Moab.

The term in its proper interpretation refers to a sheep owner who had other shepherds under him. This may suggest that Amos was a substantial and respected man in his community. It will therefore be wrong to think of him as just a simple and uncultured person. Sycamore fig trees do not grow at Tekoa but by the Dead Sea. His migrant work took him into the Northern Kingdom. Little did he realize that one day he would go there, not to pick fruit, but to preach God's message at Bethel.

reference.chapter: IV. THE BOOK OF AMOS
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — The Prophet Amos (syllabus ¶251)

topics.title: The Historical Background to Amos' Ministry

blocks.text:
Amos delivered his message during the reign of Jeroboam II, who ruled Israel from 786 to 746 BC. This was the period when the fortunes of the Northern Kingdom of Israel were at its 
highest point of prosperity and peace.

Jeroboam's father, Jehoash, who reigned in Israel from 801 to 786 BC had taken advantage of 
the political and military change in the Middle East, to improve upon the economic situation 
of his country. Syria's aggressive wars of conquest to the North had been stopped by the 
Assyrians. For that reason both Israel and Philistia who had been vassals of Syria, took the 
opportunity to revolt against the rule of Syria. Since the Assyrians were pre-occupied with 
wars elsewhere, Jehoash took the opportunity to consolidate his own position, and regained 
the territories which had previously been lost to Syria.

Therefore, at the time Jeroboam II ascended the throne of Israel, the lost Israelite lands had been recovered and there was relative peace with the Southern Kingdom of Judah. There was then a spirit of co-operation and mutual enterprise resulting in a flow of trade or commerce 
between the two kingdoms. It was a time of prosperity and splendour that was matched by a 
corresponding economic advance in Judah under Uzziah who was Jeroboam's contemporary. 
Jeroboam II himself continued the military success of his father, took advantage of the 
internal weakness of Syria at that time to extend his frontiers to almost those of the old 
Davidic kingdom and also pursued an expansionist policy into Trans-Jordan (2 Kings 14: 23 - 
29).

reference.subject: Old Testament Studies
reference.chapter: IV. THE BOOK OF AMOS
reference.topic: 4.2 The Historical Background to Amos' Ministry
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — The Historical Background to Amos' Ministry (syllabus ¶264)

blocks.text:
The military success of Jeroboam II also brought with it improved economic development. 
Israel at this time built a close relationship with Phoenicia, which remained the dominant 
commercial power in the Middle East. Among the economic policies of Jeroboam were:

The imposition of tolls upon all caravans passing through Israel. This brought a lot of 
revenue to the treasury.
Increased opportunities for international trade
Development of Samaria into a strong commercial centre

"The splendid buildings erected by Jeroboam II in Samaria demonstrated well enough the 
prosperity of the Northern State. Many people became very rich as a result of the increased 
opportunities for International trade" (John Drane 1987).

One important feature of the period was that the rich became richer while the poor became 
poorer. It is noteworthy how Amos repeatedly attacked this division between the rich and the poor. He attacked, especially, the luxury of the rich as against the misery of the poor. Amos indeed gives a clear picture of the circumstances of the time. He talks about the many fine buildings in the capital Samaria (3: 10) and also the fact that those who owned such buildings, the rich merchants and others, had one aim: to increase their profit, no matter the means. Amos stated that these merchants hated the day in which they could not do any business (8:5). These rich men were supported by their wives who demanded more and more luxury (4: 1 f; 6: 1-6).

While the houses of the rich were loaded with goods and other luxurious items (3:12; 6:4) the poor were subjected to a cruel economic exploitation (2: 6-8; 4: 1; 5: 10- 12; 8: 4-6). Small 
businessmen were forced out of their business by the big monopolies without any possibility 
of redress at the courts. Justice was perverted by the judges who took bribes (2: 6; 8:5ff; 5: 
10). Justice offered to the poor was a bitter pill (5: 7). The legal process had been totally 
corrupted and was used as instruments of oppression. The courts had become little more 
than a market where the poor man was enslaved and his rights totally violated (2: 7).

reference.subject: Old Testament Studies
reference.chapter: IV. THE BOOK OF AMOS
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Socio-Economic Situation (syllabus ¶271)

blocks.text:
Another major concern at the time was the corruption of Israel's religion which Amos, the 
prophet, attacked seriously. The worship of Yahweh even though appeared to continue, had 
become inextricably bound up with practices associated with Canaanite worship. Religion 
certainly flourished in the nation but it was a religion that was completely divorced from 
reality. Many people thronged to the shrines at the time of the great festivals (4: 4 & 5; 5: 5) 
with a great deal of activities and outward show. Ritual was elaborate (5: 21-24) but was 
accompanied by those features such as sanctuary prostitution and bacchanalian orgies (noisy, drunkenness, dancing and other merrymaking associated with the worship of the god 
Bacchus (the god of wine) which were part of the fertility cults of the surrounding nations (2: 
7f). There was no evidence of true spiritual value in the worship of Yahweh but only 
presumption bordering on arrogance (5: 14-20; 6: 3).
It was during these times that the Prophet Amos came with his prophetic message.

reference.chapter: IV. THE BOOK OF AMOS
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — Religious Situation (syllabus ¶284)

blocks.text: Amos is one of the prophets who is neither mentioned in the Book of 2 Kings nor 2 Chronicles, but his own work provides much information which accords with the history of the Kings.
4.5.1	The Call to His Ministry

Amos 7:10-17, gives a clear picture of how Amos became a prophet. "Then Amos answered and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was shepherd and took care of sycamore fig-trees. BUT THE LORD TOOK ME FROM TENDING THE FLOCK AND SAID TO ME,' "GO PROPHESY TO MY PEOPLE ISRAEL". Then again, in 3:7-8 "Surely the Sovereign LORD does nothing without revealing his plan to his servants the prophets. The lion has roared - who will not fear? The sovereign LORD HAS SPOKEN - WHO CAN BUT PROPHESY?" These statements show that Amos had no training as a prophet. He was not a professional prophet ("I was no prophet"), nor a member of the schools of prophets ("neither was I a prophet's son"). Indeed that made no difference because it was God who had called him. It is God's calling that makes the prophet. Heritage and education might be good, but they do not account for, or take the place of, the call of God.

We should take note that it was while Amos was involved in his occupation of shepherding 
that God's call came. Many of the people that God used and continue to use have had similar 
experiences. It was while they were engaged in secular work, that God called them into full- 
time service for Him.
4.5.2 	The Place of His Ministry

Although Amos was from the Southern Kingdom - Judah, he was commissioned by God to 
preach in the Northern Kingdom city of Bethel. Historically Bethel was one of the places 
where significant events had taken place. Abraham had encamped there (Gen. 12: 8). It was 
there that Jacob had his famous dream (Gen. 28: 10-22) which motivated him to give the 
name "Bethel" (meaning "House of God") to the place, which was formerly known as Luz (Gen 28: 19).

However, when the United Kingdom was divided in 931BC (1 Kings 12) Bethel became one of 
the two major religious sites of the Northern Kingdom (2 Kings 12: 25-31). At Bethel, the 
idolatrous worship of the golden calf was instituted and continued to the end of the Northern 
Kingdom. Thus, Bethel (The house of God) became the house of iniquity. It was about this 
place - Bethel (Amos 7:10-13) that Amos prophesied.
4.5.3.	The Message of Amos
Amos' message is dominated by the idea of God's righteousness. The essence of the teaching of Amos is found in Amos 5:24.

The word "RIGHTEOUSNESS" in the Old Testament belongs to the vocabulary of SALVATION. 
When the word is used of God it refers to God keeping His promises, being just to His people, and persevering in his love towards them.

Righteousness is a covenant word, and the righteousness of God refers to God's faithfulness in keeping His covenant. When the word is used of people, righteousness, in an ethical sense, 
means the people's faithfulness in keeping the covenant. They keep their promises, persevere 
in love and respond to God in love and faith. Towards their neighbour, a righteous man is 
compassionate, kind and charitable. Therefore, the basic understanding of Righteousness in 
the Old Testament comes from the covenant idea. A righteous man does what he is supposed 
to do, fulfils his obligation and the pattern for him is the God of the Covenant whose 
righteousness is love and care for His people. The opposite of a righteous man is a wicked 
man. In the Old Testament the contrast is between the righteous and the wicked. The wicked 
are the nasty, cruel, selfish, greedy, violent, hateful and unpleasant people who treat their 
neighbours badly instead of loving them. In the Old Testament righteousness is not a legal 
concept. It is a moral and spiritual concept. A righteous man in the Old Testament is a good 
man and a nice man. He is pleasant, kind, charitable, understanding and warm.

In the New Testament a distinction is made between a good man and a righteous man. In 
Romans 5:7 Paul contrasts a righteous man and a good man. Paul uses righteous to mean 
someone who keeps the Law etc. but very hard, upright in an inflexible, strict moral 
righteousness without very much compassion for man. He is very harsh and strict, whereas a 
good man has the moral righteousness, but in a kind benevolent manner and has compassion 
for other people.

There is, however very little difference between righteousness, justice, faithfulness, steadfast 
love, peace and salvation. God saves the sinner because God is just or righteous. This is the 
heart of Old Testament Theology.

AMOS speaks about the righteousness of God. It is the dominant theme in his message. By 
righteousness Amos means the goodness of God expressed for the people's salvation. Amos 
condemns the people because they have failed to respond' to God with righteousness 
themselves. Amos prophesied against a nation in which the weak, the poor, the afflicted and 
the innocent were suffering under various forms of injustice. God had been righteous to them 
as His people but they had failed to be righteous to their fellow men. He condemned the 
people for their unrighteous acts.

Their unrighteousness is the exploitation of the poor and denial of human rights (Amos 
2:6 & 7; 3:9; 4:1; 5:10-13; & 6:4-7). All these deal with social injustice. He was particularly 
concerned with the administration of justice at the law courts. Amos believed that the courts 
should represent the central institution of the nation's life. This is because it is at the courts 
that righteousness should be revealed and justice established. The courts should defend the 
weak and the poor but, as it was observed, the courts rather denied the weak and the poor 
real justice, and as Amos observed the "justice which was given to the poor was as bitter as 
wormwood" (5:7). The legal processes were totally corrupted and were used as instruments 
of oppression (5:12 & 13). Amos again condemned the affluence of the wealthy classes 
because, according to him, the wealth had been gained by the oppression of the poor through 
social injustices (2:6 & 7; 5:11).

Secondly, he condemned their Religion which was without righteousness. At this time of 
peace, there was a lot of religious activity. The people worshipped YAHWEH but this was 
condemned by Amos because as he said, you cannot worship Yahweh without righteousness 
(5:21-24). Their religion was full of rituals, but empty in content. He proclaimed that God 
had no time for ritualistic religion without righteousness. True religion must be 
demonstrated in terms of compassion, and social justice.

Thirdly, Amos asserted that God's punishment was coming upon the people for their lack of 
righteousness. The punishment would include - exile, political and military defeat and the 
destruction of the nation. He stated that judgment was already at the door. Like the lion ready 
to spring on its prey so Yahweh was ready to bring judgment upon His people (5:16-17; 7:8; 
8:2-3). "The God who gave Israel its past will give them no future as a vindication of His will 
against theirs. The oracles that derive from Amos did not offer any hope for the future to 
Jeroboam's Israel" (J. L. Mays, 1969).

reference.chapter: IV. THE BOOK OF AMOS
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF AMOS — The Ministry of Amos (syllabus ¶289)

topics.title: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos

blocks.text: 4.6.1 	Introduction

Amos 1:1 & 2 is regarded as the general introduction to the whole of the oracles. Verse 1 is 
viewed as the title placed at the beginning of the collection. It tells who spoke those words, to 
whom and when. The dating is specific, two years before the earthquake (see Zech.14:5). It was a catastrophic event which is mentioned only in these two passages. Verse 2 contains the content of the message - the judgment which is to come as a result of the evils of Israel. The nation had reached such a point that God had no option but to act in righteous judgment. yh
4.6.2 	Oracles against the Eight Nations

Amos 1:3-2:16 consists of eight oracles or messages of judgment first against the nations 
surrounding Israel, and then against Israel itself. Each of the oracles has a basic structure: 
opening "Messenger Formula" thus says the Lord, followed by the offence, then by the 
punishment and finally the concluding messenger formula, "says the Lord."

Each of the offences also begins with the words for three sins ... and for four I will not 
turn back my wrath. Amos uses this statement to indicate the certainty of the judgment to
come upon the nations mentioned.

The significance of the prophecy against the nations is to indicate the concept of Yahweh's 
sovereignty beyond His covenant people. God is portrayed as the King of His world who 
judges sin and unrighteousness irrespective of where it may occur. He is ruler of all nations 
and all people stand under His authority. The following nations are mentioned:
Syria - Capital City, DAMASCUS (1:3-5).
Offence: that it had often harassed Israel, especially under Ben-Hadad and King Hazael (read 1 Kings 20:1; 2 Kings 6:24; 10:32, 33).
Its Punishment - God would:
Burn down the palace of the capital city.
Break down their strongholds.
Cause many Syrians to die and others to be carried back into Kir, the land of their former slavery, (2 Kings 16:9). Kir was located in Mesopotamia
Philistia - Capital GAZA (1: 6-8).
Offence: Its four chief cities - Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron sold Israelites into slavery to Edom. (2 Chronicles 21:16; Joel 3:4-8).
Punishment: God will
send fire to consume her fortresses.
destroy the King of Ashdod and kill all the Philistines.
Phoenicia - Capital, TYRE (1: 9 & 10).
Offence: They had broken their covenant of brotherhood to Israel (referring to the
agreement David and Solomon made with Tyre, 1 Kings 9:13).
Israel had been attacked by Tyre and its citizens sold into slavery to Edom  (Joel 3:4-8).
Punishment: God would burn down the forts and palaces of Tyre.
Edom - Capital Cities, TEMAN AND BOZRAH (1: 11& 12)
Teman was located southeast of Petra, and Bozrah was in north central Edom.

Offence: Though the Edomites and Israelites were closely related (Edomites from Esau and the Israelites from Jacob, Gen 25:28-34), Israel had suffered grievously at the hands of Edom (Obadiah 1:1-21).
Punishment: All their strongholds would be burned.
Ammon - Capital, Rabbah (1: 13-15).

Offence: The Ammonites, who were descendants of Lot's youngest daughter (Gen. 19: 36-38) had committed serious crimes against Israel. They ripped open pregnant 
Israelite women with swords during their wars of expansion in Gilead.
Punishment: Their cities would be destroyed and the inhabitants would be enslaved.
Moab - Capital, Kirioth (2:1-3).

Offence: The Moabites who were descendants of Lot's older daughter (Gen. 19:37) 
had, among other crimes, desecrated the tombs of the Kings of Edom, with no respect for the dead (2 King 3:26,27).
Punishment: Moab would be defeated in war and its palaces burned.
Judah - Capital, Jerusalem (2:4, 5)
Offence: Judah had rejected the word of God, and disobeyed the God of the Word. They had also hardened their hearts as their fathers had done. They had followed other gods.
Punishment: God would send fire upon Judah and burn its fortresses.
Israel- Capital, Samaria (2:6 -16).

Offence: They had perverted justice by accepting bribes, sold the poor into slavery, 
trading them for a pair of shoes, both fathers and sons were guilty of immorality with the same harlot, and lounging in stolen clothing from their debtors at religious feasts. They also offered sacrifices of wine in the temple, were absolutely ungrateful for God's past blessings and caused Nazarites to sin by tempting them to drink wine.
Punishment: God would make them groan as a loaded- down wagon would groan and cause their swiftest warriors to stumble in battle.
4.6.3 	The Corruption in Israel and Judah
AMOS 3:1-6:14 gives the details of the corruption that had engulfed the whole house of Israel and the punishment that awaited them. A summary is given below:

3:1-8 That judgment was inevitable. This is because God had chosen Israel to be the people through whom all other nations of the world would know him. This promise was made to Abraham who is regarded as the father of the Israelites (Gen 12:1-3).
3:9-15: Israel's enemies- Philistia and Egypt called upon as witnesses to Israel's wickedness which included the following:
The women of Samaria had become cruel and demanding (4: 1-3).

Israel's formal and empty religious ceremonies constitute an insult to divine holiness 
(4:4, 5; 5:21-26).

They had surrounded themselves with gross luxuries, with ivory beds to lie upon, and 
choicest food to eat (6:4).
They thought more of worldly music than that of their own Messiah (6:5).
They had drunk wine by the bucketful, perfumed themselves with sweet ointments and totally neglected the poor (6:6).

4:6-13: God had tried everything to bring them back to Himself but they had refused. 
Therefore their former saviour would now become their judge. "Therefore, I will bring upon 
you all these further disasters I have announced. Prepare to meet your God as he comes in 
judgment, you people of Israel!" (4:12).

5:4-15: God extends a final invitation to Israel to come back to him and live. This 
demonstrates how patient, merciful and loving God is to his people.
This invitation was rejected and judgment would fall:
a. 	Jacob would be consumed as a lion devours a sheep (3:12).
There would be crying in the street and every road (5: 16).

In that day they would be like a man who escaped from a lion, only to meet a bear. They 
would be as a man who leans against a wall in a dark room and puts his hand upon a 
snake! (5:19).
Ninety percent of their soldiers would fall in battle (5:3).
4.6.4 	The Five Visions of Doom

The Locust Plagues 7: 1-3: God revealed to Amos in a vision that the crops were to be 
destroyed by an invasion of locusts. Amos interceded for Israel and the destruction did 
not take place.
The Vision of Fire 7: 4-6: Amos saw a destructive fire, which dried up all the waters of

Palestine. This was to fall upon the land to punish sin. Again the prophet pleaded for 
mercy, and again God set aside this deserved punishment.

The Vision of the Plumb Line 7: 7-16: Amos saw the Lord measuring a wall with a 
plumb line to find out if the wall was straight.

God informed Amos that He will continue to test Israel with the plumb line of heavenly 
justice. That He would no longer turn away from punishing them, and that He would 
destroy the dynasty of Jeroboam II by the sword. This really occurred. Jeroboam II was 
succeeded by his son Zechariah, who was assassinated by a rebel named Shall urn after a reign of only six months (2 Kings 15:10-12). God later used this same plumb line on 
Judah during the reign of King Manasseh (2 Kings 21:13-15).

The Vision of the Basket of Summer Fruit 8:1-14: The Lord showed Amos a basket 
filled with ripe fruit. He then explained to Amos that it symbolized Israel which was now 
ripe for judgment. That the cruel and materialistic merchants of the Northern Kingdom 
had:
(i) 	robbed the poor by selling them mouldy food and trampled upon the needy;

(ii) 	longed for the Sabbath to end and various religious holidays to be over that they 
might once again start cheating, using their weighted scales and undersized measures, and

(iii) 	made slaves of the poor, buying them for their debt a piece of silver or a pair of 
shoes.
When this judgment took place, the following would result:
The sound of singing in the Temple would be turned to weeping.
Dead bodies would be scattered everywhere.
Fearful heavenly signs would occur (8:9).
There would be no comforting words from God (8:11&12).

The Vision of the Lord at the Altar 9:1-10: In the final vision Amos saw the Lord at the 
altar talking about the final destruction of Israel. The destruction of the nation would be 
pursued relentlessly, and the Lord would track down and overtake all who try to escape 
the initial disaster. This last vision was frightening because the Lord himself entered the 
scene confirming the scripture which says; lilt is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of 
the living God!" (Heb. 10: 30,31).
4.6.5 	The Promise of Restoration

Amos ends his prophecy on a positive note concerning the future restoration of Israel. There 
would be:

The Restoration of the Davidic Dynasty 9:11a: God had made a covenant with David 
that there will always be a descendant to always sit on his throne (2 Sam. 7:12-16). 
The exile made that promise seem impossible, but "in that day" God would raise up and 
restore the kingdom to its promised glory. This promise would not be fulfilled by an 
earthly, political leader, but by the promised Messiah, who would renew the spiritual 
Kingdom and reign forever (Acts 15: 16-17, Luke 1: 31-33).

The Restoration of Unity in the Nation 9:11b-12: The Kingdom of Israel was divided in 931 B.C. during the reign of King Rehoboam. In his message of hope, Amos declared that the tent will be rebuilt as it used to be, which might be referring to a restored united kingdom in view of the statement "I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel" (See Hosea 1: 10-11, Ezek. 37: 15-23).

The Restoration of Agriculture 9:13: Another area that will be restored for the benefit 
of His people Israel is that of agriculture. It states "The days are coming," declares the 
Lord, "when the reaper will be overtaken by the plowman and the planter by the one 
treading grapes. New wine will drip from the mountains and flow from all the hills". The soil will be so fertile that the plowman, who is preparing the land for the next harvest will overtake the one who is reaping. This means that seedtime and harvest will follow in rapid succession, without interruption by drought or any other plague. The hills, normally barren, will also make their contribution to the prosperity of the people.

The Restoration of the People 9:14a: During the exile the Jews would be scattered all 
over the world and this prophecy refers to the restoration of captives from all over the 
world where Israel had been scattered.

The Restoration of Liberty 9:14b: "And they will plant vineyards and gardens; and they 
will eat their crop and drink their wine". In that day they will be in control of their own 
produce. They will not be growing their crops to give to some other nations as tribute, 
but will enjoy it themselves.

blocks.text:
The prophecy of Amos began with a message of judgment and doom (Amos 1:2 ff) to show 
that God is a Just God, and when His holy laws are violated He acts impartially in judgment, 
upon those who will not repent and receive His mercy.

Amos concludes his prophecy with the message of restoration of God's people. He states 
finally that this Restoration would be permanent (9: 15), "I will plant Israel in their own land, 
never again to be uprooted from the land I have given them" says the Lord your God.

What a day that will be! Israel will back in the land permanently! When that happens, there 
will be peace. No more will God's ancient people live in fear.

This particular passage shows how God delights to bless His people. He is always ready to 
welcome the repentant sinner.

blocks.text:
The Book of Malachi is one of the post exilic prophetic books which concludes the prophetic 
books of the Hebrew canon of the Old Testament. It is one of the shortest books which make 
up "The Twelve" or the Minor Prophets. It is a book which talks about the Love of God and 
how we must love Him in return. Our love for Him will be manifest in obedience to His word. 
It also talks about God's laws concerning marriage, the justice of God and the need to give our 
resources to support His work. It insists on the need to serve the Lord faithfully.

The Book of Malachi is closely linked with the prophets Haggai and Zechariah and from them 
we get to understand better, the post exilic period of the Jewish History. The book reveals 
that the nation of Israel in Malachi's day was unevenly divided into two groups: (1) the 
great majority of the nation who doubted God's love and were living in outrageous sins, and 
(2) a remnant who believed God's love (3:16-18) and was characterized by reverence and 
obedience. A careful study of the book will help the individual to know his/her standing 
before God and his/her commitment to God's word, and work.

reference.chapter: V. THE BOOK OF MALACHI
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶440)

blocks.text:
His Name: The name MALACHI means "My Messenger". There has always been a 
debate among scholars regarding this name, Malachi. The issue is "are we to understand 
MALACHI to be the name of the person who wrote the book or delivered the oracles, or 
simply a title designating his prophetic work or office? If the term MALACHI was a title, 
then who bore this title? Those who hold the view that it is a title say it might have been 
"Ezra the Scribe". However many scholars believe that Malachi, was in fact the prophet's actual name. That is to say, there is really no strong reason to doubt that this prophet was a person named Malachi. The most important thing is, he was a communicator of God's word who delivered to God's people a message which was filled with rebuke, but with the intent of turning them back to God - that they might trust anew in His Love for them.
Personal History: There is nothing in the book of Malachi or the Historical books of Ezra and Nehemiah about his personal history. The names of his parents and his home are not known.

reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — The Prophet Malachi (syllabus ¶445)

blocks.text:
Date: The exact time of Malachi's Ministry is not given. However, there are some important 
indications which seem to put the date for the book or the Ministry of Malachi sometime after 
the return from the Babylonian Exile to Jerusalem, during the period of Ezra and Nehemiah. 
First, the Prophet must have prophesied after the exile because he mentions a "governor" as being over the land (1:8). This was a political condition which existed when the Jews 
returned from Babylon. Before the exile, the political leader of the nation was a "Kinq". 
Haggai used the word governor to describe Zerubbabel (1:1).

Second, he must have prophesied after the ministry of Haggai and Zechariah who prophesied 
during the time of the building of the temple (520 - 516 B.C.). This is because there is no 
reference to the rebuilding of the temple and the impression of a drift into casual attitude 
regarding worship shows that some time had passed since the re-building took place. Temple

services have been resumed long enough for the priests to become weary with the regular 
performance of them (1:13), and some irregularities had crept in (1:7-8, 12-14; 3:8-9).

Third, there are some details which link the Prophet to the time of Nehemiah, especially 
during the latter years of his governorship over Judah.

Nehemiah came to Jerusalem to be governor in 445 Be. He served in that capacity for some 
years and then returned temporarily to Persia in 433 B.C. (Nehemiah 5:14). After his return 
to Jerusalem, he found gross sin and violation of the Law (Neh. 13). There is a very close 
agreement between Neh. 13 and the Book of Malachi and so we can infer that Malachi 
prophesied during the return of Nehemiah probably few years after 433 B.C.

Malachi is the last prophet of the Old Testament. The Book ends the Old Testament 
revelation. There is then the four hundred years of silence after which the Prophet John the 
Baptist appeared on the scene to "prepare the way" for the Messiah the Lord Jesus Christ.

blocks.text:
Firstly, the message of Malachi is Exhortative in nature. That is, he preached to the present 
needs of the people and challenged them to repent of their sins, and to be genuine in their 
religious and spiritual life.
Secondly, the message deals with Predictive prophecies concerning the Messiah.

5.4 	Analysis of the Book of Malachi 
5.4.1	The Structure of the Book

A common feature of the book is the recurring literary method of communication of God's 
word. Charges or accusations are made against Israel, which is usually an opening statement 
(e.g.: "I have loved you" says the Lord 1:2). These are then followed by objections on the part 
of the accused (in the form of a question) put into the mouth of the hearers (e.g. But you ask, 
"How have you loved us?"). The objections are then answered clearly without recourse to 
further arguments.

The words put into the mouth of the LORD'S opponents are not necessarily to be regarded as 
actual statements of the people but rather represent the attitudes and actions of the people as the prophet understood them. This is a way of making it clear to the Israelites their true 
selves, their rebellion and their need of repentance.

According to Gasque, W. Ward, the style of Malachi, then is that of the Spoken Word. That the 
book is very much like the letter of James in the New Testament and that it resembles a 
collection of loosely connected oracles rather than a carefully organized literary work.
5.4.2 	The Theme of the Book

The theme of the Book of Malachi is "God's Rebuke of Israel's Outrageous Sins". 
This theme is developed into six charges against the Nation:
that Israel has doubted God's love - Mal. 1:1-15,
that Israel has despised God's Name, (1:6 - 2:9);
Israel has defied God's Law (2:10-16);
Israel has disdained God's Justice (2:17-3:6);
Israel has disregarded God's Tithes (3:7-12) and
Israel has discredited God's service (3:13-4:6).
