topics.title: Outline of the Book of Malachi

blocks.text: 5.5.1 	The Oracle: 1:1

The Hebrew word for Oracle - Massa is used about sixty times in the Old Testament. The 
word "Oracle" as used in Malachi means a "burden" imposed by a master or a ruler or a deity 
on his subjects. The idea here is that the messenger would not have chosen to say such a 
thing, but it is not his to decide on what to say, the burden has been placed upon him by the 
LORD, and he is obliged to accept and discharge his duty. In other words a message has been 
laid on his heart as a burden and he is to discharge it. It is the word of the Lord to His 
people Israel.
5.5.2 	Israel has Doubted God's Love: 1:2-5

Malachi reminds the people of Yahweh's great love for them which is the central theme of the 
Old Testament Prophets (e.g. Hosea 11:1-4; Jer. 31:1-3; Isa. 43:1-4; Zeph. 3:17 and Deut. 7:8, 
13; 10:15). There are many situations and incidents in which God has demonstrated His love 
to the people of Israel but they complain "How have you loved us" (1:2a). The passage says 
nothing about what caused the people of God in Malachi's day to doubt God's love. God could 
have given hundreds of examples of His love to assure them, but He answers by referring 
Israel to its own history. "Is not Esau Jacob's brother?" Declares the LORD, "Yet I have 
loved Jacob but Esau I have hated" (1:2c-5, ct. Gen. 25:19-23).

The terms LOVED and HATED could be explained as preference, not animosity. God's love for 
Israel should be obvious! He has always been with them as a nation, right from the time of 
Jacob to Malachi's day. God has not forsaken them. How do we know this? One clear proof is 
Israel's very existence as a nation. This is in contrast to Esau and Edom. The "HATE" (non 
preference) for Esau (Edom) is demonstrated in her destruction as a nation (1:3-5). By 
Malachi's day, Edom, AS A NATION dwelling in her rock fortress was no more. Edom as a 
COMMUNITY OF PEOPLE moved into Southern Judea (IDUMEA), but it was no longer a 
nation. The last time we hear of this community is 70 AD when Jerusalem was destroyed by 
the Romans under Titus. The people had no valid reason to doubt the love of God to His 
people.
5.5.3 	Israel has Despised God's Name (Read: Malachi 1:6 - 2:9)

In Malachi 1:2-5, we read about how Israel has doubted God's Love and following from this 
has despised His Name. In human relationships, especially in marriage, when you doubt the 
love of your partner for you, the relationship begins to disintegrate.

Note how many times the word "name" is used in this section - (Malachi 1:6-2:9). The word 
"name" does not refer to a proper name or title. Rather, it refers to God's person - it refers to 
"who He is".

In his presentation, Malachi first shows Yahweh's indictment against the Priests (1:6 - 2:9) 
and then against the people of Israel as a whole (2:10 - 17). Those passages show that God's 
judgment always begins in God's own house (Read also Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 25:29-30; Ezekiel 
9:6; 1 Peter 4:17).

In 1:6, Malachi uses ordinary human relationships which are familiar to the people of Israel - 
Father, Son and Master, Servant - which demand honour and respect (Read Exodus 20:12; 
Proverbs 30:11). But if honour and respect are due in human relationships how much more 
is this true in the relationship which exists between Yahweh and His people. The Priests and 
the people, have despised God's name. How have the priests despised God's name? By placing defiled (ritually unclean) food upon His altar. The real problem was not just mere ritual but 
an attitude of the heart and mind, which led to carelessness in matters of priesthood ritual 
(for example, the offering of blind, crippled or diseased animals for sacrifice). The Law of 
Moses taught that only the best animals should be brought as sacrifices to God's altar, but 
Israel was bringing the sick, the blind and the lame. (Compare Malachi 1:7-8; 12-13; with 
Exodus 12:5; Leviticus 1:3, 10; 22:18-25; Deuteronomy 15:21).

By bringing such inferior offerings they were saying in effect, "This is what we think of you, 
God. You are unworthy of our best." In 1:13b-14, Malachi stresses that God is unwilling to 
accept anything but the best. That if a person makes a promise to offer a voluntary offering to 
the Lord but offers a worthless substitute, that person who attempts to cheat God will not go 
unpunished. It is in this that we find that God is a GREAT KING as well as Father and master 
(1:6). Yahweh, therefore, warned the priests of severe punishment if they did not rectify the 
situation (Malachi 2:1-9).
5.5.4 	Israel has defied God's Law on Marriage (Read Malachi 2:10-16)

The people have defied God's Law concerning MARRIAGE. This is explained in detail in Ezra 
9-10 and Nehemiah 13. The passage in Malachi shows that the Jews were marrying pagan 
women (vs. 11), which was forbidden (on religious, not on racial grounds). The issues here 
are:
The people of Israel have defied the law forbidding mixed marriages (2: 10-13).
They have defied the original intention of god against divorce (2: 14-16).
The People of Israel have Defied the Law Forbidding Mixed Marriage

The men of Israel had "married the daughters of a strange god" (vs. 11). This means that 
they had intermarried with heathen women who were idolaters. This is an issue of 
religion. It is marrying people of other Faith which is being condemned and not because 
of ethnicity. God had expressly prohibited such marriages (Deut. 7:1-5) because they 
would eventually lead Israel into idolatry (Exodus 34:16).

God's evaluation of this Sin - 2:10, 11: Intermarriage of this nature was a treacherous act which was a rejection of God as Creator and Father. This act caused disunity (especially where divorces of Jewish women were involved) in the nation, and it was a profaning of the covenant God made with the Fathers (vs. 10b), an abomination and a profaning of the Holiness of God (or the sanctuary of the Lord) vs. 11. God does not speak lightly of this act.

God's Punishment of this Sin - 2:12, 13: Malachi makes it clear that God will not let His people get away with such acts of treachery. He will severely punish the offenders (vs. 12), and no amount of weeping at the altar will cause God to accept the offerings that are brought by such offenders (vs. 13).
They have defied the Original Intention of God against Divorce - 2:14-16

Here, God states clearly "I HATE DIVORCE" (v16). The point here is that it was bad 
enough for the men of Israel to get involved in mixed marriages, but this was made worse 
by the fact that they were divorcing their Jewish wives along with it. The older men 
were cruelly divorcing their ageing wives and marrying these attractive young foreigners 
- a situation in which family life, as always, suffered. It shows that God requires 
faithfulness from His people, faithfulness to Himself and faithfulness in human relationships.
How does God view Divorce?
It is an act of Cruelty 2:14

Divorcing one's wife was an act of cruelty because it was not merely the putting away of a woman, but the putting away of a woman who is "HIS COMPANION. . ." Here is a woman who has shared her life and life's experiences, with her husband, and he writes her off as if it were nothing. This is cruelty and callousness.
It is an act of disloyalty 2:14

The woman is not only his COMPANION, but "THE WIFE OF THY COVENANT". He has vowed his life TO HER. HE has left father and mother in order to CLEAVE UNTO HIS WIFE! He has vowed NEVER TO LET HER GO! But his vow has turned out to be empty words! This is a clear act of disloyalty.
It is an act which frustrates God's design - a godly seed - 2:15

In this passage we see that when a man divorces the wife of his youth and gets involved in a mixed marriage, the future of the children is in jeopardy. It is only when parents remain faithful to their marriage vows that God's desire for godly children will be fulfilled.
It is an act which God hates - I hate divorce 2: 16
God hates evil and we are to have the same attitude towards it. Paul states in Romans 12:9, "ABHOR WHAT IS EVIL". God hates divorce and His children are to have the same attitude toward it.
5.5.5	Israel has disdained God's Justice (Read Malachi 2:17-3:6)
Statement of Israel Disdain for God's Justice (2:17)

In this passage the Jews of Malachi's day continued to struggle with the problem of why the wicked apparently prosper while the righteous suffer. (Read: Job 21:7-16; Habakkuk 1:2-4, 13). The complain was, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord and He delights in them, or where is the God of justice?" In effect, what the people were saying was that if the people are sinning and getting away with it, it must mean that God favours the sinner or, if that is not the case, then God does not exist, because if he did exist, then He would have acted in judgment against the evil doers. Many people through the ages have held the view of the people of Malachi's day. "Why", they say, "If there were really a God, who is righteous, kind and loving He would not allow war and poverty and evil in His universe!"
What this view does not take into account is that:
God is long suffering or patient, and
God has a time table for His judgment (Read 2 Peter 3:8-16).
Note that the Day of the Lord will come, but it will come in His own time.
God responds to the People's Disdain for His Justice (3:1-6)

As indicated above, it may seem that God is indifferent to the sins of men, but that is not the 
case. The Lord is indeed coming, and when He comes He will severely judge - THE DAY OF 
THE LORD. No one will be able to endure the day of His coming, "for He is like a refiner's fire 
and like fullers' or launderer's soap. And He will sit as a smelter and purifier of silver, and He 
will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver. . ." The sinners and offenders 
(v. S) will reap severe judgment when the Lord comes, but He will not utterly consume His 
people so as to destroy them forever. This will be a violation of His own character and covenant (vs. 6).

What do we learn from this passage? We should not be deluded or deceived into thinking that because 
God does not immediately judge us for our sins, He does not know about them, or is 
indifferent to them. God is all-knowing; nothing escapes Him, and God is never indifferent to 
sin! It offends Him, and he hates it. His seeming inaction is to be understood as long-suffering 
toward sinners. The message is: REPENT! And get right with God.
5.5.6 	Israel has Disregarded God's Tithes (Read Malachi 3:7-12)

Background: The Hebrew word for Tithe is, ma'aser, and it means a 'Tenth'. It is very difficult 
to trace its origin, but it is known to have existed in Babylon in ancient times, and also in 
Persia, Egypt and China. It is quite certain that Abraham knew of it when he migrated from Ur 
(Gen. 14;17-20). Since Melchizedek was a priest of the Most High, it is certain that in 
Abraham's day giving of tithes had been recognized as a holy deed (Read: Hebrew 7:4). Some 
passages in the Bible show that it was common for rulers and religious leaders to divide the 
spoils of war, (e.g. 1 Maccabeus 10:31; 1 Samuel 8:10-18 etc.). It is recorded in Gen. 28:16-22 
that when Jacob made his covenant with God at Bethel, the payment of tithe was included.

Legal requirement of tithing developed late and so customs in its payment varied. At first the 
one who paid the tithe was entitled to share his tithe with the Levites (Deut. 14:22-23). After 
the Levitical code had been completed, tithes belonged exclusively to the Levites (Numbers 
18:21). If a Hebrew lived too far from the temple to make taking his tithes to the temple 
impracticable, he could sell his animals and use the money gained to buy substitutes at the 
temple (Deut. 14:24-26). This permit eventually led to gross abuses by the priests (Matthew 
21:12-13; Mark 11:15-17).

Later under the Levitical system provision for the upkeep of the sons of Levi was made 
through the tithes (Num. 18:21-24). A penalty of twenty percent of the tithe was exacted 
from anyone who sold his tithes and refused to use the money to pay for a substitute (Lev. 
27; 31). Leviticus 27:30 makes it clear that a tithe of everything belonged to the Lord and it is 
holy to the Lord. In Numbers 18:25-32, we are informed that when the Levites received the 
tithe, they in turn gave a tenth to provide for the priests.

In Deuteronomy 12:5-12, we are instructed that the Temple - the house of God - is the place where we are to take the tithes to. One could not partake of his tithes at home but only when delivered at the Temple (Deut. 12:17-18). To make sure that no deceit would be practiced regarding tithing, each Hebrew was compelled to make a declaration of honesty before the Lord (Deut. 26:13-15).
The Statement - Israel has Disregarded God's Tithes and Offerings

Indeed, tithing was God's way in the Old Testament days of providing the means to sustain 
His work and provide for His Ministers, the Priests. In Malachi's day, there had been a total 
disregard for this rule regarding tithes. They disobeyed the clear instructions from God's 
word on what was required (Lev. 27:30-31; Numbers 18:20-21; Deut. 14:22-23), hence they 
were robbing God. They were greedy and self centered in spite of God's goodness to them. 
How long this had been going on, we do not know, but the people were now experiencing 
God's chastisement and being deprived of His blessing (Malachi 3:7-9).

What should they do? The answer is simple. They must repent and "bring the whole tithe 
into the store house," If they are willing to do this, God will open the windows of heaven, 
and pour out a blessing on them. He will also remove the chastisement they were 
experiencing in their agriculture (Malachi 3:10-12).

It is believed that by Jesus' time this injunction by Malachi for the people to pay all the tithe 
was working and for that matter teaching on it was not very necessary as we see in Matthew 
23:23 and Luke 11:42. Here Jesus encouraged his hearers to continue to pay their tithes but 
should also be mindful of the other important matters of the law like justice, mercy and 
faithfulness.
5.5.7 	Israel has Discredited God's Service (Read: Malachi 3:13-4:6)

A. 	The majority of the people of Israel said that it does not pay to serve the Lord (3:13-15). 
The people complained that they were religious, they have kept the Law of God, they have 
kept His charge and that they have walked in mourning before the Lord, but it had not been profitable to them. God had not rewarded them for it. They complained that God let the "real sinners" get away with their sin and that they were blessed by Him. This statement in reality was not true. The ones who complained were the ungodly sinners. Although they were religious and went through the motions of religious rites, it was just superficial and external. They were hypocrites. They had no heart for God. Their arrogant complaining was a DISCREDITING OF GOD'S SERVICE.
They were saying "it is vain to serve God; and what profit is there to serve God?"

B. 	The Remnant or Minority in the Nation believed that IT DOES PAY TO SERVE THE LORD 
(3:16-4:3).

Among those who profess to know God, there is always a remnant who truly are godly. 
Though the blessing may be delayed in coming to them, they do not complain that it does not pay to serve the Lord. Such people wait patiently for Him. Three things are said about the godly: (1) They feared (or reverenced) the Lord and served Him faithfully; (2) they spoke to one another - defending God's actions, and exhorting one another not to lose heart in spite of their hard conditions of life; and (3) they esteemed his name - in contrast to the rest in the nation who by their life-style demonstrated that they "despised God's name".

God admires the faith of the humble and meek. This is by His recognition of them in Malachi's day: "the Lord paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before Him of those who feared the Lord" (3:16). It is also manifest by His Future response (Mal. 3:17-4:3). In that future day of the Lord, He will honour the believing remnant: And they will be mine, says the Lord of hosts, on that Day that I prepare My Own Possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves Him (3:17). It is not VAIN TO SERVE THE LORD! The Lord sees our service; he remembers our labours. His reward may be delayed but it won't be denied. For the godless it will be denied. Thus Malachi 4:1-3 speaks of the awful judgment awaiting those who have been superficial and not genuine God-fearers.

The Day of the Lord: The Day of the Lord has to do with the last things to happen on this 
earth in this present age - it covers the important events such as the second coming of Jesus Christ, and the creation of the new Heaven and New Earth, or the inauguration of a New age. In theological terms - THE DAY OF THE LORD is an eschatological term which refers to the consummation of the Kingdom of God and triumph over his enemies and the deliverance of His people. The Day of the Lord begins with the second coming of Jesus Christ and it includes the final judgment. That day will remove class distinction (Isa. 2:12-21); abolish sin (2 Pet. 3:11-13), accompanied by serious disasters (Matt. 24; Luke 21:7-33); Judgment (Rev. 4:1- 19:6); and culminate in the New Heaven and New Earth (Isa. 65:17; 66:22 and Rev. 21:1ff).

reference.subject: Old Testament Studies
reference.chapter: V. THE BOOK OF MALACHI
reference.topic: 5.5 Outline of the Book of Malachi
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Outline of the Book of Malachi (syllabus ¶482)

blocks.text: The concluding verse of Malachi's Prophetic book is also seen as a conclusion of the Twelve Minor prophets. It is both an admonition and a promise.

The Admonition (4:4): The people of Israel are told to "Remember the law of Moses my servant, the decrees and the laws that I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel." This was a warning to the majority of the nation who had defied and neglected the Law and were thus going to face the consequences.

The Promise (4:5-6): The promise looked forward to the coming of the Prophet Elijah – who will restore the hearts of the Fathers to their children, and the heart of their children to their fathers otherwise He, the Lord, will come and strike the land with a curse.

This passage has always been debated upon among Bible scholars. Three important views concerning the identification of Elijah have been put forward. (Read Matt. 11:14; 17:10-13; Luke 1:17; John 1:21).
That this promise of the coming of Elijah was fulfilled entirely by John the Baptist
That Elijah will someday come personally and minister again.
That one will come in the Spirit and power of Elijah, but not Elijah personally.

reference.subject: Old Testament Studies
reference.chapter: V. THE BOOK OF MALACHI
reference.citation: Old Testament Studies — THE BOOK OF MALACHI — Conclusion: (Read Malachi 4:4-6) (syllabus ¶569)

blocks.text: In Summary, we say that the message of Malachi, God's prophet, to his chosen people Israel is about their willful disobedience, while accusing God of not dealing with them well. This disobedience began with the priests (1:1-29) and then the rest of the people (2:10 - 3:15). They have shown contempt for God's name, (1:6) offered defiled sacrifices (1:7-14), led others into sin (2:7-9), broken God's laws on marriage (2;11-16), called evil "good" (2:17), kept God's tithes and offerings for themselves (3:8-9) and had become arrogant (3;13-15). The people of Israel had broken relationship with their God and judgment and punishment would be theirs. It must be noted however, that in the midst of this wickedness, there was a faithful few - the remnant - who loved and honoured God. God would shower his blessings upon these people (3:16-18).

In spite of the stunning picture of Israel's unfaithfulness painted by Malachi, and for which the people deserved to be punished, there was a message of hope, the possibility of forgiveness. This is expressed in 4:2 - "But for you who fear my name, the son of Righteousness will rise with healing in his wings. And you will go free, leaping with joy like calves let out to pasture". The book concludes with a promise of the coming of lithe Prophet Elijah", who will offer God's forgiveness to all people through repentance and faith (4:5 & 6).
The Book of Malachi is seen by many as forming a bridge between the Old Testament and the New Testament.

subjects.name: New Testament Studies
subjects.description: The Gospel according to Mark, the Acts of the Apostles, Galatians, 1 Timothy and 2 Timothy.

blocks.text: The style of Mark is concise, the stories are vivid and the tone is exciting, with everything happening "immediately" after something else, hence seen or having been described as a book of action".
Summary of Vital Information
Purpose: To present the person, work, and teachings of Jesus.

Author: John Mark. He was not one of the Twelve apostles but he accompanied Paul on his missionary journey (Acts 13: 13). The apostle Peter referred to Mark as his "son" (1 Pet. 5: 13). He was also described as Peter's interpreter by second-century Fathers Papias and Irenaeus.
To Whom Written: The Christians in Rome, where he wrote the Gospel.
Date Written: Between A. D. 55 and 65.

Setting: The Roman Empire under Tiberius Caesar. The Empire, with its common language and excellent transportation and communication systems, was ripe to hear Jesus' message, which spread quickly from nation to nation.
Key Verse: "For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many" (10: 45).
Key People: Jesus, the Twelve apostles, Pilate, the Jewish religious leaders.

Key Places: Capernaum, Nazareth, Caesarea, Philippi, Jericho, Bethany, Mount of Olives, 
Jerusalem, Golgotha.
Special Features: The Book was the first Gospel written. The other Gospels quote all except 31 verses of Mark. The Book of Mark records more miracles than does any other Gospel.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT ONE. THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Introduction (syllabus ¶648)

blocks.text: The Title of the Book (1:1)

The opening verse, as well as being the title of the book (which in actual fact is the gospel of Jesus Christ, not the gospel of Mark) is also a summary of its contents. For Mark the beginning of the gospel was the historical facts of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. The gospel is "about Jesus Christ" the Son of God. "Jesus" is His divinely given personal name (cf. Mt. 1:21; Lk 1:31; 2:21). Its Hebrew equivalent (of the Greek is) "Joshua" i.e. "Yaweh" is Salvation. "Christ" is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew title Masiah (Messiah, Anointed).
The title "Son of God" points to Jesus' unique relationship to God. He is a "Man (Jesus)" and God's "special Agent" (Messiah) - but He is also fully divine.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT ONE. THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Preparatory Events (1:1-13) (syllabus ¶672)

blocks.text: The Fore-runner (vs. 2-13)
Three preparatory events are presented in this brief passage: (i) the ministry of John the Baptist (vs. 2-8) (ii) Jesus' baptism (vs. 9-11) (iii) Jesus' temptation (vs. 12-13).
Baptism of Jesus (vs. 9-11)

Jesus received baptism from John in the Jordan (v. 9), in this way identifying Himself with sinners. Both the Spirit (v. 10) descending dovelike upon Jesus, and the Father proclaiming approval, with a voice from heaven (v. 11) all bears witness to Jesus as being the Messianic Son of God. Here we see all three members of the Trinity together – the Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
Temptation of Jesus (vs. 12-13)

V.12: "Immediately (at once) the spirit impelled Him to go out into the wilderness". 
Mark's forceful style (cf. Mt. 4:1, Lk. 4: 1) is reflected here. The thought is that of strong moral compulsion by which the Spirit led Jesus to take the offensive against temptation and evil instead of avoiding them.

V.13: Jesus was in the desert for 40 days. God put Jesus to the test (the Spirit led Him to it) to show He was qualified for His messianic mission. But also Satan tried to draw Jesus away from His divinely appointed mission of service and ultimate suffering (cf. Mt. 4:1-11, Lk. 4:1-13).

The reference to wild animals during Jesus' temptation is recorded only in Mark. In the 
Old Testament imagery, the wilderness was the place of God's curse - a place of desolation, 
loneliness and danger where frightening ravenous animals lived (cf. Isa. 13:20-22; Isa. 34: 8-15; Ps. 22:11-21; Ps. 91:11-13).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT ONE. THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 1 (syllabus ¶679)

blocks.text: Jesus' First Preaching (vs. 14-15)
V. 15: ". . .The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is at hand, repent. . ."

The urgent conviction reflected in Jesus' words sets the tone for the rest of story of His 
ministry. "The kingdom of God" here means the rule of God, and Jesus' message signifies 
that God has begun to establish his rule in a world viewed by many religious Jews as under the tyranny of Satan and evil. The kingdom of God in this way represents the triumph of God's plan of salvation over human sin and demonic opposition.
The Call of the First Disciples (vs. 16-20) Simon and his Brother
Jesus' Authority over Demons and Disease (vs. 21-45)
The four disciples accompanied Jesus into nearby Capernaum. It was their hometown and it became the hub of Jesus' Galilean ministry (cf. Lk. 4:16-31).

It is significant that the first scene of Jesus' ministry (after the calling of the four disciples) is one in which Jesus teaches and performs an exorcism. Both actions are emphasized in Mark's Gospel as characteristic aspects of Jesus' ministry. We are not told what He taught here; instead Mark emphasizes the manner of His teaching - with authority (v. 22).

In verse 22, the crowds contrast the authority affirmed in His teaching with the teachers of the Law (Scribes). The Scribes had been schooled in the written Law and its oral interpretation (their knowledge was derived from scribal tradition, so they simply quoted the sayings of their predecessors). Mark's point here is that Jesus' teaching was not seen as simply another example of the learned activity of placing His opinion alongside that of other teachers on religious matters. Rather, the people are pictured as sensing in Jesus' manner an authority beyond any they were accustomed to. In verses 23-24, the presence of Jesus and His authoritative teaching in the synagogue provoked a strong outburst from a man under the control of an evil spirit. The demon spoke through the man who cried out saying "what do we have to do with you . . .Have you come to destroy us? . . .the Holy one of God" (v. 24). Mark clearly intends this part of the episode as an illustration that Jesus was much more than simply another teacher. The demon in contrast with most people, recognized Jesus' true character and identity as the Holy one of God (cf. 3: 11; 5:7).

Vs. 25-26: Here Jesus sternly rebuked the evil spirit and ordered the demon to come out of the man: "Be quiet and come out!" (v. 25). The evil spirit convulsed the possessed man, and with a loud shriek, left him.

In verses 27-28 we are told all the people were greatly amazed. Their question "what is this?" referred both to the nature of Jesus' teaching and His expulsion of a demon with only a word of command. His teaching was qualitatively new and came with authority (cf. v. 22) that extended even to demonic forces who were forced to obey (submit to) Him (cf. 4:41).
Healing of Peter's Mother-in-law (vs. 29-31)

This domestic miracle gives one of the rare glimpses into the home lives of the apostles. Peter may have been accompanied by the wife during his travels as hinted in 1 Corinthians 9:5. The touch of Jesus brought instant healing (v. 31); and the consciousness of healing brought grateful devotion to Him, expressed in glad service.

Vs. 32-34: The townspeople kept bringing the sick and the demon-possessed. Jesus healed all those who were brought with their wide variety of diseases. He also drove out many demons. As before, however, (vs. 23-26) He repeatedly silenced their cries of recognition, showing that they were powerless before Him.
V. 35: Mark selectively portrayed Jesus at prayer on three crucial occasions, each in a setting of darkness and aloneness:
(a)	near the beginning of his account (v. 35);
(b)	near the middle (6:46);
(c)	near the end (14: 32-42).
All three were occasions when He was faced with the possibility of achieving His messianic mission. In each case He gained strength through prayer.
Cleansing of a Leper (vs. 40-45)

The Rabbis regarded leprosy as humanly incurable. Only on two occasions does the Old Testament record that God cleansed a leper (Num. 12:10-15; 2 Kings 5: 1-14). Nevertheless this leper was convinced that Jesus could cure him. The leper begged Jesus to heal him             ". . .falling on his knees before Him, and saying to Him if you are willing, you can make me clean" (vs. 41-42). Jesus moved by compassion, touched the untouchable and cured the incurable. Jesus' touch showed that He was not bound by Rabbinic regulations regarding ritual defilement.

The cleansing of the leper was an undeniable messianic sign (cf. Mt. 11: 5; Lk 7:22) that God was working in a new way. If the priests declared the leper clean but rejected the one who made him clean or cured him, their unbelief would be incriminating evidence against them.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT ONE. THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Jesus' Public Ministry in Galilee (vs. 14-8:21) (syllabus ¶700)

blocks.text: The Healing of a Paralytic Man by Forgiving his Sins (vs. 1-12)
In chapter 2 we have further glimpses of Jesus' ministry of miracles and teaching.

Vs.1-2: A few days after Jesus' arrival in Capernaum, it was reported that He was at home, possibly Peter's house (cf. 1:29). While he was speaking, a paralytic was brought around by friends. Determined to get Jesus' attention, they made an opening in the roof and lowered the disabled man through it on a mat right in front of Him.
V.5: Jesus considered the determined effort of the four as visible evidence of their faith in His ability or power to heal the man. Jesus, in healing the paralytic said, "son your sins are forgiven".
In the Old Testament, disease and death were viewed as the consequences of man's sinful condition, and healing was predicated on God's forgiveness (cf.  2 Chr. 7:14; Ps 41: 4; Isa. 19: 22, 38: 16-17.
NB: This does not mean there is a corresponding sin for each occurrence of sickness (cf. Lk 13: 1-5; Jn. 9: 1-3). Jesus simply showed that this man's physical condition had a basic spiritual cause.
Vs.8-9: The scribes expected a physical healing, but Jesus pronounced the man's sins forgiven. (He did not even say "you are healed") but a simple pronouncement of forgiveness.
To the Jewish leaders this was blasphemy, claiming to do something only God could do. This attracted the death penalty (Lev. 24:15-16).

Vs. 10-11: Jesus calls Himself son of man here. The title "Son of man" emphasizes that Jesus is fully human, while son of God emphasizes deity, i.e. He is fully God. As God's son, Jesus has the authority to forgive sin. As a man he can identify with our deepest sufferings and help us overcome sin.
The Calling of Levi (vs. 13-14)
Levi is identified in Mt. 9:9 with Matthew, a customs official in the service of Herod Antipas. He immediately responded to Jesus' call to become a disciple.
The Feast in Levi's House (vs. 15-17)

Tax collectors were hated by the Jews because of their reputation for cheating and their 
support of Rome. The Jews also hated to think that some of the money collected went to 
support pagan religions and temples.
Vs. 16-17: The word sinner is a technical term for common people regarded by the Pharisees as untaught in the Law; who did not abide by rigid pharisaic standards.

For Jesus and His disciples to share a meal (an expression of trust and fellowship) with sinners offended the Law teachers who were Pharisees. They criticized Jesus for not being a separatist, i.e. a distinction between "the righteous (they themselves) and the sinners".

V. 17: Jesus' reply to the criticism: ". . .it is not those who are healthy . . .but those who are sick; I did not come to call the righteous but sinners" Indeed He came to call sinners, those who humbly acknowledge their need and receive His gracious forgiveness, into the kingdom of God. Apparently this was why He ate with sinners (cf. 2:5-11, 19-20).
Controversy about Fasting and the New Situation (vs. 18-22)

Jesus incurred further criticism on the grounds of His disciples not observing a fast. Jesus' reply was that His presence among His people was as much an occasion for rejoicing as was that of a bridegroom among the guests at his wedding. But this situation would change, for a time would come when the Bridegroom (Jesus) would be taken from them and in that day (His crucifixion) the disciples would fast.
Controversy over Religion (vs. 21-22)

Jesus' presence with the disciples was a time of newness and it signaled the passing away of the old. Addressing this issue of the disciples not joining in with "pious" Jews who were observing a fast, He gave the critics two scenarios showing that His teaching was as incompatible with the practices of contemporary Judaism as was:
a new patch of cloth on an old garment which, as it shrunk, would pull away the adjacent threads from the old garment; and
new wine in old wineskins would ferment, and cause the old skins to burst.
In other words, salvation available through Jesus, was not to be mixed with the Old Judaistic system (cf. Jn. 1:17).
Controversy over the Sabbath (vs. 23-28)

The disciples were charged with working on the Sabbath. (Mosaic Law permitted a hungry traveller to pluck and eat corn from another person's field, so long as he only used his hands for the purpose, not a sickle (Deut. 23:25). However, the scribes regarded it technically as reaping. They, therefore, forbade the practice on the Sabbath, on which day reaping was divinely disallowed (Ex. 34: 21).

In response to this issue of "picking and eating of grain on the Sabbath", Jesus appealed to Scripture and a precedent set by David and his companions when they were hungry and in need (1 Sam. 21:1-6). Two principles emerge here:

That the Sabbath was instituted (by God) for mankind's benefit and refreshment Not 
that people were to be made to keep burdensome regulations pertaining to it.

2) 	Furthermore, since the Sabbath was ordained for the well-being of humanity, rather than as an end in itself, Jesus contended that humanity's Lord and Representative was 
authorized to be the official arbiter as to how the Sabbath should be observed (vs. 27-28).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT ONE. THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 2 (syllabus ¶743)

blocks.text: Healing of a Man with a Withered hand on the Sabbath (vs. 1-6)
Vs .1-2: On another Sabbath occasion in the synagogue, Jesus saw a man with a withered hand. Rabbinic tradition forbade practicing medicine on the Sabbath unless the person was on the verge of death.

This man's problem was not life-threatening and could wait till the next day. If Jesus healed him, they could accuse Him of being a Sabbath-violator, an offence punishable by death, (cf. Ex.1: 14-17).

Vs. 3-4: Jesus asked a rhetorical question concerning which of two kinds of action was really consistent with the purpose of the Sabbath (v. 4). The obvious answer is to do good and to save life. Yet failure to use the Sabbath to meet this man's need (cf. 2:27) was to do evil (harmful misuse of its purpose). The moral (not legal) issue of "doing good" on the Sabbath was at stake, and the Pharisees could not, or rather, refused to debate.

V. 5: ". . .grieved at their hardness of heart, He said to the man "stretch out your hand" and 
he stretched it out. . ." Hardness (hard-hearted), to us means callousness or cruel, but here (i.e. to the Hebrew) it connotes unteachableness, a stubborn resistance to the purpose of God. After Jesus healed the man, the Pharisees and the Herodians resolved to have Him put to death. Why the Herodians were involved in the plot is not very clear. It is common knowledge however, that they were supporters of Herod Antipas, who feared that political unrest might result from Jesus' actions.
Jesus' Activity around the Sea of Galilee (vs. 7-12)

Many people from Galilee followed, attracted by all that He was doing (i.e. healing miracles); many also came from areas outside Galilee - Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, Tyre and Sidon. So intense was the impact of Jesus' healing ministry and the desire of those with diseases to touch Him that He told His disciples to be ready to move away from the rush of the crowds.

Vs. 11-12: In the crowds were many people with evil sprits. They recognized Jesus as the 
son of God and were greatly threatened by His presence. Jesus did not accept their repeated cries of recognition, and ordered them not to tell who He was (cf. 1:24-25, 34; 8:30), apparently because they would be reinforcing a misconception of who He is. Though their statements were true, the gospel of Christ would be damaged by an association with demon-possessed people. The Lord wanted men to find out who He was by listening to His words and by watching His deeds.
The Selection of the Twelve (vs. 13-19)

Out of the crowds who were flocking to Him, Jesus chose twelve men and there were two 
reasons for this:
So that they could be with Him;
To be sent out by Him to preach, and to have authority to drive out demons (vs. 14-15). Verses 16-19 give a traditional list of names of the Twelve.

Five of the twelve were fishermen. One a publican, one a zealot (the zeal. for God's honour rather than being an extreme nationalist). All were Galileans except Judas who hailed from Kerith, a town in Judah.

'The Twelve became an official designation or title for those men chosen by Jesus, (cf. 4:10; 6:7; 9:35; 10:32; 11:11; 14:10, 17, 20, 43). The five fishermen among the Twelve were: (1) Peter (2) James (3) John (4) Andrew (5) Philip.
Mounting Opposition and the Beelzebub Accusation (vs. 20-30)

V. 22: A delegation from the scribes (the Law teachers) came down from Jerusalem to
investigate Jesus. They charged that He was driving out demons through a power alliance with Satan, the prince (ruler) of demons (v. 25).

Vs. 23-27: Jesus refuted their allegations in parables showing the absurdity of their thinking. He said that if a kingdom or a house (household) is divided against itself in purpose and goal, it cannot stand. The same applies to Satan if it is assumed that he opposes himself it will mean his end has come, that is, his power, not his personal existence.

Vs. 28 -30: In the light of the preceding charges Jesus issued a strong warning, declaring that all the sins and blasphemies of men (people) are open to God's gracious forgiveness with exception of that which is against the Holy Spirit. This refers to an attitude of defiant hostility towards God that rejects His saving power towards man, expressed in the Spirit empowered person and work of Jesus. It is a person's preference for darkness even though he has been exposed to light (cf. Jn 3:19). Such a persistent attitude of willful unbelief can harden into a condition in which repentance and forgiveness both mediated by God's Spirit, become impossible.
Jesus' True Family (vs. 31-32)

The arrival of Jesus' mother and His brothers is still in the context of verse 21. Standing outside (the house) they sent word to Him and called Him, requesting a private conversation in an attempt to restrain His activity. Jesus' question "who are my mother and my brothers?" (v. 23) was not a repudiation of family relationship. He was highlighting the far deeper issue of a person's relationship to Him. Jesus, addressing the disciples at this stage, asserts that their kinship went beyond natural family ties; and that whoever does God's will is a member of His family. The words brother and sister and mother figuratively denote Jesus' spiritual family.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT ONE. THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 3 (syllabus ¶795)

blocks.text: Parables depicting the character of God's kingdom (vs. 1-34)
The Parable of the Sower (vs. 1-20)

This parable shows that the reason why Jesus was opposed by the religious leaders and 
others, including His own relations, was the spiritual condition of their hearts. In the 
parable, Jesus urged them to give careful consideration to the nature of their own hearts. Some hearers of his teaching, according to Him, never understood (grasped) His message at all; others were discouraged through difficulties, and others again were seduced through prosperity; the result was that only a limited proportion became lastingly committed to it.

Before Jesus would explain the parable to His disciples, He decided to answer their question as to why He employed parables (10-12). The essence of His reply seems to be that He did so in order to test the spiritual responsiveness of His audience. Those who were provoked by them into intensive reflection could proceed thereupon to obtain enlightenment concerning them. Those who would not reflect on them could be ever seeing but never perceiving. In other words they would understand the literal meaning of the words but not the parable's deeper significance.
The Interpretation of the Sower's Parable (vs. 13 -20)
The farmer (sower), probably represents Jesus and all who sow (proclaim) the word of God which is the seed.
Vs. 15-20: The kinds of soil represent four different ways people respond to God's word. Many people give one of three negative responses:
Hard hearted indifference (v. 15); here Satan like the birds comes immediately and takes it away. In effect there is no response.

Others hear the Word with hasty, enthusiastic, but shallow profession of acceptance. They, however, last for a short time because the Word takes no root in them. Here there is lack of spiritual depth (vs. 16). When trouble (i.e. "hardship" or persecution) comes on account of the Word, they quickly fall away. Their profession proves not to be genuine.
Still others hear the Word but are preoccupied with cares and riches of this life. These things choke the Word making it unfruitful (cf. 10:22), indicating they are not true believers.

By contrast, others hear the Word, accept it ("welcome it for themselves") and
produce a crop, or bear spiritual food. Evidently these are genuine disciples who will bear fruitful yields of varying amounts: 30, 60, or 100, (cf. 4:24 with Mt. 25:14-30; Luke 19:11-27).
ii. 	The Parable of the Seed Growing Secretly (vs. 26-29)

The parable presents a comprehensive picture of the coming of God's kingdom: sowing 
(v. 26), growing (vs. 27-28) and harvesting (v. 28). Its emphasis is upon the fact that the word of God will do its own work in human hearts if given the opportunity, in exactly the same way as the earth produces of itself. Outside instrumentality is limited to two things:	*  	sowing
*  	reaping (cf. Jn. 4:35,38).
Between these initial and final activities is a matter of confidence in the vitality of the seed and in the fruitfulness of the interaction between seed and soil.
iii.	The parable of the mustard seed (vs. 30-32)

The mustard seeds, proverbially, the tiniest of seeds, but within a few weeks, when planted, could develop into a shrub of over ten feet in height. The parable may be viewed as showing the expansion of the kingdom from insignificant beginnings. There is also the view that the birds of the air which rested in the shade of the shrub, were probably intended to depict the inclusion within God's kingdom of people from Gentile nations (cf. Lk. 17:22; 31:6; Dan. 4:21 ff). The incorporation of the Gentiles into God's kingdom programme is a preferred view.
Various Sayings of Jesus (Mark 4:21-25)
Mighty Works (4:35-5:43)
From 4:35 to 5:43 are related four acts of divine power wrought by Jesus in a situation of human helplessness and despair:
calming of a violent storm (vs. 35 - 41)
the healing of a demoniac (5:1-20)
the raising of the daughter of Jairus and
the healing of the woman with an issue of blood (5:21-43).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT ONE. THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 4 (syllabus ¶829)

blocks.text: The Calming of a Storm on the Lake (vs. 35 - 41)

Vs. 35-41: here Christ is shown weary at the close of a day of teaching, resting his head and falling asleep during a voyage on the lake of Galilee. A violent storm arose, and the panic- striken disciples woke Him up with a cry of reproach suggesting He was indifferent to their peril. Jesus rebuked the wind and said to the waves "Peace! Be Sill" and the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. Jesus rebuked His disciples also for being afraid. Despite His works of wonder (vs. 11, 34) it had still not dawned on them that God's authority and power were present in Him. This explains His question to them "Have you no faith?" (v. 40).
The Healing of the Demoniac (vs. 1-20)

Jesus and His disciples went to the east side of the lake (Sea of Galilee). As soon as Jesus got 
out of the boat, He encountered a man with an evil spirit from the tombs. He was uncontrollable for "no one could bind him any more, even with chains (5:3).

Such behaviour shows clearly that demon possession is not a mere ailment or insanity but 
desperate satanic attempt to distort and destroy God's image in man.
Vs. 6-10: Three things indicate that the demon indwelling the man was fully aware of Jesus' divine origin and superior power:
He knelt before Jesus (in homage, not worship);
He used Jesus' name in an attempt to gain control over Him (cf. 1:24);
He appealed to Jesus not to punish him.

(James tells us that, concerning the truth of Jesus' Godhead, "even the demons believe, and tremble" (James 2:19). In verse 7 we read "and crying out with a loud voice, he said what have you to do with me Jesus ... I adjure you by God, do not torment me"

Jesus asked "what is your name?" - "my name is Legion for we are many" - the man replied. Apparently many evil powers controlled the man and subjected him to intense oppression. They tormented him as one combined force under the leadership of one demon, as their spokesman. This explains the alternating singular ("my") and plural ("we") pronouns. The demons were exorcized by Jesus on the utterance of a single command.
The Raising of the Daughter of Jairus and the Healing of the Woman with an issue of Blood

This section has a "sandwich" structure. The account of the raising of Jarius' daughter from 
the dead (5:21-24, 35-43) is broken by the incident of the woman with the issue of blood (5:25-34). What appeared to be a disastrous delay, in actual fact, assured the restoration of 
Jarius' daughter. It is as if it was providentially ordered to test and strengthen Jarius' faith.
"Daughter!" Jesus said "your faith has made you well, go in peace, and be healed of your disease" (v. 34).

The address "Daughter" suggested her new relationship with Him. The cure was also attributed to her faith rather than the touch of His clothing. "Go in peace and be healed" his statement assured her that her healing was complete and permanent.

Vs. 35 -36: Jesus' response to Jairus call has been "unfortunately" delayed by this incident of the cure of the woman with the issue of blood. This delay was a severe test of Jairus faith. He definitely feared that the daughter would die before Jesus got to his house. This was confirmed with the report from his house that he needed not bother Jesus any further because the little girl had died.
Jesus eventually went and raised the dead girl up (vs. 40 -42). These two miraculous stories, one within the other, illustrate Jesus' authority over disease and death.

blocks.text: Rejection at Nazareth and the Mission of the Twelve (6:1-13)
The Rejection of Jesus at Nazareth (vs. 1-6)

Jesus returned with His disciples to Nazareth, his home town. He went to the synagogue, 
the next Sabbath, to teach, and the people were astonished at His wisdom and miracles. They however refused to believe. The simple reason was that He was a local man just like themselves. He was merely a local carpenter. His mother, brothers and sisters were all known to them. Definitely He had not descended from heaven. Jesus responded to their unbelief (their rejection) with a proverb that a prophet is not appreciated at home (v. 4).

Vs. 5-6: Because of their persistent unbelief, He could not do miracles among them, apart from His healing a few sick people, who presumably, did display a "little" faith in Him. So far as is known, He never returned to Nazareth again.
The Mission of the Twelve (vs. 7-13)

The Twelve sent out two by two, was a common practice which was for legal reasons (cf. 11:1; 14:13; John 8;17; Dt. 17:6; 19:15) also for the sake of witness (2 Cor. 13:1), and fellowship. The mission was to call as many Galileans as possible to repentance. Jesus gave the disciples authority over evil spirits. The power to cast out demons would authenticate their preaching (cf. 6:13).

Vs. 8-9: The urgency of their mission required that they travel lightly and to wear sandals 
(ordinary foot wear). For the supply of their material needs, they were to trust God for them. Whenever they were invited as guests they were not to impose on the hospitality of the people or accept more attractive offers once they were settled. They were also to expect rejection. If they were not offered hospitality or their message would not be listened to, they were to leave shaking the dust off their feet.

Vs. 10-11: Devout Jews did this when they left Gentile (alien) territory to show that they were dissociating themselves from it. This would tell Jewish hearers they were acting like pagans in rejecting the disciples' message. The shaking off the dust therefore would be a token that their personal responsibility to them had been discharged, and the people would have to answer to God for themselves (cf. Acts. 13:51; 18:6).

Vs.12-13: The threefold ministry of the Twelve is summarized as preaching repentance, driving out demons and healing the sick. Evidently the disciples had learnt that Jesus' power extended beyond His personal presence.

The anointing with the oil was both because of its medicinal properties (cf. Lk. 10:34; James 
5:14) and its symbolic value indicating that the disciples acted by Jesus' authority and 
power, not their own. It is to be thought of also as an accessory to miraculous healing and a stimulus to faith.
The Beheading of John the Baptist (vs. 14-29)

Because of the miracles, many regarded Jesus as a supernatural person, the reappearance of one of the prophets of long ago (v. 25) such as Elijah. Another view was that He was the resurrected embodiment of John the Baptist (v. 14). Herod remained convinced of this latter view (v. 16).

John the Baptist had protested, presumably on the grounds of Leviticus18:16 and 20:21, against Herod's marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip's wife (v. 17). For making this protest Herod had imprisoned John (v. 17). Herodias, however, was not satisfied with his being 
merely imprisoned and schemed to have him killed (v. 19).
The Feeding of the Five Thousand (vs. 30-44)
V.30: It is here and here only in this Gospel that the Twelve are called apostles (cf. 3:14).

Vs. 30-31: The apostles returned to Jesus and reported to Him all that they had done. Jesus directed them to come with Him to a solitary place for a brief rest. This was necessary because the crowd kept coming to them.

When Jesus saw the large crowd, He felt compassion for them. He was moved to help them, for He viewed them as sheep without a shepherd; that is, lost and helpless people without guidance, nourishment or protection.

Since it was late (after 3pm, Jewish time) and they were in a remote place, the disciples asked Jesus to dismiss the people so that they could go and buy food in the surrounding villages before sunset.

To their surprise, Jesus told them (the disciples) to feed the crowd, emphasing the word you. According to their calculations, feeding such a crowd would take, literally 200 denarii. This is roughly equivalent to eight months of a worker's wages, an amount beyond their means.

Jesus insisted they should find out what bread was available, perhaps back at the boat and 
also in the crowd. The disciples returned with the answer: a mere "five loaves of bread 
and two fish".

Vs. 29-44: To ensure orderly distribution, Jesus commanded the disciples to have everybody sit down in groups on the green grass (suggesting spring time). The people sat down in groups of 100s and 50s. The command was a challenge to faith for both the disciples and the crowd. Jesus, having blessed the food, broke the loaves into pieces, divided the fish into portions, and gave (literally, "kept giving") them to His disciples to set before the people.

Mark has not stated how the miracle took place but the word "gave" (imperfect tense) indicates that the bread multiplied in Jesus' hands (cf. Mk. 8:6). Mark tells us that all ate and were fully satisfied. This was confirmed by the fact that the disciples collected 12 basketfuls of leftovers.
The Walking on the Water (vs. 45-52)

Vs.45-46: Here, Jesus literally compelled His disciples to return to their boat and go before (Him). The reason for the hasty decision is not explained but In.6:14-15 might have been the reason, i.e. recognizing Him as the promised future prophet (Mk 6:14-15); and the determination of the people to make Him a king by force. Jesus sensed the potential danger of this "messianic enthusiasm" and its effect on the disciples, hence His decision to hasten them to embark while He dismissed the crowd, and thereafter he left by Himself to pray on the mountains (v. 46).

Their journey, however, proved difficult, because they encountered a strong "northern wind" (v. 48 the wind during the previous few hours having changed direction). From the mountains, Jesus saw the disciples in distress, presumably by the light of the moon, and between 3:00 and 6:00 am (the fourth watch of the night).

Jesus walked towards them across the surface of the water (v. 48). "He meant to pass by them" (v. 48d), probably in order that they might make a personal appeal to Him for help (cf. Lk 24:29). The disciples cried out of fear rather than an appeal for help. Jesus responded to it and calmed their fears (v. 50), after which He entered the boat and the wind ceased (v. 51). The disciples fear though natural, Mark considered them blameworthy, because having just witnessed the miracle of multiplication of loaves (and fish) v. 52, they should have been more conscious of the divine power with which He was endued.
Jesus' Healing Ministry at Gennesaret (vs. 53-56)

Gennesaret was presumably a small village, but heavily populated. When Jesus arrived the people recognized Him at once, "and ran about the whole neighbourhood and began to bring sick people on their pallets to any place where they heard He was (v. 55).

In this neighbourhood Jesus healed many invalids. They had faith in Him and were even 
healed by touching the edge of his cloak.

blocks.text: The Discussion Concerning Purification (vs. 1-23)

Jesus and his disciples were engaged in an itinerant ministry, proclaiming the imminent arrival of the kingdom of God and taking food wherever it was offered, eating with those who offered it. For Jesus, the central concern was this ministry, which was based on the conviction that the arrival of the kingdom was not dependent upon ritual preparation or ceremonies but upon God's will to bring it.

The religious leaders sent some investigators from their headquarters in Jerusalem to check up on Jesus. They did not like what they found; that the disciples ate their meals without submitting their hands to a ritual cleansing, thereby infringing one of the regulations contained in the tradition of the elders.
The Jews Observed many other Traditions
The radiant: a legislation which had been formulated by the rabbis, in which were prescribed detailed application of the law of Moses.

Vs. 3-4: Mark gives us a background to what had become the tradition of the elders. The religious leaders directed their critical inquiry to Jesus, who as the disciples teacher was held responsible for their conduct (cf. 2:18, 24). Jesus rejected this supplementary legislation, called tradition of the elders, pointing out to them its human origin which stood in antithesis to the commands of God.

Vs. 6-8: Jesus quoted Is. 29:13 (almost verbatim), and applied Isaiah's description of his contemporaries to the religious leaders whom He called hypocrites. They were "hypocrites" because they made an outward profession of worshipping God but gave Him no genuine worship from their hearts.

Vs.9-13: Jesus consequently charged them with abandoning the commands of God, His law, and instead adhering to traditions of men. Jesus cited a scribal tradition that side stepped the divine command. In their tradition, it was possible for a person to declare all his possessions to be Corban and thereby absolve oneself from the fifth commandment which enjoins respect to parents. The "Corban" vow was only one example of many things like it (e.g. restrictive Sabbath rules; (cf. 2:23-3:5; Num. 30:1-16) whose scribal tradition distorted and obscured the Old Testament.
Jesus' Explanation of Real Defilement (vs. 14-23)

In these verses, Jesus gave a more direct reply to the defilement question and in effect set 
aside the whole idea that certain foods make a person religiously unclean or unfit to 
participate in worship and fellowship with others.

He disclosed to the people the true source of defilement. Negatively, Nothing outside a man by going into him can make him "unclean" (cf. 7:2). Jesus spoke in a moral sense, not 
literally. In other words, a person is not defiled morally by what he eats even if his hands are not ceremonially washed.

Positively what comes out of a man makes him "unclean". In other words, a person is 
defiled morally by what he thinks in his heart even though he may scrupulously observe 
outward rituals on hygiene.
Jesus' Ministry beyond Galilee: The Cure of the Daughter of the Syro-Phoenician woman (vs. 24-30)

Jesus left Galilee and went to the vicinity of Tyre. He went there not to minister publicly to the people but to secure privacy; to instruct His disciples the previous one having been 
interrupted (cf. 6:32-34, 53-66). This explains the reason He did not want anyone to know 
He was there. He could not, however, hide His presence because news of His healing 
power had preceded Him (cf. 3:8).

Vs. 25-26: A woman whose daughter was demon possessed came and fell at His feet and 
begged Him to exorcise the demon from the girl. This, Jesus declined at first to do, telling 
her that His ministry lay among the Jews, not among the Gentiles. The figure of speech Jesus used in stating that fact was that in which the Jews were represented as children, 
the Gentiles as dogs.

Jesus was in actual fact telling the woman that His first priority in being there was to instruct His disciples. It was, therefore, not appropriate to interrupt a family meal to give the dogs food from the table. Jesus' reluctance to help rather stimulated her faith.

V.28: The woman agreed with Jesus. "Yes Lord" she said; and added, "even the dogs. . . eat the children's crumbs". The woman's point was that the dogs get some food at the same time as the children, and would therefore not have to wait.

Vs. 29-30: Because of such a demonstration of humility and faith, Jesus asked her to go home, assuring her of the cure of her daughter. The woman returned and found her daughter resting peacefully and the demon was gone. This miracle is the only one in the book of Mark that Jesus performed without even setting eyes on the sick person and without giving any vocal command.
The Healing of the Man who was Deaf and Dumb (vs. 31-37)

Jesus was requested to heal a deaf and dumb man (v. 32). In healing this man Jesus used sign language and symbolic acts which uniquely suited the man's needs thus causing him to exercise faith. Jesus took the man aside privately in order to communicate one-to-one with him. He used saliva (v. 31), touching also the ears and tongue, apparently to awaken in the man faith by encouraging him to expect healing. Being deaf, the man would not have been able to hear a vocal prayer. As Jesus looked up to heaven, therefore, he indicated to the man that He was praying.

blocks.text: The Feeding of the Four Thousand (vs. 1-10)
Vs. 1-3: During His ministry in the Decapolis region, Jesus fed another large crowd, miraculously, similar in many respects to that of His feeding of the five thousand.

After listening to Jesus' teaching for three days, they had nothing to eat. They were so weakened by hunger that if they were to be sent away hungry, many were those who would collapse on the way, for some had come from afar.
Jesus had compassion on them in their physical plight and asked the disciples to address the issue.

Vs. 4-5: The disciples' question "where will anyone be able to find enough to satisfy these men. . ." showed their slowness in understanding the significance of Jesus' presence with them in crises. It also showed their inadequacy to meet the need. They indirectly referred the matter back to Jesus (contrast 6:37).
Vs. 8-9a: Here Mark stresses the sufficiency of the miracle, "and they ate and were satisfied…" (v. 8a)
The abundance of the food 	-    seven basketfuls of the food remained
The size of the crowd 		-    four thousand men (besides women and children)

The basket on this occasion differed from those used in feeding the five thousand (Mk. 6:43; cf. 8: 19-20) they were probably rope or mat baskets, sometimes large enough to carry an adult. (cf. Acts 9: 25). Therefore, the seven basketfuls of Mk. 8:8 could hold more than the twelve basketfuls of 6:43.
Vs. 9b-l0: Having dismissed the crowd, Jesus moved together with His disciples to Dalmanutha, near Tiberias (cf. v. 13). This ended His public ministry in Galilee.
Demand by the Pharisees for a Sign (vs. 11-13)

The Pharisees came to Jesus, "seeking from Him a sign from heaven. . ." They were not necessarily demanding a spectacular miracle, but that Jesus give unmistakable proof that He and His mission were authorized by God. In fact they believed the opposite. Jesus rejected their demand. "Truly I say to you, not a sign shall be given to this generation" (v. 12c).

An appeal for a miracle can be a legitimate expression of one's faith (e.g. Mk. 5: 23; 7: 26; 32). But that of the Pharisees here arose out of unbelief. Jesus' abrupt departure was evidently out of indignation.
Jesus Warns Against Wrong Teaching (vs. 14-21)

In this section, Mark brings up the lack of spiritual perception of the disciples. While in the 
ship (v. 13) on their way from Dalmanutha to Bethsaida, Jesus warned His disciples against 
the yeast of the Pharisees and that of Herod (i.e. irreligion, v. 15). The disciples supposing that Jesus was speaking about literal leaven, instead of using the word metaphorically to denote moral evil of a corrupting nature, assumed that Jesus was complaining about the fact that they had not brought sufficient bread for their communal needs on this journey (v. 16). Jesus used the occasion to warn the disciples of those corrupting influences which more than anything cause blindness of heart (cf. Mt. 16: 5-12).

We learn from Luke 12:1 that leaven of the Pharisees was hypocrisy; the leaven of bread 
was probably worldliness and sensuality.

In context the yeast referred to a gradual increase of unbelief. This lay behind the Pharisees' request for a sign even though their minds were already made up (cf. 8:11-12, 3:6). It was the same with Herod (cf. 6:14-16; Lk. 13:31-33, 23:8-9). As Jesus hinted in His question (Mk. 8:12) this attitude had affected the whole nation of Israel. He therefore, warned His disciples against it. In contrast He called them to faith and understanding without signs (cf. vs.17-21).

topics.title: From Galilee to Jerusalem: Jesus Concentrates on Ministry to His Disciples

blocks.text: The Healing of the Blindman at Bethsaida (vs. 22-26)

In this narrative we see remarkable similarities between this miracle and that of the deaf 
mute (7:31-37).

Vs. 23-24: Jesus leading the blind man outside the village was perhaps to establish a one- to-one relationship with him (cf. 7:33) and to avoid publicity (v. 26). The touch of saliva and Jesus' hands (cf. 7:33) conveyed His intentions and stimulated the blind man's faith. At first the healing was just partial. He looked up and saw people (perhaps the Twelve) moving around. Jesus questioned him "Do you see anything?"

V.25: Jesus again put His hands on the man's eyes, his sight was restored; and he began to see everything clearly. The man's eyes were now perfect. This was the outcome the disciples could anticipate in spite of difficulties in the process.
Peter's Acknowledgement of Jesus' Messiahship (vs. 27-30)

The main task of Jesus in undertaking this journey from Galilee to Jerusalem was to prepare His disciples for His impending crucifixion. Jesus explained the nature of His messianic vocation and its implications for those who choose to follow Him. There is a balanced tension between His veiledness in suffering and His future revelation in glory.
The narrative, from this point is dominated by the thought of the approaching passion, of which there are three definite predictions. (8:31; 9:31; 10:33)
The First Prediction of the Passion (vs. 31-33)

With the disciples now convinced that Jesus was the Messiah, He was able at last to give them explicit teaching about His forthcoming death (though incidental allusions to it had been made previously (cf. 2:20). The son of man must suffer: the cause of it being the will of God (cf. Isaiah 53). Peter, even though was convinced that Jesus was the Messiah (v. 29), was appalled at the thought of it carrying such implications. He therefore protested against the assertion concerning this "defeatist approach". This reaction which probably was shared by the other disciples was a satanic attempt similar to the wilderness temptations (cf. 1: 12-13), to divert Jesus from the cross. Jesus rebuked Peter for the benefit of them all. This was not a personal attack. It was an attack on Satan, for he (Satan) was the source of Peter's thoughts.

reference.topic: 1.3 From Galilee to Jerusalem: Jesus Concentrates on Ministry to His Disciples
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — From Galilee to Jerusalem: Jesus Concentrates on Ministry to His Disciples (syllabus ¶1021)

blocks.text: Jesus' Teaching on the Cost of Discipleship (8: 34-9:1)

Having indicated what Messiahship would mean for Him, Jesus now explains what discipleship would mean for the apostles and His other hearers. Any person who enlisted in His cause would need to deny himself (v. 34) that is, abandon the attitude of self- centeredness, and take up his own (not His) cross, in other words be prepared to die.

Paradoxically, a person who wants to save (preserve) his life will lose it; he will not be saved to eternal life. But a person who loses (will lose) his life for the sake of Jesus and the gospel, will save it; that is, he will be saved to eternal life.

9:1 ". . .Truly I say to you, there are some of those who are standing here who shall not taste death until they see the kingdom of God. . .". The precise meaning of this verse remains somewhat uncertain. Four possible interpretations have been suggested, namely: the transfiguration, the resurrection and ascension, the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70; Pentecost and the beginning of missionary enterprise. The transfiguration is the most reasonable view in this context. The specific reference in the following account of Jesus' transfiguration (9:2a) indicates that Mark understood a definite connection between Jesus' prediction (v. 1) and this event. Jesus' transfiguration was a striking preview and guarantee of His future glory (cf. 2 Pet. 1:16-19).
The Transfiguration (vs. 2-13)

V.2. Jesus selected Peter, James, and John (cf. Mk. 5:37; 14:33) and took them up a high mountain where they were all alone. Jesus was transfigured in the presence of the three disciples (cf. 2 Pet. 1:16). "Transfigured" means "to be changed into another form", not just a
change in outward appearance (cf. Rom. 12:2; 2 Cor. 3:18). Jesus' human body was transformed (glorified) which the disciples saw. This obviously impressed upon them as what He will be when He returns visibly in power and glory to establish His kingdom on earth (cf15:14-18; 1 Cor. 15:20-28; Rev. 1:14-15; 19:15; 20:4-6).
The discussion concerning Elijah (vs. 11-13)

Two significant Old Testament men, Elijah and Moses, appeared miraculously and 
conversed with Jesus (v. 4). Both were prominent mediators of God's rule to the nation of Israel (cf. Ex. 3:6; 4:16; 7:1; Dt. 18: 15-18; l Kgs. 19:13; Acts 7:35). The three disciples wanted to know why Jesus' coming had not been preceded, as the scribes or scriptures had taught them (Mal. 4:5), by the coming of Elijah (v. 11).

Vs.12-13: In His reply, Jesus made two things clear. First, He acknowledged the Scripture which says that Elijah does come first (before the Messiah) and restores all things through spiritual renewal (Mal. 4:5-6). On the other hand Elijah's coming did not take away the coming of the Son of Man to suffer much and be rejected (Ps. 22; Isa. 53, esp. v. 3). Jesus added, however that indeed Elijah had come.

The progression of thought is this: If Elijah is to come before the last day and "restore the hearts" (Mal. 4:5-6), why should the Son of Man have to die? Jesus' reply is that they are correct about Elijah but their concept of the Son of Man was deficient, since it did not include the truths of His suffering and death (Ps. 22: 6; Is. 53). Christ then adds (Mk 9:13) that Elijah had already come in John the Baptist but had not been recognized.
The Healing of the Demon - Possessed Boy (vs. 14-29)
While on the Mount of Transfiguration, a disturbed father brought his demon-possed son to the disciples, who could not exorcise the demon.

Vs 18-19: 0 unbelieving generation (v. 19). It was probably the nine disciples, rather than the crowd or the scribes or the boy's father, to whom Jesus was here referring (cf. Mt. 17: 19-20). "Because of your little faith": This statement emphasizes the characteristic cause of all spiritual failure, i.e. lack of faith in God (cf. 9:23; 10:27). Jesus was apparently unhappy with the disciples' spiritual dullness (cf. 4:40; 6:50-52; 8:17-21). He therefore commanded, "Bring the boy to me". Jesus challenged the father not to doubt: for everything is possible for him who believes (cf. v. 9:29). The father's response was quick. He declared his faith, "I do believe". In contrast to the disciples who were "unbelieving", the boy's father possessed faith, though being imperfect (v. 24). Jesus informed him that a person who had faith should not say to Him "if you can" (v. 22); he should set no limit to His divine authority (v. 23). This ability was displayed thereupon in the healing of the boy (vs. 25-27).
The Second Prediction of the Passion (vs. 30-32)
His imminent death was a constant theme of His teaching on this journey. Jesus said He the son of man would be betrayed, to both Jews and Gentiles.

"Betrayed" means "deliver up" or "hand over". It was used both of Judas' betrayal of Jesus (3:19; 14:41; Lk. 24:7) and of God's delivering up Jesus to death for the redemption of sinners (Isa. 53:6, 12; Acts 2:23; Rotn.8:32). The latter idea (of betrayal) is probably intended here, suggesting that the implied Agent of the (passive) verb is God, not Judas.
The Discussion Concerning Greatness (vs. 33-37)

Evidently Jesus had been walking in front of His disciples as they drew near Capernaum (as in 10:32); but He knew what they had been discussing among themselves on the journey (Lk. 9:47). When they were in the house, Jesus asked them frankly what they were. . . arguing about on the road. Jesus' question opened the way once again for more teaching (cf. vs. 27, 29). The apostles were ashamed to admit they had argued who was the greatest among them. Matters of rank were important to the Jews (cf. Lk. 14:7-11). It was, therefore, natural for the disciples to think about their status in the forthcoming kingdom. It showed that they had not understood or had not accepted what Jesus' passion prediction (v. 31) meant for them. Jesus told them that the essence of greatness lay in performing acts of service for other people (v. 35, also 10:43-44).

Vs. 36-37: To illustrate servant-leadership, Jesus proceeded to take up in His arms a child (cf. 10:13-16). To welcome, that is, to serve or show kindness to (cf. 6:11; Lk 9:53) one of these little children, who represented the lowliest disciple (cf. Mk 9:42), in Jesus' name (on His behalf) is equivalent to welcoming Jesus Himself (cf. Mt 25:40). But to do this was not to welcome Jesus only but also the heavenly Father who sent Him (cf. In. 3:17; 8:42).
This, Jesus says, gives dignity to the task of serving others.
The Disciples Forbid Another to Use Jesus' Name: Rebukes and Warnings (vs. 38-42)

John reported to Jesus that they had stepped an anonymous exorcist who was driving out 
demons in His (Jesus') name. They did this because the man was not one of them; he was a disciple but not one of the Twelve commissioned by Jesus to do the work (cf. 6:7, 12-13). Clearly it was not the man's misuse of Jesus' name that troubled them, but rather his unauthorized use of the name. This incident shows us or exposes the narrow exclusivism 
of the Twelve. Jesus criticized John's action in the matter, pointing out that the man was 
not against them (v. 40), and that it was highly unlikely that the man would perform miracles in His name and then immediately turn around and publicly speak evil of Him (v. 39).

Vs.41-42: Here, Jesus broadened His comments verses in 39-40 to include activity besides exorcism. Even one who performs the smallest act of hospitality in Jesus' name (cf. v. 37) such as giving a cup of water to someone because the one belongs to Christ will certainly not lose his reward. In verse 42, Jesus sternly warned anyone who would deliberately turn somebody away from believing in Him. The punishment for such an offence was so severe that it would be better for him to be drowned in the sea.
Lessons in Discipleship (vs. 43-50)

The disciples' are here strongly warned about the danger of letting themselves be led astray. In these verses, the focus shifts (momentarily) from causing others to fall to causing one's own fall. The hyperboles (exaggerated statements) in the passage, though not to be pressed literally, the point is not to be lost that participation in the kingdom of God is worth any sacrifice. The organs mentioned here are really symbols for various types of activity, for example, (1) the hand that snatches for things it should not, (2) the foot that goes where it ought not; (3) the eye that desires what it ought not. Jesus meant that a disciple should take prompt, decisive action against whatever would draw him away from his allegiance to Him.
