blocks.text: Jesus' Teaching on Marriage and Divorce (vs. 1-12)

Once again the question put by the Pharisees was malicious. It was put to Him in order to test Him, i.e. to try to induce Him to incriminate Himself by contradicting the Mosaic Law. The Mosaic enactment (Dt. 24: 1-4) stated that a husband was allowed to divorce his wife by writing and giving to her a certificate of divorce (v. 4) if he had found some unseemly thing in her. The question turned upon what constituted an unseemly thing. Shammai and Hillel were authorities in the interpretation of the Mosaic Law and different groups took their authority from them. The school of Shammai maintained the strict interpretation of this, that the marriage band was indissoluble except in the event of the wife's infidelity. The school of Hillel took the liberal view allowing divorce for almost any cause (v. 5). In reply, Jesus first pointed out that Moses' legislation was a concession to human weakness and rightly introduced to regulate divorce in a defective state of society. In verse 5, we read "Because of the hardness of your heart he wrote to you this commandment".

Secondly, Jesus took them back beyond Moses to God's ideal at the beginning of creation, from which we discover that marriage was instituted as the divine ideal for man and woman, and that the bond is permanent and indissoluble, (vs. 10-12).
The Reception of God's Kingdom in Childlike Trust (vs. 13-16)

The disciples felt it was an unwarranted intrusion into Jesus' busy schedule for parents to 
bring their children to have Him touch them (v. 13). Jesus' sharp double command - "Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them. . ." was a rebuke to the disciples; for he not only received the children, but went beyond that which was asked of Him. He took the children in His arms and blessed them (v. 16). In saying "for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these" Jesus meant, that the kingdom of God belonged to people who, though not literally children, were imbued with such characteristics of children as trust and receptiveness. God's kingdom is not gained by human achievement or merit; it must be received as God's gift through simple trust by those who acknowledge their inability to gain it any other way.
The Reception of God's Kingdom made impossible by Trust in Riches (vs. 17-27)

The wealthy man here (vs. 22b), despite his having observed the Mosaic Law as best he knew or could (v. 20), was nevertheless spiritually dissatisfied, and so asked Jesus what he needed to do to inherit eternal life (v. 17). His approach, however, did not depict normal Jewish custom, because he addressed Jesus as "Good Teacher", not used by Jews to address a Rabbi. His kneeling posture and profound question however, revealed his earnestness and respect for Jesus. Jesus rebuked him for his address, reminding him that "good" was a designation which was normally reserved for God. Jesus was not hereby disclaiming being either "God" or "good", but was merely criticizing His being addressed thus by someone who clearly was completely unaware of His divine nature. In reply to the man's enquiry Jesus tried to deepen in the man a consciousness of sin by quoting to him five commandments dealing with human relationships that are more easily verified in a person's conduct. The command Do not defraud occurring only in Mark is interpreted "Do not covet" (from the so-called second Table of the Decalogue - 10 commandments). The implication to be derived from the man's retort is that he had no understanding as to all that these requirements involved. There were qualities about this man, however, which moved Jesus greatly to love him (21a). The one necessary thing the rich man lacked was unrivalled allegiance to God since wealth was his god (v. 22). He was devoted to it rather than God, thereby breaking the first commandment (Ex. 20:3). Jesus commanded two things: (1) He was to go and sell all his assets and give to the poor, thereby removing the stumbling block that was preventing him from eternal life, namely, self-righteous achievement coupled with love for money. (2) Jesus asked the man to follow Him (v. 21d). Jesus was trying to show the man that, in reality, his love of money violated the law and made him a sinner. The man, saddened by Jesus' directives, went away. Commenting on the man's decision, Jesus told His disciples that it was as impossible for a man who made riches his "god", to receive salvation, as for a camel, (the largest animal in Palestine at that time) to go through the eye of a needle (v. 25). Jesus, however, allayed the disciples' fear or amazement by reminding them that all things are possible with God (v. 27).
The Third Prediction of Jesus' Death and Resurrection (vs. 32-34)

Jesus and His disciples continued on their way from the Jordan valley (cf. v. 1) to Jerusalem. 
He was leading them in accord with Rabbinic custom. His steadfast determination in the face of the impending danger astonished the disciples; those who followed were also afraid.

Vs. 33b-34: Once again Jesus gathered the Twelve around Him and revealed what would 
soon happen to Him. This third prediction of His approaching Passion which He thereupon made to them was fuller than the earlier ones. He included the additional facts that the Jewish leaders would cause His death to be carried out at the hands of the Gentiles (v. 33) who, prior to executing Him, would mock Him, and spit upon Him, and flog Him (v. 34).
The Essential Meaning of Discipleship (vs. 35-45)

The fact that the disciples no more understood Jesus' third prediction of His Passion than they did His earlier ones (8:32; 9:32) is proved not only by the explicit statement of Lk. 8:44, but also by this request from James and John to be allowed to sit on either side of his throne in the glory of His throne (v. 37). Jesus refused their request, explaining that the matter in question did not come within the scope of His personal jurisdiction (v. 40). The disreputable request of James and John was met by an equally disreputable reaction from their fellow apostles (v. 41). Addressing all the Twelve Jesus emphasized that the highest honour to which a man could aspire consisted not in occupying a kingdom's chief seats, but in serving other people. And Jesus cited Himself, as an example of one who came to serve (v. 45).
The Faith of Blind Bartimaeus (vs. 46-52)

Jesus and His disciples followed by a large crowd were on their way to Jerusalem from Perea when they saw a blind beggar, by name Bartimaeus. When Bartimaeus was informed that Jesus of Nazareth (cf. 1:24) was passing by, he clamored for His attention and relentlessly shouted for Jesus to have mercy on him. Apparently, Bartimaeus had heard reports that Jesus restored sight. His apparent conviction that Jesus could cure his blindness might also be due to his knowledge that the Messiah would enable the blind to see (Isa. 61:1 (LXX) cf. Mt.ll:5). Bartimaeus was rebuked by those around for making a nuisance of himself (v. 48 cf. 10: 13). They might have been opposed to him addressing Jesus as son of David (occurring here for the first time in Mark) which designated the Messiah as David's descendant. Bartimaeus using that title probably indicated that despite his physical blindness he believed Jesus of Nazareth was Israel's Messiah, in contrast with the blind unbelief of most Jews. Later he addressed Jesus more personally "Rabbi" (v.51).  He was healed and then followed Him (cf. v. 52b). Jesus did not silence him, implying He accepted the title.

blocks.text: Knowing that the time was now ripe for Him to publicly declare His Messiahship (cf. 10:47) Jesus decided to do so by an act which constituted a claim that the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9 applied to Him. Therefore, instead of entering Jerusalem on foot, as was customary in the case of pilgrims, He resolved to enter the city mounted on a colt (v. 2). Jesus' choice of riding on the animal which had never been ridden before, was in accordance with the prophet's description of such a creature as a new colt (LXX). Matthew 21:2 and John 12:14 indicate that the colt in question was that of a donkey. Jesus' use of a donkey was to show that, despite popular opinion, it was not as a warrior that he would fulfill His messianic office (in which event a more appropriate beast would have been a horse). As a homage to Jesus, cloaks (cf. 2 Kgs. 9:13) and leafy branches cut from surrounding fields (Palm branches are mentioned in (Jn. 12:13) were spread on the road before Him. The word "Hosanna" (v. 9) which the crowd cried out, is derived from the Hebrew exclamation 'save now', as is written in Ps. 118: 25. It may have been an appeal to God to save the nation Israel now that the Messiah had appeared among them.

topics.title: The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)

blocks.text: Cursing of the Fig-tree and Cleansing of the Temple on Monday (vs. 12-19)

In this passage we have another example of Mark's sandwiching of two stories together in order to relate them to each other. In other words each episode helps explain the other. Mark begins the story of the barren fig tree in 11:12-14, interrupting it to relate Jesus' cleansing of the Temple in 11: 15-19, and completing the fig tree story in 11: 20-26. Both episodes signify God's impending judgment on Israel for religious hypocrisy.
Jesus' Judgment on the Unproductive Fig-tree (vs. 12-14)

The next day, (early Monday morning), after leaving Bethany for Jerusalem, Jesus was hungry and from a distance, he saw a wayside fig tree full of green leaves, and went to see if it had any fruit. Unfortunately it had nothing but leaves. We need to note that in Palestine fig trees produced crops of small edible buds in March followed by the appearance of large green leaves in early April. 'This early green "fruit" (buds) was common food for local peasants. Mark explained that "it was not the season for figs" (v. 13). The fact here, therefore, is this: the tree's leaves promised fruit; the absence of the green fruits, therefore, meant that the tree's appearance was deceptive. It is this that Jesus uses as a symbol for the Temple. It has the appearance of dedication to God, but the substance falls short of doing His will (vs. 15-17).
Jesus' Judgement the Misuse of the Temple (vs. 15-19)

When Jesus arrived in Jerusalem He went into the temple area. There was a large outer court of the Gentiles surrounding the inner sacred courts of the temple itself. No Gentile was allowed beyond this outer court. In it the High priest Caiaphas had authorized a market for the sale of ritually pure items necessary for temple sacrifice: wine, oil, salt, approved sacrificial animals and birds.

The merchants and the money changers who exchanged various currencies for the kind of coinage accepted for paying the annual Temple tax (Ex. 30: 13-16), apparently turned the Court of the Gentiles into some sort of bazaar, making it impossible for any Gentile to use the area for prayer or serious devotion to God.

Jesus was outraged by this blatant disregard for the temple area specifically set apart for Gentile use. He, therefore, overturned the tables of the money changers, and would also not allow people to use the area as a thoroughfare. Jesus' action captured people's attention, and He used the occasion to teach them about God's purpose for the temple, intended also as a house of prayer for all nations.
The Meaning of the Withered Fig-tree (vs. 20-26)

Early next morning, (i.e., Tuesday), as Jesus and His disciples were returning to Jerusalem, they saw the fig tree withered from the root. The disciples were all surprised and Peter drew Jesus' attention to it. Jesus did not explain the meaning of the incident but many believe it was a vivid picture of God's impending judgment on Israel. However, He used the incident as a practical demonstration of the power of faith (v. 22) which could effect, not merely the withering of a tree, but the removal of a mountain (v. 23), implying that by exercise of faith in God, people can do what humanly appears utterly impossible. When engaged in prayer, we must have an attitude of faith in God (v. 24), and forgiveness towards one's fellow men (v. 25) and, the petitions which are made (assuming that these are not contrary to the will of God, (cf. 1 Jn. 5:14) will assuredly be granted.
Religious Leaders Challenge Jesus' Authority (vs. 27-33)

Jesus and His disciples arrived at the Temple, and in the Temple courts, Jesus was confronted by representatives of the Sanhedrin. They required from Him who had authorized Him to chase the merchants out of the temple the previous day (v. 28). As guardians of Israel's religious life, they asked two questions: (1) what was the nature of his authority (cf. 1:22, 27) i.e., what were His credentials; (2) who was the source of his authority. In reply Jesus reminded them of the case of John the Baptist, and asked whether John had ministered by divine appointment, or whether, by contrast, he had been commissioned by the Jewish authorities [i.e., "from men?" (v. 30). They could not face the questions honestly because of the perplexing consequences involved. To have admitted that John had been divinely authorized for his ministry would have invited from Jesus the question "Then why did you not believe him?", whereas to have alleged that John acted purely from some source other than heaven, would have incurred the wrath of the people who had always believed John to be a prophet (v. 32). Being in dilemma in this way, they declined to answer the questions (v. 33). Jesus, therefore, also refused to answer theirs (v. 33).

reference.topic: 2.2 The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44) (syllabus ¶1110)

blocks.text: The Parable of the Wicked Husbandmen (vs. 1-12)

This parable is obviously a description of the leaders of Israel who had been unwilling to receive God's word sent to them by the prophets (cf. v. 12). In answer to their question Jesus had shown them that they had rejected John the Baptist and himself as messengers sent from God. This parable is intended to tell them that they are as guilty as their ancestors who had rejected the ministry of earlier prophets.
Religious Leaders Question Jesus about Paying Taxes (vs. 13-17)

Despite Jesus' warning to the religious leaders as given in the foregoing parable, they continued their campaign against Him by sending some Pharisees (2:16) and Herodians (3:6) to catch Him in His words [i.e., through an unguarded statement they could use against Him, cf. 10:2). Their question was whether it was in accordance with the Law of God to pay to Caesar the poll tax or not (v. 14). This particular tax was exceptionally unpopular, being the token of the Jews' status as subjects of Rome. The questioners felt that for Jesus to insist on its payment would alienate the people from Him, whereas for Him to deny the legitimacy of the tax would be something for which He could conveniently be reported to the Romans as a rebel against their authority. Obviously the question was designed to place Jesus in a religious and political dilemma. Jesus' reply was to the effect that since the money they possessed, having embossed on it the image of the Emperor (probably Tiberius), was, according to the contemporary view point, Caesar's property, so they should pay to him the poll tax. This tax was a debt they owed to Caesar for use of his money and other benefits of his rule. Jesus added, however, that they give back to God what is God's (literary, "the things belonging to God". This could refer to paying God the temple tax due Him.
The Question Concerning the Resurrection (vs. 18-27)

The Sadducees came to Jesus with a question in another attempt to discredit Him. (cf. 11:27; 12:13). The Sadducees (generally believed to be Jewish aristocrats) denied the truth of the resurrection, future judgment, and existence of angels and spirits (Acts 23:6-8). The Pharisees acknowledged them all (Acts 23:8b).

Whereas the former question had aimed at placing Jesus in political difficulty, this one was aimed at placing Him in a theological difficulty. They tried to make the doctrine of the resurrection, in which they disbelieved, look ridiculous. Their contention, ultimately, was that it was incompatible with the levirate marriage, as laid down in Dt. 25:5-10, which they quoted loosely to Jesus (v. 19). The Sadducees made up a story about seven brothers who successively fulfilled the duty of levirate marriage to their first brother's wife but all the seven brothers died childless. The woman died also. They asked Jesus: At the resurrection whose wife will she be? Clearly they were ridiculing belief in the resurrection.
V. 24: Jesus cited two reasons why they were in error:

(a) they did not know the scriptures; (b) they did not know the power of God, and His power to overcome death and give life. Jesus then amplified each reason starting with the second (v. 25). The Sadducees wrongly assumed that marriages would be resumed after the resurrection. In resurrection life people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Rather like the angels in heaven they will be immortal beings in God's presence.

Vs. 26-27: The Sadducees wrongly alleged that the idea of the resurrection was absent from the Pentateuch. But Jesus referred them to Ex. 3:1-6. In this passage God revealed Himself to Moses, as the God of Abraham. . . Isaac, and. . . Jacob (Ex. 3:6). God implied that the Patriarchs were still alive and that He had a continuing relationship with them as their covenant keeping God, even though they had died long ago. Jesus concluded He is not the God of the dead in the Sadducees understanding of death as extinction, but of the living.
The Question Concerning the Greatest Commandment (vs. 28-34)

V. 28: One of the Law teachers (cf. 1: 22) had heard Jesus' discussion with the Sadducees (12:18-27) and was impressed with His good answers to them. In the light of the debate, the Law teacher asked Jesus which commandment is the most important of them all?

V. 28: By Jesus' time, the Jews had accumulated hundreds of Laws, totaling 613. Some religious leaders tried to distinguish between major and minor laws, and some taught that all laws were actually binding and that it was dangerous to make any distinctions. The teacher's question could have provoked controversy among these groups, but Jesus' answer summarized all of God's Laws.

Vs. 29-31: God's laws ate not burdensome in number or detail. They can be reduced to two simple rules for life, love God, and love others. These commands are from the Old Testament (Lev. 19: 18; Dt. 6:5). When you love God completely and care for others as yourself, then you have fulfilled the intent of the Ten Commandments and the other Old Testament Laws.
According to Jesus, these two rules summarize all God's laws.

V. 34: "not far from the kingdom of God". The meaning is that the religious teacher had 
demonstrated by his answer to Jesus that he is sincere and that he is not guilty of the kind of manipulation of religious tradition for which Jesus condemned the scribes elsewhere (12: 38-40, 7: 1-13) That which separates him from the kingdom of God is his failure to become a follower of Jesus.

V. 34b: Jesus had effectively thwarted all attempts to discredit Him and had exposed the 
hostile motives and errors of His opponents so skillfully that nobody else dared ask Him 
any more questions.
Jesus' Question Concerning David's Son (vs. 35-37)
Later, as Jesus was teaching in the Temple area, He asked the question "How is it that the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David?" (v. 35).

Vs. 36-37a: To prove that the Messiah is David's Lord, Jesus quoted what David Himself speaking by the Holy Spirit declared in Ps. 110: 1. He said "The Lord said to my Lord. Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet." The indisputable fact was that David called the Messiah Lord. How then can He (The Messiah, Lord) be his (David's) son? Jesus' rhetorical question here, pointed His listeners to only one valid answer: the Messiah is David's son and David's Lord at the same time. This strongly implies that the Messiah is both God (David's Lord) and man (David's son: cf. Rom. 1:3-4; 2 Tim. 2:8) He will restore the future Davidic kingdom on earth (2Sam. 7:16; Amos 9:11-12; Mt. 19:25; Lk. l:31-33).
Jesus' Condemnation of Hypocrisy (vs. 38-40)

Vs. 38-39: Jesus kept warning people to watch out for those law teachers who sought praise from men and abuse their privileges. They liked to (a) go around in flowing robes, (b) be greeted in the market places with formalities - Rabbi (teacher); (c) have the most important synagogue seats; (d) have the places of honour at banquets. Jesus condemned their ostentatious conduct, greed and hypocrisy. Instead of pointing people's attention to God, they pointed attention to themselves under the pretense of piety. Teachers such as these will be punished most severely.
A Poor Widow gives all she had (vs. 41-44)

Having spoken of the greediness or avarice of the scribes (v. 40), Jesus spoke now about a 
woman whom He noticed surrendering everything she had for the work of God (v. 44). It 
was a sacrificial gift that left her with nothing for herself, whereas the rich retained plenty 
for themselves.

topics.title: The Last Things: Jesus Tells about the Future (vs. 1-37)

blocks.text: Vs. 1-4: Having concluded a day of teaching in the Temple one of the disciples directed His attention to the magnificence of the temple, its stone walls, as he was leaving (v. 1). Jesus' response was to predict the temple's complete destruction and devastation (v. 2). Jesus spent the nights, at this time, on the Mount of Olives (Lk. 21:37). When Jesus and His disciples were on their way after having crossed the Kidron valley and ascended the hill (where they would have a magnificent view of the city and its Temple) the four senior disciples, Peter, James, John and Andrew got alone with Him and asked Him when the Temple's destruction would occur. They enquired also to know what sign would indicate the imminence of this (v. 3-4).
The Olivet Discourse (vs. 5-37)

Vs. 6-8: The disciples are warned against deception. There would be imposters in the religious sphere, uprisings or disturbances in political and international field and calamities in the physical realm. Such things, however, are incidental to the course of the age, and are not necessarily to be taken as the signs of the end. Rather they are the beginning of the sufferings (stated, beginning of birth pains).

V.9-13: A second warning follows against spiritual failure in view of what will happen to them personally and within the Christian community. Opposition will come through official channels. It will be so severe that family members, brother verses brother, father verses child, and children verses parents - will betray each other to hostile authorities, thereby causing Christian members to be put to death. The disciples also, because of their allegiance to Jesus, will be hated continually by all men, that is, all kinds of people, not just hostile authorities or family members (cf. Phil. 1:29; 3:11; Col. 1:24; 1 Pet. 4:4, 16) He who stands firm that is, remained loyal to Jesus Christ and the gospel (cf. Mk. 8:35) to the end will be saved.

Vs. 14-23: Jesus then answered the disciples' second question, verse 14b. The sign that "these things" were about to be fulfilled (cf. v. 4b) was the appearance of the abomination that causes desolation standing where it does not belong (a reference to the temple sanctuary) let the reader understand . . . flee to the mountains.

"The abomination" is a future person "standing where he does not belong". This person is seen to be end-time Anti-Christ (Dan. 7:23-26; 9:25-27; 2 Thess 2:3-4; 8-9; Rev. 13:1-10,      14-15). He will make a covenant with the Jewish people at the beginning of the seven- year period preceeding Christ's second coming (Dan. 9:27).

V. 20: If the Lord had not already decided in His sovereign plan to cut short those days no one would survive. But God set limits on the duration of the end-time Tribulation, because of the elect, whom He has chosen. In verses 21-22, the disciples are told, at that-time if someone should claim that the Christ was here or there, His disciples were not to believe it because false Christs and false prophets would appear and perform miraculous deeds that would seem to validate their claims. Their purpose would be to mislead the elect, i.e. the believers in the true Messiah.
Jesus' Triumphant Return (vs. 24-27)
These verses tell us of a variety of cosmic disorders involving, the sun, moon, and stars which will immediately precede the second coming of Christ Jesus (cf. Isa. 3:10; 34:4).

When the cosmic events have taken place, people will see the Son of Man coming in clouds. He will exercise great power and display heavenly glory. This is Jesus' personal, visible, bodily return (Acts 1: 11; Rev. 1:7; 19:11-16).

V. 27: Also at that time the Son of Man will send His angels (cf. 8:38, Mt. 25:31) and gather His elect from four winds i.e. from all directions, a reference to people living in all parts of the world. None of the elect will be left out.
Parables and Sayings on Watchfulness (vs. 28-37)

This end is the practical application of all that has gone before. The chapter concludes with a plain assertion that these injunctions belong not to that generation alone, but to every generation of the Christian church.

V. 28: The lesson of the fig tree draws attention once more to what is the true purpose of prophecy (cf. v. 5), not that the disciples may prophesy but that they may, with spiritual insight, discern the unfolding of God's purpose in the moving spectacle of events.

V. 30: We are to learn that the fact of Christ's personal return is unalterably sure. The time 
alone is uncertain, being locked in the counsels of the Father, so that even the Son, in the voluntarily-accepted limitations of His incarnation, does not share the secret. Vs. 35-37: The entire passage (vs. 3-37) tells us how to live while we wait for Christ's return.

We are not to be misled by confusing claims or idle interpretations of what will happen 
(vs.5-6).
We should not be afraid to tell anyone about Christ, despite what they might say or do to us (vs. 9-11).
We must endure by faith and not be surprised by persecutions (v. 13)
We must be morally alert and obedient to the commands for living found in God's word.

blocks.text: The Plot to Arrest Jesus (vs. 1-2)

The Jewish leaders here made their final attempt to have Jesus killed, after having failed to implement previous plots (3:6; 12:12). However, they resolved not to let it occur during the feast. Their reason was that it might provoke violent opposition on the part of supporters of Jesus who would be coming to Jerusalem from Galilee to observe the Passover. The religious leaders' desire was fulfilled with the assistance of Judas Iscariot, who disclosed to the authorities where Jesus might be found at night and almost alone (cf. vs. 10-11, 43-50).
The Anointing of Jesus' Head (vs. 3-9)

Simon the Leper had been healed, apparently by Jesus and at this time was hosting Him. An unnamed woman believed to be Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus On. 12:13), came with an alabaster jar of costly perfume, broke it and poured it over Jesus' head. Anointing a guest's head was a common custom at festive Jewish meals [cf. Ps. 23:5, Lk. 7:46) but Mary's act here had a greater meaning (vs. 8-9).

However, some of the disciples, led by Judas Iscariot, criticised it (v.4 cf. Jn. 12:4-6). In their 
view the act was uncalled for because the perfume could have been sold for more than a year's wages and the money given to the poor.
It is necessary to note that Jewish custom called for special remembrance of the poor at Passover time (Jn. 13:28-29).

Vs. 6-9: Jesus rebuked the woman's critics and defended what she had done, calling it a beautiful thing. Jesus saw the woman's action as an expression of love and devotion to Him in the light of His impending death. Jesus added that opportunities to help the poor would always be present and the disciples should take advantage of them. He concluded here that wherever the gospel is preached throughout the world the woman's deed of love would also be mentioned.
Judas Agrees to Betray Jesus (vs. 10-11)

Judas went to the chief priests (v. 11) and offered to betray Jesus to them (cf. v. 11; 9:31). 
He suggested doing it when no crowd was present (Lk. 22:6). This would avoid a riot by the people, which was the priests' primary concern (cf. v. 2). Why did Judas offer to betray Jesus?
The following suggestions have been made

Judas, the only non-Galilean member of the Twelve, may have responded to the official 
notice-orders to report Jesus' where about (Jn. 11:57).

He was disillusioned by Jesus' failure to establish a political kingdom and his hopes for 
material gain seemed doomed.

His love for money moved him to acquire something for himself. What is clear, 
however, is that he came under satanic control (cf. Lk 22:3; In. 13:2, 27).

We find in Judas' life a combination of divine sovereignty and human responsibility. That is, according to God's plan of ages, Jesus must suffer and die (Rev. 13:8) yet Judas, though not compelled to be the traitor, was held responsible for submitting to Satan's directives (cf. Mk. 14:21;Jn.13:27).
The Disciples Prepare for the Passover (vs. 12-16)

"On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when it was customary to sacrifice the Passover Lamb. . ." (v.12). This is the day we know as Good Friday (14th Nisan) But according to Jewish reckoning this day began at the sunset the day before. The events of this section therefore took place on the Thursday evening. The question of whether the supper was in fact the Passover meal remains unsettled despite prolonged discussion on both sides.

Vs. 13-15: Jesus and His disciples, were probably in Bethany (cf. 11:1a, 11), Thursday morning, from where He sent two of His disciples, Peter and John (Lk. 22:8) into Jerusalem with instructions for locating the reserved room. For security reasons (cf. Mk. 14:11;Jn 11:57) the participants were not disclosed and the location was also kept secret. A man carrying a jar of water would meet the two disciples. Normally only women carried water jars (men carried wineskins). This unusual eye-catching sight suggests that it was a prearranged signal. The two disciples were to follow this man to the right house. Tradition has it that the room where the Last Supper was eaten was in the home of John Mark (the author of the Gospel according to Mark) therefore the owner of the house (v. 14) may well have been Mark's father. The two disciples, having prepared the Passover (v.16), i.e. the lamb, the wine, the bitter herbs etc.) returned to Jesus.
The Parting Words of the Last Supper (vs. 17-21)

As proof that Judas' treachery did not take Jesus by surprise, He announced, during their participation of this meal that one of the apostles would betray Him (v. 18); that the person was one of those who were dipping bread with Him into the common bowl placed 
centrally on the table. Jesus added that although the traitor's treachery was foretold (Ps. 41:9) he (the traitor) was not thereby absolved from personal responsibility for his deed     (v. 21). The added words, one who was dipping bread into the dish with me, grieved the disciples deeply, for to eat with a person and then betray him was the height of treachery. One by one (even Judas cf. Mt. 26:25) they sought to clear themselves. The form of their question in Greek (lit. It is not I, is it?) expects a reassuring negative answer from Jesus. He did not, however, disclose the offender to the group.
The Institution of the Lord's Supper (vs. 22-25)

While they were eating (v. 18), apparently before the main part of the meal but after Judas had left (In. 13:30). Jesus took bread gave thanks to God, broke it and gave it to them with the words take it, this is my body. That is, it represented the fact that, shortly, this body would be broken (v. 22). Jesus, after the meal (cf.  1 Cor. 11:25) took the cup containing wine, gave thanks and offered it to them telling them it represented the blood which He would shed on the morrow. Jesus explained that His which is poured out for many, inaugurates a new covenant. This is a reference to His vicarious sacrificial death for mankind (cf. 10:45); just as sacrificial blood ratified the Old (Mosaic) Covenant at Sinai (cf. Ex. 24: 6-8), so Jesus' bloodshed at Calvary inaugurated the New Covenant (Jer. 31:31-34). This supper, Jesus added, would be the last occasion of His drinking wine before doing so at the Messianic banquet of the future age (v. 25) in the kingdom of God.
Jesus' Prediction of the Disciples Desertion and Peter's Denial (vs. 26-31)

v. 26: The hymn they sang was most likely taken from Psalms 115-118, the Hallel, which were traditionally sung to conclude the Passover. After the group had sung the hymn, Jesus led out the disciples to the Mount of Olives where He had spent the previous nights (Lk. 21:37). Quoting Zechariah 13:7, He told them that they were about to become like a scattered flock of sheep when the shepherd is slaughtered. That is, their loyalty would collapse (v. 27) and they will flee in all directions.

Vs. 29-31: As before (cf. 8:32) Peter insisted that he was an exception - all the rest might fall away as Jesus predicted (v. 27) but he would not. He claimed greater allegiance to Jesus than the rest. Jesus told Peter that before the rooster crowed twice (i.e. before dawn) he would not only desert Him but actually disown (deny) Him three times (the "cockcrow" was a proverbial expression for early morning before sunrise, cf. 13:35).
The Agony in the Garden (vs. 32-42)
As a final preparation before the coming violent events, Jesus resorts to a quiet area just outside the eastern wall of Jerusalem for prayer. Two scenes that seem to dominate the passage here are:
Jesus' obedience to God in spite of His dread in the knowledge of what is to follow.
The disciples continued failure to sense how important the moment at hand was.

Jesus and His eleven disciples came to Gethsemane, and here He told them to sit down 
near the entrance and wait, i.e. "until I have prayed". Then He selected Peter, James and John to go along with him. In the "garden" Jesus became noticeably distressed and troubled. He prayed aloud with great emotion (Heb. 5:7) prostrating Himself on the ground (cf. Mt. 26:39, Lk. 22:41). His request was that if possible the hour might pass from Him (vs. 35-36). We shall never know exactly what this cup was from which Jesus shrank in such horror. It was certainly more than physical suffering, otherwise many a martyr has since shown greater courage than His. We may say that it was the agony to His sinless soul being "made sin" (2 Cor. 5: 21) and exposed to the Divine judgment of sin.

In other words, this "cup" was the alienation Jesus knew would occur when separated from God the Father, at the cross (Heb. 5:7-9). The sinless son of God took on our sins and was separated in that moment from the Father.

The three disciples, however, soon fell asleep (v. 37), sleeping in the face of Jesus' agony, as they had slept in the presence of His glory at the Transfiguration (Lk. 9:32). Having found them sleeping on three occasions (vs. 40-41), he woke them up finally, and said to them ("enough") (i.e. enough of sleeping). Then He announced that the hour has come. The son of man was about to be betrayed into the hands of sinners. Instead of fleeing, Jesus and the three disciples (no doubt now joined by the other eight) advanced to meet Judas.
Jesus' Betrayal and Arrest and the Disciples' Desertion (vs. 43-52)

While Jesus was still speaking to the disciples Judas, who had left earlier On. 13:30) and had established contact with the servants of the chief priests, came with a crowd of Roman soldiers (cf. In. 18:12) armed with swords and clubs (Lk. 22:32). Judas had told them that the person to be arrested was the one whom he would Kiss (v. 44). He did this in order to guard against the possibility of their arresting the wrong person in the dark. For a disciple to greet his teacher as "Rabbi" (v. 45), and kiss him, was a common practice; but Judas, contemptibly, used these tokens of love as an instrument of betrayal. When Jesus was seized (v. 40), one of His disciples (Peter, In. 18:10, who apparently was carrying one of the "two swords" mentioned in Lk. 22:38) attempted to fight back and succeeded in cutting someone's ear (v. 47). This man is identified as a servant of the high priest, Malchus (Jn. 18:10). Luke tells us that Jesus restored the severed ear (cf. 22:51), after having condemned Peter's act of violence.

Vs. 51-52: This unusual episode, unique to Mark, supplements verse 50 emphasizing the fact that all fled, leaving Jesus completely forsaken. A certain young man was following (v. 51). No hint is given of the identity of the young man. Because of that, and of the fact that this appears on the surface such a trivial and pointless episode to relate in the middle of such a solemn story, it has been plausibly suggested that Mark is here placing on record how he personally figured in this scene. If so, and if he was the son of the house owner (vs. 14-15, cf. Acts 12:12) that night's events may have occurred as follows: After Jesus and His disciples left Mark's father's house after the Passover, Mark removed his outer cloak (cf. Mk. 13:16) and went to bed wrapped in a linen sleeping garment (lit. "cloth"). Shortly afterward a servant may have aroused him with the news about Judas' treachery since Judas and the arresting force had come there looking for Jesus. Without stopping to dress Mark rushed to Gethsemane perhaps to warn Jesus, who had already been arrested when Mark arrived. After all the disciples fled, Mark was following Jesus and His captors into the city. On catching up with Jesus and His captors, he was himself assaulted, but escaped, though with the loss of his sleeping garment in someone's hands. So no one remained with Jesus - not even the courageous young man who intended to follow Him.
Jesus' Trials before the Sanhedrin and Pilate (14: 53-15:20)

14:53-65: This trial by the Sanhedrin - the Jewish Supreme Court - had two phases. A small group met at night (Jn. 18:12-24) and then the full Council met at daybreak (Lk. 22:66-71). They tried Jesus for religious offences such as calling himself the Son of God, which according to Law, was blasphemy. The trial was obviously fixed, because these religious leaders had already decided to kill Jesus (Lk. 22:2).

Vs. 55-56: The Sanhedrin began their deliberations by seeking evidence against Jesus in order to justify a death sentence but they found none. Many witnesses testified falsely against Jesus, but their testimonies did not corroborate. In Jewish trials the witnesses served as the prosecution, giving their testimonies separately. Convicting a person for a crime, the Mosaic Law required precise agreement in the testimony of at least two witnesses (Num. 35:30; Dt. 17:6; 19:15).
V.58: "We heard Him say I will destroy this temple. . ."

This claim about which the false witnesses finally agreed twisted Jesus' actual words. He did not say "I will destroy this Temple," He said "Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up" (Jn. 2:19). Jesus was not talking about Herod's Temple, but about His own death and resurrection.

Vs. 61-64: To the first accusation of destroying the Temple, Jesus gave no response because the evidence itself was confusing and erroneous. Not answering was wiser than trying to clarify the fabricated accusations. But if Jesus had refused to answer the second question, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" by the high priest, it could have been taken as a denial of His mission. Instead, His answer predicted a powerful role- reversal. Sitting at the right hand of God meant He would come to judge them and they would be answering questions (Ps. 110:1; Rev. 20:11-13). By tearing his clothes, the high priest showed that he regarded Jesus' bold declaration as blasphemy. This symbolic expression of horror and indignation was required of the high priest whenever he heard blasphemy. His reaction also expressed relief since Jesus' self-incriminating answer removed the need for more witnesses. Without further investigation the high priest called for a verdict from the v Sanhedrin. Since there were no objections they all condemned Him (cf. Mk. 10:33) as worthy of death. Thereafter, some Sanhedrin members showed their contempt through mockery and physical abuse (v. 58), spat at Him in the face - an act of gross personal insult (cf. Num. 12:14, Dt.25: 9, Job 30: 10; Is. 50:6). On account of His messianic claims they blindfolded Him, struck Him with their fists and demanded that He prophesy who hit Him.
Peter's Denial of Jesus (vs. 66-72)

Caiaphas' house, where Jesus was tried (v. 53), was part of a huge palace with several courtyards. John was apparently acquainted with the high priest and some of his servants, and he was let into the courtyard along with Peter On. 18: 15-16). One of the servant girls of the High Priest had previously seen Peter in Jesus' company; but Peter denied both to her and twice to those standing around (vs.66-70) that he had ever been associated with Jesus, and on the final occasion calling down curses on himself. Peter's denial was the strongest denial he could think of by denying with oath that he did not know Jesus. He said in effect "May God strike me dead if am lying".

V. 72: Peter's third denial in less than two hours was immediately punctuated by the cock's second crowing. This time he suddenly remembered Jesus' prediction. Peter also saw Jesus looking down at him (Lk. 22:61). He became overwhelmed and broke down weeping bitterly.

In contrast with Judas (Mt. 27: 3-5) Peter's remorse opened the way for repentance and a reaffirmation of his loyalty to Jesus as the risen Lord (cf. Mk. 16:7; Jn. 21: 15-19). Peter had faith in Jesus that could be renewed, but Judas did not.

blocks.text: Jesus Stands Trial before Pilate (vs. 1-15)

V. 1: Jesus is being tried by Pilate, a Roman governor for the following reason: During this period, the Romans had taken away the Jews' right to inflict capital punishment, therefore in order for Jesus to be condemned to death, He had to be sentenced by a Roman Leader. More important, the Jewish leaders wanted Jesus executed on a cross, a method of crucifixion they believed brought a curse from God, (cf. Dt. 21:23). They hoped to persuade the people that Jesus was cursed, not blessed by God.

Vs. 3-4: The Jews had to fabricate new accusations against Jesus when they brought Him before Pilate. The charge of blasphemy was a religious crime and would mean nothing to Pilate, the Roman governor, so they accused Jesus of three other non-religious crimes:
encouraging the people not to pay taxes to Rome;
claiming He was a king;
causing riots all over the countryside.
Tax evasion, treason, and terrorism - all of these would be cause for Pilate's concern.

V.5: Jesus did not answer Pilate's questions, apparently because it would have been futile to answer and the time had come to give his life to save the world. Nothing would stop Him from completing the work He had come to earth to do (Is. 53: 7).

Vs. 7-11: While bringing down an uprising in Jerusalem, the Roman authorities had 
arrested Barabbas, a freedom fighter and a robber (Jn. 18:40), and murderer (v. 7).

The people approached Pilate's elevated judgment seat and asked him to grant the annual Passover amnesty (cf. v. 6). Many of them were probably supporters of Barabbas. Pilate began to discern that the real crime of Jesus was not hostility to Rome, which the Jews would not normally resent, but that He had been too popular and the priests were envious of Him. Pilate saw this as an opportunity to show his contempt for the Jews, especially their leaders. He offered to release to them the King of the Jews (cf. v. 2). Pilate hoped to achieve Jesus' release and in this way to undo the religious leaders' plan. But Pilate's plan did not work. The chief priests incited the emotional crowd to pressure him into releasing Barabbas instead of Jesus. Apparently they knew that the Sanhedrin had already condemned Jesus (cf. 14:64). Surprisingly, Pilate did not seem to know that the crowd would never side with him against their leaders (cf. Jn. 19:6-7).

Vs. 12-14: Since the crowd had rejected Pilate's offer and requested the release of Barabbas, he inquired about what they wanted done to Jesus. They said crucify Him! The punishment which awaited Barabbas was now thrust on Jesus. Pilate, though he believed Jesus was innocent (cf. v. 14), followed political expedience rather than justice. Wishing to satisfy the people lest they complain to the Emperor - thereby putting his position in jeopardy (cf. Jn. 19:12) - he released Barabbas to them. . . had Jesus flogged, and sentenced Him to death by crucifixion, (v. 15).
Mockery of Jesus by the Soldiers (vs. 16-20)

After the flogging the soldiers entertained themselves with "the king". Jesus was loaded with ludicrous honours - a mock crown, a mock scepter, a mock robe of office after which they pressed a crown of thorns on the head. They placed a staff in His hand. They then ridiculed Him with derisive greeting Hail (rejoice), king of the Jews. The soldiers eventually removed the mock royal attire and dressed Him in His own clothes. Then a four soldier execution squad (cf. Jn. 19:23) led Him outside the city to crucify Him.
Jesus' Crucifixion and the Crowd's Mockery (vs. 21-23)

Customarily a condemned man carried his own cross (here, a crossbeam weighing about 100 pounds) through the city streets out to the place of crucifixion. Jesus began to carry His (cf. Jn. 19: 17) but was so weak from the flogging that His strength gave out near the city gate. The soldiers randomly seized a passerby named Simon and forced him to carry the beam for the rest of the journey.

V. 24: "They. . . divided up His garments. . . casting lots for them. . .". The dice the soldiers threw was used to decide by chance, who would receive Jesus' clothing. The Roman soldiers had the right to take for themselves the clothing of those crucified. This act fulfilled the prophecy of Psalm 22:18.

V.26: A sign stating the condemned man's crime was often placed on a cross as a warning to the people. Since Jesus was never found guilty, the only accusation placed on his sign board was the "crime" of being king of the Jews.

V.27-28: Pilate had Jesus crucified between two robbers. They may have been convicted of treason at the same time as Jesus because they were familiar with His case (Lk. 23:12, Lk. 22:37). Jesus was again subjected to verbal abuse (cfMk.14: 65; 15:17-19). Passersby hurled insults at Him. They taunted Him for His alleged claim regarding the temple (cf. Mk. 14:58). If He could rebuild the temple in three days then surely He could save Himself from death by coming down from the cross. V. 32. Jesus promised one of the robbers that he would be with Him in paradise (cf. Lk. 23:39-43).
Jesus' Death and Accompanying Supernatural Events (vs. 33-41)

In this portion of the narrative Mark recorded five supernatural events that accompanied 
Jesus death: (a) darkness (v. 33). (b) Jesus' cry "My God ... " (v. 34), (c) Jesus' loud cry (v. 37)
(d) the temple curtain torn from top to bottom (v. 38); and (e) the Roman centurion's confession(v. 39).

V.33: Jesus hanged on the cross for three hours in the daylight (9am till noon) and then at the sixth hour (noon) total darkness engulfed the whole land (Palestine and environs) until the ninth hour (3 pm).

The darkness was probably a cosmic sign of God's judgment on human sin (cf. Is. 5:25-30; Amos 8:9-10; Micah 3:5-7; Zeph. 1: 14-15) which was placed on Jesus (cf. Isa. 53:5-6; 2 Cor. 5:21). The darkness visualized what Jesus' cry (v. 34) expressed. Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani (Aramaic words for Heb. Eli. Eli from Ps. 22:1), which means My God, My God, why have you forsaken me? This cry was more than a righteous sufferer affirming His faith that the Father would cause Him to triumph (contrast Ps. 22:1 with Ps. 22: 28). Jesus' cry combined (a) abandonment by the Father in a judicial (not relational) sense, and (b) a genuine affirmation of His relationship to the Father. Jesus was bearing the curse of sin and the Father's judgment on sin (cf. Dt. 21: 22-23; 2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 3:31). Jesus experienced the horror of separation, for the first time, from God, who cannot look on sin (cf. Hab. 1:13) and therefore hid His face. Jesus was offered some vinegar by the soldiers; and although seemingly so exhausted, uttered a loud cry (v. 37) after which He breathed His last.

A heavy veil hung in front of the Holy of Holies, a place reserved by God for Himself. Symbolically, the veil separated the Holy God from sinful mankind. The place was entered only once a year, on the Day of Atonement by the High Priest as he made a sacrifice to gain forgiveness for the sins of all people. When Jesus died, the veil was split in two, showing that Jesus' death for our sins had opened the way for us to approach our Holy God.
The Burial of Jesus (vs. 42-47)

The Sabbath began at sundown on Friday and ended at sundown on Saturday. Jesus died just a few hours before sundown on Friday. It was against Jewish law to do physical work or to travel on the Sabbath. It was also against Jewish law to let a dead body remain exposed overnight (Dt. 21:23). Joseph of Arimathea came to bury Jesus' body before the Sabbath began. If Jesus had died on the Sabbath when Joseph was unavailable, His body would have been taken down by the soldiers. And had the Roman soldiers taken Jesus' body, no Jew could have confirmed His death, and they could have disputed His resurrection.

Vs. 42: Joseph, an honoured member of the Sanhedrin, sealed Jesus' body in his own unused tomb hewn out of rock. He undoubtedly had servants help him to perform a befitting burial within a time span of two hours. Nicodemus, a fellow Sanhedrin member, joined in, apparently by prearrangement (19:39-40). The tomb was sealed i.e. shut with a circular flat stone that could be rolled down a sloping groove till it was securely in front of the entrance to keep out intruders. To roll it back would require the strength of several men.
V. 47: Two women, Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Jesus who had witnessed Jesus' death (v. 40), saw where Jesus was buried.

topics.title: The Women's Visit to the Sepulchre (vs. 1-8)

blocks.text: Vs. 1-2: The women who had witnessed Jesus' death and burial (cf. v. 40, 47) bought spices to anoint Jesus' body the next morning, i.e. Sunday. On their way they asked themselves a question as to who would roll away the stone from the tomb's entrance (v. 3). Apparently they were ignorant of the tomb having been sealed and guarded (Mt. 27:62- 66). They entered the tomb, and were astonished to see a young man, robed in white, sitting there. The young man was clearly an angel.

V. 6-7: Sensing the women's distress, the angel told them not to fear for, Jesus of Nazareth whom they sought, had risen. The angel added that they should rather notify the disciples and Peter to meet Jesus in Galilee as He had told them before (cf. 14:28). The women's encounter with the angel startled them so much that they fled from the tomb and temporarily said nothing to anyone (v. 8).

blocks.text: Nearly all (i. e. most) scholars believe that this section (verses 9-20) is not part of the original text of Mark. The evidence for this inference being their considerable dissimilarity from the rest of this Gospel both with regards to vocabulary and style, and especially their absence from the oldest and best manuscripts of the Gospel, namely Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Nevertheless it is not to be deduced that they are not part of the inspired Word of God.
Jesus' Appearance to Mary Magdalene and His Followers' Unbelief (vs. 9-11)

The attention is now turned to Mary Magdalene's return visit to the tomb while it was still early (v. 2) that same morning. Mary went and told the disciples that she had seen Jesus. They were mourning and weeping (v.10) over Jesus' death. On hearing that Jesus was alive and had been seen by Mary, the disciples refused to believe it (cf. Lk. 24:11).

Vs. 12-13: These verses summarize the story about the two Emmaus followers (Lk. 24:13-35) while they were walking to Emmaus (which is about seven miles - North West- from Jerusalem). Jesus appeared to them, apparently in a different form from that in which they had previously recognized Him as Jesus. When the two men finally realized who Jesus was, they rushed back to Jerusalem and reported the event to the rest of the disciples. Again the disciples did not believe it (v. 11). The disciples seemed to regard post-resurrection appearances at this stage as apparitions (cf. Lk. 24:37).

V. 14-15: Jesus later appeared to the eleven while they were eating. He rebuked them because they had refused to believe the testimony of eyewitnesses to His resurrection. He later gave them the great (missionary) Commission that they should "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to the whole creation" (i.e. to all people).

V.16: In response to their message, "whoever believes and is baptized" would be saved. (Note: V. 16 does not mean that baptism is a necessary requirement for salvation. The second half of the verse indicates by contrast that one who does not believe the gospel will be condemned. In other words baptism alone without faith does not save).

Vs.17-18: In fulfilling their commission (v. 15) believers would be given the ability to do miraculous things in Jesus' name. They would be given the power to perform miracles, also drive out demons, thereby demonstrating Jesus' victory over Satan. The apostles would speak in new tongues, presumably a reference to intelligible foreign languages not previously known to the speakers. This was demonstrated at Pentecost (cf. Acts 2:4-11) and later in the life of the early church (cf. Acts 10:46; 19:6; 1 Cor. 12:10; 14:1-24).

The final emphasis of Mark, however, is that the Lord Jesus is still present with His apostles, and confirming as authentic the message they preach by various signs and wonders (vs. 17 and 18; v. 20 cf. Heb. 2:3-4).

blocks.text: Authorship

There is no question about who the author of the Book of Acts is Luke, a medical officer, was a companion of Paul in his missionary endeavours. Paul refers to him as "Our dear friend Luke, the doctor" (Col. 4:14) and as a colleague (Philemon 24). He was a loyal friend of Paul who did not abandon him even during his imprisonment. (2 Tim 4:11). It can be inferred that he was Greek (Col. 4:10-14).

The prefaces to both the Gospel according to Luke and Acts refer to one Theophilus to whom the author is writing. The preface of Acts also refers to an earlier narrative to this Theophilus. It is therefore certain that Luke wrote both books. Some scholars even regard these two books as comprising a two-part work, and hence they are often referred to as Luke-Acts.
Place and Date of Authorship
It seems that Acts was written in Rome during the two years (AD 59-61) when Paul was a prisoner there.
Purpose

Many people consider Luke as a careful historian whose aim was to provide information 
about what he considered to be the most significant events in the early days of the church. 
He was also guided by his theological beliefs.

In terms of its historical context, Acts can be seen as a defence of the Christian faith to the Roman authorities or as an attempt to mediate as they were continuing to reject the Gospel message. Acts also has an evangelistic spread to all of the known world.
In terms of its theology, Acts gives guidance to the church on how to live until Jesus comes again and on how to transmit the gospel to people who had never seen Jesus in the flesh.

blocks.text: The Forty Days (vs. 1-5)

In the 40 days between His Resurrection and Ascension, Jesus made 10 recorded appearances to the disciples. (He later made a special appearance to Paul). This definitely would free their minds of any doubt as to His continued existence as a living person.

In those 40 days, He talked with them, ate with them, felt with their hands. In his actual crucified and glorified body also, He appeared and disappeared, through closed doors, out of nowhere, and back into nowhere. He climaxed all these with His disappearance in the clouds (Ascension).
Jesus Sets an Agenda for the Expansion of the Church The Ascension (vs. 6-11)
Jesus' last meeting with the disciples was in Jerusalem (1:4). From there He led them to Bethany where He ascended or was lifted up from their sight (Lk 24:50; cf. Acts 1:9).

"Lord is it at this time you are restoring the kingdom to Israel?" (v6). They had their minds still on political independence for their nation. In the Old Testament the out pouring of the Holy Spirit and the promised kingdom were closely associated (cf. Isa. 32:15-20; 44:3-5; Ez. 39: 28-29; Joel 2:28-31; Zech. 12:8-10). This is why when Jesus told them of the soon- coming Holy Spirit Baptism they immediately concluded that the restoration of the kingdom was near.
The Ascension is the withdrawal of Jesus from our vision but not from the world (Mt. 28:20).
The Return of the Disciples to Jerusalem (vs. 12-14)

The apostles were gathered upstairs for prayer. It was large enough to accommodate 120 people. The prayer (v. 14) may be specific prayer for the promise of the descent of the Holy Spirit (vs. 4-5). (v. 14) "Mary the mother of Jesus." NB: This is the New Testament's last mention of her; and the Apostles never gave a slightest hint of feeling the need of her mediation between them and Christ.
The Completion of the Apostolate: The Twelfth Apostle (vs. 15-26)
Vs. 23-26: Concerning the matter of a twelfth apostle, two important qualifications of the candidates are mentioned (vs. 21-22):
They must be well-known members of the apostolic band, associated with them during the ministry of Jesus.
ii) 	They must be witness to His resurrection.

Perhaps what v. 25 states is the saddest and most revealing verdict on Judas "He turned aside, to go to his own place". The place he had chosen for Himself and God confirmed Him in that dreadful choice.
Pentecost - The Birth of the Church

blocks.text: The Pouring Out of the Holy Spirit in the Early Church (vs.1-13)

Pentecost is the New Testament name for the Feast of Weeks, when the wheat harvest was celebrated. A One-Day festival during which special sacrifices were offered (Ex 23:16; Lev. 23:15-21; Dt. 16:9-12).

The significance of the descent of the Holy Spirit is that the church is now equipped for the task of witness and mission. This Pentecostal glossolalia (tongue speaking) is apparently different from the spiritual gift in 1 Corinthians 14. The 1 Corinthians account of "tongue speaking" is to be used in private and public worship, and with caution and restraint.
Peter's Speech (vs. 14-36)

The Holy Spirit's presence and power are traced to the fulfillment of O. T. prophecy (v. 16) "This is that which was spoken by the Prophet Joel" (Joel 2:26-32). The sermon has basically one theme: Jesus is the Messiah and Lord (v. 36).
Application of Peter's Sermon (vs.37-41)
"Brethren, what shall we do?" (v. 37c) If the Jews had crucified their Messiah and He was now exalted, what was left for them to do?

Peter's answer was forthright; "Repent". That is, "have a change of heart; reverse the direction of your life". On that day about three thousand persons believed and were baptized. This group of people immediately joined the fellowship of the believers i.e. the church.
The Description of the Church (vs. 42- 47)

This has been described as the church's birthday: "And they were continually devoting 
themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to 
prayer" (v. 42).

The church grew rapidly after its inception "And the Lord was adding to their number day 
by day those who were being saved" (v. 47b).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 2 (syllabus ¶1427)

blocks.text: The Healing of a Lame Man (vs. 1-10)
"The ninth hour" - Three in the afternoon was the hour of national prayer associated with the evening sacrifice. The apostles worshiped as Jews with no sense of a need to break away from the Temple.

Luke's purpose, however, in recording this incident of healing of a lame man is, apparently, to indicate the important consequences which followed, leading to severance of the church with Judaism, as Jesus had foretold (Mk. 2:21-22).

The details of the healing stress the hopeless lameness of the temple beggar and the material poverty of the apostles. Nevertheless, the "name" (the Name of Jesus Christ) was there, and by its power the man's feet and ankles were strengthened.
Peter's Second Speech: He Explains the Incident (vs. 11-26)

The healing (a noteworthy miracle) gave Peter a chance to deliver an address which explained the reason for the event, disclaiming all personal credit (v. 12) and attributing all to the glory of God. Peter's point is that it was Jesus whom the Jews had killed who had been glorified by God and was still active.

This passage focuses also on God and His purposes. In v. 24 Peter declares that the entire fabric of the Old Testament is a preparation for the events which have taken place concerning Jesus. God's redeeming purposes began with Abraham whose family is blessed in succeeding generations (v. 25).
The Persecution of the Church in Jerusalem

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 3 (syllabus ¶1448)

blocks.text: The Arrest of Peter and John (vs. 1-3)

The healing of the lame man and Peter's sermon made a great impression on the ordinary people, but it incurred the anger of the rulers. They were certainly alarmed at the growing 
popularity of Jesus' "Name". Peter and John were brought before a meeting of the Sanhedrin in order to make enquires as to what they were doing.

Peter's brief address re-echoed the essential facts concerning the Resurrection, emphasising that salvation was in Jesus alone. That, in fact, Jesus is the Christ and the Author of Messianic blessedness. In the face of the popular support of the ordinary people for the apostles, the rulers could not take any stern measures or action against them, except to warn them to stop speaking in the Name of Jesus, to which the apostles refused to obey.
The principal accusers were Sadducees who did not believe in a bodily resurrection and the existence of angels or spirits (Acts 23:8; cf. Lk. 20:27-40).
After one night in prison (vs. 5, 21). Peter and John were released. And, by an earthquake, God approved their boldness (4:29, 31).
Continued Growth of the Church (vs.32-35)
The arrest of Peter and John had little impact on the growth of the Church. The church kept growing. 3,000 converts the first day (2:41) Then 5000 (4:4). Then multitudes both men and women.
Purging and Persecution

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 4 (syllabus ¶1462)

blocks.text: The Sin of Ananias and Sapphira, purging from within (vs. 1-11)

This chapter shows a second example of the church's communal life being negative in character. The first insight into the communal life of the church was one of unity and generosity in which Barnabas is singled out for special mention (4:32-37). But here, we have a negative example concerning Ananias and Sapphira. Their sin was one of vain pretention and hypocrisy. Their unholy motive was discerned by Peter (v. 4), which had a startling effect (v. 5).
The continuing growth of the church (vs. 12-42)

The major significance of the first disciplinary case was that; "No one else dared join them, 
even though they were highly regarded by the people. Nevertheless more and more men 
believed in the Lord and were added to their number." This was a paradox.
The second detention and release of the apostles (vs. 17-20)

As the religious leaders became more uncomfortable with the growth of the Church, they caused the arrest of all the apostles and put them in prison. God supernaturally released them and commanded them by means of an angel to continue the public proclamation (in the temple courts, near the church's gathering place; cf. v. 12) of the whole message of this new life (v. 20), that is, the gospel.
In Acts this is the first of three miraculous jail releases (cf. Peter, 12:6-10; Paul and Silas, 16:26-27).

When they were eventually arraigned before the Sanhedrim, Peter boldly stood before them and told the story of Jesus in its impressive simplicity: IIGod sent Jesus to Israel as their Messiah; the Jewish leaders rejected Him and engineered His crucifixion; God stepped in, and reversed this judgment of condemnation by raising Him from the dead and installing Him as a life-giving saviour; we are eyewitnesses of these facts under the guidance and empowering of the Holy Spirit."
At Pentecost the reaction to Peter's Gospel call was penitent acceptance; here it was enraged hatred and refusal.

Gamaliel saved the day, temporarily, for the apostles (vs. 34-40). Gamaliel's policy speech picks up the leading point in their theology - that God rules the world by a wise providence which is over all. Everything is under divine control, and man is to obey God and leave the issues with him.

Vs. 34-42: The venerated Gamaliel, a Pharisee and a teacher, influenced the Sanhedrin not to oppose the apostles. He spoke not from sympathy for the church, but from insight into God's sovereign working on earth (cf. v. 39).

Gamaliel said or reminded them that two notable uprisings had already proved abortive. Therefore, he went on, the new movement should be allowed to work itself out; if it is not of God, it is bound to fail, as did the Messianic rebellions of Theudas and Judas the Galilean. If God is really in it, no human opposition can break it.

Not considering it adequate simply to admonish the apostles, the rulers had them flogged and ordered them not to speak in the "name" of Jesus. In spite of the flogging, which was apparently severe, the apostles left the Sanhedrin rejoicing. The apostles felt honoured having suffered disgrace for the "name" (on the "name" see vs. 40-41 cf. 1Pet. 4:14,16).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 5 (syllabus ¶1475)

blocks.text: The Administration of the early Church (vs. 1-7)
In the Jewish world tensions existed between the Grecian Jews (Hellenists) and the Aramaic-speaking Jews (Hebrews). Unfortunately, these strains were brought into the church.

The Greek-speaking Christians complained against the Hebrews that their widows were neglected in the distribution of supplies. The apostles accepted the criticism which, in reality, was directed against them but recognized that their first priority was the ministry of the word of God and prayer (v. 4).

They gave the Greek-speaking Christians (the Hellenists) a share in the administration: seven assistants were appointed, all being Hellenists, judging from their names (v. 5). They were commissioned with the full blessing of the Twelve (v. 6). The solution was timely and yielded positive results (v. 7)
The Martyrdom of Stephen (6:8-8:1a)

The most outstanding (prominent) member of the "seven" who were appointed to represent the Hellenists was Stephen. He became a key-figure in early Christian history. He had a grasp of the universal character of the Gospel. This explains the reason his speech is reported in detail. One other prominent member of the "seven" was Philip who carried the Gospel to Samaria and West Judea.

Stephen performed great wonders and signs among the people (v. 9). Besides being a wonder-worker, Stephen was also a skilled debater. His opponents could not stand up against his wisdom or the spirit by which he spoke (v. 10). To remove Stephen, the men of the synagogue persuaded people to make an accusation against him.

They charged him with blasphemy (v. 11): "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and against God". These words were sufficient to arouse the laity and leaders to arrest Stephen and accuse him before the Sanhedrin (vs. 12-14).

V. 15: "And fixing their gaze on him, all who were sitting in the council saw his face like 
the face of an angel."

This is exactly what happened to Moses' face when he came down from Mount Sinai with the Law (Ex. 34:29). Apparently God was showing that both Moses' ministry of the Law and Stephen's interpretation of it have His approval. In fact God's blessing on Stephen is evident throughout:
The grace and power of his ministry (v. 8)
His irresistible wisdom (v. 10)
His shining face (v. 15)
All these were tokens that the favour of God rested upon him.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 6 (syllabus ¶1501)

blocks.text: Stephen's Martyrdom (7:1-53)

Stephen's address before the Sanhedrin is sometimes considered as his defense (i.e., an answer to the legal charges brought against him); but it is clearly more of an apology - that is, a statement of teaching or a recital of Old Testament history, climaxing in a stinging rebuke for their murder of Jesus (vs. 51-53).
There are three chief ideas which Stephen's Old Testament story is designed to emphasize:
The Jewish people, throughout their long history have rebelled against God and His accredited messengers.

God does not live in, nor does He desire, a material and fixed shrine or temple. His presence is not confined to sacred sites, but accompanies His people, who are to be always a "pilgrim church" on earth.

A subsidiary theme: that the Jewish people have not only rebelled against God and their leaders, but have consistently rejected the messengers (saviours) whom God sent to them. The outstanding proof is to be seen in their recent rejection of their 
Messiah.
Other commentators, especially Bruce, suggest the following two themes as running through the speech.

Throughout their history God raised up men to act as deliverers of his people, but the Jews repeatedly rejected them and disobeyed the law given by God. After dealing with the establishment of the nation through God's call of Abraham and his promises to him (7:2-8), the speech deals with Joseph, who was rejected by his brothers but rescued by God (7:9-16), and then, at greater length, with Moses, who came to deliver the people but was rejected by them (7:25-48).

The Jews had the tabernacle in the wilderness and later the temple built by Solomon but they fell into idolatry (7:39-43) and made the mistake of thinking that God actually dwelt in the temple (7:44-50). These two themes are intermingled in the speech.
The Attack on Stephen (vs.S4-8:1a)
Stephen's indictment of unbelieving Jews amply illustrated in their history (vs. 51-53) touched his hearers on a tender spot. They became furious, gnashed their teeth at him, and stoned him to death.

Stephen's death looked more like a lynching than a judicial execution for blasphemy. There was no trial; and Jewish Law had an elaborate arrangement to safeguard the accused person. If he should recant or if a witness for the defence should suddenly appear on the scene, the stoning must be stopped. It is clear that no such precautions were made for Stephen's benefit.

The most impressionable person in this violent scene seem to have been Saul who looked after the witnesses' clothes. In other words he agreed that Stephen should be stoned. Paul never forgot this awful sight (Acts 22:20).
The Expansion of the Church to Judea & Samaria

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 7 (syllabus ¶1522)

blocks.text: The Persecution ofthe Church (vs. lb-40)
V. 1b: On that day indicates that the persecution of the church was signaled by the martyrdom of Stephen.

As a direct consequence of Stephen's speech and its sequel, an anti-Christian outbreak scattered the Jerusalem Church and led to the consequent spread of evangelism (8:4-40; 11:19-30). The conflict was leading to the fulfillment of the agenda set by Jesus.
The Gospel Spreads to Samaria (vs. 9-24)

As the disciples began to flee to the countryside of Judea and Samaria in order to escape persecution, they carried the Gospel message along. We have an account of Philip's ministry in Samaria and his interaction with one Simon a sorcerer who had feigned belief.

The apostles exercised their supervisory and leadership role when Peter and John were sent to confirm their faith. The church in Samaria was born when the apostles prayed for them and the Holy Spirit was poured on them in a similar fashion as it happened in Jerusalem. Again, Peter exercised the gift of discernment when he saw that Simon who had been following Philip was phony (cf. the Ananias and Sapphira incident).
The Conversion of an Ethiopian (vs. 25-40)

The church leaders now leave Samaria (v. 25) once their mission is achieved. The Holy Spirit, however, sends Philip on a lonely assignment on the Gaza road (v. 26). He was to go and evangelize an official (an eunuch) of an African queen. This would relay the Gospel to the heart of Africa.

The first consequence of Philip's evangelization was the eunuch's conversion. After his baptism, the Holy Spirit led Philip away. Whatever happened to the Ethiopian eunuch after that is unknown. Philip, however, found himself in Azotus where he proclaimed the gospel in the vicinity as well as Caesarea (vs. 10-11).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 8 (syllabus ¶1549)

blocks.text: The Conversion of Saul 9:1-19a

The conversion of Paul marked a significant turning point in the missionary agenda of the Church. From now till the end of chapter 12, we have an account of how Peter, the apparent leader of the apostles, became convinced of the universal nature of the Gospel. From there on, we have an account of Paul's mission to the rest of the world thus fulfilling Jesus' agenda for missions. Saul is the Hebrew name and Paul the Greek name of the same person.

Saul was determined to destroy the church; so having scattered the disciples (except the apostles) he set out for Damascus to search for the believers who had fled there and to bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem.

On the way, he encountered Jesus: "I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. . ." (vs. 4-6). The super-natural nature of what Saul saw and heard was clear. The travellers with him heard the sound (v. 7) but did not understand what Christ said (22:9). Only Saul was able to understand the meaning of what the voice said. Not much was revealed at that time to the future apostle (v. 6); but he was "a new man in Christ" (2 Cor. 5:7) from that moment.

Meanwhile a disciple in Damascus (Ananias) was prepared (by the Lord) to meet him, and heal his blindness and baptize him as a believer who would witness for Jesus before both Gentiles and Jews (v. 15). The price to be paid, however, would be costly (v. 16).

Vs.17-19a: "Brother Saul" (v. 17); Ananias identified with Saul by "placing his hands" on him. His apprehension of Saul was turned to love for Saul because of the Lord's directive. He prayed for him as he was bidden. The return of Saul's sight was indicated by falling away of some kind of film from his eyes.

Vs. 19b-22: Saul took his new vocation seriously as a man saved to serve. After only a few days with the believers in Damascus, Saul began to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the son of God. The Jews were astonished. The response was understandable, ("they were struck out of their senses" the Greek). He had gone to Damascus to persecute the 
church; and then ended up preaching Jesus. No wonder the Jews were baffled.
Conspiracies against Saul (vs. 23-31)

The first conspiracy to kill Saul was in Damascus. It is clear from 2Cor. 11:32-33 that this was a joint effort of the Jews and the governor under King Aretas, though the Jews were the prime movers. Saul's followers, aware that the Jews conspired to kill him, lowered him in a basket outside the wall through an opening since the city gates were guarded.

Having escaped assassination, he eventually returned to Jerusalem (vs. 26-29). He joined the work in Jerusalem, but the believers there refused to trust him. He finds an advocate in Barnabas (v. 27), who disabused the minds of the critics of their negative thoughts on the score that,
Saul had met the risen Lord who spoke to him.
Saul had boldly preached Christ, implying that he thereby placed his own safety at risk.
Paul's activity thereafter was among the Hellenists (i.e. Jews from the Diaspora resident in Jerusalem). It is clear therefore that he did not do missionary work in the country area of Judea.
V 30: As a result of the threat to his life, Saul was taken by friends and sent to his home town, Tarsus.

V 31: Saul now leaves the scene until he reappears in 11:25. An important point has, 
however, now been achieved in Luke's narrative. All the preparations have been made for 
the decisive step forward in the mission of the church to the Gentiles.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 9 (syllabus ¶1566)

topics.title: THE BEGINNING OF THE GENTILE MISSION - LEADERSHIP OF PETER (9:32-12:25)

blocks.text: Vs. 32-35: Peter is represented as travelling among the churches outside Jerusalem in order to give them apostolic teaching (cf. 2:42). His activity, however, was not confined to teaching alone, but also included evangelism. This brought him to Lydda. Here, Peter healed one Aeneas, a paralytic who had been bed-ridden for eight years. This led many to come to faith in Christ. The gospel was beginning to attract a wider audience, Gentiles in particular.

Vs. 36-38: While Peter was at Lydda, a well-beloved Christian woman (a disciple) in Joppa, called Dorcas, died. She was known for her help to the poor. (Lydda and Joppa are 12 miles apart.) The brethren in Lydda invited Peter. He came over and prayed for Dorcas, after which he commanded her to get up. To avoid "ceremonial defilement" (cf. Lev. 21:1; Num. 5:2; 9:6-10; 19:11), Peter, apparently, did not touch her until after God restored her to life.

As with the healing of Aeneas, the news of the miracle became widely known and this also led to many conversions. It was natural for Peter to stay on in the neighbourhood to follow up this mass movement. It is noteworthy to note that Peter stayed with a tanner (Simon), one engaged in a ceremonially and defiling occupation from the Jewish point of view.
