Conversion of Cornelius (10:1-11:18)

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.topic: 4.0 THE BEGINNING OF THE GENTILE MISSION - LEADERSHIP OF PETER (9:32-12:25)
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — THE BEGINNING OF THE GENTILE MISSION - LEADERSHIP OF PETER (9:32-12:25) (syllabus ¶1591)

blocks.text: By separate visions, Peter and Cornelius were prepared (by the Lord) for this momentous event- entry of Gentiles into the church. Cornelius, the Centurion, became one of the first Gentiles, after Pentecost, to hear the good news of Jesus Christ's forgiveness.

From the description of Cornelius as devout and God- fearing (v. 2), it can be inferred he was not a full-fledged proselyte to Judaism (he had not been circumcised (11:3) but he did worship Yahweh. Evidently he attended the synagogue and to the best of his knowledge and ability followed the Old Testament salvation (cf. 11:14).

Peter went to Caesarea where he met with Cornelius and his family as well as his friends; and responded to their invitation to speak to them by preaching the gospel to them. Even as he spoke the Holy Spirit fell upon the assembled company in a manner that reminded Peter of Pentecost. This made him realize also that, if God has accepted the Gentiles in this way, he should be prepared to accept them into the church by baptism.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 10 (syllabus ¶1600)

blocks.text: The Preparation of the Apostles for a Universal Gospel (vs. 1-18)

The accusation (vs. 1-3): When Peter returned to Jerusalem, he was called to account for his action in fellowship ping or eating with Gentiles. The reaction of the Jewish Christians shows that they still held to the Law of Moses (cf. 15:5; 21:20, Gal. 2:12). The primary problem was not his preaching to Gentiles but his eating with them (cf. Mk. 2:16; Lk. 15:2; Gal. 2:12) (Acts 10:9-16). Eating with someone is a mark of acceptance and fellowship (1 Cor. 5:11 cf. the vision of Peter eating a meal involved with all kinds of meat).

Peter's Answer (vs. 4-17): Luke has obviously taken pains to repeat the details of this incident - the accusation levelled against Peter and his defense because the action of the Judaistic believers was going to be a major factor in the ministry of Paul. Note that Peter's response did not rest on what he himself did, but on what God did. If God made no distinction between Jew and Gentile, how could he (Peter) do it.
Peter's Acquittal (v. 18): The Judaistic believers recognized that the conversion of the Gentiles was initiated by God Himself and that they should not stand in His way.
Two significant results ensued from Peter's response:
First, it preserved the unity of the body of Christ, the church.

Second, it brought a wedge between the true believers and temple-worshippers (Judaizers) in Jerusalem. Hitherto, the common Jewish people looked on Christians with favour (cf. 2:47, 5:13, 26), but soon thereafter the Jews opposed the church (12:2-3 cf. 12:11).
The Church in Antioch (vs. 19-30) - The Springboard for Missions to the Gentiles

The Confirmation of the Church (vs. 22-24): Those who had been scattered by the persecution in connection with Stephen came to Antioch and began to reach out to outsiders. They actively proselytized the Gentiles, the uncircumcised Greeks. The Jerusalem church heard of it. Convinced by Peter's story of Cornelius that the work was of God, they sent Barnabas to carry the blessing of the mother church to them. Antioch eventually became the springboard for mission to the Gentile world (13:1).
The choice of Barnabas has been described as a wise choice for several reasons:
He was a Levite, and like some of Christian ambassadors came from Cyprus (4:36; 11:20)
He was a generous person (4:31) and therefore thoughtful of others.
He was a gracious person, attested to by his nick name, "Son of encouragement" (4:36).
Luke's summary of his perception about Barnabas is that "he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith" (11:24).

Barnabas Introduces Paul to the Work at Antioch (vs. 25-26): The work in Antioch grew so much that Barnabas needed assistance. He could think of no other person better suited for the work than Paul. He went to Tarsus and brought him to Antioch. Barnabas and Paul ministered a full year in Antioch, teaching great numbers of people (NIV). The church continued to grow numerically (d. 2:41, 47; 4:4; 5:14; 6:1; 9:31; 11:21, 24).
Significantly, the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.
The charity of the church (vs. 27-30): There was a prophecy by one Agabus (from amongst the believers from Jerusalem) that a great famine would occur.

(Josephus reports that a great famine occurred in about AD 46. These were actually a series of severe famines that struck various sections of the Roman Empire during the reign of Emperor Claudius - AD 41-54.)

The prophecy encouraged the Christians in Antioch to make contribution of money to enable their brothers in Judea to buy food against the coming crisis. This was an act of Christian fellowship, in which the members of the church gave voluntarily according to their means. The collection was brought to the elders in Judea by Barnabas and Paul.

Note that, a certain kind of church governance and its structure was emerging and for the first time the leaders in Jerusalem were referred to as elders and received financial contributions from the emerging churches.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 11 (syllabus ¶1607)

blocks.text: The Persecution of the Church at Jerusalem (vs. 1-25)

Before describing the major missionary advance into the Gentile world, Luke here describes another serious setback in the work at Jerusalem among the Jews. James becomes the first member of the Twelve to be martyred and there was an attempt on the life of Peter.

Luke's narrative shows how Herod's plan was thwarted by the direct intervention of God. It also shows how God acts to bring retribution or judgment upon those who oppose His work and exalt themselves. Those who set themselves up against God ultimately perish.
a) 	The Death of James (vs. 1-2)

Vs 1-2. Herod mentioned here is Agrippa I. He was known for doing everything to win favour with the Jews, so he found it politically expedient to arrest Christians. James, brother of John, was the first of the Twelve to suffer martyrdom in the hands of "Herod the King" (v. 1). He attempted to execute Peter also. "Intending ... to bring him out before the people" (v. 4) implies an intended execution, after a public trial. Herod found that it would please the Jews to kill Peter, at least for two reasons. First, he was the leader of the Christians, and second, he had socialized with Gentiles (an association which was not acceptable to the Jews).

Note that these persecutions clearly show that the church was now an identifiable group 
which had become hated and despised by the Jews.
b) 	The Imprisonment and Escape of Peter (vs. 3-19)
Peter was under tight security, but the church was earnestly praying to God/or him (v. 5).

Here then were two communities, the world and the church arrayed against one another, each wielding an appropriate weapon. On the one side was the authority of Herod, the power of the world and the security of the prison. On the other side, the church turned to prayer, which is the only weapon the powerless possesses.
Vs. 7-10: God delivered Peter through an angel. Supernaturally, God caused the chains to fall off his wrists kept the guards asleep, and opened the Iron Gate.

Vs 12-17: Although the believers were praying earnestly (v5) for Peter's release, they did not believe Rhoda, the servant girl, when she reported that Peter was at the door. "You are out of your mind. It must be his angel": that was their reply. This statement implies a belief in personal angels (cf. Dan. 10:21; Mt. 18:10). F. F. Bruce says "the angel is here conceived of as a man's spiritual counterpart, capable of assuming his appearance and being mistaken for him".
c) 	The Death of Herod (vs. 18-25)

Vs 18-25: The news of Peter's "escape" from prison led to the ruthless execution of the guards. Herod then left to stay for a while in Caesarea. Nevertheless he soon met a fateful end (vs. 20-21). "On the appointed day", in verse 21, on which the people of Tyre and Sidon were to make a representation to the king (vs. 20-21) refers to a festival in honour of the Emperor. He was greeted as a god (v. 22).

A piece of secular history from Josephus adds: "He did not rebuke them nor did he repudiate their impious flattery': Josephus' story goes on "he saw an owl, which he recognized as a messenger of evil tidings, and a pang of grief pierced his heart."

Luke attributes this to a divine action (v. 23) stating he was eaten by worms and died. By contrast "the word of God grew and multiplied" (v. 24). In other words, in spite of opposition and persecution the Lord prospered the work of His church. With this progress report Luke has brought the section on the growth of the church in Jerusalem, Judea, & Samaria, following Jesus agenda, to a conclusion (cf. 2:47; 6:7; 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20; 28:30-31). Now the gospel message will be ready to go to Asia Minor (i.e. to the outermost parts of the world - the last stage in Jesus' agenda for the apostles).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 12 (syllabus ¶1637)

blocks.text: Concerning Paul's missionary work, E. Best, ('Acts 13:1-3', JTS II, 1960, pp344 - 348) a commentator wrote; "The importance of the present narrative is that it describes the first piece of planned "overseas mission" carried out by representatives of a particular church, rather than by solitary individuals, and begun by a deliberate church decision, inspired by the spirit, rather than somewhat more casually as a result of persecution". The details given by Luke show that he was aware he was describing a crucial event in the history of the church.

NB: (The Acts of the Apostles may conveniently be called the Acts of the Holy Spirit as well.) 
From now on, the Church at Antioch became the base of operation for Saul's ministry (v. l). Jerusalem was still the mother church, but the missionary church was Antioch. Peter was no longer the central figure, Saul had become the central figure. Antioch became Saul's headquarters for missionary work. From Antioch he started his missionary journeys, and to Antioch he returned to report.
a) 	First Missionary Journey: Details (vs. 4-12)

From Seleucia, the port of Antioch, then to Salamis, the chief town of Cyprus. Their next point of ministry was Paphos (100 miles south west of Salamis) v6. The major event here was the conversion of the pro-consul, Sergius Paulus, whiles the false prophet, Bar-Jesus, wanted to prevent this. This is the first time Luke uses the name Paul and thereafter consistently calls him so. NB: Paul is the Roman equivalent of Saul. He was born in Tarsus a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 21:39; 22:25). Both Saul and Paul were given at the time of his birth. Now he begins to use the name Paul as he finds himself in this Gentile environment.
b) 	Evangelism in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (vs. 13-52)
From here on, Barnabas slips into second place (contrast 12:25; 13:2 and 13:43). Barnabas' greatness is displayed by his willingness to let Paul be the leader.

Paul's selection of Pisidian Antioch was of strategic importance as a centre and base of apostolic ministry. This is because Antioch was a Roman Colony, and he would make full use of the synagogue as a sounding board from which his message might go out.

Jewish worship gave opportunity for any qualified visitor to expound the scriptures in the form of a "homily" (sermon). This explains the invitation of verse 15. Paul's speech was effective in convicting both Jews and proselytes in the synagogue, so much that great crowds came together the following week to hear more. Unfortunately, some other Jews were envious of Paul's success and therefore opposed the message.

Their rejection led Paul to pronounce openly the principle that he would now go to the Gentiles, which he did with significant results. Further opposition forced him to leave an infant church before he had time to consolidate his work.
John Mark's defection (v. 13b)
(v. 13) "Now Paul and his companions put out to sea (sailed) from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia, and John left them and returned to Jerusalem" (NAS).

What caused John Mark to desert is open to speculation. Did he resent the fact that Paul was now the leader, while his cousin Barnabas was relegated to second place? Or did he not want to go further than Cyprus? Or did he lose courage? Or was there some other reason? We are not told, but it is clear from 15:38 that Paul regarded the defection of Mark as a serious matter, while Barnabas was prepared to make allowances for him. Whatever the reason, Paul considered it a fault. (cf. 15:38) "but Paul did not think it wise to take him. . ."

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 13 (syllabus ¶1663)

blocks.text: Iconuim, Lystra and Derbe

(Vs. 1-6) The next city to be visited was Iconium where, in the same manner, the apostles entered the synagogue, and as a result of their preaching a large number, both Jews and Gentiles believed. The unbelievers drove them out of the city and they went to Lystra.

(Vs. 7-20a) In Lystra, about 20 miles south of Iconium, Paul healed a cripple, and the multitudes thought he was a god. Later they stoned him, and left him for dead. Lystra was the hometown of Timothy (16:1). It is possible Timothy witnessed the events (2 Tim. 3:11).
(20b-21a) In Derbe, about 30 miles south east of Lystra, they made many disciples. They then returned through Lystra, Iconium to Antioch.
The Return to Antioch (Vs.21-28)

Tarsus, Paul's home town was about 160 miles farther on from Derbe, nevertheless the two apostles retraced their steps in Asia Minor in order to strengthen and encourage the churches recently planted, in anticipation of many hardships and also to anticipate entry of the kingdom of God. In particular, the missionaries made sure that some kind of leadership was established in order to consolidate the groups for the future.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 14 (syllabus ¶1685)

blocks.text: This was probably the second most significant event in the missionary advance of the Gospel to the Gentiles. The first was the experience Peter went through concerning the conversion of the household of Cornelius and Peter's subsequent report to the Church in Jerusalem and their acceptance of the report.

This second event was crucial as it was to settle for the Gentiles the very critical question of whether one has to become a "Jew" before he could become a Christian or that God accepts us in Christ irrespective of our background.

The issue has very profound implication for the issue of culture in relation to our faith in Christ. For example, since the Gospel came to us from Europe, do we have to adopt the European "cultural clothing" that came with it or we can be truly African and be accepted by God in Christ?
The Proponents
Those who belonged to the party of the Pharisees presented their case as follows:
"The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses."
Peter: He spoke about the experience he went through in Cornelius' house and how the Gentiles also experienced the same outpouring of the Holy Spirit as had occurred to the Jews at Pentecost.
Barnabas and Paul: They spoke about "the miraculous signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them."

James: The brother of Jesus had become an important person among the elders in the 
Church at Jerusalem. Though the Lord's brothers did not believe in him, after the resurrection, they called him Lord. James speech clarified the position of the Church on the issue and his proposals were accepted.
The Major Conclusions

"It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" - This means that the conclusions arrived at 
were based on human reasoning and conviction by the Holy Spirit. Both agents are very important in knowing the will of God when taking decisions. The Major conclusions were:

The Gentiles were not to be circumcised like the Jews before they could become 
Christians.
So far as the Law of Moses is concerned they were to abstain from the following:
Food sacrificed to idols;
Eating of blood;
Eating animals whose blood has not been poured out.

The basis for this prohibition as suggested by James was that the Gentile Christians must 
be alert to the sensitivities of their Jewish brethren. Since both Jews and Gentiles may be 
worshipping together, they must have fellow-feeling for the Jews and not become careless 
about something which the Jews cared for most.

They were to abstain from sexual immorality - There were even shrine-prostitutes in some Gentile cities and this and similar blatant exhibition of immorality was to be avoided by the Gentile Christians.
The Emissaries

In order to authenticate the conclusions and directives as coming from the leadership of the Church in Jerusalem, two people, Judas and Silas, were sent along with Barnabas and Paul to deliver the message contained in the letter written by the apostles in Jerusalem.
The Response

In Antioch, the centre of Gentile missionary advance, when the letter was read and the 
message delivered, "The people were glad for its encouraging message."
Silas, who was one of those sent by the Council, stayed on in Antioch and later became a partner with Paul, replacing Barnabas on the second and Third Missionary journeys.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — THE JERUSALEM COUNCIL (CHAPTER 15:1-35) (syllabus ¶1697)

blocks.text: Contention between Paul and Barnabas (15:36-41)

After the satisfactory settlement of the Gentile question, Paul proposed a return trip to the places where they had previously evangelized and planted churches. Barnabas agreed to Paul's proposal, and suggested inclusion of John Mark. Paul disagreed with Barnabas because Mark had deserted them during their previous campaign. Obviously, Paul was so concerned for the mission that he was unwilling to take a doubtful partner. He felt Mark might do it again. There was sharp disagreement between the two, and they parted company. God certainly over-ruled this dissention for, two missionary journeys rather emerged from it. Barnabas went to Cyrus with Mark, and Paul went to Syria and Cilicia with Silas; ultimately reaching Europe. Paul, some time later, acknowledged the worth of Mark and regarded him as a colleague (CoI. 4:10; especially 2 Tim. 4:11, cf. 1 Pet. 5:12) Barnabas must be commended for living up to his name (Son of Encouragement) as he took on Mark and made him a useful servant to the Lord.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — THE SECOND MISSIONARY JOURNEY (15:36-18:22) (syllabus ¶1728)

blocks.text: First Stop: They went through Syria and Cilicia strengthening the churches (vs. 40- 41).
Second Stop: Derbe and Lystra - The Conscription of Timothy (16:1-5).
Timothy was the son of a Jewess who had also become a Christian. His father was a Greek.

Timothy had a good reputation (v 2); and because of that Paul wanted to take him along, probably as a helper just as Mark had been. There was a problem, however, because Timothy was uncircumcised, though the mother was a Jewess; and this would be offensive to the Jewish community. The mother might not have taken her Jewish responsibility seriously, or the son (Timothy) had remained so because of the father's influence. That Timothy was not circumcised was probably well known among the Jews in the area. Paul therefore had him circumcised. F. F. Bruce thinks, Paul simply "regularized Timothy's status" as a half-Jew in having him circumcised.
He was also guided by the decision of the Jerusalem Council, by being sensitive to issues that concerned the Jews, Timothy himself being a Jew.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — The Details Of Paul'S 2Nd Missionary 'Durney: (syllabus ¶1732)

blocks.text: Third Stop: The call from Macedonia (vs. 6-10)

The ministry of the Holy Spirit here is seen in both restraining (vs. 6-7) and constraining the missionaries (v 9). Paul was making his way towards Ephesus (v 6) but God stopped him. Then he started to move northward into Bithynia and again God stopped him (v 7). Finally, at Troas, God gave positive direction by means of a vision to Paul to go to Macedonia to help (apparently with the gospel outreach programme).
Philippi: The First Macedonian Church (vs.11-40)

The missionaries had a successful evangelism among the women associated with the Jewish faith. They were also persecuted in this community (which is predominantly Roman citizens) as the result of an exorcism performed by Paul (vs. 16-24). The Jewish population at Philippi must have been limited, because there was no synagogue there (v13).
Two Notable Conversions are described:

Vs. 13-15: Lydia, a seller of purple cloth. She hailed from Thyatira, a centre of dyeing trade. Evidently, she was doing business in Philippi, and had some attachment to the Jewish faith as a God-fearing woman, who was apparently rich.

Her conviction is what is described as "prevenient grace" in theology i.e. God took 
the initiative (went before), in her readiness to hear the word by pre-disposing her 
to give a ready acceptance to the gospel (v 14b).

When a demon-possed slave girl who had made her masters rich by her fortune- telling was exorcised by Paul, the team was arrested, falsely accused, tried and put behind bars. But there were a series of supernatural interventions which led to their release. The following miracles or events were involved:
Paul and Silas were thrown into prison, after severe flogging. They displayed their trust in God by praying and singing praises to Him all night.

In answer to the praying and singing, there suddenly occurred an earthquake which shook the prison, causing the doors to fly open and the chains securing the prisoners to the walls to be loosened. In this way, escape became possible. The point of the story is that the prisoners made no attempt to escape.
The jailer become convicted by the events and the two prisoners' reaction, and he asked the question which every convicted sinner must ask:

Vs. 31-34: "What must I do to be saved?" The answer they gave, "Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved," shows that all that is needed for justification is faith in the Lord Jesus. The jailer had asked what he should do. The answer was that he did not need to perform any work; he only needed to believe in Jesus who is the Lord.

Note: The words and your household mean those members of his house who were of 
sufficient age to believe would be saved (cf. 34) as they trusted Christ. Each member had 
to believe to be saved. It could also mean that as Joshua said on behalf of his family, the 
whole household including children could benefit from the covenant grace that was now 
available to them. It seems clear that the jailer sent Paul and Silas back to prison. What 
prompted the magistrates to change their minds is also not stated.

Vs. 34 -40: Paul's demand that the magistrates escort him and Silas out of prison appears 
to be vindictive. The news brought by the policemen would apparently put the magistrates in perplexity. This is because they knew that if an account of what had happened reached a higher authority they would be in trouble. They, therefore, made the best of a bad situation by personally coming out and conciliating the missionaries.

The escort demand by Paul and the upper hand he gained over the magistrates (rulers) would certainly spare the young church in Philippi from further harassment. The believers would be in a far more secure position before the officials.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 16 (syllabus ¶1742)

blocks.text: The Mission in Thessalonica
Thessalonica (vs. 1-9): The 2nd Macedonian Church

From Philippi Paul moved directly to Thessalonica, the capital city of Macedonia. Here he had successful mission in the Jewish synagogue. Testimony in the synagogue often took the form of discussion (vs. 2, 3). Paul won many converts among the Jews and the Gentile adherents, among whom were some highly-placed women (v. 4).

The three Sabbath days (v. 2) must refer to three Sabbaths, of unhindered testimony in the synagogue, which were followed by long periods of preaching in the house of his host, Jason, before the riot and Paul's flight. The riot was organized by the Judaizers who had become envious of Paul's success and hoped to use it to get Paul into trouble with the civil authorities.

Vs. 6-7: The brethren planned for Paul and Silas to escape and they forced their frustration on Jason. This church suffered from persecution by the Judaizers as can be seen from Paul's two letters to this church.
4th Stop: The Church in Berea (vs. 11-15)

On arriving at Berea, the missionaries again went first to the Jewish synagogue. These Jews, whom Luke calls the Bereans, were more open-minded than the Thessalonians. They received the message with great eagerness and "examined the Scriptures to see if what Paul said was true. Paul's approach to preaching actually encouraged people to investigate the scriptures for themselves. It was not surprising, therefore, that many people believed (v 12).
5th Stop: The Mission in Athens - Paul in Athens (vs. 16-34)
Background
Athens - the capital city of the district of Atlica in ancient times and the capital of modernGreece was named after the patron goddess Athena.

"In New Testament times, Athens could still boast of being one of the most famous centres of wisdom, architecture, and art. Though it had been surpassed economically by Corinth and intellectually by Alexandria, the city nevertheless maintained a great reputation."
Significant features of the city which could attract any visitor including Paul were the following:
The rocky hill Acropolis about 156m(516ft) high where many temples which were centres of worship stood.

West-northwest of the Acropolis was the Areopagus, which was the seat of Athens 
highest court of justice.

There was also the Agora, or the market place - a large open place surrounded by colonnades, temples, bazaars and government buildings. It was here that the Athenians spent their time discussing political issues and exchanging goods and services.
Philosophies: In additions to the temple worship, there were two schools of philosophy which reigned in Athens which Paul had to address in the Areopagus:

Epicureans: Founded by Epicurus (341-270BC) this philosophical school held a materialistic view of life. Death is the end of everything and therefore nothing is to be feared. Therefore, the pursuit of happiness (hedonism) was to be the goal of human existence. Therefore, Paul's message of divine judgement and resurrection delivered at the Areopagus was contrary to their beliefs.

Stoicism: Founded by Zeno of Citium (ca. 335-263 BC) who taught in a building called (Stoa Poikete - Gk) in the Agora, hence the name. In Stoicism, the primary focus is on how life is to be lived, with the attainment of virtue stressed above all. For the Stoics virtuous living was living in accordance with nature. Stoics were in Paul's audience at the Areopagus and some scholars contended that the Apostle himself was influenced by stoicism. They reflected in his letters which stressed self-sufficiency, contentment in all circumstances that nature or destiny brings to an individual and indifference to whether one is poor or wealthy, suffering or not suffering (cf. 2 Cor. 7:17, 20, 24 cf. 1 Tim 6:6-8).
Paul's message in Athens
In the synagogue were Jews and God-fearing Gentiles (v 4); and he certainly used his normal approach proving from the Old Testament Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah (vs 2-3).

In the market place or Areopagus ("Agora" (Greek), centre of civic life) where philosophers debated and presented their views. Paul's approach was different. With the background that has been given of Athens, it can be appreciated how Paul's message was geared towards moving the audience from what they knew to what they did not know. The key here is that the message was made relevant to their needs. The idol worshippers needed to move from the "Unknown God" to the "Known God" and the philosophers needed to know that there is a God who will judge all the affairs of men after death and to prove this He has raised Jesus from death. This pattern of preaching (making the message relevant to people's needs) is key to good preaching. Not many converts were won here as Paul appeared to be in transition and no church appeared to have been established here.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 17 (syllabus ¶1765)

blocks.text: 6th Stop: Paul in Corinth (vs. 1 -18)

Paul left Athens and went to Corinth (v. 1). The two cities though close (50 miles apart) were quite different. Athens was noted for its culture and learning, Corinth for its commerce and extravagance.

Corinth was marked by profligate and licentious living. It was a centre for the worship of Aphrodite, the goddess of love, who promoted immorality in the name of religion. This is borne out by Paul's discussion of the issue in his letters to the Corinthian church. Politically, Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia. Paul met Aquila, a Jew and his wife Priscilla in this city. He was a tentmaker, a trade which Paul also practiced. Corinth and Ephesus were the two most important cities visited by Paul in the course of his missionary work. He stayed in each for quite a considerable period (a year and half) in order to establish a church (vs. 10, 11) which would then evangelize the surrounding areas.
Paul turns to the Gentiles (vs. 4-11)

V. 4: Here, Paul began his work of evangelism in the synagogue as has been his custom (cf. 9:20, 13:5, 14; 1; 17:2, to. 17; 18:19; 19:8). Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia and joined him (v. 5). With their arrival, Paul devoted himself exclusively to preaching. Certain factors about Silas and Timothy's arrival encouraged Paul;
The two evidently brought financial aid from Macedonia (cf. 2 Cor. 11:9; Phil. 4:15); and this made possible a full-time ministry for him (v. 6b).
The good news about the steadfastness of the Thessalonians cheered up the apostle (cf. 1 Thess. 3:6-8). They were faithful and generous in the midst of persecution.

V. 9: Some threatening circumstances must have prompted the vision from the Lord. He might have expected reprisals from the Jews in view of his success in drawing away many of their adherents including their leader Crispus. The Lord urged him to keep on ministering in Corinth, assuring him that no harm would be done him.
Gallio Ignores the Jews (vs. 12-17)

Vs. 12-17: When Paul was drawn to court a critical decision was taken by the Romans. Gallio was a Roman proconsul, or governor of Achaia. Any judgment pronounced by him would establish legal precedent. Vs. 14-16: Here it is necessary to note that Judaism was a "licensed religion" under Roman Law. Christianity could take advantage of this protection as long as it sheltered itself under the tent of Judaism. The Jews must have complained that the Christians were not a division or sect of Judaism, but GaIlio refused to see it their way. To him Christianity came under the aegis of Judaism and therefore was not a matter to be settled in a civil court. This decision was crucial for it was tantamount to legitimatizing Christianity in the eyes of Roman Law.
The Conclusion of the Second Missionary Journey (vs. 19-22)

Paul's itinery took him from Corinth via Ephesus to Antioch. Paul was accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila, whose destination was Ephesus. Luke adds that when they reached Cenchrea Paul had his hair cut, for "he was keeping a vow".

Note: Jews made vows to God either in thankfulness for past blessings (such as Paul's 
safekeeping in Corinth) or as part of a petition for future blessing (such as safekeeping 
on Paul's impending journey). The present context inclines towards the former 
interpretation. There is an alternative view that Paul's action there marked the end of a 
vow previously taken. This view is usually rejected on the ground that vows could not 
be terminated outside Jerusalem. Paul left his companions, Priscilla and Aquila, in Ephesus while he continued his journey. Probably it was for them to continue the work while he went away, with the promise to return.
The End of the Second Missionary Journey (v. 22)
Paul moved on to Caesarea, went and greeted the church, and then went to Antioch. Thus he ended his second missionary journey.
The Ministry of Apollos in Ephesus (vs. 24-28)

Apollos is an abbreviated form of the name Apollonius. He was a native of Alexandria, an educated Jew well versed in the scriptures. It is not known where he became a Christian but there is every reason to suppose that his faith would have been developed at an early date in Alexandria.

(Alexandria was a centre of education and philosophy, and it was here that Philo, the Jewish philosopher, worked. Apollos may well have owed his eloquence and debating ability to his upbringing in Alexandria)

Paul's friends, Aquila and Priscilla, realized that Apollos' message was incomplete, so they invited him home for further instruction. God, in this way, raised up an outstanding witness to the truth who became a special blessing in Corinth. He became an important figure, apparently a leader, in the Corinthian church (1 Cor. 3:6), and in Ephesus (1 Cor. 16:12). Some years later he was still helping Paul in Crete (Titus 3:13).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 18 (syllabus ¶1798)

blocks.text: The Twelve Disciples at Ephesus (vs. 1-7)

"After spending some time in Antioch, Paul set out from there and travelled from place to place throughout the region of Galatia and Phrygias, strengthening all the disciples" (18:23). After Apollos had left Ephesus, Paul moved in. This time round, Paul stayed in Ephesus for about two years and carried on a very powerful ministry. Some of the significant events were the following:

In connection with the story of Apollos (19:1), Luke tells us how Paul found people in Ephesus who claimed to be Christians but lacked any experience of the Spirit. He instructed them, baptized them and laid hands on them, with the result that they spoke in tongues. In other words, they demonstrated manifest signs of the gift of the Holy Spirit This story has often been used as the basis for doctrines about the reception of gifts of the Spirit subsequent to conversion. This, however, has no real connection with these. Paul was dealing with an unusual situation which required special treatment.
The Twelve Disciples and the Baptism of the Holy Spirit

Vs. 3-4: Here, like Apollos (18:25) these Ephesian disciples knew only of John's baptism, a sign of repentance towards God (Mt. 3:2, 6, 8, 11; Mk. 1: 4 -5; Lk. 3:8). Paul told them that John pointed to Jesus Christ as the one in whom they should believe (Mt. 3: 11-12; Mk. 1: 7-8; Lk. 3:16-17).
Pre-Pentecostal baptism and Laying of hands (vs. 5-6)

Vs. 5: "baptized in the name of Jesus", It is only here in the New Testament that mention is made of anyone being re-baptized. It is clear that John's ministry was anticipatory; Christ is the fulfillment of all things.

The result of the laying on of hands was tongue speaking and prophesying by the Twelve disciples. The purpose of tongues in Acts was to address the issue of unbelief on the part of the Jews doubting acceptance of Gentiles by God. The chart below compares the usages of tongue-speaking in Acts and points to its purpose.
Speaking in Tongues in Acts

NB: As seen above (on the chart) the reception of the Holy Spirit in Acts does not follow any set patterns. In Acts 2:1-4 the Holy Spirit came after salvation. In Acts 10:44, the Holy Spirit came to believers before baptism. In Acts 19:6 He was manifested at the time of or after baptism. It is quite clear that these instances as seen in the Book of Acts cannot be used as a doctrinal source on how to receive the Holy Spirit.
Paul's work in Ephesus (vs. 8-22)

Paul did return to the Ephesus synagogue and spoke boldly for three months. Three months in a synagogue without a riot was something of a record for Paul. It appears the cosmopolitan nature of Ephesus caused the Jews there to be more tolerant.

In this synagogue, the topic for Paul's discussion was the kingdom of God which would obviously include the person and work of Christ (cf. 28:31). Paul's association with the synagogue was brought to an end by the opposition of some Jews who were hardened against the message. The strength of the opposition was such that Paul felt that he could no longer use the synagogue as a base for evangelism. He moved, therefore, to a neutral ground - a lecture hall belonging to Tyranus. Apparently Tyranus made his lecture hall available to travelling teachers. Paul ministered there (in Ephesus) for two years (v 10). According to Acts 20:31, however, he was there for three years (since it was customary to count part of a unit of time as whole, ". . .remembering that night and day for a period of three years" - Acts 20:31); his ministry was actually between two and three years.
Paul's ministry was so effective that the gospel spread throughout the province of Asia. During this time the churches at Colosse, Laodicea, and Hierapolis were founded (cf. Col.4:13).

Vs. 11-12: Here, Paul gained some notoriety as a worker of miracles (v. 11). This reputation induced some itinerant Jewish magicians to capitalize on his success, and try their hands at using the name of Jesus as a formula for exorcism (v. 13).

Christ's Victory over occultism (vs. 13-20) 
(cf. 8:9-14; 13:6-12; 16:16-18)

V. 13: Some Jewish exorcists who obviously used various kinds of clairvoyant powers tried to invoke Jesus' name over demon-possessed people. Apparently their action was an endevour to rival Paul's powers.

The misguided exorcists (cf. v. 14) thought that they could put the names of Jesus and Paul into their basket of tricks (cf. 8: 19) and use them for casting out demons. The first attempt was so disastrous that they ended up in bloodshed, having been severely beaten by the demon possessed people.

Vs. 17-20: Many Christians had been in sorcery and spiritism. After their open confession they burnt satanic literature (handbooks and compilation of invocations and formulae) despite the high market price of these materials. It also meant loss of their power. Again and again, however, emphasis is placed not on the miracle but on the name and the word which spread and grew in power (v. 20).
Paul's Future Plans, the Riot in Ephesus and Departure

Verses 21-22 are an intimation of Paul's future plans, including the expression of his desire, to visit Rome. First, however, he desired to visit the churches of Macedonia and Achaia. The purposes of this itinerary were (a) to confirm the churches and (b) to take up an offering for the saints in Jerusalem.

Paul sends two of his colleagues, Timothy and Erastus, ahead of him to Macedonia to prepare for his coming, while he stayed in Ephesus a little longer (v 22) because "a great door for effective work" had opened before him, and many were opposing him. "Both the opportunity and the opposition necessitated his continued presence in Ephesus." (John Stott)

Note: The words the Way in verse 23. Saul (Paul) referred to Christianity as "the Way", a 
term used only in Acts (19: 9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22).
The Reaction of Paganism in Ephesus (vs. 23-41)

Luke tells us that a riot arose because of 'the Way'. The root cause was neither doctrinal 
nor ethical, but economic. Demetrius and his colleague silver-smiths saw their business 
declining as more people became believers and accepted Paul's teaching that "man-made 
gods are no gods at all". The city clerk and other Christian leaders ensured that Paul was 
protected.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 19 (syllabus ¶1830)

blocks.text: Paul's journey from Ephesus to Miletus (vs.1-16)

After these events Paul left Ephesus, having spent the best part of three years there during his third missionary expedition. Second Corinthians 2:12-13, 7:5-7, gives further information on this segment.
A Change of Plan and Arrival in Jerusalem

It is noteworthy that in this final trip, Paul's intention was not to return to Antioch and report to the church but to go to Jerusalem and from there to go to Rome. Paul's plans included a return visit to Macedonia and Achaia before his journey to Jerusalem (19:21). His original plan would have been to go directly from Corinth to Palestine, going along the west coast of Asia, but in view of his fears of a Jewish plot against him, he resolved to return by the way he had come, i.e. through Macedonia, via Troas.
Events in Troas (vs. 7-16)

This section gives us an insight into the kind of worship services that were held by these churches. They were held on "the first day of the week" - Sunday. There was breaking of bread - the Eucharist, and a sermon was preached. On this occasion the service was held in the evening and dragged on till there was a fatal accident.

Luke, the physician, affirmed that Eutychus was picked dead after he had fallen from a third-story window. After the manner of Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings. 17: 21; 2 Kings 4: 34- 35), Paul embraced Eutychus and the young man came alive.
(NB: The name Eutychus, literary means "fortunate". The restoration proved to be true to his name).
Paul's Farewell Address at Miletus (vs. 17-38)

In this address, he recounted his ministry among them and the need for the leaders to follow his selfless leadership in taking care of the sheep. He spoke of his conviction that they were not likely to meet personally again as he travelled to Jerusalem. It was an emotional departure.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 20 (syllabus ¶1869)

blocks.text: Paul's journey to Jerusalem (vs. 1-16) and the warnings

Luke narrates a sea voyage from Miletus to Tyre. On their way they called at various ports of call (vs.1-3) until they reached Tyre. The persecution of the early church in Jerusalem had scattered the believers to Phoenicia (11:29).

The lengthy process of unloading the ship's cargo meant a delay (v. 4), but Paul redeemed the time by making acquaintance with the believers at Tyre. Here Paul received the first warning not to go to Jerusalem. "Through the spirit" means they had a revelation of what would happen to Paul at Jerusalem.
The Second Warning at Caesarea (vs. 4-14)

Paul's host here was Philip the evangelist He was one of the seven (cf. 6:1-5) who ministered to widows in Jerusalem. He had four unmarried daughters who had the gift of prophecy. Note that this spiritual gift, evident in the early church, was not limited to men (cf1Cor.11:5).

It is seen as surprising, however, that despite their prophetic powers, they did not prophesy about Paul's fate. Nevertheless, a prophet called Agabus, who came from Judea, dramatically illustrated how Paul would be bound in Jerusalem. (Prophets often symbolized their prediction: cf. 1Kgs 11:29-31; Isa. 20:2-4; Jer. 13:1-7; Ezek. 4.) Agabus' prophecy was a combination of act and spoken interpretation, very much in the style of Old Testament prophetic ministry. It gave rise to renewed appeals that Paul should spare himself bonds and imprisonment. Paul persisted in his willingness to suffer all things for the name of the Lord Jesus. Why did Paul not heed these warnings? We must note that the prophecies did not say Paul was not to go, they only spoke of the sufferings that he would undergo, and Paul was convinced that his plans were in the will of God.
Paul's Arrest in Jerusalem (vs. 15-36)
A day after their arrival, Paul and his companions had audience with James, the Lord's brother and head of the church at Jerusalem (cf 15:13-21), and with all the elders.
A very significant decision took place at this meeting which did not remove the fears of the elders but made matters worse, becoming a source of embarrassment.

To allay Jewish suspicions that Paul was advocating a wholesale rejection of the Mosaic 
Law and its relevance to Jews who became Christians, James and the elders suggested that Paul join in the purification rites of four men who had taken a vow and pay their expenses (vs. 22-24). This involved the presentation of an offering at the Temple. (The four men evidently had a Nazirite vow). This action of Paul was to demonstrate to the believers that Paul respected the Mosaic Law.

This action of Paul confirms one of the principles of his ministry which was to become like a Jew to win the Jews, to become like one under the Law to win those under it (1 Cor. 9:20). The solution proposed by the elders however, did not work!

Trophimus, a Gentile in his company was spotted by certain Asian Jews. These Jews drew conclusion that Paul had taken him into the most sacred and restricted part of the Temple to defile the Holy place (v 28). The crowd was incited and Paul was seized. The Roman troops came to the rescue and took Paul into protective custody (vs. 32-33). The fury of the crowd is seen both in their uncontrolled demonstration (v. 34) and their determination to get at Paul, who was carried into the safety of the barracks by the soldiers (v. 35).
Paul's Defence before the Mob (vs. 37-Chapter 22: 29)

The army commander's plan of taking Paul inside the barracks for interrogation was 
interrupted by Paul's request to speak to the people. When he began to speak, the people 
became surprisingly quiet. The reason was that he spoke Aramaic. Undoubtedly, the Jews at home were pleased if not surprised that a Jew of the Dispersion, as Paul was, could 
speak Aramaic as well as Greek. They, therefore, settled and listened (22:3-9). He also 
spoke of his mentor, Gamaliel, a respected member of the Sanhedrin.

(22:12-19) He also spoke of Ananias and his role in his (Paul's) conversion. Ananias, was 
a devout observer of the Law and highly respected by all the Jews living there. (These facts 
about Paul are not given in Acts 9.)

Vs. 14-16: The reference to "seeing Christ" The Righteous One (v. 14) was important 
because it qualified Paul to be an apostle (cf. 1 Cor. 9:1; 15:8). They listened to Paul quietly 
until he began to speak about his commission to the Gentiles.
Paul Protected by Roman Law (22:23-29)

In this episode, Roman Law twice came to Paul's aid. The soldiers heard the tumult and rescued him from lynching. Secondly, he was saved from flogging by the soldiers when he appealed to his Roman citizenship.

22:25-27: By Law a Roman citizen not proven guilty of a crime could not be flogged. He was actually being prepared for flogging when he divulged his Roman citizenship. Similarly in Philippi he had not revealed his Roman citizenship until after he had been beaten, imprisoned and put in stocks (Acts 16:37). Paul seems for some reason not to have wanted to take advantage of being a citizen except in some dire extremity. The commander, knowing he had put Paul in chains, was afraid that Rome would learn he had violated Roman Law.
Paul's Trial before the Sanhedrin (22:30-Chapter 23:10)

By this time the commander has understood that the accusations against Paul were Jewish (vs. 23-29), and the best way to unearth these was to have a hearing before the Sanhedrin. If the prisoner was found innocent he could be released, but if the charges were valid the case could be remitted to the procurator. Therefore Paul was arraigned before the Sanhedrin, with the high priest Ananias in the chair. Four significant things took place:
Paul and Ananias (23:1-5)

(a) 	Paul claimed all good conscience in his ministry (cf. 24:16, 1 Cor. 4:4) The high priest, Ananias, ordered his underlings to strike him on the mouth. (Josephus describes Ananias as insolent, hot-tempered, profane and greedy.)

Why the high priest was so enraged is not easily conceivable. It seems to Ananias 
that Paul was arrogant, even of guilty blasphemy.
(b) 	Paul, the Pharisees and the Sadducees (23:6-10)
Evidently Paul's protest divided the council (v7). At all events two things stand out in the sequel:

Paul addressed the Pharisees by appealing to a doctrine which they believed in as he, a Christian, did - the resurrection of the dead (denied by Sadducees, the high-priestly party, Acts 4:1-2; Mk. 12:8.) Therefore, he gained the support of this section of the Jewish legislature (v 9).

ii) 	Subsequently, his main enemies were the Sadducees (23:14). The division 
between the two was so intense that the army had to remove Paul to the barracks.
(c) 	Paul and the Lord Jesus (23:11)

The importance of this vision was not only in its comfort and encouragement (cf. 18:9-10) but also in the confirmation it gave of Paul's plans to go to Rome. The gospel of 
Christ would literary go from Jerusalem to Rome by means of the Apostle Paul. This 
was the fourth vision given Paul by the Lord (cf. 9:46; 16:9; 18:9-10).
(d) 	Paul rescued from a Jewish plot (23:17-35)

Fanatical Jews had taken an oath to kill Paul (v. 14) and sought the cooperation of the religious authority (v. 15). The conspiracy was discovered by Paul's nephew (vs. 16- 22). The following scene, set in the Roman garrison-house, is a drama of suspense and mystery, with hurried exchanges of information, quick decisions, and sworn secrecy (v.22).
(e) 	Lysia's letter (23:25-35)

The counter-plan, devised to foil the conspiracy was to secretly transfer Paul by night from Jerusalem to Caesarea (vs. 23-24). A formidable bodyguard of foot soldiers, cavalry, and light-armed troops was detailed to escort Paul, a prisoner, to Felix, the Roman procurator at Caesarea, the headquarters of Roman authority in Palestine. Caesarea would be a far more secure place, not subject to rioting as was Jerusalem. Paul was accompanied by a letter explaining the reason why he had been sent. It is the only secular letter in the New Testament.

When a prisoner was forwarded to a superior, the subordinate officer was required to accompany the subject with a written statement. This letter from Claudius Lysias presents the essentials of the case. Clearly, however, the letter had been designed to enhance the commander's own reputation for prompt and decisive action. He bent the truth in saying he rescued Paul (v 27) because he actually learnt from a subordinate that Paul was a Roman citizen (23:16). He also tactfully omitted an incident which had clearly embarrassed him, his preparing to have Paul flogged (22:24-26).
Paul Appears before Felix (24:1-27)

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — PAUL'S ARREST AND IMPRISONMENT (vs. 1-28:31) (syllabus ¶1885)

blocks.text:
In this section we look at Paul in the eyes of his enemies (v. 5) and also at how the earliest 
Christians had to contend with misrepresentation and implacable hate.
Vs. 5-8: The accusations were three:
Paul was a worldwide trouble maker, stirring up riots everywhere.
He was a leader of the Nazarene sect.
He attempted to desecrate the temple.

The first charge had political overtones because Rome desired to maintain order throughout its empire. The second charge was also concerned with the government because Tertullus (the accuser, v. 2) made it appear that Christianity was divorced from the Jewish religion. (Rome permitted Judaism as a legal religion, but it would not tolerate any new religions.) By describing Christianity as a "sect" of the Nazarenes, the attorney made Paul's faith appear to be cultic and bizarre.

The third charge of desecrating the temple also had political overtones because the Romans had given the Jews permission to execute any Gentile who went inside the barrier of the Temple (cf. 21:28. This was an offence punishable by death). At this point Tertullus modified the original charge made in 21:28. Paul was accused of bringing a Gentile (Trophimus from Ephesus) into the Temple courts; but here Paul is said to have tried (i.e. attempted) desecration. After the Jews had agreed to the veracity of their prosecuting attorney's charges, Paul was given an opportunity to answer.
Vs. 9-21: In his defence Paul shows that he is innocent of all political charges, and that the real issue between him and the Jews is a theological one (vs. 20-21).
The following are the rebuttals he made to the list of accusations which faced him:
His visit to Jerusalem was a recent event and the facts of the case should be known to all.
ii) 	His slanderers could not cite an instance when he instigated a riot in the city.

iii) 	He was and always had been a loyal Israelite (v 14) with a faith built on the Old 
Testatement revelation which looks beyond itself to the fulfillment of divine 
promises. In other words, Paul worshiped the God of Israel in full conformity with the Law and the Prophets (cf. 26:22; 28:23)
Adjournment of the Trial by Felix (vs. 24-27)

Evidently Felix was not prepared to settle the dispute there and then, so he deferred the case (vs. 22-23). His intention was clear; he was in a dilemma. He could not convict Paul, since Lysias had found no fault in him (23:29); so also the Sanhedrin (23:9), nor had Tertullus been able to substantiate his charges. On the other hand Felix was unwilling to release Paul because he hoped for a bribe (v. 26), and partly because he wanted to pacify the Jews. He left Paul in prison even though he knew Paul was innocent.
Felix eventually lost his position because he was cruelly intemperate in putting down a Jewish and Gentile conflict in Caesarea.
Paul's Defence before Festus

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 24 (syllabus ¶1945)

blocks.text: Vs. 1-12: Paul's fortunes seem to be unchanged. The Roman authorities were unwilling to decide his case; one motive for such slowness is given in 24:27. (Porcius Festus was Felix's successor. The change came about AD 58. A Roman magistrate could decide when a case would be called; often the delays were long, as here.) Next, the Jews sent a second deputation from Jerusalem with nothing new to say, for they repeated the unfounded charges as on the former occasion (v. 7). Paul simply denied any complicity (v. 8), after which came the question "Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem?" (v. 9). Paul was at crossroads here. If he said yes, he would play himself into the hands of his accusers, perhaps admitting that there was a case to answer and that they were competent to act in this matter. Besides, his safety was at stake, considering the assassination plan hatched by his enemies (v. 3). On the other hand, to refuse now might put Festus out of his way and thereby lose the protection of Roman custody. In his reply, therefore, Paul wisely used a technical phrase to which he was entitled as a citizen of the empire "I appeal to Caesar" (v. 11). This exercise of his privilege quashed all local proceedings, and transferred his case to the imperial court in Rome (v. 12). Divine purpose would, therefore, in a strange way be carried forward (23:11).
Festus Asks Agrippa's Advice (vs. 13-22)

A state visit of Herod, along with his sister Bernice, gave Festus a chance to mention Paul's case (vs. 13-14). It was not Festus' intention to get Paul re-tried (which was now beyond the powers of both Festus and Agrippa, since Paul had appealed directly to the emperor), but simply to get his views and thereby to have information for the dossier to be sent to the imperial court. Festus must have expected that a prisoner whom the Jews were so zealous to prosecute must have been charged with particularly grave crimes.

Festus had come to understand that the whole issue was ("about a certain dead man Jesus" (v. 19), which proves that the general debate over the resurrection of the dead (24:15, 21) turned upon the case of one particular resurrection - namely, that of the Messiah. This special application of a principle was more than the Pharisees could allow or believe; but at least the pagan Roman had the wit to see what Paul was continually talking about. In verses 23-27, it is clear that Luke was in close touch with these proceedings. His detailed descriptions prove that (v. 23).
Paul's defence before Agrippa

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 25 (syllabus ¶1967)

blocks.text: Paul had already made his defence to Festus (25:6-12) so now he directed his address to Agrippa. After a brief introduction (2-3) designed to draw attention to his defence before King Agrippa, whose Jewish ancestry would give him a special sympathy with Paul's case, the apostle opened up his defence in three parts.

The story of his past life (vs. 4-11): This may be summed up as "sincere, but wrong", Nevertheless the believers were asserting the Messiah's resurrection (i.e. resurrection message) v. 8, a special application of a belief cherished by all good Pharisees (vs. 6-7).

ii) 	The crisis of his conversion (12-15). He recounted his encounter with the living Lord. The encounter is seen as crisis, i.e. a judgment upon his past life and a new beginning, memorably stated in 2Cor.4:6; 5:17 as a new creation. In the darkness of his ignorance and folly, the light of God had shone (v13); and the real meaning of his persecution of the church was made known to him (v. 14-15). In attacking the Christians, Saul (Paul) was wounding Christ Himself.

iii) 	The terms of his commission (vs. 16-18). The life-work of Paul to the Gentiles is sketched, from the initial experience of personal knowledge of Christ (v. 16, "to the things which you have seen") to the establishing of Pauline churches (v. 18; ". . .those who have been sanctified by 'faith in me').

Agrippa was Herod Agrippa II, the grandson of Agrippa I. He is now asked to assist Festus. Bernice was his sister, living with him as his wife (Bernice was a woman of rare beauty. Later she became mistress to Emperor Vespasian and to Emperor Titus. Think of Paul making his defence before such a couple.) Agrippa was profoundly impressed (26:28). However, to Festus, the idea of a Resurrection from the Dead was so unthinkable that he cried out that Paul must be crazy (26:34).
Paul's Voyage and Shipwreck

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 26 (syllabus ¶1979)

blocks.text: The Beginning of the Voyage (vs. 1-12)

The vividness and accuracy of this narrative which describes Paul's sea voyage from Palestine to Italy has been commended by commentators, calling it "one of the most instructive documents for the knowledge of ancient seamanship". Soon after leaving Myra, they ran into fierce adverse winds, were driven off course, and, after many days, when all hope was gone, God appeared to Paul to assure him that He would make good His word (27:24). Paul had travelling companions all the way, one of them is named Aristarchus and at least one other, the narrator i.e. Luke. The use of the pronoun we points to him.

Having trans-shipped at Myra, the party sailed on a corn-ship bound for Italy. The next stage of the voyage was slow and difficult, owing to unfavourable winds and dangerous rocks. At Fair Havens (v. 8) Paul came forward with a suggestion but was ignored by the ship's captain.
Storm and Shipwreck (vs. 13-20)

The ship set out from Fair Havens and headed for Crete, only to be struck suddenly by the fearsome wind called the 'north-easter' (also known as Euraquilo – v. 14) which swept down from the Cretan mountains (v. 14) putting the ship out of control.

Vs. 18-26: The storm raged on, so the next day they threw the cargo overboard. So awesome was the storm that after many days, they gave up all hope of getting out of the situation alive. Paul's commanding position was evident. It was not the first time he had faced the perils of the storm (2 Cor. 11:26); and out of his past experience and faith in God he spoke words of cheer. Twice the apostle urged his shipmates (all 276 of them cf. 27:37) to keep up their courage (vs. 22, 25) Paul, even as a prisoner, did not hesitate to make known his faith in God.

Vs. 27-32: After two weeks in the storm the sailors finally sensed they were coming to some land. The water was becoming shallower (from 120 feet to 90 feet) as their soundings (measurement of the depth of water) showed. As they came into even shallower water they dropped four anchors, to brake the vessel (v. 29); and Paul once again showed his leadership in preventing a party of sailors from saving their own skin at the expense of the rest (vs. 30-32).

Vs. 33-35: Because of Paul's confidence in the Lord to keep them all safe (v. 24), he encouraged them to eat (vs. 33-34). He then took some bread, thanked God for it, broke it and started eating. This sounds like an observance of the Lord's Supper, but it wasn't. Most of those 276 people were not Christians. Rather it was a public practical expedient demonstration of eating in order to muster strength for the ordeal ahead.
The Shipwreck (vs. 39-44)

The shipwreck scene is dramatically painted in the remaining verses of the chapter (i.e. vs. 39-44). Seeing a bay with a sandy beach at dawn, they decided to try running the ship aground. The sailors severed the cables and left the anchors in the sea; at the same time unleashing the steering-paddles, and hoisting the foresail to catch the wind, they drove the ship on to the shore (v. 40).

V. 41: The ship struck a sandbar which the sailors had not seen. Because of the beating of 
the waves, the back of the ship was broken to pieces while the bow was stuck in the sand.

Vs. 42-44: Because soldiers were accountable with their own lives for any prisoners who escaped (cf. 12:19, 16:27) they planned to kill the prisoners to prevent any of them from swimming away and escaping. For soldiers this was simply a matter of self- preservation.

The centurion, however, wanted to spare Paul's life so he forestalled the soldiers' plan. Evidently, however, God was sovereignly at work to spare Paul for ministry at Rome and to guarantee the fulfillment of his promise (v. 24). In the cold rain (28:2) the passengers (soldiers and prisoners) and crewmen who could swim were urged to swim ashore, while the rest held onto the ship's debris.

As Paul had predicted, the ship was lost (27:22), they ran aground on an island (v. 26), and 
no one perished (v. 22).
Paul in Malta and on to Rome (28: 1-16)

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 27 (syllabus ¶1990)

blocks.text: The Sojourn at Malta (vs. 1-10)

The island on which the sailors were shipwrecked was Malta - a Phoenician word, which by a strange coincidence, means "escape". The islanders showed the shipwrecked seafarers unusual kindness by building a fire in the cold and rain of the early morning (v. 2). Paul played his part by gathering "a bundle of sticks" out of which emerged a viper, dislodged by the heat. Luke does not explicitly say that Paul was bitten, although perhaps his statements that the snake fastened itself on his hand (v. 3) and was hanging from his hand (v. 4) are meant to imply this. Apparently the islanders took it for granted that Paul had been bitten. The Maltese were superstitious, and kept changing their mind about Paul in relation to things that happened to Paul.

Vs. 7-10: One benefit of Paul's ministry was healing of Publius' father who had fever and 
dysentery, and the rest of the sick on the island.

The Summation of Service at Rome (vs. 11-31) 
Arrival in Rome (11-16)

V. l1: The ship-wrecked men spent the three months of winter on the island, (perhaps from mid-November to mid-February). In that time they saw another ship docked at the island. The ship had a carving of twin gods, namely, Castor and Pollux on it. These were supposed to be the heavenly twin sons of Zeus and Leda according to Greek mythology.

Vs. 12-14: The journey was carefully traced by Luke; from Malta to Syracus, Sicily; to Rhegium (Reggio today) of Italy; to Puteoli (Pozzuoli today, 152 miles south of Rome); and finally to Rome itself. At Puteoli there were already many Christians there (see his greetings in Romans 16 written three years before). This is significant because it shows that the gospel had already spread from Rome to the Italian Seaport. Certainly a church had been planted in Rome by Roman Jews who had gone to the Pentecost feast (2:10). Paul accepted an invitation of a Christian fellowship there to spend a week with them.
V. 16: Evidently, Paul, had by this time become a trusted prisoner; and was, therefore, allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him. He resided in a rented house (v. 30).
Paul and the Jews in Rome (vs. 17-31)

These closing verses (17, 24) speak of another rejection of the gospel and of Paul's taking the message to the Gentiles (v. 28). When he arrived in Rome, as usual, with the principle of speaking first with Jews, he called the Jewish leaders to meet with him, because he could not go to their synagogues.
In his presentation Paul made several significant points:
He was innocent of damaging the Jews or their customs (v. 17).
The Roman authorities in Judea thought he was innocent (v. 18).
His only option was to appeal to Caesar because the Jews refused to deal with him justly (v. 18 cf. 25:11).
This fourth point is a major one: he was not pressing charges against Israel; he only wanted to be acquitted (v. 19).
His primary objective in calling the leaders was to talk with them about the hope of Israel (v. 20).

The hope of Israel was more than the resurrection; it meant fulfillment of the Old Testament promises to Israel (cf. 26:6-7). Paul firmly believed Jesus is the Messiah of Israel who will return someday and establish Himself as the king of Israel and Lord of the nations (cf. 1:6).

As on many previous occasions, his address divided the people into two camps (v. 24 cf. 1 Cor. 1:18; 2 Cor. 2:15-16). As the unconvinced Jews left in disarray, Paul with prophetic insight applied the words of Isaiah (Is. 6:9-10). That obstinate refusal to believe results in calloused hearts, deafened ears, and spiritually blinded eyes. This had happened to Israel both in Isaiah's day and in Paul's as well (cf. Rom. 11:7-10).

While Paul was in Rome during this incarceration, the gospel was never hindered. Men 
may bind preachers, but the gospel cannot be chained. So the kingdom message went from 
Jew to Gentile and from Jerusalem to Rome.

It is important to take note of the factors that worked to bring to pass, Paul's decision of 
reaching Rome with the Gospel. Most important of all were:
The overruling hand of God which was obvious throughout.
The Roman system of governance which ensured the security and right of individuals.
Paul's knowledge and use of his civil rights.

Paul's knowledge of the Jewish religion and the fulfillment of the Jewish hope in the 
Messiah - Jesus Christ.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT TWO. THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 28 (syllabus ¶2023)

blocks.text: Paul addresses the issues of "nominalism" and "carnality" and also "true Christianity", in many of his letters. In his letter to the Galatians the local preacher has a mirror to look at himself/herself and his/her message. Here, Paul calls Christians from legalism/good deeds to grace. Note: Regeneration (new-birth) is the most important characteristic of a preacher (cf. Luke.6:39).
Problems in Galatia and Paul's Purpose of Writing
There was one basic problem disturbing the churches in Galatia, the teaching of Judaizers. That problem threatened the peace and spiritual welfare of the Christians in these churches on two fronts:
Firstly, Paul's gospel of justification by faith was threatened by the teaching that Christians, both Gentile and Jews, must keep Moses' law.
Secondly, Paul's personal authority as an apostle was attacked, a tactic used to undermine the authenticity of Paul's teachings.

Paul represented the chief obstacle to the success of the Judaizers. As the leader of the mission to the Gentiles, his voice carried great weight. Paul was as relentless in opposing the Judaizers as they were in pushing their teaching. He said "to them we did not yield submission even for a moment that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you" 
(Gal. 2:5).

In order to prevail, they would have to destroy his influence. Therefore they attacked him at his "Archilles heel". In other words they dealt with him in such a way that he would be so silenced as if he were dead or no more. Their strategy was this: because he was not one of the Twelve Apostles, his authority was not apostolic; that whatever he knew he got second-hand and got it garbled at that.

Paul saw clearly that the issues raised by the subversive activities of the Judaizers had wider implications than were realized by the dominant Jewish Christian element, and the rapidity with which the Galatians had departed from the freedom of the gospel served as goad to the apostle. "I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting Him who called you by the grace of Christ for a different gospel" (1:6).

Paul, therefore, wrote to defend his place and authority as a genuine apostle of Jesus Christ 
(Chaps. 1 and 2 primarily), which included establishing that his commission and gospel 
came directly from Jesus (Chapter l: 11 ff). Paul stated also that the gospel he preached had been vindicated before the other apostles (2: 1-14) d. 2: 2. He then wrote to correct the error of the Judaizers and to prove the truth of the gospel he preached (Chapters. 3-4). This includes a demonstration that justification is by faith and not by the law.

Paul's writing was also to teach about the spirit-controlled life that accompanies justification by faith (Chapters 5 & 6). His detractors seemed to say that his doctrine of grace led to licentiousness. In this last section (5: 1-6:10) Paul appeals to total inward moral change. It may be seen as Paul's ethics.

Key word: Faith 
Key Verse: 3:2
Theme: Justification by Faith

reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Introduction (syllabus ¶2084)

blocks.text:
1.1 	Greeting and Reproof 
The Greeting (vs. 1-5)

With a few words of salutation he introduces the atonement, a truth which he holds fast 
and has imparted to the Galatians, but now practically rejected by them.

After the opening greeting, Paul normally in his letters moves on to some prayer for the local church. He very often finds some point on which he can commend them. Then gradually he introduces the real purpose of the letter. On this occasion, however, there is no easy and gradual transition to the subject. Paul is too deeply moved for that. He states: "I am astonished that you are quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and turning to a different gospel" (RSV).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — CHAPTER 1 (syllabus ¶2106)

blocks.text: Was Paul taught the gospel he preaches, by man?
Revelation of Paul's Gospel (vs. 10-24)

Here, he proves that he received his gospel direct from our Lord Jesus Christ himself, in 
Arabia.
Paul's Protest (vs. 10-12)

Paul emphasizes the fact that he was not pleasing men. He states "If I were pleasing men I should not be a servant of Christ". In other words the gospel he preached was no human gospel. That he neither received it by human tradition, nor was he taught it: it came through an unveiling of Jesus Christ.
Paul's Life before His Knowledge of the Truth or His Salvation (vs. 13-14)

"For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God 
violently and tried to destroy it" (v. 13).

Paul is concerned to show that, before his experience on the road to Damascus, he certainly did not believe this gospel. Paul was in no way disposed to believe the gospel. He regarded it, as a Jew, as a blasphemy perhaps just as a pious Moslem would regard it today. Later, he was to sum this period of his life by describing himself thus, "as to zeal a persecutor of the church..." (Phil. 3:6).

reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Paul's Apostolic Authority (syllabus ¶2112)

blocks.text: What was Paul's relationship with Peter and the other apostles?
Here Paul shows how he had always resisted the Judaisers, even going to the length of openly correcting Peter.

Note: Whereas in Chapter 1, he emphasized his independence from the other apostles, he now 
demonstrated that there was a basic unity between himself and them.
