reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Contentions (vs. 1-15) (syllabus ¶2127)

topics.title: Defense and Exposition of Salvation and Sanctification by Faith Alone

blocks.text: Justification by faith alone (vs. 16-18)

Paul's opponents argued that since justification by faith eliminated the Law, it encouraged sinful living. That it is possible that a man could believe in Christ for salvation and then do as he pleased, having no need to do good works. Paul vigorously denied the charge, especially noting this made Christ the promoter of sin. "May it never be!"

On the contrary, if a believer would return to the Law after trusting in Christ alone for salvation, that Law would only demonstrate or make him a sinner and therefore a Law breaker. We see Peter here withdrawing from Gentile fellowship and as such returning to
the Law.

Paul argues that, as Jews, they (he and Peter) had experienced the inability of the Law to save. What the Law could not do, grace had done. Justification clearly therefore, is by faith, and faith alone. 	.
Divine union by faith (2:20-21)
Here Paul says faith not only leads us unto justification, but also into identification with Christ, in his death and resurrection, and union of the soul with the Lord.

Paul described the transformation in a person who has come to God by faith in Christ in 
terms of a death and a resurrection.

The Law demanded death for those who broke it, but Christ paid that death penalty for all 
sinners. In this way the Law killed him and those joined to him by faith, freeing them to live 
for God (cf. Rom. 7:4). Having been united to Christ, believers share in his death, burial and 
resurrection.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.topic: 2.2 Defense and Exposition of Salvation and Sanctification by Faith Alone
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Defense and Exposition of Salvation and Sanctification by Faith Alone (syllabus ¶2132)

topics.title: Reception of the Spirit by faith (vs. 1-22)

blocks.text: The Galatian Christians accepted what the Judaizers taught, that a more complete salvation and a greater sanctification can only be achieved if they would obey the Law. But Paul argued that to supplement the work of Christ is to supplant it. There can only be one way of salvation, and that is by faith in Christ alone.

"You foolish Galatians!" To embrace a doctrine which declared the death of Christ unnecessary was irrational (cf. 2:21). It would almost appear they had been bewitched, cast under some evil spell by a wicked influence. "This is the only thing I want to find out from you: did you receive the spirit by the works of the Law, or by hearing with faith?" (3:2). The implication here is that we are not only justified, we also receive the sanctifying Spirit; so the justified state leads to a state of sanctification, and that by faith.

God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3 does not mention the Holy Spirit. But Paul tells us here, by inspiration of God, that the gift of the Holy Spirit was included in God's unconditional covenant of salvation with Abraham. It was there in embryo. The Holy Spirit could not come as long as the Law was in the way. Christ had to die and be glorified before the Spirit could be given (John 16:7).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.topic: 3.1 Reception of the Spirit by faith (vs. 1-22)
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Reception of the Spirit by faith (vs. 1-22) (syllabus ¶2149)

blocks.text: Purpose of the Law (vs. 23-25)
The passage here tells us that not only are we justified by faith, but we also become the children of God through faith, and are enabled to realize our sonship by the indwelling spirit.

Commenting on the purpose of the Law, Paul used two figures of speech, likening the Law 
to a person and a child-custodian relationship.

"Before faith came" (v 23) means before the advent of faith in Jesus Christ (see v 22). Justifying faith was operative in the Old Testament but faith in the person and work of Christ did not come until he was revealed. Before that Israel was under the protective custody of the Law. God was in this way shielding his people from the evil heathen rites surrounding them. The Law served as a "teacher", a custodian, usually a slave whose job it was to insure the safe arrival of the child at school. This was the Law's function until Christ came and then people could now be justified by faith in him. The law was also the disciplinarian until Christ came.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Sonship through Faith (vs. 23-4:31) (syllabus ¶2157)

topics.title: An appeal not to turn to legalism (vs. 8-11)

blocks.text: Paul turned from a formal argument to a personal appeal for the Galatians not to return to a slavery similar to their former bondage in paganism.
Prior to conversion the Galatians, in their ignorance of the one true God, were in bondage to false gods such as Zeus and Hermes (cf. Acts 14:11-13).

But a great change took place and they came to know God (salvation from the perspective of man), or to be known by God (salvation from God's perspective). Yet having come to know the true God, the Galatians were turning back. Paul was amazed and dismayed. "But now that you have come to know God, or known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elemental spirits, whose slaves you want to be once more?" (4:9).

Reflecting concern for the Galatians, the apostle expressed the fear that his efforts would 
be in vain or wasted. "I am afraid I have labored over you in vain." (4: 11).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.topic: 4.1 An appeal not to turn to legalism (vs. 8-11)
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — An appeal not to turn to legalism (vs. 8-11) (syllabus ¶2165)

blocks.text: Christ leads into glorious freedom; there is the need to preserve it (vs. 1-12)

The last verse of chapter 4 describes the believer's position: he is free. This first verse of chapter 5 refers to his practice: he should live as a free man. Here in this chapter Paul illustrates the difference between the law and grace. The law would say "if you earn your freedom you will become free". But grace says "you have been made free at the tremendous cost of the death of Christ, now in gratitude to God, you should stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ has made you free".
Turning to Law ruins Grace (Vs. 1-2)
The Law commands but does not enable. Grace provides what the law demands, and then enables man to live a life consistent with his position by the power of the Holy Spirit.

C. H. Mackintosh has said "The Law demands strength from one who has none and curses him if he cannot display it. The Gospel gives strength to one who has none and blesses him in the exhibition of it."

In this chapter Paul tells us also that legalism (undue respect for the law and legal forms) makes Christ of no value. The Judaizers insisted on the necessity of Gentile believers being circumcised for salvation. Paul also insists that to depend on circumcision is to make Christ of no benefit. If observing a mere ritual could help, then Christ is unnecessary.
Legalism requires men to keep the whole Law (James 2:10). You cannot accept the easy commandments and reject the others.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Contrast between Law and Grace (syllabus ¶2175)

blocks.text: Paul teaches us how we can fulfill the just requirements of the law, not by our own strength, but by the saving grace which comes through faith in the atoning work of Christ.

By believing in Jesus, He fills us with His Holy Spirit and we live the Christian life in the (Spirit, controlled by God's Holy Spirit and no longer by our human (freshly) desires. The Christian who walks by the spirit (a life lived in the power of the Holy spirit) therefore does not manifest the true desires of the flesh (vs. 19-21); rather he bears the fruit of the spirit (vs. 22-26) and thus fulfills the just requirements of the law summed up in the commandment, "you shall love your neighbor as yourself' (v. 14). Note: all the virtues listed in verses 22 and 23 constitute one fruit (singular); so all the virtues must be manifested in all Christian because he/she walks by the spirit; he/she lives a life controlled by the Holy Spirit and in the power of the Holy Spirit.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Walk by the Spirit (vs. 16-25) (syllabus ¶2188)

blocks.text: Question: How do we relate to each other as Christians? We must deal compassionately and sympathetically with each other, especially the erring ones.

A believer is free from the Law of Moses and possesses liberty in the spirit but must fulfill the Law of Christ, and this can be done in the power of the Spirit. Such a life involves sacrificial service directed towards sinning Christians, burdened Christians, the pastor- teachers and all people.
Compassion towards the Christian who has sinned (vs. 2-3)

We must deal compassionately and sympathetically with each other, especially the erring 
ones. In this passage (Gal. 5:26 - 6:1-10) Paul gives some practical examples of what the 
spirit filled life is like, both negatively and positively. He shows us how a sinning believer is 
to be restored.

The fallen Christian here is a man who has committed an act of sin rather than one who is 
habitually sinful. Such a person is to be dealt with by spiritual Christians. A casual Christian 
might, by a hard, cold attitude, do more harm than good. These attitudes should be 
avoided.
Compassion towards the Pastor-teacher (vs. 6-9)

Vs. 7-8: A warning is given that God cannot be mocked. God's rule is; "a man reaps what he sows" and this rule is unchangeable. In other words, each sower decides what his harvest will be. If a person sows to please his sinful nature, that is, if he spends his money to indulge the flesh, he will reap a harvest that will fade into oblivion. On the other hand if he 
uses his funds to support the Lord's work, or sows to please the spirit, and promotes his 
own spiritual growth, he will reap a harvest that will last forever.

V. 9: Christians may become discouraged with spiritual sowing because the harvest is often long in coming. In the face of this reality, Paul charges his hearers (the Galatians) not to become weary or give up, because the harvest is sure. The reaping will come in God's proper time, which may be only in part in this life and in full in the life to come at the judgment seat of Christ.
Compassion towards all Men, especially Christians (v. 10)

Christians have a responsibility to do good to all people, when the occasion demands. When Jesus fed the 5000, both the saved and the unsaved participated. Therefore the benevolence of Christians should not be limited, except that fellow believers are to have the priority.
Illustration: In a home, family needs are met first, then those of the neighbors.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Service in Compassion and Faith (v. 1) (syllabus ¶2193)

blocks.text: As Paul brought this letter to a close, he again emphasized some of the great issues discussed throughout the epistle. The conclusion, therefore, contains both summary and final statement of the issues he felt so strongly about.
V. 11: At this point he decided to write the rest of the letter himself. He used large letters, probably to give a final emphatic thrust to his message.
The aim of the false teachers (vs. 11-13)

It is clear that the Judaizers wanted to attract or build up a large group of followers. They 
could do this by insisting that circumcision was necessary for salvation (Acts 15:1). People 
are often comfortable with observation of rites and ceremonies as long they are not 
required to change their habits. It would not be difficult today to build up a large church 
membership by lowering the standards. Paul sees through the insincerity of these false 
teachers and accuses them of seeking to avoid persecution for the cross. The cross means 
separation from evil. Therefore, men hate the glorious message of the cross, and persecute 
those who preach it.

Benediction (v.18) 
Grace not law.

The word which characterized Paul's gospel was grace. "Grace to you and peace from God 
our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (Gal. 1:3). It is still the theme with which he closes: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen" (6:18).
Concluding Observation
The Message of the Galatian Epistle for Today
Question: Has the problem of legalism adequately been addressed in Christianity?

On studying the book of Galatians one might conclude that Paul had defeated the teachers of legalism so effectively that the issue would never again trouble the church. History and experience, however, prove otherwise. We are still confronted with the teachings that baptism, confirmation or church membership are necessary for salvation; that the law is the believer's rule of life, (this includes keeping of the Sabbath) if they are to be saved at.

reference.chapter: UNIT THREE. GALATIANS
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — GALATIANS — Conclusion (vs. 11-18) (syllabus ¶2213)

blocks.text: Timothy: Who is He?

Timothy was Paul's spiritual child (1 Tim. 1:2; 2 Tim. 1:2). He was the son of a Greek father and a devout Jewish mother, Eunice (Acts 16:1; 2 Tim. 1:5). He was converted at the age of fifteen, during Paul's ministry at Lystra (d. 20:4).

From the days of his childhood Timothy had been instructed in the writings of the O'I' (2Tim. 3:15). Timothy became Paul's companion (Acts 16). A companionship of old and young can yield a fruitful ministry. Here the older man seems to have had the vigor and the younger, quiet, reserved and even timid. Their coming together was very helpful to both (Phil. 2:22).
Circumstances

On his release from his first imprisonment before he visited Spain (Rom. 15:24; Philem. v. 22). Paul probably visited Macedonia, Ephesus and other places. Not being able to stay long at Ephesus, he left Timothy to take charge of the work. This parting was a bitter moment to Timothy (1 Tim. 1:3; 2 Tim. 1:4). To encourage and instruct Timothy (who was sensitive, timid, and not strong 5:23) Paul wrote this letter to him from Corinth.
Character

The two letters to Timothy and the one to Titus are known as Pastoral Epistles. They were addressed to individuals and not to congregations. Paul was advanced in age (about 70 years) when he wrote the letters; consequently we have in them his farewell address to ministers and Christian workers. In them we see the mellow wisdom of old age. Christian workers have, for centuries, found these letters a source of encouragement and help.
The epistles are highly personal, practical, and unsystematic.
Analyses

The purpose of the epistle is clearly given in 1 Tim. 3:15, - how people ought to conduct themselves in God's household. The letter was written to instruct the young worker to be a good and effective leader (1 Tim 4:12). That Timothy should not let anyone "despise" his youth. Instead Timothy was to demonstrate his maturity by living a godly life, in speech and conduct, in love, in faith and in purity, i.e. moral cleanness.
Key phrase: How one ought to behave in the household of God
Key verse: 3:15

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FOUR. 1 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 1 TIMOTHY — Introduction (syllabus ¶2229)

blocks.text:
Paul's typical salutation includes an identification of himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus. 
In several of his other epistles he stresses his apostolic "calling" according to "the will of God" (1 Cor. 1:1; 2 Cor. 1:1; Eph. 1:1; Col. 1:1; 2 Tim. 1:1). Paul was often in the position of having to defend his authority which came from both God the Father and God the Son. Paul needed to establish his apostleship otherwise his message would be considered second-hand (d. Galatians 1:11- 2:21).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FOUR. 1 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 1 TIMOTHY — Opening Greeting (vs. 1-2) (syllabus ¶2250)

blocks.text: Doctrinal error is to be forbidden. False doctrine is not only untrue but also unprofitable. Pretensions to teaching the Law do not justify an ignorant use of it. Its lawful use agrees with the gospel, of which Paul himself has deep, personal experience. He charges Timothy to continue his Christian warfare.
What does Paul say about false teaching?

Doctrinal distortion and irrelevant theories must be abandoned. Such activities do not promote Christian faith and life. On the contrary they result in fruitless discussion and misuse of the Law. There is a right use of the Law which is in line with the gospel entrusted to Paul (vs. 3-11).

reference.chapter: UNIT FOUR. 1 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 1 TIMOTHY — Instructions Concerning False Teachers (vs. 3 -20) (syllabus ¶2255)

topics.title: Standards of the Church: What are they? (2:1-3:16)

blocks.text: There are certain patterns of conduct which should be observed. Public worship is considered first. Directions for prayer are here given by Paul with a theological reason. Paul further looks at the demeanor (social esteem) appropriate to Christian women. He defines their status. Paul next deals with the qualifications of bishops or pastoral supervisors as well as those of deacons and women. Finally he lays stress on right conduct in the church broadly (cf. 3:14 - 15)
Public Worship (vs. 1-15)

There are certain patterns of conduct which should be observed. Public worship is considered first. Concerning this, directions for prayer are outlined by Paul, with theological reason. He also addresses the demeanor (social conduct) appropriate to Christian women. He defines their status. Paul next deals with the qualifications of bishops or supervisors as well as those of deacons and women. Finally he stresses on right conduct in the church broadly (cf. 3:14-15).
Prayer (vs. 1-8)

Prayer of every kind is to be offered for all men, with intercession and thanksgiving. Rulers are specially mentioned because of their wide influence. The object of prayer is social peace and godly life, and certainly for their salvation. As in modern times, some in the Ephesian church were prepared to question the validity of prayer for the salvation of all men. Paul therefore defended his instructions by pointing out that such a prayer is good, and pleases God our Saviour.

One reason Paul gives for praying for rulers is "that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life, godly and respectful in every way." He thinks it is for our own good that the government should be stable and the country should be preserved from revolution, civil war, turmoil and anarchy.
Women (vs. 9-15)

Prayers for all men are followed with instructions that Christian women dress moderately and not extravagantly. In other words they should not emphasize the external but the internal. Instead of stressing external beauty according to the world's standards, Christian women should manifest a different set of values. They should adorn themselves with (lit. "by means of') good deeds. They should depend on their faithful service in the name of Christ to render them attractive to others.

Note: This was no plea for women to make themselves unattractive; it was simply an exhortation to reject the world's yardstick for measuring beauty and adopt heaven's standard 
(1 Sam. 16:7). One should expect nothing less from women who profess to worship God.

reference.topic: 2.1 Standards of the Church: What are they? (2:1-3:16)

topics.title: Qualifications Necessary for Spiritual Oversight or the Ministry

blocks.text: The seriousness with which Paul regarded the ministry is revealed in the detailed qualification required of those who were to be appointed to the office of bishop or deacon. He wanted to encourage respect for the congregation's leaders. Bishops must be men of integrity, sobriety and conscientiousness. Both bishop and deacon should be husband of one wife and a model of a family head.
Bishops (vs. 1-7)

The office of bishop is a noble one and the qualifications required are high and of permanent significance. The bishop must be a man of able mind and excellent character, socially adaptable and tactful, and able to teach and lead. In everything he must be above reproach, including marital and family relationships, deeply grounded in the faith and commanding the respect of all.
Deacons (vs. 8-13)

"Deacon" means "servant, helper" and refers to the bishops' assistant. Deacons take care of mundane (worldly contrasted with spiritual or heavenly) matters of church life, particularly the distribution of charity. Like the bishops, deacons must also be men of quality, even though their function in the congregation is significantly different. Deacons should be proved blameless through examination before entering office. Desirable characteristics are sincerity in speech and faith, sobriety and unselfishness. Their private life ought to manifest a true Christian home. Good service in the diaconate results in higher position and confidence, with consequent influence.
"Women" in verse 11 may imply a female order of deaconesses or may refer to deacons' wives, who were expected to help in the charitable work of their husbands.

Vs. 14-15 is a statement of the purpose of this letter (see the analyses in the introduction). 
Chapter 3 closes with the quotation of an early Christian hymn or creed, which traces the career of Christ from incarnation to ascension ("he was revealed in the flesh ... taken up in glory" 3:16) - See Commentary: Know the Bible, by Thomas Oseku-Afful.

topics.title: Threats to the Safety of the Church

blocks.text: Error and Apostasy (vs. 1-5)

Here Paul gives warning against false doctrine. The false teaching comprised two prohibitions: marriage and eating of certain foods. Paul's strong opposition to these practices is due to their dangerous implications. The apostle argues that prohibitions such as these are in conflict with the divine ordinance. The reason which Paul supplies is based on a general or fundamental principle concerning God's creation that what a good Creator creates must be good (cf. Gen. 1:31).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FOUR. 1 TIMOTHY
reference.topic: 4.1 Threats to the Safety of the Church
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 1 TIMOTHY — Threats to the Safety of the Church (syllabus ¶2293)

blocks.text: It is necessary that a good minister instructs the people in sound doctrine, which is the diet of his own soul. Superstition is to be avoided. In other words taboos should have no place in an intelligent Christian approach, in contrast to many systems of taboos in heathen cults (i.e. world religions).
Living on One's own Message (v. 6)

Paul here begins a personal directive to Timothy. That a good minister is not a theorizer. He teaches the apostolic doctrine which he has made his own both as nourishment by which to live and as standard by which to judge himself. "If you put these instructions before the brethren, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of the faith and of the doctrine which you have followed".
These instructions are primarily the contents of verses 1-5, though the earlier words of guidance lie in the background.
Avoiding Superstition (v. 7)

Apparently, the church was at this stage confronted with invented stories and untrue fables. Timothy is reminded of this "Have nothing to do with godless and silly myths. Train yourself in godliness" (v. 7).

It is clear that in this section, Paul is thinking of Christian service as a form of athletic contest. Paul often used athletic analogies to drive home the need for spiritual discipline (cf. 1 Cor. 9:24-27).

In the preceding verse, he has been speaking of the suitable diet for one who is serving Christ. That a Christian should be nourished in the words of faith and of the good doctrine. In this verse, however, he speaks of exercise that has godliness as its aim.
Self Training (vs. 8-10)

The apostle Paul is of the opinion that the minister's own spiritual life does not come 
automatically. He must train himself in spiritual exercises, since the prize for the good fight 
is both here and hereafter. "For while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in 
every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come" (v. 8) (RSV).
Example (vs. 11-12)

The injunctions here are more directly concerned with Timothy himself. There is to be a note of authority in Timothy's teaching. Paul's purpose is therefore to inspire him (being timid) to display firmness. Many of the Ephesian Christians, and especially the elders, were almost certainly of matured years; and as they had served under Paul, a veteran, it is obvious that some would look with disfavour and contempt on the youthful missionary, Timothy. As a counter-balance to contempt, Timothy would have to live in an exemplary manner. In this way it would become evident to the believers that in Christianity, authority is contingent upon character and not age.
Spiritual Ministry (vs. 13-16)

In the interim before Paul's arrival, Timothy was to concentrate on his ministerial duties. 
Paul exhorted him to attend to his public ministry as well as his private life. The public service or ministry's to consist of at least three ministerial essentials:

(i) 	Public Reading of Scripture (V. 13): Paul emphasizes the public reading of the word 
of God. It has always been the practice of God's people to read the Word of God 
aloud in the congregation (cf. Ex. 24:7; Dt. 31:11; Neh. 8: 7-8; Lk 4: 16; Acts 15: 21; 
Col. 4:16 etc.).

(ii) 	Preaching (V. 13): This is "exhortation". The term includes exposition and application of the passages read. It suggests preaching to Christians. Preaching to non-Christians is evangelism rather than exhortation, though in actual fact it is certainly "persuasion with authority."

(iii) 	Teaching (V. 16): This may refer primarily to a more catechetical (catechism) 
treatment of the truth of the Christian faith (cf. 1 Tim. 1:10; 1 Tim. 4:6 etc).

V. 14: Here we are not told exactly what gift had been given to Timothy, whether he was an evangelist, a pastor or a teacher. The general tenor of the epistles would lead us to think that he was a pastor-teacher.

The chapter opened with a description of the false teachers who were causing havoc among the people of God. Paul is telling Timothy that by faithful adherence to a godly life and to the Word of God, he will save himself from these false teachings and he will also save his hearers from them as well.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FOUR. 1 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 1 TIMOTHY — Countermeasures (vs. 6-16) (syllabus ¶2297)

topics.title: Instructions Concerning Various Groups in the Church (vs. 1-6:10)

blocks.text: From a further warning against false doctrine (chapter 4) Paul turned to advice on how to relate effectively to individuals who make up various groups in the church.

Provision for widows is primarily a family responsibility, neglect of which is infidelity. Widows who are officially recognized by the church should bear the marks of piety as well as of age. Younger widows should not be enrolled, because of their tendency to a shallow and faithless life and partly because they should remarry and set up Christian households. The church must not be burdened unnecessarily if the family can help, so that its resources may be applied to widows in genuine need. Elders need honor and financial support.
Concerning Various Age-groups (vs. 1-2)
Paul's overall advice about how to treat various age-groups was that Timothy handles different people as he would members of his own family.

Timothy is not to rebuke an elder sharply but exhort or appeal to him as he would his own father. He should treat other young men as brothers. Older women were to receive all the respect Timothy would accord his own mother. Younger women were likewise to be treated as sisters. This would safeguard him from reproach.
Concerning Widows (vs. 3-16)

In this passage, Paul says widows should be supported by their families. But widows who are elderly and godly and without family support should receive economic assistance from the church. Younger widows should marry, so that they do not fall into temptation of resorting to an immoral life as a means of support.
Concerning Elders (vs. 17 - 25)

Faithful elders, especially those who preach and teach deserve respect and financial support. No accusation against an elder is to be entertained except on the testimony of two or three witnesses, but those who are duly convicted must be rebuked publicly as a deterrent to others. Timothy is also not to ordain ("lay hands on") a man to eldership hastily, i.e., without first proving his character over a period of time.
Note: Speed is frowned upon as it involves action without full knowledge.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FOUR. 1 TIMOTHY
reference.topic: 5.1 Instructions Concerning Various Groups in the Church (vs. 1-6:10)
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 1 TIMOTHY — Instructions Concerning Various Groups in the Church (vs. 1-6:10) (syllabus ¶2332)

blocks.text: Concerning Slaves and Masters (vs. 1-2)

The apostle speaks of slaves who have unbelieving (unsaved) masters. Should slaves in such a case act insolently towards their masters? Should they rebel or run away? Should they do as little work as possible? On the contrary, they should count their masters worthy of all honour. In other words they should give them due respect, work obediently and faithfully, and in general, seek to be a help rather than a hindrance. The motive for such diligent service is the testimony for Christ that is involved. If a Christian slave should act rudely or rebelliously, the master would blaspheme God and the Christian faith.

In verse 2, Paul deals with slaves who have Christian masters. It is not at all unlikely that when the local church met together for the Lord's Supper, there would be Christian masters and Christian slaves around the table - all one in Christ Jesus. But the slaves were no, on this account, to think that social distinctions of life were thereby abolished. Just because a master was a Christian did not mean that the slave did not owe him honor and service.
Concerning the Motives of the False Teachers (vs. 3-10)

Paul now turns his attention to those who might be disposed to teach new and strange doctrines in the Christian church. These men are described as not agreeing with sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ. They are puffed up. They profess to have knowledge, but actually they know nothing. Their teaching stirs up "envy, dissensions, slander, base (evil) suspicions and wrangling (constant friction) among men" (RSV).
Life's True Gain (vs. 6-8)

Furthermore the false teachers think that piety is mere gain, forgetting to add the qualification of contentment. In verse 6, we read: "There is a great gain in godliness with contentment". Picking up the words "godliness" and "gain", Paul shifted their meaning from the erroneous to the truthful. That godliness does not give financial gain. It is a gain when accompanied with contentment. In other words, godliness without contentment would give a one-sided testimony. Contentment also without godliness would not be distinctively Christian at all.
But to have real godliness and at same the time to be satisfied with one's personal circumstances is more than money can buy.
The Peril of Greed for Money (vs. 9-10)

Here, Paul contrasted the proper attitude of contentment with its opposite - the craving to get rich and the love of money. The grasping after riches leads people to "fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge men into ruin and destruction" (v. 9).
To illustrate his point Paul referred indirectly to some people (undoubtedly known to Timothy), who had fallen into the trap Paul was discussing. Eager for money, they wandered from the faith.

6.2	 Final Charge to Timothy: Flee, Follow, Fight (vs. 11-21) 
Exhortation to Godliness (vs. 11-16)

As he concludes the epistle he turns directly to Timothy "But as for you" an emphatic contrast with "some people" of verse 10, who chase after riches. Timothy as a man of God, was to be different - to flee from all this, but chase instead after personal virtues that are of eternal value. Here the elements of eternal value (Christian character) are given as righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. In verse 12, not only is Timothy to flee from ungodliness, but he is also to fight the - good fight of the faith. Repeatedly in this epistle Paul directly addressed Timothy with personal charges, the second steepest of which is found in 5: 21. Here, however, is Paul's strongest and most solemn charge of all (I charge you. . .). The content of Paul's charge is that Timothy keeps this commandment without spot or blame. The "commandment" is probably broader than any simple law. It refers to the entire body of sound teaching which Paul had been describing throughout the letter.

Vs. 15 - 16: Early in his ministry Paul was convinced that Christ would return soon. Now near the end of his ministry he showed both an awareness that Christ might not return before he died and a desire to encourage Timothy to leave the timing of this great event to the Lord. Hence Paul stressed that God will bring about Christ's appearing in His own time.

Paul ends this section with an inspiring doxology to the God who is the cause and object of it all: the ultimate Ruler of the universe, the King of kings and Lord of lords (cf. Rev. 17: 14; 19: 16) the only eternal one, who dwells where no man can survive or approach or even see (cf. In. 1:18). Such a Lord deserves an awesome reverence combined with complete humility (cf. Job 42: 1-6). To him be honour and might forever, Amen (cf. 1 Tim. 1:17).
Instructions for the Rich (vs. 17 - 19)

Paul had earlier dealt with those who did not possess wealth, but who deeply desired it (vs. 3-10). Here he deals with those who have it, and instructs them as to what their attitude should be towards it. The rich are to give up arrogant behavior inspired by wealth. They must not put their hope in wealth, which is so uncertain. This seems to be the greatest temptation to wealthy Christians. Wealthy Christians should put their hope in God, who is the Source of material things. Again material possessions are among those things God has given for our enjoyment (v. 17).

Vs.18-19: Here Christians are reminded that possessions are to be shared with those who 
have less. The implication is that the money a Christian possesses is given to him as a steward. He is responsible to use it for the glory of God and for the well-being of his fellow men. Thus Timothy was to charge the rich to do good, to be rich, not ultimately in money, but in good deeds. The wealthy should make every effort to be generous and willing to share what they have. If they do this they will lay up treasure for themselves in heaven.
Exhortations to Remain Faithful (vs. 20-21)

Here we are told of the apostle's final charge and farewell. Timothy is to guard (to keep) 
the Christian "deposit" or "trust" which Paul had passed on to him in preference to the 
empty talk and contradictions of so-called "knowledge." The fate of some men is a warning. 
They have professed the "knowledge" and missed the faith. A farewell prayer is offered for 
grace upon all the hearers.

Note: The deposit in Timothy's care was no less than the gospel, the message of salvation (1:18). It was his task and responsibility to see that it was kept intact: not diminished by being toned down, not increased by speculative additions, and not distorted by false perspective or proportion. (The "deposit" appears again in 2 Tim. 1:12, 14; cf. 2:2).

Paul closes his letter with the simple benediction, Grace be with you, "You" is in the plural, (an indication of his awareness that this letter would be read widely in the churches (cf. Col. 4: 18; 2 Tim. 4:22, Titus 3:15) . . .The letter was addressed to Timothy (v. 2), but it was surely to be read to the church for its own edification and to the young minister.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FOUR. 1 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 1 TIMOTHY — Instruction Concerning Various Groups (Continued) (syllabus ¶2352)

blocks.text: Apostle Paul was in prison when he wrote this epistle. It was his last letter to Timothy (4:6-13). Not long afterwards, according to traditions, the apostle was beheaded.
The purpose of 2 Timothy was to encourage Timothy in his ministry at Ephesus. The primary theme of the letter is the need for faithfulness in the face of hardship.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Introduction (syllabus ¶2428)

blocks.text: Paul introduces himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus.
The words "according to the promise of the life which is in Christ Jesus" relate to Paul's apostleship.

The question asked regarding this statement is this: Do these words "according to the promise of life which is Christ Jesus" refer to a promise of life Paul personally received, or to a promise he was to proclaim to others? In other words was-his apostleship "because of' the promise or "in conformity to" the promise?

Answer: The original word (i.e. the Greek, "Kata") gives the picture of a merger of the two. 
Therefore, the promise of life in Christ, the gospel, was the reason for and the yardstick of Paul's apostleship (cf. Titus 1:2-3).
"To Timothy my son", here we see emphasis on the close fatherly relationship which Paul maintained with his "spiritual son" or protege.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Greetings (vs. 1-2) (syllabus ¶2435)

blocks.text: Thanksgiving (vs. 3-5)

The remembrance of Timothy inspires the apostle with thanksgiving to God. He is moved by Timothy's love but dwells more on his (Timothy's) sincere faith, the salvation and 
ministry.

Paul viewed his own faith in Christ, not as a break with his Jewish forefathers, but in 
continuity with their faith.

As Paul prayed for Timothy night and day, his gratitude to God for Timothy kept increasing. As he sat chained in prison there was little else he could do but pray. He would definitely bear Timothy in prayer as he ministered to the church which he (Paul) knew best.

In v. 4 we are told Paul remembers Timothy's tears on their last parting. He had longed for his companionship which was such a joy to him. It is interesting to learn that even the great apostle at times became lonely, discouraged, and in need of support from fellow Christians. Probably many had opposed him (1:15; 2:17; 3:1-9, 13; 4:3-4, 10-21). Timothy's sincere faith therefore gave him relief.

V. 5: The apostle was convinced that Timothy possessed true faith ,therefore he urged him to fan (rekindle, stir up) into flame his God-given ability for ministry. God's gift must be used to reach and maintain their full potential.

In v. 7 we read "for God did not, give us a spirit of timidity, but a spirit of power and love and self control". We may ask here, why did Timothy need such a reminder? He might have been intimidated by the opposition to both Paul and the gospel, possibly threatened and also ashamed (2 Tim. 1:8) at having to defend a prisoner (cf. 2:9) and the 'foolishness" which they both (Paul and Timothy) preached about a despised and crucified Jesus (cf. 1 Cor. 1:18-25). However, Paul thinks such timidity (cowardice) has no place in God's service. Instead God gives a spirit of power (1 Cor. 2:4) oflove (cf. 1 Tim. 1:5) and of self-discipline (cf. 1 Tim. 4:7). These three virtues which are supplied by the Holy Spirit are supposed to or should characterize Timothy.
Call to Courage (vs. 8-13)

In this passage, Timothy is told that he should not be ashamed. In fact this would be the case (not being ashamed) if his ministry were marked by the virtue mentioned (v.7b). He, in this way, would be able to stand against his opponents, and would not be ashamed to testify about our Lord (cf. 1 Cor. 1:6), or ashamed of Paul his prisoner. Paul exhorted Timothy to join with him in suffering for the gospel (cf. 2Tim. 2:3) for it is in such circumstances that the power of God will show (cf. 2 Cor. 12:9-10). Paul now spells out some important details of the gospel, that God saved us and called us to a holy life. However, this salvation had nothing to do with a believer's merits but was purely because of his own purpose and grace (cf. Rom. 8: 28; 9:11; Eph. 1:11; 3:11 and 1 Tim. 1:14).
Call to Guard the Truth (vs. 13-14)

Timothy was to view what he had heard from Paul as the essential outline or sketch of sound teaching ("sound doctrine" cf. 1 Tim. 1:10) and was to guard or maintain it. Timothy was to hold the truth with faith and love in Christ Jesus.

First, he had been given a trust or stewardship from God (cf. 1 Tim. 1:11); second, he had in turn entrusted himself and his destiny to God (2 Tim. 1:12). Here Paul spoke of stewardship, the first of the two. The stewardship of the truth he had received had now been passed into the hands of Timothy who was to pass it on yet again to other faithful Christians, who were to pass it on to still others (2:2). While it was in Timothy's possession, it was his responsibility to guard it through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. In fact he was to do so with faith and love in Christ Jesus.
Examples of Unfaithfulness and Faithfulness (vs. 15-18)

In v. 15 we read "You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me and among them Phygelus and Herrnogenes" (RSV). It is likely that the Christians in Asia severed their connections with Paul when they learned that he had been arrested and imprisoned. They forsook him at the very time when he needed them most. Probably their reason was that they feared for their own safety. The failure consisted of a total defection from the faith. From these sad examples of unfaithfulness, Paul turned to the good example shown by Onesiphorus, who had supported him, not only in Ephesus but also in Rome. Depicted in this passage is the contrast between the faithful and the unfaithful, the strong and the weak, the trustworthy and the unreliable.

The "all who are in Asia" (v. 15) portray the very things Paul had been warning Timothy against, that is, cowardice, shame, self-indulgence, infidelity. Onesiphorus, on the other hand, demonstrated the characteristics Paul had been recommending to Timothy which include courage, love, self-discipline, boldness and faithfulness.

It is perceived or concluded here that the negative and the positive examples were designed to strengthen Timothy's resolve to be counted among those who were willing to stand shoulder to shoulder with Paul.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Call to Faithfulness (vs. 3-18) (syllabus ¶2445)

blocks.text: Enduring Hardship for Christ (vs. 1-7)

Timothy is to realize that power is not a matter of his own strength of mind. He is to be empowered. In other words Timothy's strength was not his own, it was a divine "gift" (grace) found only in Christ (Phil. 4:13). "You then, my son be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus" (V1).

V. 2: As Timothy travelled with Paul, he had heard him address many diverse audiences. The essence of Paul's message had not changed. It was the same truth Paul had taught Timothy personally. Now, with the apostle nearing the end of his own ministry, what Timothy had heard from Paul he was in turn to entrust (cf. 1:14) to reliable men who will also be qualified to teach others (cf. 1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:9).
This principle has come to be called "the ministry of multiplication".

In Vs. 3-7, Paul helps Timothy to understand hardship: "Take your share of suffering as a 
good soldier of Christ Jesus". As a soldier Timothy should expect hardship and have the 
right priorities; as an athlete he should recognize the need for training and of maintaining 
a high standard; as a farmer he should expect the divine blessing on his labour.
Christ's Example of Endurance (vs. 8-10)

Here Paul gives the ultimate example of endurance leading to success. The example of Jesus Christ: "Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, descended from David, as preached in my gospel" (RSV). The thought is not that Timothy is to remember certain things about the Lord Jesus, but rather that he is to remember the person himself, alive from the dead. In one sense, this verse is a brief summary of the gospel which Paul preached. The crucial point is that the gospel is the resurrection of the saviour. "Not the vision of a crucified Jesus but the vision of a risen Lord is held up before Timothy" - Hiebert.

The expression "of the seed of David" is a simple statement of the fact that Jesus is the Messiah, the descendant of David, in whom the Messianic promises of God are fulfilled. Paul gives another example of suffering or endurance with his incarceration. He was chained in prison. He was looked upon as an evildoer, as a common criminal. There was much to discourage. Not only was the Roman Government determined to put him to death, but some of his own Christian friends had turned away from him. And yet in spite of these bitter circumstances, Paul's spirit soars high above the prison walls. He forgets his own miserable outlook when he remembers that "the word of God is not bound" ". . .the gospel for which I am suffering and wearing fetters like a criminal. But the word of God is not fettered" (V.9).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Challenge to Endurance (vs. 1-13) (syllabus ¶2473)

blocks.text: Faithfulness in Ministry vs. 14-19)

The instruction of the previous verses was not for Timothy only. "Remind them of this, and charge them before the Lord to avoid disputing about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers" (RSV). Timothy was to keep reminding others of these things. Timothy was to charge his people solemnly to avoid argumentation, for its effects may be ruinous.

As for Timothy, he was to do his best to be sure he would meet with God's approval, a 
workman (Tabourer") who does not need to be ashamed. Paul had spoken of shame 
before men (2 Tim. 1:8, 12, 16); but shame before God is worse. Timothy need not fear 
such shame if he would correctly handle the word of truth.

Timothy was also to avoid godless chatter (lit. "Shun profane empty utterances" cf. 1 Tim. 6:20) which only advance ungodliness like gangrene (gangrene refers to the mortification of a part of the body caused when it is cut off from its normal supply of blood and nutrition).

Two men are named whose teachings were corrupting the local church. They were Hymenaeus and Philetus, whom Paul had already "delivered over to Satan". These two had wandered away from the truth (cf. 1 Tim. 1:6, 6:21) regarding the crucial doctrine of the resurrection. According to Paul these two false teachers destroy the faith of some (cf. 1 Tim. 1:19).
A Clean Instrument (vs. 20-21)

Here Paul turns to the variety of people who are found in the church, some good, others unworthy. The apostle uses a metaphor of a household here. That in a large household are all sorts of containers. Some are made of gold and silver and others of wood and clay. More importantly, some are for noble purposes and some for ignoble. Apparently the reference so far is to the faithful and the unfaithful within the church. The metaphor is clearly showing how one can be an instrument for noble purposes, by cleansing himself from the ignoble vessels. If a Christian cleanses himself he can be used by God in the noble duties of ministry. Timothy was to have nothing to do with the false teachers. In this way he would be a vessel (1) for noble use; (2) made holy; (3) useful to the master; (4) prepared for any good work (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16).

What is clean and set apart for special use can easily get contaminated and rendered unusable through contact with the corrupt. Paul was concerned that Timothy keeps himself in a usable condition for the Lord.
Faithfulness in Conduct (vs. 22-26)
V. 22: "So shun youthful passion and aim at righteousness, faith, love, and peace. . ." (RSV) "Flee . . .youthful lusts. . ." (KJV).

Probably Paul did not have sexual passions in mind here at least not primarily. The youthful passion (the evil desires of youth) here would include all the unholy desires that would characterize young people (Timothy was a young man cf. 1 Tim. 4:12), e.g. self- assertion, love of argument, partiality, intolerance and impatience.

Timothy was to flee the evil desires of youth and pursue the opposite virtues, namely 
righteousness, faith, love and peace.

Vs: 24-25: "And the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kindly to everyone. . . correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant that they will repent and come to know the truth".

Here, Paul says: when brethren fall into false teaching they must be treated with gentleness and Christian love in the hope that they will come to their senses and escape from the trap of the devil (cf. Gal. 5:1; 1 Tim. 3:7; 6:9) who has taken them captive to do his will. False teaching and all its negative consequences in the church are always the handiwork of Satan but God in His grace often salvages the situation through the Christ- like ministry of his servants.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Marks of a Good Workman (vs. 14-26) (syllabus ¶2487)

topics.title: Predictions of Faithlessness in the Last Days (vs. 1-9)

blocks.text: Vs. 1-5: As in his previous letter, Paul warned Timothy about the collapse predicted for the last days (cf. Tim. 4: 1-3). During this interim, according to the prediction, the world will see terrible times of general moral decadence. People will be (1) lovers of themselves (self-centered); (2) lovers of money; (3) boastful (they think that they have the future in their hands and can determine everything. Why bother about salvation? They are therefore (4) arrogant (proud). (5) They are abusive towards others (evil speakers and insulting and blasphemous); (6) disobedient to their parents; (7) ungrateful (lacking in appreciation); (8) unholy (impious, holding nothing sacred, irreverent); (9) inhuman (without natural affection, unfeeling); (10) implacable (refusing to make peace, refusing efforts towards reconciliation); (11) slanderers (false accusers, spreading false and malicious reports); (12) profligates (men of uncontrolled passions, without self-control); (13) fierce (savage, brutal, unprincipled); (14) haters of good (not lovers of the good, haters of whatever is good); (15) treacherous (detractors, betrayers); (16) reckless (rash, self-willed); (17) swollen with conceit (puffed up, making empty pretensions); (18) lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God (loving pleasure more than God).

Though these characteristics are cataloged under the auspices of a prediction about "the last days" it is clear that Paul considered them to be already present in Ephesus, though they would intensify with time. Timothy had to beware of such people and have nothing to do with them.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.topic: 3.1 Predictions of Faithlessness in the Last Days (vs. 1-9)
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Predictions of Faithlessness in the Last Days (vs. 1-9) (syllabus ¶2514)

blocks.text: Paul's Example of Faithfulness and Suffering in the Face of Opposition (Vs. 10-14)

In his direct exhortation to Timothy (cf. 2:1), the apostle returned to his own example of 
endurance and faithfulness.

In marked contrast to these false teachers was the life and ministry of the apostle Paul. Timothy was well aware of the nine prominent features which characterized the apostle. He had followed Paul closely and could testify to the fact that Paul was a man who was faithful to Christ and to his word. The contrast with the false teachers is a strong one. "But as for you, continue what you have learned."
Faithfulness to God's Word (Vs. 14- chapter 4:5)

The exhortation is to continue in the things Timothy had learned and become convinced of (cf. 1 Cor. 15:1-2). These things had come from two sources, which Paul set side by side as of equal importance: his own testimony, and the Holy Scriptures, which at that time consisted of the Old Testament. Timothy's complete confidence in both sources would be enough to prevent any slippage in his commitment to the truth.

In 3:16, Paul tells Timothy that all Scripture is God breathed (inspired), that is, God's 
words were given through men superintended by the Holy Spirit so that their writings are without error. This fact was virtually taken for granted by the Jews. This led Paul to declare the "usefulness" of the word. For each aspect of Timothy's ministry, whatever it might be: teaching (instructing believers in God's truths), rebuking those in sin (cf. 1 Tim. 5:20; 2Tim. 4:2), correcting those in error (cf. 2 Tim. 2:25; 4:2), and training (literary "child- training") in righteousness (guiding new believers in God's ways) - for all of these and more the written word of God is profitable.

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Challenge to Faithful preaching (vs. 10- chapter 4:8) (syllabus ¶2519)

blocks.text: Paul was about to die. He viewed his death now as certain; he was already being poured out like a drink offering (Phil. 2:17). This refers to the libation connected with daily offerings of the lambs (cf. Num. 28:4-7). Paul knew, sitting in a jail, that he would not be released. "My departure has come" (v. 6). Now looking over his life, he could say: I have fought the good fight (cf. 1 Tim. 6:12) finished the race (cf. Acts 20:24) and kept the faith (cf. 1 Tim. 6:10). As a result of his faithfulness to duty Paul had no fear of meeting the Lord, the righteous judge, but only anticipation of reward in the form of a crown of righteousness which was already waiting in store for him on that day (a reference to Christ's return, not Paul's death), side by side with the rest of the faithful who have longed for his appearing (cf. Phil 3:20-21; Titus 2:13).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Faithfulness of Paul (vs. 6-8) (syllabus ¶2530)

topics.title: Reminder of God's Faithfulness in Paul's adversity (vs. 9-18)

blocks.text: Paul's Enemies and Friends (Vs. 9-16)

V. 9: Here the apostle requires the presence of Timothy urgently, "Do your best to come soon". Paul's need for Timothy was intensified by the defection of Demas who, instead of loving the Lord's appearing (v. 8), loved this world. Demas deserted the apostle to embrace the deceptive, freedom or comfort of Thessalonica. There is no suggestion or hint of blame or of any disaffection concerning the absence of Crescens and Titus. It seems they might have been dispatched to the Lord's work elsewhere, Crescens to Galatia and Titus to Dalmatia.

V. 11: Of all Paul's close associates only Luke maintained contact with Paul in Rome. In joining the two of them, Timothy was to bring Mark along, picking him along the way "Get Mark and bring him with you". Paul had once considered Mark untrustworthy (Acts 15:36-40) but he was now considered helpful to the apostle in his ministry.
Paul's Deliverance by the Lord (vs. 17-18)

The apostle may have been forsaken by men, but the Lord stood by him. Not only so, but 
he was divinely empowered to preach the gospel at his trial. The message went forth 
without hindrance and a Gentile law court heard the message of salvation: "all the 
Gentiles might hear it so I was rescued from the lion's mouth."

The expression "I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion" is seen by some as a general 
way of saying that Paul was granted a temporary delay. The trial was continued. The 
danger was temporarily averted.

V. 18: Paul, despite every evil attack, had complete confidence that God would bring him safely to his heavenly kingdom (cf. v. 1). For this Paul, even in the face of his death, could praise God: To him be glory forever and ever. Amen (Eph. 3:21; 2 Peter 3:18).

reference.subject: New Testament Studies
reference.chapter: UNIT FIVE. 2 TIMOTHY
reference.topic: 4.2 Reminder of God's Faithfulness in Paul's adversity (vs. 9-18)
reference.citation: New Testament Studies — 2 TIMOTHY — Reminder of God's Faithfulness in Paul's adversity (vs. 9-18) (syllabus ¶2533)

blocks.text: Greetings are sent from Paul and others expressing personal interest and association. There is a small item of news and a request for Timothy to come before winter. The epistle ends characteristically with grace.

V. 19: Prisca (or Priscilla) and Aquila - Devoted friends of Paul (Acts 18:2,26; Rom. 16:3; 1 Cor. 16:19. Onesiphrous (cf. 2 Tim. 1:16) and his faithful household were singled out by Paul for greeting. V. 20, Erastus: an old associate of Timothy (Acts 19:22), Trophimus an Ephesian (cf. Acts 20:4, 21; 29), he had accompanied Paul to Jerusalem.

V. 21: The appeal in v. 9 is repeated with the addition of the words before winter. Paul may have desired his cloak before the weather turned cold (v. 13), but he was more likely concerned about sailing conditions on the Adriatic Sea. Of the four individuals listed, Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, and Claudia, nothing is known. Though "everyone" had deserted Paul at his first defense, still in the spirit of forgiveness expressed in verse 16, Paul had not cut the Roman Christians off. The greeting is from all the brethren.

V. 22: Paul's closing benediction is first directed to Timothy (your spirit - singular), and then to other readers (you, plural) once again demonstrating that the epistle was meant or designed to be read widely (cf. 1 Tim. 6:21; Titus 3:15).

subjects.name: Christian Doctrine
subjects.description: The Doctrine of Christ, the Holy Spirit, the Trinity, the Affirmation of Faith (the Creeds) and the Doctrine of the Last Things.

blocks.text: The doctrine of Christ (Christology) "is enquiry into the significance of Jesus for Christian faith. In the classical Christian tradition, faith is understood as faith in the person of Jesus Christ."

The Jews had been looking for the "anointed one" for hundreds of years when Jesus finally came into the world. The prophet Isaiah had written about the promised Messiah as one who would bear the sins and sorrows of the people (Isa. 53:1-12). However, the Jews were looking for a king who would lead their nation into political victory over Rome; they did not believe that the Messiah would be God himself come to earth as a man, or that their Messiah would die on a cross.

But this Messiah whom Christians identify as Jesus Christ of Nazareth, is the one on whom Christians have obviously placed their entire hope for salvation from their own and this world's sins. How could a mere man bear the sins of the entire world? Or is he God? To answer these questions we shall look at the Person and Work of Christ.
A. The Person of Christ

reference.subject: Christian Doctrine
reference.chapter: I. THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — Introduction (syllabus ¶2619)

blocks.text:
The name Jesus is often referred to as the proper name of Christ. Jesus is the Greek form 
of the Hebrew Yeshua or Joshua. In Hebrew it means Yahweh is salvation - God helps or God saves. The interpretation of this name, as applied to the Christ (Jesus of Nazareth), is in Matthew 1:21 - "She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." Here, it can be said that the name "Jesus" means "Saviour."

Who is Jesus? We cannot answer that question by speculating about his "essence" or his "nature." We can only answer by looking at what he has done and what has happened to him. This means that we cannot separate the "person" of Jesus from his "work". As we go about our study the question before us, then, is "Who is this person who stands at the centre of the Christian faith, and wham we come to know in the story of his life and works?" We shall try to answer this question by looking at the Incarnation, the Atonement and the Resurrection of Christ.

reference.subject: Christian Doctrine
reference.chapter: I. THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — JESUS - WHO IS HE? (syllabus ¶2627)

blocks.text:
The word Incarnation "comes from the Latin incarnare which means "to make flesh" or in a general sense, it means bodily manifestation of a supernatural being. The idea that 
God or the gods have made themselves present amongst humankind in human form is widespread in the history of religions. However, in Christianity, the doctrine of the Incarnation which is central states that "God, in one of the modes of his triune being and 
without in any way ceasing to be God, has revealed himself to mankind for their salvation by coming amongst them as a man."

As Livingstone K. Buama aptly puts it, "The word incarnation directs our attention to the bringing together in one person (Jesus Christ our Lord) both Godhood and manhood to become 'human' . . .the incarnation has to do with how the eternal word became flesh - the bodily manifestation of the eternal word (John 1:14)." The New Testament tells us that God became a human being. This person, Jesus Christ, was fully God and fully man. According to St. Augustine, "The meaning of the Word being made flesh is not that the divine nature was changed into flesh (human nature), but that the divine nature assumed our flesh (our nature) except without sin."

The story of Jesus' birth is recorded only in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke. It is not mentioned in Mark or John. Paul never mentions it in any of his letters, nor do any of the other New Testament writings. The story of the birth of Jesus which emphasizes the Christian belief that "God is with us" (Matthew 1:23) is not just a beautiful idea or an abstract theological truth. It is historical. We need to note the following facts about the Incarnation:

Christ was Son of God from Eternity: The New Testament teaches that Jesus existed long before He was born; He did not come into being at the time of His birth, but that he has always existed as the Son of God (John 1:1-3). It was through him that God created the universe, and in him all things hold together (Col. 1:15- 17).

It was by Supernatural Conception: The circumstances of Jesus Christ's birth help us to understand that he was born without sin. The human inclination to sin is inherited from our parents. Because of the unique conception of Jesus, he was born without this bias.

Though Christ's birth was as normal as that of any human's, his conception occurred through the intervention of the Holy Spirit. Because of this, Jesus was both God and man (Matt. 1:18-25; 1 Pet. 2:22; Heb. 4:15).

It Upholds Christ's Full Deity: As the New Testament unfolds, the fact that Christ is God is increasingly revealed. We learn about Christ's character (he lived his life 
without a taint of sin); his claims (to be the centre of all truth, to be the world's judge, and to have a unique relationship to the Father); and his conduct (in performing miracles, forgiving sins and accepting worship) (John 8:46, 50-58; Luke 5:20, 21; John 20:26-29).

It Establishes Christ's Full Humanity: The New Testament shows that Christ was fully human, born into a Hebrew family, and subject to the Hebrew law. He experienced all the problems that people have to face. He was exposed to hunger and thirst, fatigue and sorrow, and he faced the full force of temptation. Although he was still fully God, Jesus (as a man) shared completely the weaknesses of all humankind except sin. Because of this, he was perfectly qualified to be the unique go-between, bringing humankind and God together (Gal. 4:4-5; Heb. 2:14-18; 5:7).

It Explains Christ's Unique Personality: Jesus Christ is parallel, for he is both God and man, in two distinct natures, and one person for ever. It was the same Jesus who declared that he was thirsty, who also referred, in prayer, to the glory which he shared eternally with the Father.

The New Testament writers do not try to explain, as a philosophy, how one personality could be both human and divine. But the portrait they give us identifies him both with humankind and with God (Matt. 8:24, 27; John. 19:28, 17:5).

f)	It Validates Christ's Saving Ministry: There are aspects of the Incarnation that are beyond our understanding. But one thing is clear. We know enough to realize that Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, is the one Saviour that humankind needs.

By laying aside his eternal splendour, and involving himself in humankind's burdens - even to the point of death on the cross for our sins - he becomes the reconciler between God and humankind, and by his resurrection he brings our humanity to heaven (1 Tim. 2:5; Phil. 2:5-11).

blocks.text: The Virgin Birth (Parthenogenesis) is the biblical doctrine that Jesus was miraculously begotten by God and born of Mary, who was a virgin. The term virgin birth explains the way in which the Son of God entered human existence; it means that Mary had not had sexual relations with any man when she conceived Jesus.

This incomparable act of God is described beautifully in Luke 1:26-38. The angel of God appeared to a virgin who was engaged to Joseph. In those days engagement was a legal 
arrangement in which a woman was betrothed, or pledged, to a man. But engagement did not permit sexual relations. Since Mary had not "known" Joseph sexually, she wondered how she could bear a child. The angel explained that this would be encouraged by "the power of the Highest" as the Holy Spirit would "overshadow her." There was nothing physical about this divine act; this is emphasized by the statement that the child would be the "Holy One" (Luke 1:35).

The angel also declared that the child would be called "the Son of God." This clearly teaches that it was only through the virgin birth that Jesus, a human being, could also be properly identified as the Son of God. The one person, Jesus, has two natures divine and human. The eternal, divine nature of the Son of God was joined, in Mary's womb, with a human nature by the direct act of God.

The parallel account in Matthew 1:18-25 views the virgin birth from Joseph's perspective. Because of the legal nature of engagement, a man who found his fiancée pregnant would normally divorce her. Because Joseph was a fair and just man, he did not want to shame Mary by divorcing her publicly, so he decided to do so privately. But the angel prevented this by assuring him that Mary was still a virgin. Her child was conceived by the Holy Spirit, as prophesied by Isaiah seven hundred years before the birth of Christ. The prophet Isaiah said, "Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will be with child and bear a son, and she will call His name Immanuel" (Isa. 7:14). After this revelation, Joseph took Mary as his wife but did not unite with her sexually until Jesus was born.

The New Testament records the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy: "Now in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, called Nazareth, to a virgin engaged to a man whose name was Joseph, of the descendants of David; and the virgin's name was Mary. . . And the angel said to her, 'Do not be afraid, Mary; for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb, and bear a son, and you shall name Him Jesus. . .' And Mary said to the angel, 'How can this be, since I am a virgin?' And the angel answered and said to her, 'The Holy Spirit, will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and for that reason the holy offspring shall be called the Son of God. . . For nothing will be impossible with God' " (Luke 1:27, 30, 31, 34, 35, 37).
The Gospels record that Mary and Joseph did not have sexual relations until after Christ was born, and he "kept her a virgin until she gave birth to a Son; and he called His name Jesus" (Matt.1:25).

topics.title: The Necessity of the Virgin Birth

blocks.text: There are several reasons why the virgin birth was a necessity. The following are some of them:
1.3.1 	Christ's Pre-existence

The Bible teaches that the Word who became flesh was with God from the very beginning (John 1:1). The fact of the pre-existence of Christ is testified many times in the New Testament (John 8:58; Philippians 2:5-11; Colossians 1:15, 16).

When Jesus came into the world, He was not a newly-created individual such as we are, but was rather the eternal Son of God. To be born into this world of the Virgin Mary required divine intervention and this is exactly what the Gospels record.
1.3.2 	Transmission of Original Sin

Another reason why Jesus needed to be virgin-born was because of His sinless nature. According to Ambrose and Augustine (both Early Church Fathers) the transmission of original sin is bound up with the sexual nature of propagation and the carnal desires aroused by procreation. That Jesus was conceived not through any sexual relations explains how he was free of original sin.

A basic New Testament teaching is that from the day He was born until the day He died, Jesus was without sin. To be a perfect sacrifice, He must Himself be perfect-without sin. Since our race is contaminated with sin, a miraculous entrance into the world would be required, hence the virgin birth.
1.3.3 	Jesus' Inheritance of the Throne of David

Moreover, if Jesus had been fathered by Joseph, He would not have been able to assume the throne of David. According to the prophecy of Jeremiah 22:28-30, there could be no king in Israel who was a descendant of King Jeconiah, and Matthew 1:12 relates that Joseph was from the line of Jeconiah. If Jesus had been fathered by Joseph, He could not rightly inherit the throne of David, since he was a relative of the cursed line.
There are possibly other ways which God could have chosen to send His Son into the world, but the fact is the way He chose to do it was through the virgin birth.

blocks.text: Even though the virgin birth is given as a historical fact and certain things made the virgin birth essential, many still have objections to its occurrence for the following reasons:
1.4.1 	Later Addition to the Christian Tradition

Some scholars claim that the reference in Luke 2:27, 33, and 41 to Jesus' parents (Joseph and Mary) implies that the virgin birth was not a part of early Christian tradition. But these words were written by the same writer who described the annunciation of the virgin birth in Luke 1:26-38. Some Bible students also express concern over the lack of reference to the virgin birth elsewhere in the New Testament.

Response: The other Gospels say nothing about Jesus' birth, so it is not strange that they do not speak of the virgin birth. Since the gospel message concerns the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ (1 Cor. 15:1-3), the virgin birth is not generally a part of its proclamation. But the virgin birth is an essential, wonderful, and powerful truth noted in historic Christian doctrine because it is revealed in the eternal Word of God.

The passages in both Matthew and Luke are authentic, with no evidence at all that they were later additions to the text. The doctrine of the virgin birth has been believed by the church from its beginning.
1.4.2 	It is a miracle
The main problem that people have with the virgin birth is that it is a miracle. Scripture does not treat this event as an ordinary occurrence but rather as a supernatural act of God.

Response: The miracle of the virgin birth should not pose any special problem if one accepts the possibility of miracles. If an all-powerful God does exist, who spoke all creation into existence, a virgin birth would not be beyond His capability.
1.4.3 It is Biologically Impossible
A common objection to the virgin birth is that it is a biological impossibility, which was accepted by people ignorant of these things. C. S. Lewis made some pertinent observations on this view:

Thus you will hear people say, 'The early Christians believed that Christ was the son 
of a virgin, but we know that this is a scientific impossibility.' Such people seem to have an idea that belief in miracles arose at a period when men were so ignorant of the course of nature that they did not perceive a miracle to be contrary to it.
Response: C. S. Lewis continues his observations in response to the objection thus:

A moment's thought shows this to be foolish, with the story of the virgin birth as a particularly striking example. When Joseph discovered that his fiancée was going to have a baby, he not unnaturally decided to repudiate her. Why? Because he knew just as well as any modern gynecologist that in the ordinary course of nature, women do not have babies unless they have lain with men.

No doubt the modern gynecologist knows several things about birth and begetting 
which Joseph did not know. But those things do not concern the main point-that a virgin birth is contrary to the course of nature. And Joseph obviously knew that."
1.4.4 	It is a Myth

Some have attempted to account for the virgin birth by tracing it to Greek or Babylonian mythology. They argue that the Gospel writers borrowed this story from the mythology of their day. Many deities among the Greeks, Babylonians, and Egyptians were reported born in an unusual manner, but for the most part these beings never actually existed. The myths are accounts of a god or goddess being born into the world by sexual relations between some heavenly being and an earthly woman, or by some adulterous affair among the gods and goddesses.

Response: This view does not fit the facts, for there is no hero in pagan mythology for which a virgin birth is claimed, and moreover it would be unthinkable to the Jewish mind to construct such a story from mythology.
Obviously, the Gospel narratives contain no mythological elements. Dr. Thomas Thorburn comments appropriately that,

All these various stories of supernatural conceptions and births, which we meet within folklore and the history of mythology, have this one point in common-they serve to point not so much to the similarity as to the complete contrast and dissimilarity which exists between the Christian birth-story and the tales which are current in various pagan circles.

The virgin birth is set down in the Bible as a historical fact and a necessary historical fact at that when one considers all the facts. Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch (one of the early Church Fathers) who lived at the beginning of the second century, wrote to the Ephesians and said, "For our God, Jesus the Christ, was conceived in the womb by Mary, according to a dispensation, of the seed of David but also of the Holy Ghost."

Thus when we closely consider the objections to the virgin birth, we become more 
convinced that it did indeed occur just as the historical records in the Gospels state.
