blocks.text: The many different names of Jesus Christ reveal the distinctive characteristics of his person and the work that he came to do. Jesus has many names or titles.
1.5.1 	Messiah

For hundreds of years the Jews had been looking for a future King who would be a 
descendant of David when Jesus finally came into the world. This person was called the "Messiah" by the Jews (which in the Greek language is Christos, from which we get Christ). Both "Christ" and "Messiah" mean the "anointed one" or "one who has been anointed."He would have God's authority and power to bring in the end of the age and establish the kingdom of God.

It was Simon Peter who made the first clear declaration that Jesus was the Christ, but it is important to note that Jesus totally rejected the popular idea of the Messiah as being a political deliverer from the Roman Empire. He saw his messianic role as one of suffering and death for the salvation of humankind (John 6:15; Matt. 16:16, 21; Jn4:25, 26).

The name "Jesus" itself means the "one who saves." We usually add the term "Christ" 
after his name. The prophet Isaiah had written about the promised Messiah as one who would bear the sins and sorrows of the people (Isa. 53:1-12). Isaiah even said that this Messiah would be called the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father, and the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6).

However, the Jews were looking for a king who would lead their nation into political victory over Rome; they did not believe that the Messiah would be God himself come to earth as a man, or that their Messiah would die on a cross. As John Macquarrie puts it, "The messiah was visualized as a victor, not a sufferer."
1.5.2 	The Holy One of God
This title was given to Jesus by Peter On. 6:69). This was a name belonging to him as the Messiah - especially set apart for God.
1.5.3 	Son of God

The term "Son of God" occurs most frequently in John's Gospel (John 20:17; 5:18, 25; 20:31). It usually emphasizes Jesus' deity. Jesus was acclaimed as the Son of God at his baptism (Mark 1:11). He also was given this title by the angel Gabriel at the annunciation: "That Holy One who is to be born will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35).

Jesus does not appear to have called himself "Son of God", but the tradition indicates 
that he had a special sense of the fatherhood of God, and expressed this in a word, abba 
which demonstrates peculiar intimacy. Jesus taught his disciples to think of God as their 
Father in a particularly intimate way when he taught them to pray, "Our Father ... n But 
because of his use of the terms "my Father" and "your Father," it is clear that he saw his 
own relationship to the Father in a quite different way from that of his followers. The 
Jewish authorities recognized this and accused Jesus of making himself equal with God.
1.5.4 	Son of Man

The expression "Son of Man" (in Hebrew, ben adam; in Aramaic, bar nasha) was commonly used in these languages as a periphrasis for "man". Thus, when the psalmist asks, "What is man that you are mindful of him, the son of man that you care for him?"(Ps. 8:4), the expressions "man" and "son of man" are used synonymously in a parallelism, and each of them means simply "human being". This is the common informal sense of" son of man".

Jesus used this title more than any other to describe himself. Although it seems to speak of his humanity, in reality it is a pointer to his deity, for the term is drawn from the book of Daniel, where the Son of Man, who is an apocalyptic figure, rules an everlasting kingdom (Dan. 7:9-14).

The term "Son of Man" usually emphasizes Jesus' messianic role. In the Old Testament, the Messiah was called the "Son of Man" (Daniel 7:13-14). Although this messianic "Son of Man" comes from heaven and accepts divine worship, Jesus often used the term "Son 
of Man" when emphasizing his own humanness (Matthew 8:20; 11:19; 17:22-23).

Jesus used the title in three ways - when speaking of his earthly ministry, his death and his coming glory. It is suggested that he favoured this title because it carried no nationalistic associations, it implied an identification with humans, and it had both "overtones of divinity and undertones of humanity" (Matt. 8:19, 20; 20:17-19; 24:30).
Note: The terms "Son of God" and "Son of Man" are used interchangeably in Matthew 26:63-65. (See also Mark 2:10; John 1:14, 18, 34; 5:25-27).
1.5.5 	Word and Wisdom

Jesus is also designated the Word or Logos. The use of the Greek expression Logos has perhaps led to the belief that this term came from Greek philosophy. The Old Testament tells us that God created all things by his Word. He spoke and it came to be. The Apostle John shows that this Word was, in fact, God's Son, without whom nothing would exist (John 1:1-4, 14).

The Word is also involved in God's creation in another important way. He is the perfect expression of God to humankind. Because Christ is the Word, he did not merely bring us God's good news, but he is himself that good news (Ps. 33:6-9; Rev. 19:11-13).
Christ is also portrayed in the New Testament as the personal wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24, 30) - the one through whom all things were created (1 Cor. 8:6; Col. 1:16; Heb. 1:2).
1.5.6 High Priest

This title, given to Christ in the Book of Hebrews, is drawn from the Old Testament system of sacrifices. A sacrifice had to be made every year by the High Priest on behalf of God's people to atone for their sins. Christ, by his sacrificial death (never to be repeated) is the perfect mediator and High Priest (Lev. 9:7-8; Heb. 7:23-28).
1.5.7 	Lord

Several words denoting lordship were used of Jesus in the New Testament. The most requent, and the most important in relation to the doctrine of his person, was the Greek word kurios, spoken of him as "The Lord" or "The Master." To call Jesus Lord was, in the New Testament Church, the mark of a true Christian. To use this name invited opposition - from the Jewish authorities on the grounds of blasphemy, and from the Romans on the grounds of treason against the Emperor. This was the name that ascribed all authority to Jesus (1 Cor. 12:1-3; In. 13:13; Phil. 2:9-11).

The title "Lord" is somewhat different from the other titles of Jesus. This is because whilst the other titles are descriptive terms "Lord' expresses rank or worth. To acknowledge Jesus Christ as Lord (Rom. 10:9) appears to have been one of the earliest Christian confessions of faith. "Jesus is Lord" is the ultimate Christian creed. When we call Jesus "Lord," we are certainly saying something about him as well as expressing our devotion and allegiance to him. We recognize him as an exalted being. As Graham Stanton puts it, "The kyrios Christology expresses the authority of the Lord over the individual and the Christian community, and is often related to ethical statements."

Jesus is called God in the New Testament. Thomas, convinced that the risen Christ stood before him, abandoned his doubts with the confession, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20; 28). But the classic text is John 1:1. John declared that the Word existed not only "in the beginning," where he was "with God," but also actually "was God." In the epistle to the Hebrews a psalm is addressed to Jesus as God, "But about the Son he says, 'Your throne, 0 God, will last forever and ever. .. '" (Heb. 1:8). This is the Word that became incarnate as a real man in Jesus Christ, without ceasing to be what he had been from eternity.
The Bible thus presents Christ as altogether God and altogether man - the perfect mediator between God and humankind because he partakes fully of the nature of both.

blocks.text: Heresies have arisen in Christian history when either Christ's deity or his humanity has been neglected. There is hardly a doctrine of Christianity that has not been denied by someone sometime. From the very beginning, the Church faced trouble from those who taught false doctrines about Jesus. Even today there are those who continue to be led astray by false teachings about Jesus. We examine two of them here:
1.6.1 	Arianism

The first false idea is that Jesus was just a man, not God at all. The heresy of the denial of Christ's divinity usually goes by the name of Arianism (after Arius of Alexandria; died 335). Arius taught that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit were beings willed into existence by God for the purposes of redemption. Thus they were not eternal, as God is. There was a time "before which they were not." Those who believe this agree that Jesus was a great moral teacher, and that God blessed him, but they deny that Jesus was God. (More will be said about this under our discussion of the Creeds).
1.6.2	 Docetism

The second false idea is just the opposite; that Jesus was God but not man. The heresy of denying Christ's humanity, goes by the name Docetism. The word Docetism comes from the Greek verb dokeo which means "to appear" or "to seem." Docetism asserts very strongly that Jesus was divine, but denies that he really was human. He only seemed to be a man. His human nature was only a mask behind which his true divine self was concealed. Jesus was not a real man, but only a spiritual being, who looked like a man, acted like a man, seemed to be a man, but was not really subject to all the limitations and problems of earthly human existence. In Him God was only pretending to be with us in the midst of our sinful, suffering, creaturely existence. His purpose was not to help us in the world but to help us escape from the world.
1.6.3 	The Early Church's Arguments against Docetism as Emphasized in the New Testament
Jesus was a Jewish man, not a heavenly ideal man. (See the birth narratives of Jesus in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke). Jesus was "born ofa woman" (Gal. 4:4).
ii) 	Jesus was a "real man" - a man of strength and determination (Matt. 23:17; 23:33; Luke 12:49-53; Matt. 10:34-39).

iii) 	Jesus experienced every human need and appetite. He was completely human in all aspects of life. Like any other man, Jesus was limited also in his knowledge. He had to grow in wisdom as well as in stature (Lk. 2:52). He himself admitted that He did not know everything (Mk. 13:32). Like any other normal man, He did not want to die (Matt. 26:36-39).

iv) 	Jesus was tempted to sin, just as every other man is (Matt. 4:1-11; Lk.4:1-14). He was a man subject to the same pressures, doubts, fears, and desires as we are. If He was not, how could He be God with us? How could He "sympathize with our weaknesses" (Heb. 4:15)?
v)	Jesus was without sin - perfectly fulfilling His humanity. He was tempted in every respect as we are, "yet without sinning" (Heb. 4:15).
B.   The Work of Christ

blocks.text: It has been said that "Christianity is Christ" and that Christian Theology is therefore an explanation of who Christ is and what it means to have faith in him. For one thing, the most important statement to be made about Jesus is that he is both God and man. For another, the doctrines of Christ's person (Christology) pass quickly and inevitably into the area of Christ's work (soteriology). So it is impossible to talk meaningfully about who Jesus is without also talking about what he did and about the importance of that for us. We can understand who Jesus is only by looking at his whole life and activity; the person and work of Christ are inseparable.

Why did Jesus become man? The answer to that question is to be seen in the passion and death of Jesus, which paradoxically, has been seen as a saving event, in spite of its horror as a public execution. Jesus became man in order to die for those who were to believe in him. We shall now look at the various aspects of the work of Christ.

blocks.text: Many theories of atonement have been produced but we shall not have any discussions of such theories. For our purpose here, we shall look at the importance of the death of Jesus Christ.
2.1.1	 It initiated a new relationship

The Bible teaches that man's sin has created a barrier of guilt between him and his creator. However, Jesus accepted the responsibility for human sin and willingly took its penalty on the cross. A new relationship is now available for those who respond to the good news that their sins can be forgiven. Hostility has been replaced by friendship.

Those who unite themselves to Christ are viewed by God as though they had never been 
rebels at all. Indeed, the Christian is seen as a new person altogether (2 Cor. 5:15-19; Rom. 5:8-11).
2.1.2 	It fulfilled Old Testament scripture
The Old Testament showed that God and man could not be reconciled unless a sacrifice was made. Only then could the guilt of sin be removed.

The Old Testament animal sacrifices could not in themselves take away sin, nor could they be a final solution to the problem of sin. The New Testament sees them as illustrations of the perfect sacrifice Jesus was to make (Heb. 10:1-12; Isa. 53:4-12).
2.1.3 	It destroyed Satan's kingdom

The power of Satan's kingdom was broken through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. The final destruction of the Devil is yet to be. The Christian is aware of his activity and influence - but is confident of victory and protection through the power of the cross (Col. 2:15; 1 John 3:8).
2.1.4 	It reversed sin's dominion

In the Bible, the idea of redeeming (or "buying back") a person who is enslaved is very strong. Christ is presented as the one who, by his death, redeems his people from the 
penalty of God's moral law.

Because Christ has taken our guilt upon himself, sin no longer has the power to 
dominate the life of the Christian (Gal. 3:13; Rom. 6:6-11).
2.1.5 	It provided a way of victory

With the power of the Devil limited (and ultimately doomed), and with the guilt of sin removed, the cross of Jesus Christ has set the Christian free. The Christian is not set free from the fight for moral purity - rather he is set free for the fight. The "tenses" of salvation are as follows: we have been saved from the penalty of sin by a crucified Saviour; we are being saved from the power of sin by a living Saviour; we shall be saved from the presence of sin by a coming Saviour. From the cross onwards, the message is one of victory (1 John 1:7-9; Titus 2:14).
2.1.5 	It guaranteed an eternity with God

The cross is the guarantee that God has set his eternal love upon his people; there could 
be no stronger demonstration than the death of his son.

Death is still an enemy, but it is an enemy that is defeated because of the death and resurrection of Christ. Like the Devil, death will face ultimate annihilation. The cross assures the Christian of a promised inheritance in God's eternal kingdom (Rom. 8:31-39; Heb. 2:14, 15).

The work of Christ has often been stated in relation to his threefold office as prophet, priest, and king. As prophet, He is the perfect spokesman of God to the world, fully revealing God's character and will. As priest, Jesus has offered to God by His death a sufficient sacrifice for the sins of the world. Now, on the basis of that sacrifice, He exercises a ministry of intercession on behalf of His people. As king, He is "the ruler over the kings of the earth" (Rev. 1:5) - the one who has already introduced that kingdom of God to earth, and whose rule over the whole world will ultimately be revealed.

reference.chapter: I. THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — The Atoning Death of Christ (syllabus ¶2794)

topics.title: The Work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present, and future:

blocks.text: 2.2.1 	The finished work of Christ

By the "finished" work of Christ is meant the work of atonement or redemption for the human race which He completed by His death on the Cross. This work is so perfect in itself that it requires neither repetition nor addition. Because of this work, He is called "Saviour of the world" (1 John 4:14) and "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29).

Further, His finished work broke hell's powers. Colossians 2:15 speaks of the "principalities and powers" as those evil powers which have controlled humanity. There was no hope of successful resistance against them, when it looked as if death and hell had conquered Him too. But on the cross He conquered death itself, along with all other hostile forces. In His victory all who believe in Him have a share: "Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Cor. 15:57).

Thus, the saving work of Christ includes the reconciliation of sinners to God (2 Cor. 5:19; Col. 1:20). It also brings them together as human beings. Hostile divisions of humanity have peace with one another through Him (Eph. 2:14).
2.2.2 	The present work of Christ

The present work of Christ begins with the exaltation by God, after the completion of His "finished" work in His death and resurrection. The first aspect of His present work was the sending of the Holy Spirit to dwell in His people (John 16:7). The fulfillment of this promise was announced by Peter on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:33), a promise that can be traced back to John the Baptist, who prophesied that Jesus would "baptize you with the Holy Spirit" (Mark 1:8).

The present work of Christ that receives the main emphasis in the New Testament is His 
intercession. Paul, quoting what appears to be an early Christian confession of faith, spoke of "Christ who died, and furthermore is also risen, who is even at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us" (Rom. 8:34; Heb. 7:25).

Jesus' presence with God as His people's representative provides the assurance that their requests for spiritual help are heard and granted. To know that He is there is a powerful incentive for His followers. No good thing that Jesus seeks for them is withheld by the Father.

The exaltation of Christ is repeatedly presented in the New Testament as the fulfillment of Psalm 110:1: "Sit at My right hand, till I make your enemies your footstool." This means that Christ reigns from His present place of exaltation and must do so until all His enemies are overthrown. Those enemies belong to the spiritual realm: "The last enemy that will be destroyed is death" (1 Cor. 15:26).
2.2.3 	The future work of Christ

During His earthly ministry, Jesus declared that He had works to do in the future: the raising of the dead and the passing of final judgment. To raise the dead and to judge the world are prerogatives of God, but He delegated these works to His Son, to discharge at the time of the end.

The raising of the dead and the passing of judgment are associated with the Second Coming of Christ. When Paul dealt with this subject, he viewed Christ's appearing in glory as the occasion when His people would share His glory and be displayed to the universe as the sons and daughters of God, heirs of the new order. He added that all creation looks forward to that time, when it "will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God" (Rom. 8:21).

Both the present work of Christ and His future work are dependent on His "finished" work. That "finished" work was the beginning of God's "good work" in His people. This work will not be completed until "the day of Jesus Christ" (Phil. 1:6), when the entire universe will be united "in Christ" (Eph. 1:10).

blocks.text: This is a central doctrine of Christianity that affirms that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day. Without the resurrection, the apostle Paul declared, Christian preaching and belief are meaningless (1 Cor. 15:14). The resurrection is the point at which God's intention for Jesus becomes clear (Rom. 1:4) and believers are assured that Jesus is the Christ. So significant is the resurrection of Jesus that without it there would be no church or Christianity, and we would still be in our sins (1 Cor. 15:17). What do we need to know about the resurrection?
3.1.1 	It is the Foundation of the Christian Faith

The resurrection of Jesus Christ lifts Christianity from the level of philosophy, or a mere code of conduct, to the supreme stature of God's good news for the human race. In the resurrection God set His seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God, and underlined the value of His death. It was the resurrection that transformed the followers of Jesus, and sent them out into the world to preach the good news. The resurrection is the pivot of the Christian faith (1 Cor. 15:12-19; Rom. 1:4). It is non-negotiable.
3.1.2 	It is an Event Supported by Evidence

If we enquire into the evidence for the resurrection, we are confronted first by the factual evidence. There is the empty tomb, containing only the abandoned grave clothes, and the persistent failure of all explanations other than that Christ had risen. Also to be faced are the numerous reported appearances of the risen Jesus, at different times and before different people.

There is also the psychological evidence. For example, there are the transformed disciples, the conviction of the early church in the face of persecution, and the change from Saturday to Sunday as the Christian day of worship (after centuries of Sabbath worship) (John 20:1-29; 1 Cor. 15:1-8).
3.1.3 	It is a Promise of Ultimate Victory

If Christ had not been raised from the tomb, His death would have been evidence enough for the failure of his mission. Thus the resurrection gives positive assurance that the Christian believer has not believed in vain. The mission of Jesus did not end in failure, but in triumph. Ultimately all things, even the "last enemy", death itself, must submit to the victory and rule of Jesus (1 Cor. 15:24-28; Acts 17:30, 31).
3.1.4	It is the Power of Christian Experience

To the Christian, the resurrection of Christ is far more than a past event of history. It plays a vital part in Christian living in the present, and colours the outlook, hopes and motives of every believer.

The New Testament teaches that Christians must be ready to be like Jesus Christ in His life and death. This means that when we are willing to die to self interest (as Jesus died) then we will be able to live a new life (as Jesus rose to new life). The Christian lives and works in the very power by which God raised Jesus from the dead (Phil. 3:10, 11; Rom. 6:5-14).
3.1.5 	It is the Assurance of Eternal Security

Christ's victory over death has made immense changes in the area of sorrow and bereavement. The finality has been taken out of death. All those who die can know that Christ has been through this experience before them, and will bring them through it to be with Him.

Furthermore, because Christ's body was raised from death, the Christian has the guarantee that he or she too will receive in eternity a resurrection body of beauty and strength. This new body will be related to the old, but without weakness or decay (John 11:25, 26; 1 Cor. 15:20, 42-57).

blocks.text: Christ was unlike any prophet or religious teacher that ever lived. By his authority and deeds and by the power of his teaching and his example, he challenged his hearers to believe in him as the unique Son of God. The following are the aspects of Christ's ministry that distinguish him from any religious leader who ever lived:
4.1.1 	Authority that convinced

The authority with which Jesus taught astonished the people who heard him. The prophets of old repeatedly declared "The Lord says. . ." but Jesus directed his hearers towards himself saying, "But I tell you. . ." The Jewish leaders of Jesus' day took their authority from the great teachers of the past, but Christ taught in his own name and authority (Matt. 5:21, 22, 27, 28, 31-34; 7:24-29).
4.1.2 	Parables that provoked
The teaching of Jesus Christ was given in terms and images understood in daily life, and this is particularly true of his unforgettable parables which both concealed and revealed truth.

People would often be fascinated by the story of the Great Banquet, the Prodigal Son or the Rich Fool, only to discover that the parable had been about themselves (Mark. 4:2; Matt. 13:10-17; Luke 15:11-32).
4.1.3 	Miracles that confirmed

Christ's authority was further demonstrated by his miracles. The wind and the waves were obedient to his command, and even the dead were brought back to life. But most of his miracles were acts of healing that were part of his mission of love. They also pointed to his identity as the Son of God and to the coming of God's kingdom (Mk. 1:23-28; In. 10:31-33).
4.1.4 	Compassion that attracted

Christ's deep concern for people was born from his understanding that human beings are created in God's own image, but that they are also fallen and live in a fallen world. Because of this, Christ showed care and concern for the individual. This can be seen in his many encounters with the bereaved, the sick and the demon-possessed. The crowds were quick to recognize the high value that Jesus placed on the individual, and they came to him in large numbers (Matt. 9:35-38; 15:32-39; John. 11:30-44).
4.1.5 	Training that prepared

Towards the beginning of the second year of Jesus' public ministry, the twelve disciples were chosen to share in his work of teaching, preaching and healing. These men learned 
from Christ's example and from the private instruction he gave them. He also trained them for their future work as they (and some seventy others) were sent out to do his work.

The Twelve did not understand all that was being taught them at the time, but their training was to be vitally important in the future development of the Church (Matt. 10:1-15; 16:13-21; 1 John 1:1-4).
4.1.6 	Controversy that challenged

From the outset the words and actions of Jesus had a controversial cutting edge that finally provoked a collision between him and the Jewish authorities. Jesus clashed with the Jewish leaders over the following issues: that he mixed with sinners, challenged traditions, liberated the Sabbath, and that he claimed to be God (Mark 2:5-7, 15, 16; Matt. 23:13-36; 26:62-66).
It is a remarkable fact that while Jesus directed his hearers towards himself, he never at any time gave the impression of being conceited, arrogant or selfish.

blocks.text:
The four Gospels present the reader with selected significant events in Christ's life. The 
following are of particular importance:
5.1.1 	His Humble Birth

Jesus was born during the reign of the Roman emperor Caesar Augustus, into an extremely poor family. He was born in alien surroundings during a Roman census, and he was born into immediate danger - as King Herod searched to kill him.

These two elements, the humility and insecurity of Jesus' birth, were to set the pattern 
of his whole life (Luke 2:1-7; Matt. 2:1-18; Luke 9:57, 58).
5.1.2 	His Sinless Baptism

The baptism of Jesus marks the beginning of his ministry. John the Baptist was calling his hearers to a baptism of repentance. Jesus, however, had no sin of which he could repent. But by his submission to John's baptism, he showed his identification with sinful humanity. The descent of the Spirit like a dove and the Father's words of acceptance, which accompanied the baptism, came as God's approval of the ministry that was to follow (Matt. 3:13-17).
5.1.3 	His Prolonged Temptation
Immediately following his baptism, Jesus went into the desert for a period of forty days, during which he fasted, and was tempted by the Devil.

The temptations that are recorded for us took the form of challenging Jesus to by-pass his mission. Jesus successfully resisted these and all the other temptations that occurred throughout his life (Matt. 4:1-11; Luke 4:1-13).
5.1.4 	His Revealing Transfiguration
Towards the end of his public ministry Jesus took three of his disciples to a mountain- top where he became brilliantly irradiated before them.

Moses and Elijah appeared, and spoke with Jesus about his coming ordeal in Jerusalem. 
The disciples also heard a voice of divine approval, as at Christ's baptism. The event was clearly a preview, in miniature, of Christ's glory that lay ahead (Luke 9:28-36).
5.1.5 	His Obedient Death

The tide of events turned against Jesus after his triumphant entry into Jerusalem. The Passover meal that he celebrated with his disciples was swiftly followed by his betrayal, 
by a series of unjust trials, by death on a cross and by burial.

It was a dark hour, but it was the hour for which Jesus had come into the world. He 
made it clear that he had come, not only to teach and heal, but also to suffer and die for 
all humanity (Matt. 26; 27; Luke 22:53).
5.1.6 	His Victorious Resurrection

Thirty-six hours after the burial, Jesus' tomb was found empty, except for the discarded 
grave clothes. It was sufficient for John who 'saw and believed'.

Then Jesus began to appear to his friends over a period of forty days. This was not an 
illusion, for he took food, could be touched, and was seen alive by hundreds of people. 
And yet he was uniquely and powerfully different - the victor over death (John 20; 21; Luke
24:36-43).
5.1.7 	His Glorious Ascension

The last time the disciples were to see Jesus was on the Mount of Olives. He commanded them to make disciples everywhere and he promised them the gift of the Spirit, who would give them the power to do this. He was then taken from them, visibly. He would not be seen again until his return (Matt. 28:16-20; Luke 24:44-53).

chapters.title: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

blocks.text:
During the latter period of his earthly life Jesus promised his disciples that after he had departed this world he would send the Counsellor (Comforter) to them (John 16:7). After 
the Lord had ascended into heaven the promise was fulfilled on the Day of Pentecost. 
After the Pentecost experience, the disciples realized that although Jesus was no longer 
with them in the flesh, he was with them in an even more effective way through the 
presence of the Holy Spirit in their hearts, The disciples no longer had to depend upon 
Jesus' bodily presence since they were aware of his power at work within and through 
them.

Consequently, as the disciples went into Europe and Asia Minor, around the Eastern 
Mediterranean, spreading the Good News of what the love of God had done in Jesus, all 
those who heard them and believed also came to experience Jesus as their Lord and 
Saviour though they had neither seen nor heard him speak. The gospel continues to be 
preached and the power which made, and still makes possible, the miracle experienced by the disciples then and today, has never diminished. This is the work of the Holy 
Spirit.
Who then is the Holy Spirit?

reference.chapter: II. THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶2930)

topics.title: The Deity of the Holy Spirit

blocks.text: In this section we shall try and find out whether the Holy Spirit is God.

The Spirit was associated with the work of creation; he gives the Christian new life; he is the source of all knowledge, the guide and helper of the Church in all ages; and he makes salvation a real experience to individuals. Also the apostle Peter equated lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God (Acts 5:3, 4).
The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity (Matt. 28:19; 2 Cor. 13:14). He is presented in the Bible as a person fully worthy of worship.
1.1.1	The Spirit possesses divine attributes; he is:
Holy 		-	Luke 11:13 (". . .the Holy Spirit. . ." The word holy is not a noun
but an adjective describing his character)
Eternal 		-	Hebrews 9:14
Omnipotent	-	Genesis 1:2; Job 26:13; Luke 1:3:35
Omniscient	-	1 Corinthians 2:10, 11; John 14:26; 16:12, 13
Omnipresent	-	Psalm 139:7-10
Truth 		-	1 John 5:6
1.1.2 	The Holy Spirit does things that only God can do
a) 	He was associated with the work of creation (Gen. 1:1, 2; Job 33:4; Ps. 104:30).
He makes salvation a real experience to individuals (1 Cor. 6:11; Eph. 1:13).
He gives the Christian new life (John 6:63).
He is the author of the new birth John 3:5,6).
He makes prophecy possible (2 Peter 1:21).
He convinces people of righteousness and of judgment to come (John 16:8-11).
1.1.3 	The Descent of the Holy Spirit
One of the clearest indications of the full divinity of the Holy Spirit is given by Jesus when he promised to send the Spirit to the disciples (In. 14: 16; 15:26).
He is included in the Christian formula of baptism and in the apostolic blessing (Matt. 28:19; 2 Cor. 13:14).
The apostle Peter equated lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God (Acts 5:3,4).

When Christ had left the world, the Spirit was given his most specific work. The book of Acts (which is the account of the early Church) portrays the Spirit as directing and controlling the new Christian movement.

topics.title: The Person of the Holy Spirit

blocks.text: 2.1.1 	The Importance of Knowing the Holy Spirit as a Person

The Holy Spirit is a living Person, the Holy God, equal to the Father and Son, therefore, he ought to be worshipped as they are. Theoretically this is done in the Doxology and Gloria Patri. His name is linked with the Father and Son in the Benediction and Baptismal formula.

The Spirit is not just an influence or power, so we cannot refer to him as "It" as some people erroneously do, and desire to get more of "it" instead of allowing him to get more of them. He is a Person, for this reason, we must address him with proper nouns such as "He" and "Him."

The Holy Spirit is a Person. Consequently, we must get to know him more intimately and personally. The Holy Spirit, being God, is personal. He is much greater than any individual person we have ever known and the relationship between him and us can best be understood in personal terms. That is how Jesus taught us to think about God.
2.1.2 	Characteristics of the Holy Spirit

As discussed earlier, the Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force, and therefore cannot be 
referred to as "It." The Holy Spirit is a living being who is self-conscious and therefore, 
has the following characteristics:

He has Knowledge: The Holy Spirit is more than a force; he is a person, with a character of his own. The Bible teaches that it is through the Holy Spirit that God knows us completely. It is the mind of the Spirit that helps to shape the life of the Christian.
Jesus declared that the Holy Spirit would remind the apostles of his words and teaching (John 14:26). He reveals, interprets and applies the deep things of God (1 Cor. 2:9-14).
He has Intelligence: It is only a person who has the ability to search, know things and to teach (Neh. 9:20; Rom. 8:27).

He has Emotion: Because the Holy Spirit is a person, naturally, he has feeling, as we understand the term, for humanity has been made in God's image. As a result, he loves (Rom. 15:30); it is possible to make him sad (Eph. 4:30); he can also be insulted (Heb. 10:29) – and therefore we must be careful, in what we say and do, not to insult the Spirit who lives in us. The Bible challenges us to bring glory to God by the quality of our lives and characters. In this way we will please the Holy Spirit.

He Acts: The same Spirit who was involved in the creation, who equipped God's leaders in the past and inspired the prophets, is the same Spirit who came in power upon the early Church, and acted in it and through it. Throughout the Bible we can see his active personality.

For example, the New Testament shows us that the Spirit convicts people of their sins (John 16:8); he leads and instructs Christ's followers On.16: 13); he speaks Rev. 2:7; he assures Christians that they belong to Christ (Rom. 8:16); he intercedes  (Rom. 8:26, 27); he forbids certain courses of action and appoints leaders for the Church (Acts 8:29; 16:6-8; 20:28). In such ways we see that the Spirit is a person who acts decisively in executing God's plans.
e) 	He has will Power: The Spirit makes decisions (1 Cor. 12:11).
2.1.3 	His Names and Emblems (Descriptions)
The character and activities of the Holy Spirit are emphasized through the various names and descriptions by which he is known.

reference.subject: Christian Doctrine
reference.chapter: II. THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
reference.topic: 2.1 The Person of the Holy Spirit
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT — The Person of the Holy Spirit (syllabus ¶2970)

blocks.text: The Holy Spirit: The third person of the Trinity is best known by this name. It was the name used by Jesus in his final words of promise to his disciples, and by Peter in his sermon on the Day of Pentecost. The name conveys the Spirit's holiness and opposition to sin (Acts 2:32, 33).

The Spirit of God: This title is used many times in both Old and New Testaments. It signifies both that the Spirit is God, and that he has God's power. He is not an attribute of God, but God himself. Jesus claimed that it was by the Spirit of God that he confronted the demonic world of his day (Matt. 12:28).

The Spirit of Christ: This title brings great comfort and assurance to Christian believers, because it shows us that Christ was true to his word by not leaving his followers desolate when he ascended to heaven. The Spirit was sent in fulfillment of Christ's promise: "I will come to you" (Rom. 8:9).

The Spirit of Truth: The apostles were assured that the Holy Spirit would enable them to' remember Christ's teaching and lead them into all the truth. The reader of the Bible may be thankful for its trustworthy, divine authorship (John. 16:13, 14).

The Counsellor or Helper: The literal meaning of the term "Counsellor" is one who comes alongside. This name is reassuring for Christians facing temptation, doubt, demanding service or opposition (John 16:5-7).

topics.title: The Emblems of the Holy Spirit

blocks.text: The emblems of the Holy Spirit throw light upon both his nature and mission.

Wind: Wind here indicates unseen power, and the main ideas conveyed are mystery, 
sovereignty and energy. This vivid description of the Spirit's activity is used in the Bible as in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones being given new life (Ezek. 37:1-14); Christ's words to Nicodemus in John Chapter-S On. 3:8), and the sound of rushing wind at Pentecost (Acts 2:1, 2).

Water: Water indicates life and cleansing (Isa. 44:3). The key reference to the Spirit's work as water comes from some words Christ spoke. Jesus talked about streams of life-giving water flowing from those who believe in him. He was clearly talking about the life-giving activity of the Holy Spirit On. 7:37-39).
Fire: Fire indicates
the presence of the Lord (Ex. 3:2)
the protection of the Lord (Ex. 13:21)
the approval of the Lord (Lev. 9:24)
the purifying from the Lord (lsa. 6: 1-8)
the judgment of the Lord (Heb. 12:29)

The Prophet Malachi predicts the coming of God's messenger in terms of refining fire (Mal. 3:1-3), and this picture is reiterated in the New Testament; John the Baptist said that Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire (Matt. 3:10-12). It is possible that the tongues of flame at Pentecost were meant to show the Spirit's refining activity (Acts 2:3).

Oil: Oil indicates light, healing, and anointing for service. In the Old Testament, anointing with oil was a sign that God had chosen someone for a particular task. In this way, priests or kings were set apart for God's service. The Bible tells us that Jesus was "anointed" by the Spirit, and this is also true for his followers (Ex. 30:30; Luke 4:18; Acts 10:37, 38; Heb. 1:9; 1 In. 2:20).

The Dove: The dove indicates purity, peace, and modesty. The Spirit, in the form of a dove, descended upon Jesus at his baptism (Mk. 1:9-11; In. 1:32, 33). Without doubt Jesus possessed the Spirit already, however, this event pictures the gentleness associated with the dove. This gentleness would characterize Christ's work.
A Seal: A seal indicates ownership, finished transaction, identification, security, value, authority, genuineness (2 Cor. 1:22; Eph. 1:13; 4:30).
It is important to note that these images are nothing more than pictures meant to help us appropriately describe the work of the Spirit.

topics.title: The Work of the Holy Spirit

blocks.text: 3.1.1 	His Activity (General)
The Holy Spirit is mainly featured in the Bible for his work in the lives of men and women. He is responsible for the following activities:
He Convinces of Sin: Because the Holy Spirit knows as a person, it follows that the lives of individuals are open to his scrutiny. Our needs can be fully met by him, for he is God.

As Spirit of truth, his work is to convince the unbeliever of being wrong. This is not achieved by human means - it only takes place as the Holy Spirit makes the message of the Bible a living force in a person's heart and conscience. In this way, the Holy Spirit opens the eyes of men and women to their true spiritual condition (John 16:8- 11; Eph. 6:17; Heb. 4:12).

He Illuminates Truth: As it was the Holy Spirit who inspired the writing of God's word, so it is he who shows us what the Bible means. He makes the words of the Bible understandable and relevant to our lives.
Without the enlightening work of the Holy Spirit, the truth of God's message remains misty, and can even appear nonsensical and offensive (John 14:25, 26; 16:13; 1 Cor. 2:1214).

He Reveals Christ: The apostles were taught that when the Spirit came in power upon them, his task would be to focus the spotlight not on himself, but on Christ. This is the pattern of Christian experience. From Pentecost, the disciples became aware, not so much of the Spirit who was now controlling their lives, but of Christ and his love. It was indeed the Spirit of Christ who ruled them (John 15:26; 16:14; Acts 7:55).

In having the Holy Spirit, we have Christ. Thus the late Archbishop William Temple described the Holy Spirit as "first and foremost the special and distinctive influence which God exerts over our souls as we respond to his love in the human life of Christ."

He Lives in Believers: The Old Testament recognizes that the Spirit works in a selective way, limiting his activity to certain individuals and tasks. But the prophets predicted a coming time when God would put his Spirit permanently within the lives of all his people. This prophecy was finally fulfilled on the day of Pentecost.

The apostle Paul writes of Christ making his home in the hearts of his disciples, for it is the Spirit's work to make Christ real to the Christian. No one who belongs to Christ is without the Spirit. He empowers and equips us for the whole of life (Ezek. 36:26, 27; Eph. 3:16, 17; Rom. 8:9-11).
He Inspires Prayer: Because the Spirit is the Counsellor or Helper, we may look to him for assistance in all forms of Christian service and spiritual warfare.
In particular, the Spirit helps us to pray, because he understands our weaknesses. He prevents prayer from degenerating into mere mechanical drudgery or powerless routine (Rom. 8:26; Eph. 6:18).

He Prepares for Heaven: The entire Christian life is a life directed by the Spirit. The Christian has been set free from the control of sin, and God no longer judges him for it. However, although sin no longer controls, the disciple of Christ faces a life-long battle to develop a holy character (Rom. 8:1-4,16,17; 2 Cor. 3:18).

It is the Spirit who helps a Christian in this battle and prepares him or her for the glory of heaven. It is vital that we do not underestimate what takes place when the Holy Spirit enters a person's life and personality. All Christian growth happens because of him.
3.1.2 His Activity in the Christian
From the beginning of Christian discipleship, the Holy Spirit lives within the Christian. He gives the Christian the power to follow Christ, confidence in believing, and unity with other Christians.

Life - New Birth by the Spirit: Without the power of God, an individual is considered to be "dead", spiritually. He shows no signs of life as far as God is concerned. The Bible teaches that the gift of new life is available because of the death of Christ on the cross.

This new birth is brought about by the Holy Spirit in the life of a person who responds to the good news of Christ. According to the Bible, that person can be described as a new being and an inheritor of God's kingdom. The new birth is not earned by personal achievement - it is God's free gift (John 3:3-8; 2 Cor. 5:17; Titus 3:4- 7).

Assurance - The Witness of the Spirit: The Holy Spirit comes to assure the Christian of the reality of his new relationship with Christ. He confirms that Christ's death will always be sufficient to provide complete forgiveness for sins.

He also confirms that the new believer is a child of God, and that the Bible's promise of eternal life is to be believed. The changing life and desires of the new Christian are a part of this inner witness by the Holy Spirit (Rom. 8:15, 16).

Unity - Fellowship in the Spirit: Every Christian has received the Holy Spirit, and is
said to have been "baptized in the Spirit". "Baptism" includes the ideas of entrance and membership. The Christian is brought into the life of the Spirit at conversion and is united to all other Christians in the body of Christ's Church (Mark 1:8; 1 Cor. 12:13; Eph. 4:3-6).
Ownership - The Seal of the Spirit: The presence of the Holy Spirit in a person's life is the invisible yet permanent stamp of God's ownership upon that life.

Two ideas are present here. First, we belong to God - and therefore cannot be separated from his love Rom. (8:38, 39). Second, we are given guarantee that God will keep us securely (Eph. 1:13, 14). Eventually, God will claim his own people finally and completely (Eph. 4:30).

Power - the Fullness of the Spirit: Christians are commanded to be filled with the spirit, as a continuous and regular experience (Eph. 5:18). This is not something that only happens once. We are filled with the Spirit so that our lives may be holy and our work for Christ effective (Acts 4:31). To be filled, we must obey God and submit to his rule; we must turn from evil daily and depend upon God's power; we must give ourselves in the service of other people.

Confidence - The Pledge of the Spirit: The Bible teaches that the Holy Spirit is given to the Christian as a foretaste of all that God has prepared for his people in the future. As we experience a small part of the fullness of life that God will one day give us, the Holy Spirit encourages us to press on. He makes us more confident about the future God has planned for us. A great deal of our life in the Spirit consists in living out and developing what God has already given us. (2 Cor. 5:5; 1 Cor. 2:9, 10)
3.1.3 	The Fruit of the Spirit

In Galatians Chapter 5, Paul states the principle of fruit bearing. The fruit is produced by yielding to the sweet influences that are about us. "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such, there is no law" (Gal. 5:22-23). Notice it is singular; is, not are. One can argue about the grammar used here, but it happens to be singular in the Greek. There are not nine fruits, but one fruit composed of nine elements. The Holy Spirit produces one kind of fruit, that is, Christ-likeness.
The word fruit is significant for the following reasons:

It means the result, product, outcome, or effect produced by the Spirit in the 
believer's life.
Unlike "the gifts of the Spirit" (plural), only some of which are given to a Christian, each believer is to have all nine virtues composing "the fruit of the Spirit" (singular).
As a fruit on a tree takes time to grow and mature, so the Spirit does not cultivate these virtues in the believer's life overnight.
We shall look briefly at each of the nine elements of the fruit of the Spirit:

Love: Love is what God is, and what we ought to be. Christ said that his 'new' commandment was that believers should love one another. It was new because the love he had in mind was modelled on his own - a selfless, sacrificial and practical love that is revolutionary in any age. It is this self-denying, self-sacrificing, Christ- like love which is the foundation of all other graces. This kind of love is beautifully described in 1 Cor. 13.

Joy: Joy is contentment and satisfaction with God and with his dealings. This kind of New Testament joy is totally independent of circumstances. The joy of the Holy Spirit (1 Thess. 1:6), is that deep abiding, inner rejoicing in the Lord (Phil. 4:4) which differs from happiness. It is the joy of Christ's reign in the lives of Christians, inspired by the Spirit.

Christ displayed it in John 4:34. The person who is reading the Bible for the first time will be surprised to find that joy and persecution go hand in hand in numerous instances (e.g. Matt. 5:11, 12; Acts 5:41; James 1:2,3; 1 Pet. 1:3-9; 1 Pet. 4:12-14).

Peace: This could include the peace of God (Rom.5:1) as well as harmonious relations among Christians and with others (see Rom. 12:18). It is tranquility of soul (Phil. 4:7), the peace that Christ gives and which the world cannot take away.

The peace which "passes all understanding" was described by Jesus to his disciples as "my" peace (John 14:27). It does not mean the absence of trouble, but the deep peace that protects the life that is hidden in Christ.

Longsuffering: This means patience in affliction, annoyance, and persecution. Its supreme example is found in Luke 23:34. In other words, it is patient endurance and steadfastness under provocation; forbearance under ill-will, with no thought of retaliation.

The Apostle Paul longed for the readers of his letters to be tolerant and patient in the face of each other's faults. Peter pointed to the example of Christ's endurance and patience under suffering (1 Pet. 2:23).

Kindness: Kindness is gentleness, perhaps best explained in the attitude of the Lord 
toward little children (Mark 10:14). This means graciousness and kindly disposition. 
Wherever the Spirit of Christ is involved in a situation or person, kindness will be 
seen in action. We can see Christ's unique brand of kindness in his parables, in his breaking of conventions to help the outcast, and in the value he placed on the individual (Titus 3:1-5, 8).

Goodness: Goodness is kindness shown to others. This means kind but firm, beneficence, ready to do good. It was the transparent goodness of Jesus that drew people to him long before his true identity was known. Goodness is love in action. It expects no rewards, and it stems from a heart of purity and openness. It points other people to God (1 Pet. 2:11, 12).

Faith: Faith here means fidelity or faithfulness which makes one true to his or her promise and faithful to his or her task. God delights to give his servants responsibilities. As we are faithful in the small tasks God gives us, he will trust us to do greater things. The Bible reminds the Christian servant of the final day when the faithfulness of his service will be assessed (Matt. 25:14-30).

Gentleness: Gentleness is taking the lowly place as Jesus did when he washed his disciples' feet (John 13:1-17). This does not mean mildness; it is not weakness, but controlled strength. This word conveys the idea of a listening ear to hear what God has to say. It is submission to God and unselfishness to our fellow human beings. Two men who were truly meek were Moses (cf. Ex. 32) and the Lord Jesus Christ. True gentleness was seen in Jesus Christ. In the face of extreme provocation he never lost control and never flaunted his immense power (Matt. 11:28-30).

Self-control: This is rational restraint of the natural impulses. It means holding oneself in, especially regarding sex. Excess and a lack of discipline result from moral weakness, while self-control is a sign of strength and growth in character. Paul said that we should be like athletes, who go into strict training before a sporting event. Thus, when the Spirit is in control, we experience the difference he makes (1 Cor. 9:24-27).

The fruit of the Spirit is not produced by human effort. It is produced as Christians live in communion with the Lord. It is the evidence of salvation and the genuine work of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 7:17). The life of Christ is manifested by the fruit of the Spirit.
3.1.4 The Gifts of the Holy Spirit

After the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples at Pentecost, he began his ministry of gift-giving to Christians, and will continue till Christ comes again. Spiritual gifts are supernatural abilities given by the Holy Spirit to believers.

topics.title: Hallmark of the Gifts of the Spirit

blocks.text: The Gifts Glorify Christ: The main purpose of spiritual gifts is that they glorify Christ. The Holy Spirit was sent for this very purpose - to illuminate the Lordship of Jesus (1 Pet. 4:10, 11; In. 16:14).

The Gifts Involve All: It is important to note that the gifts of the Spirit are not restricted to outstanding individuals, or leaders in the Church. Each believer has at least one gift, and these gifts are to be discovered and developed, for all God's people are to be involved in Christian ministry and service of some kind (1 Cor. 12:7-11). No believer is without a gift just as no one believer possesses all the gifts. Thus, the individual members of the Church need each other (1 Cor. 12:4-12, 27-30).

The Gifts Should Unite All: The Church of Christ is likened to a body, composed of many limbs and parts, each part relating to the whole. The Holy Spirit shares various gifts to whom he wills as he wills. The gifts are given to the body of Christ. They are for the building up of the whole body, not merely for the enjoyment or enrichment of the individual members with the gifts (1 Cor. 12:7; 14:5, 12). Though not all the gifts are obvious, all the gifts are important (1 Cor. 12:22-26).

The individual believers, then, should see the abilities and functions that God has given them as gifts available for the whole body. In this respect, Paul had to correct the divided Corinthian church (Rom. 12:4, 5; 1 Cor. 12:12-26).

Gifts Lay Foundations: The Church of Christ is also likened to a building, built upon the unique and powerful ministry of the apostles and prophets, Christ himself being the stone that holds the whole building together.

The gifts which characterized the apostles may not be in evidence today in the highest sense of those callings, but there are Christians who in a sense have been sent (as the apostles) to establish the Church across new frontiers, or who speak to the Church in relevant terms (as the prophets) to encourage and build it up (Eph. 2:19-22).

Gifts Edify the Church: There is a great variety of spiritual gifts featured in the New Testament. The Christian is to make careful use of every gift received, to build up harmony and unity in the fellowship.

It is important that individual believers are not jealous of the gifts of others, nor insist on the superiority of their own. As we use God's gifts, we should be humble and look for ways in which we can serve others (Eph. 4:11-13).

Gifts Promote Mission: The gifts of the Spirit are given for more than building up the Church - they are given to widen its boundaries. However corrupt and challenging their environment, Christ's followers are called - individually and collectively - to use their gifts in proclaiming the good news, vigorously co-operating with the Spirit of God in making mature disciples (Col. 1:27-29; 1 Cor.14:24, 25).
Below is a Table of Reference of the Gifts of the Holy Spirit: Four passages of Scripture list some of the gifts: Roman. 12:6-8; 1 Corinthians 12:8-10; Ephesians 4:11, 12; 1 Peter 4:10, 11.
h) 	The Abuse of the Spiritual Gifts
Not using the gifts in love (1 Cor. 13:1).
Not using those gifts imparted to us (1 Tim. 4:14; 2 Tim. 1:6).
Attempting to use those gifts not imparted to us.

While the fruit of the Spirit is concerned with character, the gifts of the Spirit relate to abilities and functions distributed among believers. All the fruit should be exhibited in every Christian but the gifts differ widely from person to person.
Everyone has "natural" gifts from birth, which are given by God. By giving these back to him, they can be enhanced and made use of by Christ as they learn to follow him.

blocks.text: It is true that "three persons-in-one-Godhead" is a mystery no one can understand. St. Augustine, who wrote a long book about it, said that he spoke of it only in order not to keep silent. And the great contemporary theologian, Karl Barth, has written, "When we have said what is meant by Father, Son and Spirit in God, we must continue, and say that we have said nothing." But this mystery is far too central to the Christian faith either to be unthinkingly accepted because we are supposed to, or to be casually shrugged off because no one can explain it.

blocks.text:
The Church slowly formulated this doctrine in opposition to false interpretations of the 
Christian faith, specifically with the question of the deity of Jesus Christ. Early Church Fathers such as Irenaeus, Origen and Tertullian were responsible for the formulation of the doctrine. Under the leadership of Bishop Athanasius the doctrine was proclaimed as the faith of the Church at the Council of Nicaea in AD 325, and at the hands of Bishop Augustine, a century (one hundred years) later, it was accepted by Trinitarian churches. Without going into the details of a debate which went on for a century (one hundred years) long, we shall look briefly at some ancient trinitarian heresies (false views).

topics.title: Some Heresies (False Views about the Trinity)

blocks.text: Modalism: This view teaches that the one God assumes different forms, or plays different roles. In the beginning God acted as Creator and Law-giver. Later in history when things went wrong, he revealed himself as the Redeemer, and then later, he revealed himself as the Holy Spirit who is the Enlightener and Sanctifier.

It must, however, be noted that God did not as a matter of urgency become threefold for the purpose of creation, redemption and sanctification. As William Barclay emphasizes, "God is always, from eternity (before time), through time, and when time shall end, Creator, Redeemer, Sustainer and Enlightener." And as A. Wainwright puts it, "God redeems through Christ in the power of the Holy Spirit."
ii) Tri-Theism: This teaching pictures and presents the three persons of the Godhead (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) as consisting of three separate (but co-operating) Gods.
The emphasis of Tri-theism is the Three-ness of God but it overlooks the Oneness or the indivisible unity of God.

reference.chapter: III. THE DOCTRINE OF THE TRINITY
reference.topic: 1.2 Some Heresies (False Views about the Trinity)
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF THE TRINITY — Some Heresies (False Views about the Trinity) (syllabus ¶3154)

blocks.text: The early Church rejected the false solutions of Tri-Theism and Modalism and worked out its own statement about the Trinity. Its alternative was not really a solution to the problem of how God is one and yet three, three and yet one. All it really did was to affirm both God's oneness and his genuine presence and work in Christ (and in the Spirit). The one God makes Himself known to us and works in our world and our individual lives in three different ways. But in each of these three ways of his presence and working, we really have to do with the one God himself, not with three gods, nor with a hierarchy of divine beings, nor with masks which hide who the one behind them really is.

The ancient Church said this in the language and concepts available to it at the time. Even then it had no adequate way of expressing what it wanted to affirm; its formulation was open to misunderstanding, and it was often misunderstood. The ancient formula is even more difficult to understand in our time; they have actually changed meaning over the years. Let us look briefly at what this doctrine affirms.

One God in Three Persons: The Westminster Confession preserves the doctrine of the Trinity formulated by the ancient Church with these words: "In the unity of the Godhead there are three persons of one substance, power, and eternity. . ." The Belgic Confession says the same thing: "God is one in essence, yet distinguished in three persons." If we are to understand what the doctrine affirms, then, we must try to understand what it means when it expresses the unity of God with the concepts "one essence" or "one substance," and what it means when it expresses the distinctions in God and his work by speaking of "three persons."

Unity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit: One essence or one substance originally meant that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are the same in being or identical in being. It meant, as Karl Barth has put it, in God there are not three divine "I's" but one "I." In other words when we have to do with the Father or with the Son or with the Spirit, we have to do not with a part of God, or someone possessing divine characteristics, or with a different God; we have to db with the one God himself. The Father is God; the Son is God; the Spirit is God - all one and the same God, expressing Himself simultaneously in different ways.

The Distinctions within God and His Work: It is very important to note that there are not three persons or personalities in God. God is only one person. When we speak of God as personal or as a person, we refer to the one person who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, the fact that we can speak of this one person only in a three-fold way does mean that there are distinctions within the richness of God's being and work. "One God in three persons" means one God who has at the same time three distinct "ways of existence" as God or "ways of being" God.
We should, however, be careful not to fall back into the heresy of modalism:
So long as we remember that these three ways of being are not just masks behind which the real God is hidden, but ways in which God himself lives and works;

So long as we remember that God lives and works in these three ways, not in temporal succession (as if there were first the Father, then the Son, then the Spirit), but simultaneously. God always has been, is and always will be the one God who both in Himself and in His work has three ways of existence.

The one God lives and works as Father, as Son, and as Holy Spirit. In order to express the richness of God's being and work in these three ways, the church (following the Bible) has attributed different works to each. For example, Paul Tillich says, ". . .the threefold manifestation of God as creative power, as saving love, and as ecstatic transformation."

Also, R.P.C. Hanson says, "We know God in three different activities and three different manifestations of himself; we find him and know him as the Father who is approaching us in Christ, as the Son who is God entering human history and human life to save us, and as the Holy Spirit who is God in whom we perceive God's activity towards us and in whom we respond to that activity."

Many analogies have been devised to express these distinctions in the life and work of God. None of them is really adequate. The unity and distinction between God the Father, Son and Spirit are absolutely unique, comparable to nothing else. Nevertheless, these analogies can perhaps help us to catch a glimpse of how the one God may exist and work in three different ways at the same time. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are like the sun, the rays of the sun and the heat generated by the sun. They are like the spring, the stream and the lake which as a single whole make up a river. They are like water in the form of liquid, ice and steam. They are like memory, understanding and love which exist in the innermost being of one person.
The doctrine of the Trinity states that "God is One in his 'Essential being' but that in this 'Being' there are three Persons, yet so as not to form separate and distinct enrichments."

It seeks to emphasize the personal distinctions as well as the indivisible unity of God. In the being of God there are not three individuals but only three personal self- distinctions within the one divine essence. Each person in the Trinity is self- conscious and self-directing, yet never acting independently or in opposition.

topics.title: The Biblical Source of the Doctrine of the Trinity

blocks.text: The Bible does not teach the doctrine of the Trinity. Neither the word "trinity" itself, nor such language as "one-in-three," "three-in-one," one "essence" or "substance," or three "persons" is biblical language. The language of the doctrine is the language of the ancient Church, taken not from the Bible but from classical Greek philosophy. The Church used the language and concepts available to it to interpret what the Bible itself says about God and his dealings with humanity in the world. The question is whether this language is adequate, or whether we ought to find new ways to say it.

While we cannot find the doctrine itself spelled out in Scripture, we can find there the 
roots of the doctrine, for example:
1.4.1 	Roots of the Trinity in the Old Testament

Creation: In the creation story, Elohim is seen to create by means of Word and Spirit 
(Gen. 1:1-3).
Here is revealed a threefold centre of activity in which God the creator thought out the universe, expressed his thought in a Word and made his Spirit its animating principle.
Also, the name Elohim in Gen. 1:1 is plural in form but is joined to a singular verb.

The creation of man and the use of personal pronouns in the plural form: It is thought that in Genesis 1:26 "And God said, 'let us make man in our image and after our likeness', by implication, reveals God as the Triune God.
ii) 	The Three Fold Aaronic Blessing: The threefold Aaronic blessing recorded in Numbers 6:24 is a prototype of the New Testament Apostolic blessing.
1.4.2 	Roots of the Trinity in the New Testament

According to Robert Culver, there are two expressions, which have been traditionally employed to designate certain inner relations between the Father and the Son, and the Father and the Son with the Spirit. These are:
The eternal generation of the Son by the Father; and
The eternal aspiration (or procession) of the Spirit from the Father and the Son.

In scriptural language, they express the idea that the Son and the Spirit were eternal with the Godhead, John 1:14 refers to our Lord as the only begotten Son of the Father. And John 14:16, 26 speak of the Spirit as proceeding from the Father and the Son.

John the Baptist's Preaching: R. A. Finlayson suggests that it is most probable that the preaching of John the Baptist had a Trinitarian reference, as he was conscious of the presence and calling of the Spirit. He called for repentance towards God, faith in the coming Messiah and spoke of a baptism of the Holy Spirit, of which his baptism with water was a prelude. Thus the Father and the Spirit were disclosed as operating in the incarnation of the Son.

ii) 	Jesus' Baptism: At the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan the three persons can be distinguished. The Son being baptized, the Father speaking from heaven and the Spirit descending in the objective symbol of a dove.

iii) 	Jesus' Public Ministry: In his public ministry as well as in his private teaching of the Twelve, Jesus constantly directed attention to the Father as the one who sent him on his mission and from whom he derived his authority (John 5:16 and 20; Matt. 22:43).

Jesus bore clearer testimony to the Father and the Spirit appeared in the work of redemption as revealed by Christ; the Father sending the Son to undertake the work, and the Father and the Son sending the Spirit to apply the salvation which Christ wrought.

iv) 	The Baptismal Formula: The most concise expression of the Trinitarian teaching by Christ is found in the baptismal formula - Baptizing into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28: 19).

The Pentecost Experience: The apostolic conception of the Holy Spirit and of his relation to the Father and the Son is clear from Acts. Peter, in explaining the incident on the Day of Pentecost presents it as the activity of the Trinity (Acts 2:32, 33).
vi) 	The Apostolic Benediction: The apostolic church was built upon faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

In the letters of Paul, Peter, John, James and Jude, as well as in the Epistle to the Hebrews, redemption is uniformly traced to the threefold source, and each Person appears as the object of worship and adoration. The apostolic Benediction, "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God and the communion/fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all" (2 Cor. 13:14), not only sums up the apostolic teaching, but it interprets the deeper meaning of the Trinity in Christian experience, the saving grace of the Son as that which gives to the Love of the Father and the Communion of the Spirit.
From both the O. T. and the N. T. we clearly see the Trinity acting in unity in:
Creation (Gen. 1:1-3; Job 26:12,13)
Incarnation (John 3:16; Luke 2:11; 1:35)
Redemption (Heb. 9:14)
Salvation (Luke 15:4, 22; Eph. 1:13)
Communion (2 Cor. 5:19; Eph. 2:18)
Prayer (In. 16:23; Rom'-8:26)
Glory (1 Cor. 15:24; Phil. 3:21; Rev. 22:17)
Regeneration (Luke 10:20; In. 3:3-6; Eph. 1:7)

topics.title: The Relevance of the Doctrine of the Trinity

blocks.text: The doctrine of the Trinity is ultimately a practical doctrine with radical consequences for the Christian experience and life.
1.6.1 	The Trinity and Relationships

According to the doctrine of the Trinity, God lives as the mystery of love among persons. If we are created in the image and likeness of this God, and if our destiny is to live forever with this God and with God's beloved creatures, then what forms of life best enable us to live as Christ lived?
i) 	Relationship with God

The doctrine of the Trinity is a way of contemplating the mystery of God and of ourselves in relation to God. It is also the framework for reflecting on the nature of the human person, on the relationship between humankind and other creatures of the earth, on the relationship between ourselves and God. The truth about both God and ourselves is that we are meant to exist as persons in communion in a common household, living as persons from and for others, not persons in isolation or withdrawal or self-centeredness.

Christians normally are baptized into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Names express personal identity; one cannot get closer to "what" someone is than "who" they are. To live in the name of another means to appropriate their personal history and relational identity; our identity is now linked intimately with theirs.
ii) 	Relationship with others

The Godhead reveals that God is truly a living one, not an impersonal but a personal God. He relates with us, and deals with us in a personal way, at one and the same time, as loving Father, a self-giving Saviour (the Son) and a sanctified spirit (the Holy Spirit). This truth is important because it helps us to accept and affirm our personhood as well as the personhood of others. As we relate to a God who is personal, we also learn to live as such, since all persons are made in the image of a personal God. This is a moral obligation.

The Triune God is Love and is always in love. According to St. Augustine, "Without the Trinity, there can be no fellowship as love in God. He has deep affection with himself and towards us (Hos. 11:8; In. 3:16; Rom. 5:5). According to Dr. Livingstone K. Buama, "Love is the distinguishing characteristic of a true Christian. Thus, the practical demand or message for all sons and daughters of God is to abide in God's love, manifest and propagate it in word and indeed" (1 John 4:7-12).

The Trinity teaches that God is indivisibly one. In him there is unity of purpose and action. The three persons live and work harmoniously together for the promotion and final realization (consummation) of the Kingdom of God. As we worship the God of Unity we also need to pursue unity in our relationships (Eph. 4:4-6).

Finally, The Trinity brings to the fore the communal nature of God. The three persons of the Godhead live in a state of mutual co-existence, solidarity, fellowship and harmony. There is no power struggle or personality conflict within the Godhead.

Those who embrace this fact are under. a moral and spiritual obligation to promote fellowship, solidarity, and communal and harmonious existence. Through this we can promote freedom, justice, peace and prosperity (Ps. 133).
1.6.2 	The Trinity and Prayer

St. Augustine acknowledged the active presence and involvement of the Triune God in the prayer of Christians, with each of the Persons of the Trinity actively playing his distinct role - that of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
i) Father - When we pray to God as Father, we do so with the assurance that it is God Himself who has given us "the power of becoming children of God."

ii) Son - In the Christian tradition, prayers have been addressed to Christ, as well as through him and in his name. Jesus taught his disciples to pray, and went further by setting an example - praying himself.

iii) Holy Spirit - In prayer, the Holy Spirit is the Christian's master, and it is He who animates the prayer. It is He who enables us to discover God as our Father as revealed to us in Jesus Christ (the Son).

blocks.text: A creed is "a brief, authoritative, formal statement of religious beliefs." The word creed comes from the Latin word credo ("I believe"), the first words of both the Nicene Creed and the Apostles' Creed.

According to J.N.D. Kelly, "A creed is a fixed formula that summarizes the essential articles of the Christian religion and enjoys the sanction of ecclesiastical authority." Hence the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds are summaries of the essential articles of the Christian Faith, i.e., God (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), the Universal Church, the Communion of Saints, the Resurrection of the body, and Everlasting life.

Though the so-called "Apostles'/Nicene Creeds" do not go back to the Apostolic times, there are clear indications that the essential elements (the creedal fragments) are clearly indicated in the New Testament. For example, there is evidence that in the primitive church there was a corpus (a collection of writings), of distinctive Christian teachings held as sacred deposit from God (see Acts 2:42; Rom. 6:17; Eph. 4:5; Phil. 2:16; Col. 2:7; 2 Thess. 2:15; and also in the Pastoral Epistles, 1 Tim. 4:6; 2 Tim. 1:13-14; Titus 1:9).

This body of instructions, also known as "the apostles teaching," "the work of life, the 
apostolic traditions," etc. formed the basis of the Christian ministry, and was to be held firmly (Jude 3; Heb. 3:1f, 4:14 f, 10:23) handed on to other believers as the apostolic men 
themselves had received it (see 1 Cor. 11:23 ff, 15:3) and made use of in public proclamation of the gospel. This was seen especially in the Eucharist, where ceremonial declarations of faith, hymnic compositions, liturgical prayers, etc. are associated. The New Testament "creed" range in scope, from simple confessions, i.e. "Jesus is Lord" to implicit Trinitarian formulations, as in the apostolic benediction of 2 Cor. 13:14 (also Matt 28:19).
The following are the three classic, or most historically important, creeds of the church:

blocks.text: This is a creed adopted by the First Council of Nicaea (AD. 325) and revised by the First Council of Constantinople (AD. 381). The First Council of Nicaea, convened by the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great (ruled AD. 306-337), rejected a heresy known as Arianism, which denied the divinity of Jesus. The Nicene Creed formally proclaimed the divinity and equality of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, in the Trinity.

blocks.text: This well-known creed lies at the basis of most other religious statements of belief. Although it bears the name of the apostles, it did not originate with them. It was written after the close of the New Testament, and it held an important place in the early church. This creed has been appealed to by all branches of the church as a test of authentic faith.
