topics.title: History of the Formulation of the Nicene Creed

blocks.text: The whole issue of the formulation of the creed began with questions about the person of Christ. "Who was he?" "Was he God or Man?" By the beginning of the fourth century, the answer to this question was not clear. One of those who attempted to give an answer was Arius, a presbyter from Alexandria. He said the Son (Jesus Christ) was a creature and not God. For him only God the Father is unbegotten and self-subsistent. The Son is begotten, so there must have been when he was not. His main reason was that there is only one God. If it is asserted and affirmed that the Son is God, then we have two Gods.

This view was strongly opposed by Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, who suspended Arius from office. But Arius stuck to his opinions and received support from his friends and sympathizers. The dispute spread and became a threat to the unity of the church as well as the empire.

Consequently, Emperor Constantine summoned the first great ecumenical council of Bishops, to meet at Nicaea in 325. The council condemned Arianism, and drafted a creed to which all the bishops were required to give assent. This creed was not, of course, the one which we now call the Nicene creed, but it attempted the very difficult task of saying affirmatively what the essentials of Christian belief are, by saying this in such a way as to exclude any possible Arian interpretation. The most noteworthy feature of the creed of 325 was its assertion that Christ is "of one substance as the Father" or "of the same being as the Father".

The hope that Nicaea would bring peace and harmony to the church was not quickly realized. In 328 Athanasius had become bishop of Alexandria. Earlier, in his treatise entitled De lncarnatione (The Incarnation), usually dated 318, he made a contribution to

Christology before he became involved in the Arian controversy. The Christology of Athanasius is a "Christology of the Word, which took a body of the virgin." For him, Christ the Word became man that we might become God. His argument was that, "We are dependent on God and must return to God. It is only God who can save us and give us life. God is the Uncreated. God alone is the eternal one and the giver of life. A creature (even the highest) cannot reveal the uncreated to us; a creature (even the highest) cannot save us and give us eternal life."

The views of Athanasius and his supporters finally triumphed only some years after his death, at an ecumenical council held at Constantinople in 381. It was this council which agreed to what we now call the Nicene creed, though it would be more accurately called the Niceno-Constantinopolitan creed. It enshrined the word homoousios, "of the same being" or "consubstantial", as the most accurate term the church could find to express the relation of Christ to the Father. Even to this day, the creed of 381 remains the most ecumenical of all dogmatic statements in Christian churches. This does not make it immune from criticism or possible revision, but it does entitle it to a very high degree of respect. The council of 381 had another important matter to consider as well as reaffirming the findings of Nicaea. However, this is not a matter for consideration here.

At Nicaea, the doctrine of the divinity (Deity) of the Holy Spirit was also discussed but denied. However, at the Council of Constantinople in 381, the doctrine of the divinity of the Holy Spirit was discussed and was officially accepted and affirmed. According to this council, the Holy Spirit is "The Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father. Together with the Father and the Son, he is worshipped and glorified. He spoke through the prophets."

The main reason for this affirmation was that it is only through the Spirit that we can come into unity with Christ who has brought salvation. For Paul Tillich, "In order to be able to unite us with Christ, the Spirit must be as divine as Christ himself, not half divine, but fully God."

According to the Constantinopolitan Creed, the Holy Spirit proceeds "from the Father." Later in the history of the Church, in the West, under the influence of St. Augustine of Hippo, the expression and the Son was added. Thus that part of the Creed reads as "And I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified." This new addition was captured in the popular Latin expression Filioque. This teaching did not originate with Augustine. It had already been expounded in one form or another by Tertullian, Hilary, Marius Victorinus and Ambrose. The Eastern Church, however, thought the phrase "from the Father and the Son" weakened the truth that all is from the Father, and preferred to say "from the Father through the Son."

topics.title: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation

blocks.text: I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth: And in Jesus Christ His only Son our Lord, Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, Born of the Virgin Mary, Suffered under Pontius Pilate, Was crucified, dead, and buried, He descended into hell; The third day He rose again from the dead, He ascended into heaven, And sitteth on the right hand of God the Father Almighty; From thence He shall come to judge the quick and the dead. J believe in the Holy Spirit; The Holy Catholic Church; The Communion of Saints; The Forgiveness of sins; The Resurrection of the body, And the life everlasting. Amen.
1.5.1 	A Brief Explanation to the Creed

The Apostles' Creed summarizes what every Christian believes. That is, whenever we say the Creed, all that we are doing is an affirmation of our FAITH, reminding ourselves of the basis of the Christian faith, as well as all that the Christian trusts and looks forward to in the future. It is the affirmation of Faith, Hope and Love of the Christian. The Christian believes in the Triune God, the Father, Son and the Holy Spirit; believes in the Church of Christ; the forgiveness of sins, and in the life hereafter where there will be no more sin, suffering, etc. (Rev. 21:1-4).
a) 	I Believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of Heaven and Earth

In this we are affirming the fact that God is the only mighty one, and also that He is the creator (Gen. 1, 2) as against Darwin's evolutionary theory. In this we are also affirming what and who we know God to be - the one who cares for us, sustains and provides for us. He is the one who brought everything, visible and invisible into being. God is therefore the only one to be worshipped.
And in Jesus Christ our Lord . . .He Will Come to Judge the Quick and the Dead

This is a summary of what was treated in Unit 1 (The Doctrine of Jesus Christ). "His only Son" - this describes the divinity of Christ (Heb. 1:1-2) "Born of the Virgin Mary" - The belief in the Virgin Birth helps us to understand the issue of Jesus being truly God and truly man. It sets our mind on the Divinity and Humanity of Jesus. "Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead and buried." - The expectation of the Jews was that they would have a Messiah who would deliver them from their enemies and bring about a glorious age of peace and righteousness for mankind (lsa. 9:1-7; Dan. 7:13-14). Because Jesus claimed to be the Messiah, criticized and vehemently attacked the teachings of the religious leaders as well as their practices, He was hated.
I Believe in the Holy Spirit
By this we are affirming our faith in the Trinity - God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Here again, much has been said in the Doctrine of the Holy Spirit).
The Holy Catholic Church

A Brief Explanation of Church: The word "church" derives from the Greek kyriake ("belonging to the Lord") and ekklesia ("assembly"). In its primary sense, 
therefore, the church is the worshipping assembly called forth by God. Indeed the noun has always had a plural as well as a singular form: the great church (or church universal) and the churches. The doctrine of the church is "ecclesiology."

The word "Church" is used in the New Testament to describe assemblies or 
meetings of Christians; it is used for:
The congregation of Christians actually meeting in one place at the same time (1 Cor. 11:18).
All those who are Christians in a town or village (Acts 11:3-8).
The Christians in a particular household (Rom. 5; Col. 4:15).
All Christians everywhere (Acts 9:31; Eph. 1:22-23).
The Church is also described as
the body of Christ as the Head (1 Cor. 12:13; Eph. 1:22-23;5:23).
the Holy Temple in which God dwells (1 Cor. 3:17; 2 Cor. 6:16; Eph. 2:21) .
the family of God (Gal. 6:19; Eph. 2:19).
ii. 	Marks of the True Church: The church of the New Testament was richly diverse.

There were various communities which placed different emphasis on various aspects of church governance. However, despite all the local differences, certain common elements stood out clearly which are described as the marks of a true church:
It accepts the full teachings of the Christian faith as spelt out in the Bible that is, faith in Jesus as Messiah and Lord.
It maintains continuity with the experience of Christians in the past - their unity and oneness of purpose, their love and joy, their devotion to duty and purity of life.
It celebrates the sacraments commanded by our Lord that is, Baptism and Holy Communion as well as other means of grace.
Its members follow the standard of life set by Christ that is different from that of other people. Even if they do not always achieve the ideal, they make the effort.
It follows the apostolic preaching and instruction.
Its members live in constant expectation of the coming kingdom of God.

iii.	Holiness of the Church: The basic meaning of the word holy is "different" or "separate". Since the Church is the "body of Christ," and Christ is pure and blameless and was set apart for a purpose, so is the Church. When we confess that the church is holy we do not mean that its members know better and are morally superior to other people. The church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives.
The following are three ways in which we can say that the church is holy or different and distinguished from other organizations or groups of people:

It is a community of people who know they are sinners, and freely admit that they are not good or superior. From the time of the prophets to the apostles, individual and social sinfulness have been identified among the people of God and have thus been addressed. (Isa. 1:1-17; Jer. 6:13; 7:1-26; Amos 5:21-27; 1 Cor. 1:10-13; 5:1, 9-13; 11:20-22; Gal. 2:11-14; Phil 1:15-17). Charles C. Morrison aptly makes the point when he says,

The church is not a society of good people; it is a society of sinners. It is the only organization in human society that takes sinners into its membership just because they are sinners. It is the only organization that keeps on saying week after week, year after year, age after age: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done, and we have done those things which we ought not to have done."

It is a community of people who are not satisfied with themselves, or with the way things are in the world around them. They are gathered together not to justify their present way of life or to publicize their holiness, but to admit publicly that they need to be forgiven for what they are, and that they want to change and need help.

It is a community which is gathered in the name of Jesus Christ who is its Head. According to Gurthrie, "Holiness is not found in the church and its members as such, but in him from whom they seek forgiveness, change, help and new direction." The church which is the body is holy only because the Head is the "Holy One."

Catholicity of the Church: The word catholic is probably derived from the Greek adverbial phrase kath' holou, which means on the whole. Hence, Catholic Church means Universal Church, that is, it consists of all people throughout the world - races, nationalities, cultures, ethnic groups, political, economic and social status, and gender, who believe in Jesus Christ as their Saviour and Lord, and believe in the Word of God. Though the word catholic is not used in the New Testament its meaning is expressed in Galatians 3:28 ". . .for you are all one in Christ Jesus" and Ephesians 4:4-6: "There is one body and one Spirit . . .one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all." (See also 1 Cor. 12:4-6.)
The Communion of Saints

The word "Communion" means sharing fellowship, and "the saints" is another name in the New Testament for the members of the Church (Eph. 1:1; Phil. 1:1). "Communion of saints" is therefore the fellowship of Christians. The phrase is not actually used in the New Testament; nevertheless the conception is there (See Col. 1:12). In 1 John 1:3f emphasis is placed on the fact that the communion of saints is based on their communion with the Father through the Son. In 2 Corinthians 13:13 we are reminded that this communion is in the Spirit.

We share our fellowship with other Christians during prayer meetings and worship 
services, Bible Class meetings, in our homes, in family prayers and as we work together. In this communion, the weak are helped by the strong, poor by the rich, and the young by the old. The meeting of this communion or this fellowship is best seen in the Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper. Prayer links all present in unity with the living Lord. The Holy Communion is central to the fellowship of the Church. As we meet at our Lord's Table, our differences and distinctions vanish, for we are all sinners in need of our Lord's forgiveness.

There are two groups of Christians - those who are still journeying on the road of life and those who have finished. Those who are still in this world and are fighting the battle on earth and have not been called home to heaven constitute the CHURCH MILITANT. Those who battled on earth and have been called home to heaven constitute the CHURCH TRIUMPHANT. As Christians we believe that the graces of the Christian character won by the soul in the fellowship of the Church are not lost with death; they live on. We who remain are linked with those who have already finished their course. They are witnesses of our lives. "As for us we have this large crowd of witnesses" (Heb. 12:1).
The Forgiveness of Sins

The issue of sin and salvation has been thoroughly discussed in Local Preachers Book 1 Part 2. (Read Rom. 3:23; 1 In. 1:8-10; Eph. 1:7). When we turn to God in sincerity and God forgives us our sins there is a remarkable change in our lives (2 Cor. 5:17).
The Resurrection of the Body and Life Everlasting

In the Christian Faith, Jesus assures us that as children of the heavenly Father, we look forward to a glorious life hereafter, usually termed "ETERNAL LIFE." It is a life, which begins here and continues after death (John 14:1-3). This life in Christ cannot be broken by physical death (Matt. 22:32; In. 6:40). According to Revelation 21:1-4; 2 Cor. 5:1, we have a home in heaven where we shall return after this earthly temple is destroyed. A home of peace and this is what we are looking forward to as Christians. (See under the Doctrine of the Last Things for further reading on the resurrection of the body).

chapters.title: THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY)

blocks.text: Christianity is a historical religion. This is so in the sense that God has acted decisively in history, revealing himself and will yet act to bring history to its predestined conclusion. The Hebrew prophets knew and attested to the fact that God decisively acts and works out his purposes in the realm of history.

Throughout the Bible we learn that humankind is accountable to God the Creator for every thought, word and deed. God the Creator and Redeemer has offered salvation in his Son Jesus Christ. This same God who is the Judge will bring every thing to judgment.

It is important to note that Christians are not in full agreement about the details of these future events. They disagree about the millennium, a period of one thousand years during which Jesus is to reign upon earth; some see this as a specific future period, some as symbolic of the age of the church in which we are now living. Even among those who accept the millennium as a specific future period there are differences as to where it fits in with other events. How do the millennium and the return of Christ relate to the period of great tribulation spoken of in Daniel 9:27 and other texts, assuming that these do in fact speak of a specific tribulation period? What about the role of Israel in prophetic events? Armageddon?

Antichrist? Regardless of the disagreements that exist among Christians concerning the millennium, the great tribulation and other problems of prophecy, most writers focus on the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body, and the final judgment as the essential and dominant elements of eschatology. Wherever the other events fit in (assuming there are other events), they at least have to fit in around those more important elements. We shall look at each of the main elements of eschatology:

reference.subject: Christian Doctrine
reference.chapter: V. THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY)
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY) — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶3376)

blocks.text: The return of Christ occupies a prominent place in the Old Testament in that most of the Old Testament prophecies concerning the coming of Christ deal, not with the first advent in which he died as our sin-bearer, but with his Second Advent in which he is to rule as king. In the New Testament, one verse in twenty-five deals with the Lord's return. The subject is mentioned 318 times in the 260 chapters. The return of Jesus Christ is mentioned in everyone of the New Testament books except Galatians (which was written with a particular and quite different problem in view) and the very short books such as 2 and 3 John and Philemon.
In the Gospels, Jesus spoke of his return quite often (See for example, Mk. 8:38; 13:26-27; John 14:3; 21:21-22).
Paul's letters are also full of the doctrine of Christ's return (1 Thess. 4:16-17; Phil. 3:20-21). Paul called the return of Jesus Christ "our blessed hope" (Titus 2:13).

Peter called the return of Christ our "living hope" (1 Pet. 1:3). John declared with conviction, "Behold, he is coming with the clouds. . ." (Rev. 1; 7). He ended the Revelation with ". . ., 'Surely I am coming soon.' Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!" (22:20).
The return of Christ is a practical doctrine and not merely an escape route for wishful thoughts. Let us look at why this is so.
1.1.1 	Reasons why the return of Jesus is a practical doctrine
During the period of the early Church Christians expressed their belief in Jesus' personal return, a return that was to be closely associated with
a period of great wickedness on earth.
the resurrection and transformation of their own bodies.
an earthly rule of the glorified Jesus and.
a final judgment of individuals and nations.

The early Christians acknowledged that their lives should be lived differently because of the return of Jesus. If we are expecting the Lord's return, that conviction ought to be seen in how we deal with social, political, economic, cultural and all other issues of concern. If we are motivated by prejudice, injustice, hatred, corruption, sexual immorality, abuse in all its forms, tearing down other people, wasting our gifts or in any other way failing to live as Christ's faithful disciples, then the return of Jesus has not made its proper impression on our thinking.

It comforts those who are suffering. It helped the early Christians. We imagine that as they suffered persecution, torment and imprisonment, entered the arena to face the lions or looked up in their cell to face their executioner, with death staring them in the face, they looked for Christ's coming and thought that perhaps in an instant and without warning Jesus would appear and call them home.

Moreover, believers in Christ have lost children, parents and close friends. Belief in the return of Jesus is comforting to them. The people of Paul's day had lost friends through death, and he wrote to them reminding them of this blessed hope. "Therefore comfort one another with these words" (1 Thess. 4:18).

The return of Christ is a practical doctrine because it is an encouragement to godly living and, at times, even to go on living - which means that it has bearing upon present history as well as upon history's end.

reference.subject: Christian Doctrine
reference.chapter: V. THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY)
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY) — Christ's Return (syllabus ¶3385)

blocks.text: The second point of the doctrine of the "end things" upon which Christians are widely agreed is the resurrection, specifically the resurrection of the bodies of believers at Christ's Second Coming. This doctrine is of tremendous importance for several reasons:

The Christian doctrine of the resurrection recognizes that death is an enemy (1 Cor. 15:26) and is therefore something unnatural, something evil that was not God's original intention for humanity. It is important to stress this because some forms of Christianity encourage a false optimism that denies the reality of the three great evils: sin, suffering and death.

On the other hand, the Christian doctrine of the resurrection speaks of victory over death provided for us by the Lord Jesus. After writing about death as an enemy, Paul went on to speak of the ultimate victory to come (1 Cor. 15:54, 57).

Death involves every part of our being. When God said to Adam and Eve in the garden, "Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall die" (Gen. 2:17), they ate of it and died. They died in every part of their being. They had a spirit, soul and body, and died in each one. They died in spirit and showed it by hiding from God. They died in soul; all the anger, lust, hate, jealousy, pride and other sins we know so well began to enter the experience of the race. Eventually their bodies died also.

When God saves us he saves us in spirit, soul and body. He gives us a new spirit in the moment of the new birth. He creates a new soul through the process of sanctification. At the resurrection he gives us a new body. The salvation he provides is a complete salvation.

Assurance of these things is ours because of Christ's resurrection. Without this, our hope of a resurrection would be no more than wishful thinking. Jesus' own resurrection provides a powerful assurance of the Christian's resurrection.

reference.subject: Christian Doctrine
reference.chapter: V. THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY)
reference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY) — Resurrection of the Body (syllabus ¶3409)

blocks.text: The coming of Christ will be a joy for Christians, who will be raised to meet him. But it will also mean the beginning of Christ's judgments for those who have contemptuously rejected the gospel. They say Jesus will come again from heaven "to judge the living and the dead."Paul told the Athenians that God "has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and of this he has given assurance to all men by raising him from the dead" (Acts 17:31). Christians acknowledge this truth every time they recite the Apostles' Creed.

This tells us that history has an end, and its end involves accountability. We shall answer for what we have done, and we shall all be judged either on the basis of our own righteousness (which will condemn us) or on the basis of the perfect righteousness of Jesus who is our Saviour.

In a sermon given on the Mount of Olives in the middle of his last week in Jerusalem, 
Jesus used three parables to teach what the final judgment would be like for those who 
refuse to face the reality of the day of accountability and go on ignoring it. These were:
The Parable of the Ten Virgins (Maidens) 	-     Matthew 25:1-13
The Parable of the Talents 			-     Matthew 25:14-30
The Parable of the Sheep and Goats 		-     Matthew 25:31-46
All three parables contain the same essential features, though each is different from the others in detail. In each case
There is a sudden return of the Lord.
Some are prepared for his coming and others are not.
There are rewards and judgments.
Those who are lost are no doubt amazed at that outcome.

chapters.title: GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD

blocks.text: Until the end of the fourth century, in both Eastern and Western Christendom, the service formally began, after a call to order by the bishop or deacon, with the reading of the lesson. While waiting for the whole congregation to assemble, Christians in earlier times either sang or had read to them other material. From the fifth century on, some of this became an invariable part of the structure of the liturgy.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: I. GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD
reference.citation: Liturgics — GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶3491)

blocks.text: These are scriptural passages selected to be read to the congregation at worship services. The selected ones in the liturgy are for guidance. Other appropriate ones could be selected to suit specific occasions. Not all are meant to be read.

Apart from preparing the congregation for a take off in the service, the sentences remind the worshiper about his/her sins which need to be confessed, and God's readiness to forgive them. This is the reason why they are not just to be read for the sake of it, but in reading them, to do it in a more meaningful way such as would appeal to the heart of the listener. Such reading of the sentences would require a responsive attitude of the listener or worshiper. Dating from the late seventh century, the readings were preceded by four distinct items: The Introit, The Kyries, The Gloria, and Collect. These are known as the preliminaries.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: I. GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD
reference.citation: Liturgics — GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD — SENTENCES (syllabus ¶3494)

blocks.text: Background Introit: comes from a Latin word "introitus" which means entry or entrance.  It is a hymn or psalm sung when the ministers enter at the opening of a service. It is a chant which accompanied the advance of the priest to the altar. Originally it was a psalm which was sung alternately with its antiphon; and later became one verse only of the psalm. The introit, according to older liturgists, dates from the fifth century, from Pope Celestine 1 (d. 432).

Sung by the choir, the Introit has a special significance, because it announces and gives an 
indication of the mystery and feast solemnized in the Holy Sacrifice. Another purpose of singing a psalm at this point was to cover the entrance of the ministers, which at a solemn 
papal mass in a large basilica would take some time. Introit introduces the service. It could be hymns sung or a psalm read.

Current Practice: This is the heritage that we have as Methodists. Today, we sing the 
Introit in preparation for the continuation of the worship service after the procession by the choir.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: I. GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD
reference.citation: Liturgics — GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD — Introit (syllabus ¶3500)

blocks.text: Background: This stands for Invocation in the Greek language, "Lord have mercy." It is found in the Old Testament (Ps. 50:1; Tobias 8:10; Judith 7:29) and in the Gospel (Matt. 9:27; 15:22; Luke17:13). It entered late into the liturgy, first in the East, perhaps in Antioch in the fourth century, then in Rome in the fifth century and thence to Gaul in the sixth century.

It was the reply of the people to the litany of the deacon which used to invite to prayer, announcing one after another the different intentions. When the diaconal litany was suppressed there remained only the invocation, and there was added to it Christe, eleison, directed to the Son. Then in the ninth century there was added a third series of Kyries addressed to the Holy Spirit, and so the number of invocations became fixed at three of the Divine Person.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: I. GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD
reference.citation: Liturgics — GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD — Kyries Eleison (Invocation) (syllabus ¶3507)

blocks.text: The Gloria is an ancient hymn of praise to the Trinity that has been in use in the Church since the second century. The opening line of the hymn is taken from Scripture (Luke 2:14), where the angels announce the birth of Christ to the shepherds. The hymn was composed in Greek some time in the second century and can be found recommended as a daily morning prayer in book VII of the Apostolic Constitutions (3rd/4th century). It was introduced to the west by St. Hilary of Poitiers (d 368), who was the first to introduce hymns into the Western Church.
In our current liturgy, the Gloria is always sung in its short form as a concluding part to some canticles and Psalms. It runs:
Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.

We do this as Methodists in recognition of the tradition to which we belong, and in  recognition that we accept the doctrine of the Trinity which is the basis of our Christian 
faith.

blocks.text: Background: It is believed to have been introduced by Leo 1 (440 61) or his immediate predecessor. The name derives from the Gallican rite, Collectio, later Collecta; and refers to the function of the prayer, to its collecting or summing up of the people's intercession, as was once thought. It is from the Latin which means to bring together into a sentence. In the fifth century, it meant "to collect prayers" i.e. to conclude the prayers, hence the concluding prayers.

It is the prayer which the priest addresses to God in the Holy Mass after the initial chants, in the name of the people, and as it were gathering together the aspirations of the assembly, and which the people make their own by the final Amen. In ancient times it perhaps concluded the Litany said by the deacon, therefore its name. Collects are noteworthy for their precision of doctrine, exquisite sense of calm religious sense, and at the same time of human understanding. In its ordinary form the collect has an invocation to, and praise of, the Father, a petition supported by a motive, and at the close introduces the meditation of our Lord. Some have expressed variant views for its purpose. While some hold that it is to conclude the entrance procession, others too believe that it is to introduce the readings.
Their form consists of:
An address to God
A clause referring to some attribute or saving act of God
The petition
The purpose for which we ask
The conclusion

blocks.text: Reading of passages from the Scripture was one of the elements of worship taken over by the Christians from the Jews (Luke 4:16-21). As early as Justin's time, readings were a feature of the pre-Eucharistic service.

In the fourth century Antiochene tradition there were two lessons from the law and 
prophets (as in the Synagogue), followed by one from the Epistle or Acts and finally one 
from the Gospel. But the use of three lessons, one Old Testament and two from the New 
Testament was far more common. It was probably the original practice in Rome, but the 
third lesson was being dropped in the fourth century. It then became customary to have 
New Testament readings on Sundays and one Old Testament reading and the Gospel on 
ferial or weekdays. Occasionally, non-scriptural texts were used. Readings from the Acts of 
the Martyrs were allowed at Mass on the appropriate feast days by the third council of 
Carthage in 397 A.D and Augustine frequently quotes from them in his sermons.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: I. GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD
reference.citation: Liturgics — GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD — THE READING/SCRIPTURAL LESSON (syllabus ¶3531)

blocks.text:
Readings should suit sermons. It is said that the selection of readings was originally  dependent on the Bishop's choice. Lessons on certain great feasts were however fixed and could not be changed e.g. the Eastertide Lectionary, the Christmas, Epiphany and Ascension Day. Sundays began to acquire fixed lessons in Antioch, in Chrysostorn's time. The period between Pentecost and Advent was the last to have fixed lessons. But the choice of readings 
was determined by various criteria.
By their appropriateness for some ceremony.
By some catchword suitable to the scene.
By the situation of the Roman stational church and the history of their martyrs.
By the proximity of the feast of some great saint honoured in Rome.

There were no authoritative lectionaries until the mid fifth century when Venerius, the Bishop of Marseilles had one drawn up for the feast days of the whole year apparently not for ferial days. The first complete Lectionary dates only from the seventh century.

blocks.text:
As early as Tertullian's time Christians used the Psalms although it was until the fourth 
century that they were sung responsorially, that is by one cantor with the people repeating a refrain between the lessons. This method was derived from Jewish practice. Psalm singing became more important in the third century. The psalm at first could be regarded as a lesson in itself and not as a response. In modern Ghanaian Methodist worship, canticles like the Te Deum Laudamus, Venite Exultemus Domino, Benedicite Omnia Opera and the Cantemus Cuncti are chanted in between the readings.

reference.citation: Liturgics — GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD — CHANT (syllabus ¶3545)

blocks.text:
The homily was one of the constituent parts of the liturgy from the earliest times, being one 
of the elements inherited from Judaism (Acts 13:15). Its essential function was to expound 
and explain the scriptures which had just been read. It was the duty of the Bishop, and the 
privilege of a priest, to preach in the liturgy. By the fourth century it had become the 
general practice in the East that all priests present who wished to do so should preach and, 
after them, the Bishop himself. In the West the danger of heresy led to priests being 
forbidden to preach. Exceptions were made in the case of Augustine when he was a priest.

blocks.text:
The recitation of the Creed belongs originally and essentially to baptism but in the 
struggles against the Christological heresies it came to be used in the Eucharist itself. It 
spread to the West where Arianism was renounced at the end of the sixth century. It was 
here recited before the Lord's Prayer as a preparation for communion.

Two centuries later Charlemagne, advised by Alcium introduced it immediately after the Gospel, and from there under imperial influence, it spread throughout the West and was eventually adopted by Rome itself after the visit of Henry II in 1014 AD.

Creeds, asstatements of faith, confirm the faithful in their faith, thus strengthening their corporate unity. Creeds should endorse what is at the core of the Christian faith as well as of the life of the wider community whose vicissitudes raise questions for the believer. The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed are the commonly used among Ghanaian Methodists in affirming our faith.

blocks.text: In the previous section, we have attempted to give a general introduction to the liturgy of the word paying critical attention to historical antecedents. The realty however, is that is that the Methodist Church Ghana, in both the new and old liturgical materials, has not been glued to these materials. We have always varied them to suit our peculiarities. In practice, every congregation has always found a way of implementing the blue prints of the liturgical material in a way that is adaptive and relevant to the people. In this section therefore, we are looking at the New Liturgy and how it can be relevant to our worship.

blocks.text:
In the new order, the call to worship is a way of calling the congregation's attention to the 
fact that the service is about to begin. After this the Choir, Singing Band and the Clergy process. In practice, however, most liturgists read an appropriate passage from the Bible 
and/or say a word of welcome and after the introit follow that by saying "we continue our 
service in the name of God the Father, Son and the Holy Spirit". It should be noted that if the procession comes before the call to worship, the service continues and does not start with the call to worship. Again in situations where the service begins with the procession rather than the call to worship the liturgist may join the call to worship and welcome as one item after the introit.

blocks.text:
Generally, the Apostle's Creed is said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on 
Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days. It is also good for all preachers and liturgists to have a good knowledge of the other new creeds that have been 
added and know when they can be appropriate.

The purpose of a creed is to act as a yardstick of correct belief. The creeds of Christianity 
have been drawn up at times of conflict about doctrine. The acceptance or rejection of a creed serves to distinguish believers and deniers of a particular doctrine or set of doctrines. For that reason a creed was called in Greek a sumbolon, meaning half of a broken object which, when placed together with the other half verified the bearer's identity. The Greek word passed through Latin symbolum into English symbol, which later took on the meaning of an outward sign of something.

The Apostles' Creed is the basic creed of Reformed churches. It is a statement of Christian belief. It is widely used by a number of Christian denominations for both liturgical and catechetical purposes. The Apostles' Creed appears to have been originally formulated as a refutation of Gnosticism, an early heresy. This can be seen in almost every phrase. For example, the creed states that Christ Jesus was born, suffered, and died on the cross. This seems to be a statement directly against the heretical teaching that Christ only appeared to become man and that he did not truly suffer and die but only appeared to do so. The Apostles' Creed, as well as other baptismal creeds, are esteemed as an example of the apostles' teachings and a defence of the Gospel of Christ. The Apostles' Creed does not address some Christological issues defined in the Nicene and other Christian Creeds. It thus says nothing explicitly about the divinity of either Jesus or of the Holy Spirit.

The Nicene Creed is the profession of faith that is most widely used in Christian Liturgy. It is called Nicene because, in its original form, it was adopted in the city of Nicaea in 325. The Nicene Creed was adopted in the face of the Arian controversy. Arius, a Libyan preacher, had declared that although Jesus Christ was divine, God had actually created him, and there was a time when he was not. This made Jesus less than the Father and contradicted the doctrine of the Trinity. The Nicene Creed, therefore, explicitly affirms the divinity of Jesus applying to him the term "God." It speaks of the Holy Spirit as worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son. As Methodists, we recite the Nicene Creed to affirm that the doctrine of the Trinity, which makes the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, equally divine, is true.

blocks.text:
This part of our service is where we do an altar call for people to give their lives to Christ, 
rededicate their lives to Christ or seek our corporate assistance in prayer in response to the Word that has been preached, and the conviction or the inner touch of the individual by the Holy Spirit. If the preacher intends to or is touched to minister to the congregation in healing, deliverance or manifestation of the gifts of the Spirit, this is the appropriate time to do so. The preacher should not use this part of the service to drag the whole service. 
He/she should factor it into the total time of the preaching and be mindful of time. It should not be a surprise to see people falling, prophesying or speaking in new tongues as they are prayed for. Notwithstanding, care must be taken not to create any unpleasant scene. It is advisable to have a standing prayer team that will deal with unique cases in order to save time. We may also allow for testimony sharing in the church at this time or any other suitable time to experience how God is dealing with other believers and to encourage the congregation.

The singing of lyrics is gaining popularity in our services these days. Both old and young 
men and women are learning more and more of it to inspire and spice our worship. The 
new liturgy provides a specific place for lyrics and this should help us to control the spontaneous ones. However, as the preacher speaks, he/she should be tolerant enough to 
accept the spontaneous ones as they are relevant to the sermon, but bold enough to curtail it if it is irrelevant and detractive. The preacher must be sensitive and tactical in this.

blocks.text:
The order of service, as we know from Part One of this Syllabus, is mainly a guideline. It is 
there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down. There should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility.

The singing of Te Deum, for instance can be varied with other canticles. In a service where 
time saving is very much needed, a shorter canticle like Canticle 6 could be sung. It should however be noted that some of the canticles are occasion specific. It is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas. Again, choruses and canticles play the same role of singing God's praise and one could be used in place of the other for the sake of time.

blocks.text:
Preaching the sermon is, essentially, telling the Good News to people. This Good News is 
about God, or from God. This has been an essential part of the church's ministry to itself 
since converted Christians would always have to be "fed" with the Good News. Sermons are therefore not personal views about current events whether social or political, not even about current theological issues; but the word of God as contained in the Scriptures with the aim of bringing home its saving and liberating truth to the hearers, enabling them to understand the truth in relation to their lives. This is not accomplished by the preacher, but by the Holy Spirit who uses the preacher as an agent, to bring the truth to the people.

Bernard Manning therefore sees preaching the sermon as "manifestation of the Incarnate 
Word, from the written word, by the spoken word". He sees it as an assault upon Hell's gate and again, a deed not of man but of God. In like manner, Alan Richardson in the book A Dictionary of Christian Theology argues "the proclamation of any kind of message other 
than the gospel message, which is the truth of God as revealed in the Bible and especially in Jesus Christ, is not preaching or sermonizing". This shows the uniqueness of sermons, as its sole purpose is to talk about the word of God through Jesus Christ. As a result, the 
discussion of politics, popular authors, and social and current issues may rightly be called 
addresses. Preaching is a subset of an address but a peculiar and unique form of address.

Bultman also defines preaching as "the communication of Biblical truth by man to man with the explicit purpose of eliciting behavourial change". Philip Brooks, considered preaching to be "communication of divine truth through human responsibility for eternal life". Thus sermons are seen to bring about changes with respect to human lives. Therefore, for sermons to be devoid of the "spiritual" component and purpose attached to it, is to miss the mark. Sermon delivery is an act of worship. The Holy Spirit is allowed to work through its delivery. Sermons are therefore expected to give a truth from Scripture. The listener then makes a decision. Our sermons should challenge people to make decision to live for Christ.

It must be noted that sermons are not prepared in order to have something to say. Rather, something must already be there to talk about. To have something to say when you mount the pulpit is far better than to have to say something. It is not man talking to men out of his own experience and views. Rather, to deliver a sermon is to speak "from God". It is in sermons that a man makes known to men, God's demands. The preacher's words are not his but God's. Unlike an address, a sermon is geared towards eliciting behavioural change. A sermon is thus aligned with decision-making. So a preacher can never adopt the "take it or leave it attitude" in his preaching.

Preaching should therefore be prophetic. It should point out what things are wrong and 
how to remedy them. It is further aimed at teaching those who do not know the way of God to know it.

The purposes of preaching then are: proclaiming the Gospel (kerygmatic), teaching (didactic) as well as it being therapeutic i.e. aimed at healing the broken spirit and broken society. The uniqueness of sermons calls for a distinctive way of preparation so that the expected end can be achieved. In fact, something that elicits behavioural change needs thorough preparation. As the word of God, it needs God's own guidance for the sermon to effectively impart the intended target. Again it must be noted that the best preacher preaches with his lifestyle. So one cannot preach virtue and practice vice. The preacher must therefore be an imitator of Christ. He should be a man of deep piety and affection for others.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶3619)

blocks.text: The word text is from the Latin 'textus'. It implies something woven. In the case of a topical sermon there may not be the need to choose a text. Your text should be in line with the sermon and not a departure from it. The choice of a text is no mean a task. It takes a lot of time and meditation to do that.

Texts help you to be effective in your delivery as you are constantly checked to talk 
within the scope.
They also awaken the interests of the congregation and help them to listen, to see how the text would be developed.

In choosing a text one must seriously consider the needs of the congregation so that the 
sermon becomes very helpful. As much as possible the preacher should be able to cover a 
sizeable number of the great themes or theological truths in the Bible.

In doing this, the preacher must not choose subjects that are above and beyond his ability 
to handle. However, one must at certain times attempt handling much difficult themes to 
bring about the much-needed growth.

In addition to reading the Bible, other good Christian literature would also be of tremendous help. Read good books of all kinds, history, science, geography, etc. but above all, the Bible. A bit of Biblical criticism is necessary if the preacher would be effective in the delivery of his message. He should know whether the language of the text is literal or figurative. When the language is to be understood literally, we should not hesitate to do so. It is a very good habit for Christians and preachers to possess more than one version of the Bible.

The wider our range, the more versatile we become and better our understanding of the Biblical text. Some versions even define and explain, as well as give other synonyms for certain words and phrases. We should also be guided by the fact that the target group of the writers of the Bible is different from ours. We should try to understand how the Scripture applied to them and how it applies to our. situation. In applying it to our condition, we must compare it with other scripture to impart to our hearers.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — The Text (syllabus ¶3632)

blocks.text:
The choice of a theme is another important aspect of sermon preparation since his 
understanding of the theme would affect how he impacts the audience. Even though the 
theme may be chosen for you as in the Almanac, it is important that the preacher 
thoroughly understands the given theme.

Effective communication is a give-and-take exercise. A preacher should try as much as 
possible to come to the level of his audience in order to be properly understood. They must receive you on the same wavelength. It has been said that one of the great qualities of the late K. A. Busia, one-time Prime Minister of Ghana was his ability to communicate the same kind of message to a highly sophisticated audience on one hand, and to the unsophisticated on the other. It is the same message but adapted to their varying conditions. When Paul 
spoke to the Athenian philosophers he referred to their "poets" while speaking to a rural 
audience he spoke of the "fruitful harvest" God had sent them.

The preacher is an educator and a good teacher imparts his knowledge in such a way as to make assimilation very easy. Our preaching should have a purpose. What do we hope to achieve by delivering that message? We must not preach for preaching sake. Paul preached with the aim of persuading men to be reconciled to God.

The theme should be suitable to the time, and occasion. Sermon preparation is not done 
over a day or two. It spans over a period of time. It is a time to pray to God for guidance and teaching. It takes time to collect sermon material, and to reflect on them.

The preacher must also be observant and abreast with current issues as these can reflect in his sermon. Christ was observant and very current as is exemplified in his teachings. Your reflections, must be written down. You will be unconsciously developing a concept or an idea to be used in your sermon preparation.

reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — The Theme (syllabus ¶3645)

blocks.text: What has so far been said may be summed up in our understanding of these two theological terms. In his book, The Foundations of Preaching, Rev. Prof. Emmanuel Asante states; "the task of the preacher is to -expose the world of the Bible to his or her audience. This task involves the interpretation of the text, which must be considered as a process involving two approaches, namely, 'Exegesis and Hermeneutics" Emmanuel Asante quotes Daniel Parte as defining the two terms in his book, What is Structural Exegesis as follows; "Exegesis aims at understanding the text in itself while hermeneutics attempts to elucidate what the text means for the modern interpreter and the people of his culture."
2.3.1 Steps in Exegesis

The following points help the preacher in his/her sermon preparation to undertake a 
proper exegesis:
i) 	The text: The passage from which the text is chosen; the full passage must be   read.
ii) 	The context: An overview of how the text was used in the Bible.
iii) 	The historical setting: The historical background surrounding the text.

iv) 		The geography of the land of the Bible: This may be very helpful for sermons on the baptism, transfiguration, temptation and death of Christ. These events involve certain landmarks which when understood can aid in the interpretation of the events.

Culture: One should also do well to explain the customs and practices of the people, to whom the word was originally spoken. This will help in applying the text to our 
modern culture.
vi) 	The circumstances peculiar to the writer: The occasion and the target audience.
