reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Exegesis and Hermeneutics (syllabus ¶3657)

blocks.text: 2.4.1 	Linking the Three Lessons, the Text and the Theme
The Methodist preacher normally has to deal with three lessons and a theme as given in the Almanac. It is the task of the preacher to link these passages to the theme.
2.4.2 	Steps

Sermon preparation has different styles that call for different steps and procedures. In our context, we are trying to link three lessons to a theme. The steps recommended below are not exhaustive but are deemed helpful in carrying out the task.

Step 1: 	Read the passages over and over again. Read them in different versions of the 
Bible including your local language and note any translational differences that may enhance your explanation and interpretation. Meditate on the passages and the theme for some time.
Step 2:  	Write down your understanding of the three passages and the lessons in them. Narrow down to those lessons related to the theme.
Step 3:   	Select your text based on your understanding of the theme. Delimit the aspect of the theme you intend treating if the theme is broad. The text can be chosen from any of the three lessons.

Step 4:	Read other parallels of your text in other books of the Bible. The Gospels, 
especially the Synoptics, have almost all the events in Jesus' life reported but with some differences, which enhance interpretation, inference and implications. The Old Testament and the Epistles also have some parallels in their presentations.

Step 5: 	Consult other materials like Bible dictionaries, commentaries, concordances and 
other writings to help you understand and know what others have said about the theme and passages. This is not meant for copying other people's options but to help you shape yours and be relevant.
The following are examples of Parallels which may be useful in your interpretation.

Old Testament Example: Compare the three passages below. Are they saying the same 
thing with different emphasis? This is where your Concordance may be very helpful in identifying parallel passages.

Psalm 1:1-3: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful. But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.

Jeremiah 17:7-8: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD 
is. For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the 
river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be 
careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.

Ezekiel 47:12: And by the river upon the bank thereof, on this side and on that side, shall 
grow all trees for meat, whose leaf shall not fade, neither shall the fruit thereof be 
consumed: it shall bring forth new fruit according to his months, because their waters they 
issued out of the sanctuary: and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine.
Gospel Example: Are Matthew and Luke saying the same thing? Are there any differences? How do the differences enhance interpretation?

Matthew 10:29 - 31: Are not two sparrows sold for a copper coin? And not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father's will. But the very hairs of your head are all 
numbered. Do not fear therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.

Luke 12:6-7: Are not five sparrows sold for two copper coins? And not one of them is 
forgotten before God. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Do not fear therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows.
Epistle Example: Are Paul and Peter saying the same thing? Are there any differences for emphasis?
2 Thessalonians 2:13: . . .Because from the beginning God chose you to be saved through the sanctifying work of the Spirit and through belief in the truth.

1 Peter 1:2: Who have been chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, 
through the sanctifying work of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling of his blood.
Step 6: 	Look critically at the background of the text and its implications to the theme and its treatment. The background of the other passages and their implications can also enhance the linkage.
Step 7: 	Look at the text in line with the theme and the other lessons. Ask these questions:
How does the text treat the theme?
What part of the theme does the text treat?
Step 8: 	Consider:
The how(s)
The why(s)
The because(s)
The therefore(s)
The notwithstanding(s)
The in addition( s)

Remember that in some cases you may need to use only one of the three lessons to help 
you treat the theme properly. When the situation calls for that, do not hesitate. However, 
this is not an opportunity for lazy work.

2.4.3 	An Outline of a Sermon (Linking the Three Passages) 
Theme: Our Life Is In God's Hands
Passages: GENESIS 21:8 - 21 (Background); ROMANS 6:1-11; MATTHEW 10:24 - 39

Text: MATTHEW 10:29 - 31 "Are not two sparrows sold for a copper coin? And not one of 
them falls to the ground apart from your Father's will. But the very hairs of your head are 
all numbered. Do not fear therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows."
Points:
Jesus promises his care for us and asks that we should not fear. (Gospel)

This is because we are more valuable among creation [explain the price of sparrows] 
(Gospel)

Hagar and Ishmael were sacked from their inheritance and yet God cared for them. 
(Old Testament)

We are God's inheritance and God is our possession, therefore he holds our life dearly 
in his hands. (Old Testament)

When we take our life into our own hands, our strife to survive and get our basic 
needs of life (food, clothing and shelter) leads us to sin. (Epistle)

We may also wrongly relax in enjoying God's provision while still in sin, thinking He is 
a merciful God. (Epistle)

But God encourages us to shun all the cares of this world that lead us to sin and rely 
on him for our precious life is in his hands. (conclusion)

There is always a link among the three lessons in treating the theme. Some may be obvious, 
others obscure. The preacher must strive to unearth the link.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — The Body of the Sermon (syllabus ¶3669)

blocks.text:
There are various types of sermons and each is good depending on who is preaching it and the situation at hand. It is never true that a type of sermon is the best and the other types are not good. Sermons have been described as personal testimony, biographical, historical incident, topical, textual, expository, springboard or narrative. It is believed that the weaknesses of the other forms of preaching generally centre around their inability to 
strictly expose the original meaning of the text, as expository preaching will do. There is however an overlap between all types as they share one text.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — TYPES OF SERMONS (syllabus ¶3737)

blocks.text: A Topical Sermon is preaching on a subject. One chooses the subject and then finds all the Scripture that relates to that subject and forms that material into a sermon. The topical sermon is the most oratorical type of sermon. It takes only its subject from the text. Its organization is based on the subject rather than distinctions of the text.

It requires the preacher to have an overall knowledge of the Bible and an ability to pull together related passages from different parts of the Bible to support the topic being preached. When preparing for a topical sermon, one must consider an effective use of a concordance, a dictionary or a topical Bible.
3.1.1 	Advantages of Topical Sermons

Topical sermons allow the preacher to get a grasp of a Bible subject completely. Everything about a particular subject is not found in one place in the Bible, so the Bible 
material must be collected together on purpose and then analyzed and preached. In 
such a task, the knowledge of the preacher about the whole Bible is broadened.

ii. 	If there is too much Scripture to cover in one sermon, a series of sermons can be 
developed to cover all of the passages that relate to that topic. The preacher is able to 
divide topics into sub-topics and deal with them in a series to ensure full coverage.

iii. 	Topical sermons acknowledge and preserve the unity of the Bible. Topical sermons 
impress the preacher, as well as the hearer, that even though the Bible is made up of 
sixty-six books written by many human authors of varied backgrounds, it is one volume 
in unity. This is because the ultimate author is God Himself and as we compare one 
passage to another, it is amazing to see the unity of God's revelation to man.

iv. 	Because of the above benefits, many writers believe that topical sermons constitute the 
best way to preach about and completely cover the great Doctrines of the Bible. The 
Bible doctrine that is chosen becomes the subject of the sermon or sermons and each 
passage of Scripture that relates to that doctrine is expounded so as to cover every 
aspect of it.
3.1.2 	Disadvantages of Topical Sermons

Topical sermons give too much room for oratory and argumentative preaching than 
concentration on the import of the Bible.

ii. 	A preacher may also choose and develop a topic with passages from the Bible to 
support but a careful study will show that the Bible does not intend that teaching. In 
other words, there is the danger of misapplication of Bible passages to support the 
topic.
3.1.3 An Outline o] a Topical Sermon
Topic: The Holy Spirit
Sub- Topic: The Holy Spirit in the Life of the Christian
His Work in Us
He dwells in us (Romans 8:9, John 14:16-17, 1 Cor. 3:16; 6:19).
He fills us or comes upon us (Joel 2:28-29; Acts 2:17-18).
He empowers us (Acts 1:8; 6:9-10)
He gives us gifts (1 Cor. 12:4-11).
Through him, we bear fruit (Gal. 5:16-25).
He convicts us of sin (John 16:7-9).
He gives us life (John 3:3-8, Psalm 104:30).
He controls us (Romans 8:9).
Our Response to Him
Be aware of his presence.
Desire him
Call upon him
Pray to receive him (Luke 11:13, Acts 8:15).
Surrender to him.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Topical Sermon (syllabus ¶3740)

blocks.text:
In Textual sermons, the preacher takes a few verses, a verse, or even a part of a verse from 
the Bible. The preacher discovers the theme of the verse in context and preaches on it in his 
own words. In the textual sermon, both the subject and the main points are based on ideas 
in the text, but, unlike the expository sermon, the development of the main ideas comes from sources outside of the immediate text. This sermon looks to the text to bring out the 
meaning. It uses the "hook-book-look-and took" method. You use something to hook your 
audience such as an interesting story that would bring people to think about the sermon. 
The book of course is turning to the Scripture and look discusses what that Scripture is 
saying. Then the last part, the took is what each person should take away from the sermon. 
You use the book of God to bring to the people a message that makes them think. It's almost 
a combination of the narrative and expository sermons.
A textual sermon is generally good for:
Preaching to audiences with short attention spans (children; elderly)
Preaching at occasions other than church services (banquets, funerals, etc.)
Preaching "Great Bible Texts" or "Favourite Bible Verses" series
3.2.1	Advantages of Textual Sermons

A textual sermon is a great technique to bringing the actual words of the Bible before 
the hearers, giving Divine authority to the message.

Since the text is short, it will be easier to remember or memorize. The preacher can 
thus easily make constant reference to the text many times during the sermon.

The preacher who employs the textual method deals with distinctively Scriptural themes that come right out of the text. Thus a well-constructed textual sermon is much more intimately in contact with the text, drawing from it not only the subject treated but all the leading thoughts of the treatment.
It also gives ample opportunity for variety, freshness, and originality.
3.2.2	Disadvantages of Textual Sermon

Like expository sermons, a textual sermon does not allow for the use of many topics 
and broader perspectives.

The use of a short text is often inadequate if one wants to do thorough treatment of 
the Scripture itself. In a textual sermon, the Bible seems chopped into fragments and 
sadly abused by the dislocation of its parts.

The unity of the Bible is not emphasized in textual sermons, as it is with the 
expository method of preaching. If texts are selected here and there throughout the Scriptures, they are not likely to impress the hearer with the unity of the Bible as a 
whole. The Bible may be made to appear as a book of isolated texts, instead of appearing as it should, a living whole and a complete revelation.
An Outline of a Textual Sermon
Theme: Be Resolute for Christ
Text: I Corinthians 15:58
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye steadfast, unmovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord (KJV).
God wants you to make these four resolutions regarding your service for Jesus Christ.
I will not quit in my service for Christ (be ye steadfast)
I will not move from my service for Christ (unmovable)
I will not become complacent in my service for Christ (always abounding)
I will have no regrets in my service for Christ. (. .. Not in vain)

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Textual Sermons (syllabus ¶3778)

blocks.text: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs. Here, the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is. When preaching expository sermons one needs to study the passage until its insight is clear to him/her and allow the content of the passage and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment. The preacher should pay attention to some three elements that aid the study of a passage for expository sermons.
1. Statements: These elements are sentences that report facts.
2. Expressions: They demonstrate emotion.
3. Prescriptive: They are sentences that describe what is to be done.

Expository sermon, like the textual sermon, takes its subject and main points from a 
particular text, but, unlike the textual sermon, it also takes its sub-points from the 
immediate text. References to other texts may occur, but they are used only to support, 
elaborate, or confirm what is already evident in the immediate text.

Again, the difference between expository preaching and topical preaching is that the former concentrates on a specific text and discusses topics covered therein, while the latter concentrates on a specific topic and finds references or texts covering the topic. A sermon is not expository merely because it addresses a subject in the Bible or because it cites numerous Scriptures. The true expository sermon discloses the thoughts of the author, covers the range of the passage, and applies its truths to the lives of the listeners.

The seeming simplicity of expository preaching entices many to attempt it. However, the 
greatest danger is that the expositor may fail to proceed from interpretation to application. In so doing, he/she may end up producing an expository lesson instead of an expository sermon. This expository lesson will only aim at the mind and impart information. On the other hand, an expository sermon will not only impart information to the mind, it will also seek to change the behaviour of the listeners. It is addressed to both the mind and the will. In a sense, therefore, proper expository preaching requires a rich knowledge of human nature and life experience to apply the text to the lives of the hearers. It relates the listener to the sermon's proposition by focusing on the hearer's responsibility toward that proposition and how that responsibility can be carried out in daily living. The preacher who fails to make the passage meaningful to the lives of his hearers may impress the audience with his (knowledge), but he will not impress them with the Saviour.  An expository sermon is meaningful when it relates God's truth to man's life, addressing hearers in the way they listen.
3.3.1 	Advantages of Expository Sermon

The main advantage of expository preaching is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible. An expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in a sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period of time no matter how long it will take.

ii. 	In addition, the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on. Very few 
preachers have preached through the entire Bible in their lifetime or with one congregation. Those who are able to finish the entire Bible with the same congregation might have done it within many years during which time a lot of new faces would have come into the congregation so they can start all over again.
iii. 	Again, expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching.
iv. 	Further, the preacher does not expound just a great book, a poem, a political passage, or his personal opinion. Rather, he/she concentrates on the authoritative word of God.
v. 	Finally, the expository sermon demands integrity on the part ofthe preacher.
3.2.2 	Disadvantages of Expository Sermon

The main disadvantage of expository preaching is that it covers many topics and 
necessitates often lengthy diversions into other passages for clarification. It does not allow for detailed coverage of a particular topic when only a specific text is covered. Therefore, in order to properly address the context and content at hand in a given passage, the preacher does become topical by concentrating on the topic at hand, and integrating other supporting passages.

ii. 	From the above, expository sermon becomes a time-consuming task and most 
expository preachers will never cover the entire Bible in their lifetime.

iii. 	Again, Exegesis (the art of critically analyzing or interpreting the passage, which must be done honestly) may give way to Eisegesis (the "art" of reading preconceived 
opinions into the text). In other words, the preacher may have what he already wants to say and force that out of the passage instead of allowing the passage to determine its own lessons.

iv. 	Finally, the expositor may wander from the text, departing from true exposition and 
may stretch and strain the text to draw from it lessons it was never intended to teach and does not teach. Thus instead of expositing or exposing the passage, the preacher may rather exploit it.
3.3.3	Outline of an Expository Sermon
Theme:  Surrender Your Life Fully to God
Passage: Romans 12:1, 2

I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a 
living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto. God, which is your reasonable service. And be not 
conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may 
prove what is the good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God (KJV).
What Does It Mean To Fully Surrender Your Life To God?
Letting God Have Your Life (A Sacrificed Life)
The Old Testament Sacrificial system as a background
What Kind of Sacrifice Does God Want?
A living sacrifice
A holy sacrifice
An acceptable sacrifice
Why Should You Give Such a Sacrifice?
It is "your reasonable service" (Sacrifice is the logical, intelligent choice)

Letting God Change Your Life (A Transformed Life) 
a. The Enemy of a Transformed Life:
• The Pattern of this World
b. The Entrance into a Transformed Life:
• A renewed mind
c. The End Result of a Transformed Life:
• The Will of God

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Expository Sermons (syllabus ¶3805)

blocks.text:
After going through all the spiritual and physical preparation needed in the work of the preacher, one of the important tasks of the preacher is how to deliver the sermon. The preacher my write a very good sermon but the effectiveness or the achievement of the 
desired end of changing lives is largely determined by the delivery.

Issues that affect sermon delivery include the appearance of the preacher and his/her body language. Other manners like the tone of the preacher, his eye contact and many others are 
also important.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — SERMON DELIVERY (syllabus ¶3860)

blocks.text:
The preacher's appearance has a major impact on the congregation. The dressing of the 
preacher must be descent. While modesty is very necessary for a preacher, it is not good to go to the pulpit shabbily dressed in the name of modesty. Depending on the social status of the congregation, the preacher should ensure that his/her dressing is generally acceptable and neither offensive nor expensive. The preacher must also be careful of wearing dresses that have the potential of drawing attention to the preacher rather than his/her message. The facial expression and the general look of the preacher are also very important. You must look cheerful, healthy and fit, ready to impart the Good News to the people of God.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Appearance (syllabus ¶3865)

blocks.text:
When in the pulpit, the preacher must be mindful of how he/she carries him/herself. Be 
yourself and imitate no one except Christ. Be natural in your voice and style. Do not put 
your hands in your pocket or your waist, it carries a wrong impression. Your body language is very important. There is the need for the preacher to preach with passion. Let the congregation see that you are up to the neck into what you are preaching. A passionate preacher is more likely to make a positive impact than the one who is him/herself emotionally detached from the message.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Posture (syllabus ¶3868)

blocks.text:
Generally, the preacher may motion the hands, the head and some other parts of the body 
to express or stress points in the sermon. This should be done with care. If you have to hold your microphone in your hand, do that with the left hand so that you can use your right hand in stressing points. Remember in some cultural settings, using the left hand to talk to people is not acceptable. Do not be glued to the use of words like Praise the Lord, 
halleluiah, Amen and so on just for the sake of it.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Gesture (syllabus ¶3871)

blocks.text:
In delivering a sermon, the preacher must check the tone of his/her voice and that of the 
message as well. The gospel is a message of joy and happiness. The preacher must not 
sound too gloomy even if the message is about sin and repentance. The good news aspect of the gospel must always call for hope and must be clear in the tone of the message. 
However, the voice and sound level of the preacher must be considered. While some point 
may need loud voice to stress them, it should not be the habit of the preacher to shout. You should be heard without necessarily shouting. You must speak clearly and confidently.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Tone (syllabus ¶3874)

blocks.text:
The preacher must of necessity involve the congregation. One of the methods is having a 
calculated eye contact with the people. In a big chapel situation where the congregation is 
spread throughout all the four corners 'of the chapel, the preacher must consciously look 
around, turning when necessary to all corners so to look at the people as they also look at 
him/her. Another way is to verbally involve them by leaving ends of some quotations and 
statements to be completed by the congregation or asking them to say some of the things 
with you. Care should be taken not to abuse this method. It is alright to consult your notes 
when preaching to ensure that you do not go off point. However, staying too glued to your sermon notes detach you from the people you are preaching to. Remember that the average listening capacity of any human being spans between ten to twenty five minutes. You should therefore be mindful of your time in order to have the congregation go along with you throughout.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Involving the Congregation (syllabus ¶3877)

blocks.text: One of the challenges many preachers have is how to end their sermon. On occasions when the response from the congregation is positive, preachers are carried away to repeat parts of the sermon unduly, prolonging the duration of delivery. On other occasions, preachers are found wanting when it comes to ending the sermon. The preacher should remember that ending a sermon does not necessarily mean you must get to your conclusion. Again, you are not forced to finish developing all your points or say all that you have written down in your notes. The sermon must end when it must. You should be very sensitive to the Holy Spirit, the time spent, the mood of your listeners and whether you have gotten to the peak of your delivery or not. The peak of your delivery is the point in your sermon where, anything said again brings down the excitement and the joy of your listeners. There are times you will hear the Holy Spirit prompting you to end your sermon. There are times too you will see that the listeners are no more following you with enthusiasm. When these signs begin to show, it does not matter where you are in the sermon, raise a song, repeat your text/theme and/ or say a prayer and end there.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: III. SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY
reference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Ending your Sermon (syllabus ¶3880)

blocks.text:
A Methodist Local Preacher once remarked: "whenever I have a preaching appointment, 
my first hymn is MHB 1 second, MHB 432, third MHB 386 and fourth, MHB 478." The understanding is that anytime this preacher had a preaching appointment, without recourse to the theme and lessons, those were the hymns the preacher chose. But there is more to choosing a hymn than those hymns being one's favourites. A choirmaster asked for the Sunday's hymns from a preacher. The preacher just entered the vestry, checked the theme and gave MHB 308 as the sermon hymn and asked the choir to select the other three. What really made the preacher choose 308? Are there any considerations aside the theme in choosing a hymn for any given service?

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: IV. SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE
reference.citation: Liturgics — SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶3889)

blocks.text:
It is quite possible that most of us have at one time or the other selected our hymns before preparing our sermons. This could be due to some form of pressure mounting up such that when the choir needs the hymn for practice, we might not have prepared our sermons. Under such pressures, it is expedient to at least read the lessons and reflect on them in line with the theme before you make your selection. The most appropriate time to select your hymns is when you have finished preparing your sermon or at least when the first draft, 
outline or sketch, as you may call it, is done. This will ensure that the hymns you choose 
will be appropriate for the service.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: IV. SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE
reference.citation: Liturgics — SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE — WHEN TO SELECT HYMNS (syllabus ¶3892)

blocks.text:
The first hymn in our services always serves as hymn of praise and/or adoration. It is the 
part of the service that sings the praise of our Maker. We use the first hymn to show our 
appreciation to God for who He is and what He does. It is therefore amazing to hear people 
singing 'Faith of our Fathers' (M.H.B.402) or 'Stand up stand up for Jesus' (M.H.B.821) as 
the first hymn unless the service is a special one that demands that. There is a whole range 
of hymns that can qualify as a hymn of praise. The common among these are those from 
MHB 1 to MHB 35 and MHB 82 to MHB 116.

The second hymn is a hymn of invocation. This hymn serves to inspire the worshipers to 
immerse themselves in the worship and encourage them to pray. Preachers have often 
chosen hymns from MHB 273 to MHB 301 as the second hymn.

The third hymn is usually the sermon hymn. It is sung to prepare the congregation for the 
day's sermon. It is expected that the third hymn will be relevant to the sermon by touching 
on the core or at least an important point of the sermon. More often than not, preachers 
who for one reason or the other could not lay hands on any hymn they deem relevant for 
their sermon rely on "Tell me the old old story" (MHB.161) or "Lord thy word abideth." 
(MHB.308). This is not good enough. Preachers often look for a hymn that can wholly 
express the core of their message but it does not always work. Rather, just a stanza or two 
or even a few lines in a hymn may be what we need. It is the duty of the preacher to show 
the congregation, in the course of the sermon delivery, that "minute" part of the hymn 
relevant to the sermon, by making reference to it at the appropriate time.

The closing hymn is the hymn of response. It should be able to state the desired response to 
the sermon. It seeks to address the question: what should we do after hearing this sermon? 
Here again, "Forth in thy name 0 Lord I go" (MHB 590) has suffered an attack by many a 
preacher and together with what has been called the Methodist-closing anthem, "Now 
thank we all our God" (MHB 10). They have been misused by preachers who are not able to 
select fitting hymns of response. Just answer the question as to what your listeners' 
response to the sermon should be and you are on the way to getting the clue to your closing 
hymn. "Beloved let us love", for example has served as a good response to sermons that 
seek to emphasize love and good neighbourliness.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: IV. SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE
reference.citation: Liturgics — SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE — THE CHOICE OF HYMNS (syllabus ¶3895)

topics.title: Factors to Consider in Choosing the Sermon Hymn and the Closing Hymn

blocks.text:
The first is the theme. Themes always serve as the first point of reflection and when well understand, could give enough clues to the hymns to be selected for the service.  In considering the theme as an indicator for hymn selection, the preacher should be able to 
delimit himself/herself as to which aspect of the theme would be handled in the sermon.

The second is the text. Even though we have commonly used text to refer to a verse or two on which the sermon may be anchored, we can also look at a text in the sense of the main Bible passage that addresses the theme directly or even all the three lessons. When read and well understood in the light of the theme, the lessons or the anchor text could give clue to selecting the sermon and the closing hymns.

The proposition, when appropriately identified and formulated, can help in the process. 
The proposition is the central thought in the sermon. It contains the main message and the desired response. Obviously when you know your main message and what behaviour 
should be exhibited in response, there cannot be a better way to identify your sermon and closing hymns. It is even thought that the proposition does the best job as an aid to hymn selection.

We have always selected Christmas and Easter hymns to make our worship meaningful. However, there are other seasons like Advent and Lent that serve as preparatory seasons for Christmas and Easter, respectively. That man or woman is sad who attends Advent Sunday service and does not hear the Messianic Antephone, "0 come 0 come Immanuel" or a fitting substitute, sung. It is heartening to hear "Sing we the King who is coming to reign" (MHB.116) as the hymn of praise for any of the advent Sundays. This same hymn has been useful on the Christ the king Sunday either as sermon or closing hymn with "Rejoice the Lord is king" being its partner. The point here is that we can do ourselves a lot of good if we do not sing songs that are out of season. The preacher must know the special occasion on which he or she is preaching and that will lead to the selection of appropriate hymns.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: IV. SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE
reference.topic: 3.1 Factors to Consider in Choosing the Sermon Hymn and the Closing Hymn
reference.citation: Liturgics — SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE — Factors to Consider in Choosing the Sermon Hymn and the Closing Hymn (syllabus ¶3905)

blocks.text: One major problem preachers commonly face is the time to get settled and prepare sermons. Some preachers have always seen sermon preparation as part time or even secondary. Many preachers prepare their sermons on Saturday night or even Sunday morning. Once enough time is not allowed for the sermon preparation, hymn selection will suffer. A simple suggestion: read the passages latest by Monday evening and keep reflecting on them and the theme. Write points down as they come and gather them by Wednesday night. You may have had enough points or ideas to help you to select your hymns by now.

Another problem is that most of us are not familiar with our hymns. We may not know the hymns by their numbers but at least certain lines should be remembered. You may consult the content of the Methodist Hymn Book to get an idea of a range of hymns that fit various subjects. It pays to ask for help from fellow Lay Preachers and Ministers.

Again, a number of us do not find it easy to understand the theme and find it difficult linking the theme to the passages, let alone selecting the appropriate hymns. Let us encourage ourselves to spend a little more time to reflect and consult other literature and 
help from other preachers so that we can contribute to a lively and spirit-led worship. But 
above all pray for guidance and the Holy Spirit's enlightenment.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: IV. SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE
reference.citation: Liturgics — SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE — COMMON PROBLEMS IN SERMON PREPARATION (syllabus ¶3914)

blocks.text:
The hymns for our services and music in general play important roles in our worship. They enhance inspirational worship and make participation by all, possible. When we sing during worship everybody feels part of what we are doing. Music unifies us during 
worship. The only time we all say the same thing, in the same "Language", with the same spirit is when we sing. Music thus makes our worship meaningful. It is therefore imperative that preachers approach sermon preparation and hymn selection with all the attention and inspiration they deserve.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: IV. SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE
reference.citation: Liturgics — SELECTION OF HYMNS FOR SERVICE — CONCLUSION (syllabus ¶3921)

blocks.text: Prayer is one of the major activities in the Christian life. Jesus prayed and ordained prayer as a means of receiving God's grace. John Wesley, in his sermon, "Means of Grace," said, "All who desire the grace of God are to wait for it in the way of prayer." Prayer is the strength of the Christian, and without it, the Christian becomes powerless and defenceless. The first line of M.H.B. 539:2 says, "We perish if we cease from prayer." It has been said that, "one week without prayer makes one weak." In the words of i.e. Ryle, the "neglect of prayer is the sure road to a fall." Great men of the Bible, including Jesus Himself, made prayer their daily and regular affair. Prayer is the very life-breath of true Christianity. For an effective ministry, the preacher must be a man or woman of fervent prayer.

The Christian church was born through prayer. The Spirit was poured on the apostles as a result of Prayer. Prayer was indispensable in the ministry of the prophets. The revelation of the Word of God was received when the prophet was in a prayerful relation with Yahweh. Daniel received the prophetic revelation while in prayer. Prayer continued to be the native air of the Early Church (Acts 2:42). There was a close connection between prayer and the Holy Spirit's presence and power. Throughout the Acts the Church leaders emerged as men of prayer who urged the Christians to pray with them.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶3926)

blocks.text: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is a means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him. Real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father, and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. Contact with God begins when we receive Jesus into our lives as Saviour and Lord (John 14:6).

Prayer is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation, but also in direct address to Him. Prayer may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, 
extempore or formal.

Throughout the Bible, Prayer is described variously as "calling upon the name of the Lord" (Gen. 4:26; 12:8; Zeph. 3:9). It is "beseeching the Lord" (Ex. 32:11); "pouring out the soul before the Lord" (1 Sam. 1:15); "crying to heaven" (2 Chron. 32:20); "seeking unto God and making supplication" (Job 8:5); "drawing near to God" (Ps. 73:28); "approaching God's throne of grace" (Heb. 4:16) and "drawing near to God" (Heb. 10:22).

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — WHAT IS PRAYER? (syllabus ¶3931)

blocks.text: The purpose of prayer is not to notify God, but to express our trust and faith in Him and our expectation and heart's desires.
Let us examine some reasons why Christians should pray:

First, we are commanded to pray. God's Word commands us to pray (Lk. 18:1; 
Acts 6:4; Mk. 14:38; Phil. 4:6; Col. 4:2; 1 Tim. 2:1, 2). Thus, if we are to live in true obedience, we should pray as commanded.
ii) 	We pray to have fellowship with God, receive spiritual nurture and strength to live a victorious life, and maintain boldness for a vital witness for Christ.

iii) 	Prayer releases God's great power to change the course of nature, people and 
nations.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — WHY SHOULD WE PRAY? (syllabus ¶3939)

blocks.text:
Jesus told His disciples a parable in Luke 18:1-8 to show them that, they should always 
pray and not give up. Jesus told them this parable of the pitiless and unjust judge, who was not interested in justice, but became so tired of a widow's persistent demand for justice that he, finally, said, "l will see that she gets justice so that she won't eventually wear me out." Jesus is not teaching that God is like the judge. He is rather teaching that we should be like the widow, who would not give up till she got her answers.

One Biblical principle for prayer is to ASK, SEEK and KNOCK. This may mean that after asking without receiving, seeking and not finding, you must knock hard. And if the door refuses to open, you may need to P.U.S.H. -literally meaning 'Pray Until Something Happens.' (Mt. 7:7 9).

Even though prayer is such an important part of the Christian life, it is the most neglected duty, especially private and personal prayer. Even those who pray, do so amiss. Their prayers are nothing short of mere repetitions of words without much meaning. There are others who use "good words" but their hearts are not in it. According to J.C. Ryle, where there is no heart, there may be lip-work and tongue work, but there is no prayer.

George Muller was a German-born English preacher and was referred to as a man of prayer who lived by faith. He said: "It is not enough to begin to pray, nor to pray aright; nor 
is it enough to continue for a time to pray; but we must patiently, believinqly, continue in 
prayer until we obtain an answer." He prayed for five people to be saved. After five years, 
one person got saved. After ten years, two of them got saved. After thirty-five years, the 
fourth person was saved, and finally, after fifty-two years, the fifth person got saved just 
after the death of Mueller.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — PERSISTENCE IN PRAYER (syllabus ¶3948)

blocks.text:
Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God. This formula is popularly known as CATS (Confession, Adoration, Thanksgiving and Supplication) or ACTS (Adoration, 
Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication).

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — THE CONTENT OF PRAYER (syllabus ¶3958)

blocks.text:
To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips (Ps. 150). We need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of 
requests before God. Prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests. To 
adore or worship God is to display our awareness of His majesty and capability. In Psalm 
95:1-7, the Psalmist praised God for who He is and what He does. This should be the entry point of our prayer.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — Adoration (syllabus ¶3961)

blocks.text:
When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to 
reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed. When Isaiah entered into the awesome glory of God, he saw how awful his sins and that of his people were. He immediately confessed them and he was purged of them. The way then opened for him to commune with God (Isa. 6:1-7). In Psalm 51:1-12, David extensively confessed his sins and pleaded for God's forgiveness. Jesus affirmed the need for confession in Matthew 6:12. Confession of sins must be sincere and specific. It is not a time to hypocritically tell God to forgive your unknown sins. Tell Him also about the known and intentional ones. Confession of sins must culminate in repentance and change.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — Confession (syllabus ¶3964)

blocks.text: An attitude of thanksgiving to God, for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy, because we belong to Him, enables us to recognize that He controls all things, not just the blessings, but the problems and adversities as well. As we approach God with a thankful heart, He becomes strong on our behalf. Psalm 136 makes a tall list of what we must thank God for, because His mercy endures forever. Philippians 4:6 calls on us to pray with thanksgiving. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God. In it, the Christian sees God as the creator of a world that was "good" (Gen. 1:4, 31), the provider of salvation to fallen and sinful humanity and the giver of every good and perfect thing. The entire Christian life is a sacrifice of thanksgiving in gratitude to God for all His mercy and His daily provision.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — Thanksgiving (syllabus ¶3967)

blocks.text: Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others.

a. 	Petition is asking God for personal things in prayer. When we petition God, we ask for 
things for ourselves in order to succeed in life. In Matthew 7:7 -9, Jesus commands us to ask, seek and knock for positive results for ourselves. We need to petition God because we have varied needs. Paul writes in Philippians 4:19 that God will supply all our needs. Examples of petitions are found in 1 Samuel 1:11; Psalm 27:7-12; Daniel 6:11; 9:17-19 
and Matthew 26:39, 42.

Intercession is prayer for others. Prayer is not a selfish enterprise, but a sharing and a 
caring ministry. Pray for others - your spouse, your children, your parents, neighbours, and friends, those in authority over you and your nation. Pray for the salvation of souls, for daily opportunity to introduce others to Christ and to the ministry of the Holy Spirit, and for the fulfilment of the Great Commission. In Psalm 122:6-9, David encourages us to pray for our nation and for its peace and prosperity. Jesus in John 17 prayed the longest prayer for His disciples. The persons you hate so much, whose thoughts come to your mind, need your prayer. You are not to brood over their offences, but to pray for 
them.

As a preacher, intercession is an integral part of your ministry. You need to pray for the 
people you preach to so that God's word will be meaningful and beneficial to them. You 
need to pray for their needs and special requests. A preacher who does not pray for those 
he/she preaches to, has an incomplete ministry, an unfulfilled one. It is worth noting that 
intercession is a ministry on its own. God is always looking for someone like you to stand in the gap on behalf of the people (Ezek. 22:30)

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — Supplication (syllabus ¶3970)

blocks.text: Prayer suggests a union of man's will with God's will and abandonment and submission of the self to God. Prayer draws us closer to God. There is intimacy which generates the attitude of trust, faith, confidence and hope. Other attitudes are humility, self-abasement, and self-surrender. Prayer leads to intense spirituality as it makes us aware of our relationship with God.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: V. PRAYER
reference.citation: Liturgics — PRAYER — ATTITUDES AND PRAYER (syllabus ¶3978)

blocks.text:
Christian festivals are occasions celebrated to mark specific land marks in the development 
and growth of the Church. There are many of these festivals depending on which tradition 
is being referred to. The general ones are listed below in the order of appearance on the 
Christian calendar and the time of year celebrated.
Advent Sunday
Christmas
Epiphany
Ash Wednesday
Lent
Palm Sunday
Good Friday
Easter (Resurrection Day)
Ascension
Pentecost
Trinity

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶3982)

blocks.text:
According to one of the Church Fathers called Justin, Sunday was the day on which 
Christians worshipped together. The name was derived from "Day of the Sun" which was 
connected with nature worship.

Christians also believe that Sunday was the day Jesus rose from the dead. It was in 
consequence of the resurrection that in the New Testament, Sunday replaced the Sabbath, 
for Christians. And according to Saint Augustine, "Sunday also prefigured eternal rest." 
Sunday was eventually declared a public holiday by Emperor Constantine in 321 AD. 
Constantine believed that he was victorious at the battle of the Milvian Bridge because of 
the help of the Christian God. If this were so, then the day that Christians cherished so mush 
ought to be made a holiday to enable them give appropriate worship to this God, hence that 
decree. Viewed as the Day of the Lord, its celebration was characterized by joy.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — SUNDAY (syllabus ¶3996)

blocks.text:
Easter is the oldest and greatest festival in Christianity, which falls on Sunday, the day 
Christ rose from the dead. According to Tertullian, Easter was the normal occasion for 
converts to be initiated into the Christian faith. So on Easter, Christians commemorated the 
death and resurrection of Christ and celebrated both baptism and the Eucharist. Previously, 
preparation for Easter spanned over two days, with prayer and fasting i.e. on Friday and 
Saturday. This was lengthened to a week and then to 40 days now called Lent in English. 
Other places organized vigils on the Friday and Saturday nights.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — EASTER (syllabus ¶4001)

topics.title: Background to the Date for Easter Celebration

blocks.text: Easter can be said- to have apostolic background because it derived from a time when Jewish influence was effective i.e. the first century A.D and it depended on the lunar calendar. For three centuries the church tolerated its celebration on different days. While Asia or the Eastern Orthodox Church celebrated it on 14 Nisan, others elsewhere had it on the Sunday after 14 Nisan. Both were accepted because they all had apostolic authenticity. So Asia celebrated it on the same day as the Jewish Passover. Those who kept Easter on the 14th Nisan were known as "Quartodecimans".

A great controversy known as the Quartodeciman controversy erupted as a result of the 
date of the celebration of Easter. It has been mentioned that Asia celebrated it on the 14th 
Nisan whatever the day of the week, whereas other churches observed it on the Sunday 
following the 14th Nisan. In 155 AD Polycarp (the Bishop of Smyrna) discussed the matter 
in Rome with Ancietus and they agreed to differ. So the matter seemed to have rested for 
some 35 years until 190 AD, when Victor of Rome made an energetic attempt to secure 
uniformity. Because of the large Asiatic population in the capital one part of the Church was still fasting when the other was feasting. Victor held a Synod and sent out requests for others to meet. Though his views were accepted the Synod of Asia under Polycrates of Ephesus refused to conform. So Victor stopped communion with Asia. In time the celebrations of Easter upon the Sunday was adopted by all, the only question remaining was whether in determining the date, the Jewish reckoning was to be followed, as was the custom at Antioch or whether it should be calculated independently as was done at Alexandria and Rome. The latter method was the one eventually agreed upon.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.topic: 3.1 Background to the Date for Easter Celebration
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — Background to the Date for Easter Celebration (syllabus ¶4004)

blocks.text:
In Judaism, Pentecost was a harvest festival which was also known as the Feast of Weeks 
(Lev. 23:5-21), the Feast of First Fruits. The descent ofthe Holy Spirit recorded in the Book of Acts was at the Jewish Pentecost and this made Christians fix their celebration of the pouring down of the Holy Spirit on the 50th day after Easter i.e. the 7th Sunday after Easter. It was a day of universal rejoicing and as Tertullian records; "we spent our time in all exaltation."

St. Athanasius calls it "Magna Dominica" the "Great Sunday" and consequently neither 
fasting nor kneeling was allowed during its celebration. Pentecost Sunday is also called 
White Sunday or Whitsunday possibly in references to the white robes won by catechumens and others who are baptized on that day. An alternative derivation is from the word "wit" or "wisdom" which implies that it was the day the Apostles were filled with wisdom from God by the Holy Spirit.

The sanctuary colour of Pentecost Sunday is red, the colour of the Church. The red symbolizes the Fire of Pentecost as well as that of the Apostles and other disciples of Jesus 
who were gathered in the Upper Room for the empowerment from God to preach the gospel to other nations. (For additional information on this topic, see Weekly Bible Lesson, 
January-June, 2009 Edition, pp 85-88)

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — PENTECOST (syllabus ¶4009)

blocks.text:
The Ascension was commemorated on either Easter Sunday itself following the Lucan and Johanine narratives (Luke 24:50-53, John 20:21ff) or the 50th day. It was not until the 
second half of the 4th century that the Ascension was commemorated as a historical event on the 40th day and the gift of the Spirit on the 50th.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — ASCENSION (syllabus ¶4014)

blocks.text:
This seems to be a combination of two elements, an extended fast before the Pascha or 
Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and a regulated period of preparation for baptism. It is a 
period of 40 days which was determined by the length of our Lord's fast in the wilderness. The word lent comes from an Anglo Saxon word "Lenten" which means "spring". The actual length of Lent varied considerably, depending on how the 40 day period was calculated: whether it included Good Friday and Holy Saturday, or the whole of Holy Week. While Athanasius alludes to a 6 week Lent beginning on a Monday and including Holy Week, Egeria has 8 weeks because Saturday and Sunday were not fast days. In today's Christianity, Lent begins on Ash-Wednesday and ends on Holy Saturday. The Sundays within the period are not counted as fast days. (For additional information on this topic, see Weekly Bible Lessons, January - June 2009 Edition. Pp 38-42.)

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — LENT (syllabus ¶4017)

blocks.text: Both Christmas and Epiphany are festivals instituted to counter pagan festivals connected with the winter solstice which in the West was reckoned to be 25th December, and 6th January in the East, in Alexandria.
In the East, 6th January was connected with the virgin birth of Aiori/Dionysus and legends of Epiphanies in which gods made themselves known to men. Epiphany is considered to be older than Christmas.

Epiphany comes from, the Greek word epiphania, which means manifestation. It also stands for "appearing". It was connected with Christ's baptism, nativity and the miracle at Cana. The Armenian Church still keeps Epiphany as Christ's birthday. Later Epiphany ceased to be connected with that event and was associated with His baptism only. Later the West associated Epiphany with Christ's appearing to the Gentiles and especially to the Magi. The word Christmas is derived from a combination of two words i.e. Christ + Mass. It is therefore the special mass or worship service, said during the celebration of Christ's birth. It comes from the season's first service; the Christ Mass. Colours used on this occasion are white, gold and materials of finest texture to express one's happiness and joy.

Christmas was instituted as an attempt to counter pagan festivals connected with the 
solstice which in the West was reckoned to be 25th December, and 6th January in the East in Alexandria. 25th December had been fixed as the date for the observance of the birthday of the Sun god in 274. The celebration took place on the Vatican Hill where the sun was  worshipped in the Mithras-cult (the Persian form). It has been recorded that Emperor Constantine may have had a hand in this because he encouraged the adaptation by the Church of various features of the sun worship. About 62 years later in 336 AD the 
Christians first celebrated the birthday of Jesus Christ, their Lord. Constantine took over 
the Vatican Hill and built St. Peter's Church. It is believed that Christmas was introduced in Rome in order to provide a Christian substitute for the pagan festivals of the Winter 
Solstice. The practice was very beneficial as it prevented the Christians from going back to an old practice of worshipping the pagan god at the beginning of the year.

It should be noted that it was not the pagan celebration which was Christianised. The 
celebration of Christ's birthday replaced the pagan one. Before this time, i.e. the 4th century AD, there were no records to show that Jesus celebrated his birthday, or his apostles or the early Church celebrated it.

Christmas is immediately preceded by the Advent season. The Advent season is for four 
Sundays preceding Christmas. These are the second coming of Christ (Advent Sunday), 
Preparation for the incarnation in Old Testament prophecy, the Ministry of John the 
Baptist, and the vocations of Blessed Virgin Mary and St. Joseph. It is a hopeful period for all Christians because we wait the coming of our Lord.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — CHRISTMAS/ EPIPHANY (syllabus ¶4020)

blocks.text:
This is a festival peculiar to Methodists all over the world. On December 25,1747, John 
Wesley strongly urged the Methodists to renew their Covenant with God. His first Covenant Service was held in the French Church at Spitfalfields on August 11, 1755, when he recited the words of "that blessed man Richard Alleine", which he published that year in the "Christian Library." Wesley issued this as a pamphlet in 1780, and the form was used without alteration for nearly a century. Various modifications were then made, till a form was prepared which gave the people a larger share in the devotions. That form has now been revised with a deep sense of the importance of a service which has been a fruitful source of blessing to Methodism ever since 1755.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — COVENANT SUNDAY (syllabus ¶4033)

blocks.text: The Christian year contains two cycles: The Christmas Cycle (Advent-Christmas-Epiphany) and the Easter Cycle (Lent-Easter-Pentecost). Within each cycle there is a preparatory season symbolized by purple and a festival season symbolized by white. After each cycle there is an ordinary time of growth symbolized by green. Thus there is a sequence of season using purple, white and green in that order twice each year.

Purple is a colour of both penitence and royalty used during the preparatory seasons of 
Advent and Lent. Blue, a colour of hope, may also be used during Advent.

White and gold are joyous and festive colours used during the Christmas and Easter 
Seasons (except on the Day of Pentecost) and in other seasons on festive day's such as 
Baptism of the Lord, Transfiguration, Trinity, All Saints, and Christ the King. White may also be used at weddings and at services where the sacrament of baptism is central. White is recommended at services of Holy Communion, white linens on top of the Lord's table are customary, but the perimeter hanging over from the sides of the table and other visuals should reflect the day or season of the year.
Green is a colour of growth, used in the seasons after Epiphany and after Pentecost except when special days call for white or red.

Red is a colour of fire, symbolizing the Hoy Spirit. It is used on the Day of Pentecost and at other times when the work of the Holy Spirit is emphasized. Red is also the colour of the blood of Christ and the blood of martyrs. Because of its intensity, red is most effective when used occasionally rather than continuously for a whole season. It is appropriate for 
evangelistic services, for ordinations and consecrations, for church anniversaries and 
homecomings. It may be used beside white and gold through the Easter season. It may be 
used during Holy Week, beginning with Passion/Palm Sunday, to symbolize the blood of 
Christ.

Although the use of these colours is based on broad ecumenical tradition, other colours 
have been and are being used in Christian Churches. Creativity with colours and other signs for the days and seasons is encouraged.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VI. THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS/CALENDAR — COLOURS FOR THE SEASONS (syllabus ¶4036)

chapters.title: THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP

blocks.text:
It has been said that, "the Bible is for culture, against culture and above culture." Others 
also say that, "the Christian gospel and worship must be biblically faithful, and culturally relevant." Even though we may be uncomfortable with some of the practices in our culture, we must also understand that this is the culture we have been called to minister to. This is our world, and God has placed us here for such a time as this. We have been called to bring the gospel of Jesus Christ to the people of this generation. If we are going to do that, and if we are going to do it effectively, we must fashion our worship and present the message of Christ in a culturally relevant fashion.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VII. THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶4052)

blocks.text: Culture may be viewed as the accumulated habits, attitudes, and beliefs of a group of people that define for them their general behavior and way of life. Culture defines a particular society at a particular time and place. Culture then depends on the human capacity for learning and transmitting knowledge from one generation to another. It can therefore be said that, Culture is Dynamic, Progressive, interactive, "Maturational" and "Acquisitional."

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VII. THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP — WHAT IS CULTURE? (syllabus ¶4055)

topics.title: THE MEANING OF CULTURAL RELEVANCE OF WORSHIP

blocks.text: Cultural relevance is not about "political correctness", or about watering down the gospel and worship. Rather it is a process by which the church, in its mission of preaching the gospel, becomes culturally sensitive and thus relevant to her context while remaining doctrinally pure. Jesus commanded us in Matthew 28:19 to "Go into all the world and make disciples of all nations baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit." In Acts1:8, Jesus' promise of the Holy Spirit was to the effect that "You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth." Our assignment, as preachers, is therefore to be men and women who live and teach the Gospel with cultural relevance, sensitivity and power, so that the eternal truth of the Gospel will be understood and received in every culture of the world, especially in our own culture. Remember Paul saying: "I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some" (1 Cor. 9:22).

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VII. THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP
reference.topic: 3.0 THE MEANING OF CULTURAL RELEVANCE OF WORSHIP
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP — THE MEANING OF CULTURAL RELEVANCE OF WORSHIP (syllabus ¶4058)

topics.title: HOW DOES WORSHIP BECOME RELEVANT IN A PARTICULAR CULTURAL SETTING?

blocks.text:
We should recognize that as far as our worship and the Gospel of Christ are concerned, 
there are unchangeable facts that cannot be compromised. Biblical truths and doctrinal 
facts are unchangeable. That Christ is the Son of God, that He died to save sinners and that He shall come again to judge the world, are all unchangeable. However, the methods of presenting this can change from pulpit preaching to PowerPoint presentation on projectors and through drama. There can be changes from recitation of sentences to singing them or from hymns to choruses.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VII. THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP
reference.topic: 4.0 HOW DOES WORSHIP BECOME RELEVANT IN A PARTICULAR CULTURAL SETTING?
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP — HOW DOES WORSHIP BECOME RELEVANT IN A PARTICULAR CULTURAL SETTING? (syllabus ¶4061)

blocks.text: 4.1.1	 Jesus

"Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Heb. 13:8). In a world of 
constant change it is good to know that Jesus Christ is always the same that He is always 
here for us, that He will always love us, and that His sacrifice on the cross and His 
resurrection from the dead will always be sufficient. Jesus' sameness yesterday, today and forever is a comfort in this day and gives us a solid foundation regardless of the changes in our culture. The place of God the Father, Son and the Holy Spirit in our worship does not change.
4.1.2 	The Word of God

It is stated in Scripture that "The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever" (Isa. 40:8) "For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God" (l Pet.1:23). "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away" (Luke 21:33). The Word of God stands for all time as a revelation from God's mouth to our ears. It will never change, and it will never take second place in the church. The Word of God is where we get our directives for worship, for our lifestyle choices, for practical instruction, for our salvation. This will never change. Thus the prominent place of reading and interpreting the Word of God in our worship cannot change and laying emphasis on hearing God's voice during worship cannot be out of place.
4.1.3 	Divine Principles

Titus 1:9 is an instruction for those who will hold leadership positions in the Church and it says that those who hold these positions "must hold firmly to the trustworthy message as it has been taught, so that he can encourage others by sound doctrine and refute those who oppose it." The doctrinal truth taught in the Bible does not change. God's truth and the divine principles He has given us do not and will not change.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VII. THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP — The "Unchangeables'" (syllabus ¶4064)

blocks.text: 4.2.1 	Change Comes with Age

We change physically as we age. We may thus need to be moderate and considerate in our tone and approach when speaking to an ageing congregation while we can comfortably jump and shout in a fairly youthful congregation. Younger people may want a radically different setting for worship where opportunity is given for self expression and spontaneous experience in songs, prophecies and revelations. But an older congregation may prefer a solemn, reflective, calm worship setting. We must be sensitive to both. In an intergenerational congregation, there must be a fair balance. We need to be sensitive to the new ways of worship that is making other churches grow rapidly. We should study and apply the viable principles in them.
4.2.2 	Ministry Methods Change

Worship styles, technology, outreach methods, teaching styles, and much more, are always being adapted to reach those who are unchurched, as well as to disciple those who are already Christ's followers.
Note the following contrasts:
Jesus preached from a boat on the Sea of Galilee, and the audience on the beach, thus creating a natural Amphitheatre but we use microphones in pulpits.

Paul wrote on papyrus with a quill and ink but we use Microsoft Word and 
PowerPoint on computer systems.

The early church studied from the scrolls and parchments which were limited and 
available to few, but we have dozens of translations bound together in our choice of bindings and colours, and Bibles on computer and mobile phones where we can look- up Scripture in milliseconds. So then in the early church "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17)." But today, we can say that faith comes by hearing, reading and probably, watching the word of God.
Paul wore a Toga while he was preaching but we wear suits and cassocks.
4.3.3 	God is a God of Change

"In the beginning, God created." God is a Creator, and He is not happy when His church tries to stop His creativity. The Bible believes in new things and so does God. Terms like "new song", "a new heaven and earth", "new wine", "new life", "new covenant", "new creation", "new man", and a "new command" are scattered in the Bible. Our God is a God of change, and He calls the Church to be willing to change with Him. It is thus true that the church cannot minister to the people of this millennium with methodology designed to reach the people of the 1950s.

reference.subject: Liturgics
reference.chapter: VII. THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP
reference.citation: Liturgics — THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP — The Changeables (syllabus ¶4074)

blocks.text: 4.3.1 	Obtain a Biblical Worldview

A worldview is quite simply the lenses through which we see our world. We need to make 
sure our worldview is in line with the Bible's. "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor 
free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal. 3:28). If we are going to see 
people through Jesus' eyes, if we are to have His worldview, we will not base our feelings 
and attitudes on a person's age or social status. We will love everyone as God's special 
creation and seek to be relevant to them in our worship and preaching. John said "Then I 
saw another angel flying in midair, and he had the eternal gospel to proclaim to those who 
live on the earth to every nation, tribe, language and people" (Rev. 14:6). The gospel is for 
all people at all times. Not only do we love these people as God's children, we embrace 
them as equals. It is good for the preacher to be aware of other world views but not be 
moved by them.
4.3.2 Embrace New Methodologies

The Pharisees approached Jesus and wondered why His disciples weren't fasting (why they weren't keeping the Law). Jesus responded in Mark 2:21-22 "No one sews a patch of 
unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the new piece will pull away from the old, 
making the tear worse. And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined. No, he pours new wine into new wineskins." These two brief parables of the old garment and old wineskins illustrates the incompatibility of the old system of Jewish law and tradition with the new cloth and new wine of the gospel of Christ. Jesus was always being questioned about the different methods He used. Jesus embraced what was new and effective for ministry. Jesus was the Master at presenting truth in the language of His culture. He used objects, seeds, soil, situational parables, coins, camels, and fig trees, all things that his audiences could readily identify with. And much of the methodology we will employ will do the same thing, whether it is drama, video, art, music, or stories, they will be used to present the gospel in ways that our culture can identify with.
4.3.3 	Be Creative in Worship

David said: "Praise the LORD. Sing to the LORD a new song, his praise in the assembly of the saints" (Psalms 149:1). John also revealed: "And they sang a new song: 'You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, because you were slain, and with your blood you purchased men for God from every tribe. and language and people and nation' " (Rev. 5:9). God wants His church to sing a new song. He wants us to creatively worship Him in our assemblies. This in no way means that we cannot continue praising God with the grand old hymns, but neither does it mean we can shut out the new songs God is calling His people to sing. This is not an "either, or" situation, it is a "both, and" situation.

blocks.text: A pastor once went to visit one of his church members admitted to a hospital. He was a new member who had recently arrived from China and could not speak English. When the pastor arrived at the hospital, he took hold of the man's hand and prayed with him. As he finished his prayer the patient began to shout something in Chinese. The pastor didn't understand what he was saying, and the man continued in vain to communicate something to the pastor.Within a few moments the patient made one last attempt to communicate, gasped for air, and then he died. The pastor was called to preach at the man's funeral. During the sermon the pastor repeated the phrase the man had been shouting to him on his hospital bed. One of the man's relatives listened and then gave the interpretation: "Move over, you are standing on my oxygen tube, I can't breathe!" indeed the pastor had virtually killed the man by standing on his oxygen tube and sucking the life out of the man.

We, like the pastor, are capable of sucking the life out of the ministry God has called us to 
and by so doing suffocating our congregation to death if we do not try to be relevant to 
them. God wants to breathe new life into His church, He wants to minister with all of His 
creativity and power, but many in the church refuse to change their methodologies because they are worshipping their tradition. Let us lead worship services with minds open to the direction of the Holy Spirit and ready to change if that can help to win all men and women for Christ.
