subjects.name: Methodist Studies
subjects.description: Key doctrinal teachings of John Wesley, Charles Wesley and Methodist hymnology, Wesley's social ethics, the controversies, and episcopal leadership in Ghana Methodism.

chapters.title: THE BASIS OF WESLEY'S THEOLOGICAL THINKING

blocks.text: It has been said that "Methodism is long on organization and short on theology." This is to suggest that the people called Methodists have no theology or have pushed theological issues to the backstage in the life of both the church and individual Christians. Many people think this way because they picture John Wesley as a leader of a revival who was not very interested in theology, but in a practical Christianity as opposed to doctrinal Christianity. However, this has been proved wrong for studies have revealed the richness of the theological legacy of John Wesley and the Wesleyan Revival in a much clearer perspective.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: I. THE BASIS OF WESLEY'S THEOLOGICAL THINKING
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THE BASIS OF WESLEY'S THEOLOGICAL THINKING — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶4150)

blocks.text: There were no doctrinal requirements for becoming members of Methodist societies, but once persons were admitted great care was taken to teach them true doctrines. Two practical problems with which Wesley had to deal show he did not have a casual attitude toward doctrinal issues. "Preaching houses" were provided in which the Methodist preachers resided, and each of these houses had a deed which contained the following clause: "In case the doctrine or practice of any preacher should, in the opinion of the major part of the trustees, be not conformable to Mr. Wesley's Sermons and Notes on the New Testament, on representing this another preacher shall be sent within three months." Another example comes from an occasion when a group of Methodists in Yorkshire were concerned because of the preaching of what they considered to be "false doctrines" by the preacher. They asked Wesley if they should continue to attend the services. His reply was that they first should attend the service of the church as often as possible. But that secondly, if the minister began either to preach the absolute decrees (Calvinist doctrine of election) or to rail at and ridicule Christian perfection, they should quickly and silently go out of the church; yet attend it again at the next opportunity.

The theological concern of Wesley was to lead men along the road of salvation, carefully leading the way that he should take and trusting the grace that will enable him to walk that way. The Source of Wesley's theological thinking is four-fold; namely Scripture, Reason, Tradition and Experience. This is normally referred to as the Wesleyan Quadrilateral. It is believed Wesley appealed to each of these individually in various settings or he often appealed to two or three of them jointly.
1.1.1 	Scripture

Wesley used the Bible as his most basic authority to determine Christian belief and practice. For him, Scripture was the sole authority in any doctrinal discourse. The Bible gave authority for all Christian life. For Wesley Scripture should be the constant rule of our tempers, the rule of our words and the rule of our actions and for determining doctrinal issues. Wesley was convinced of the value of reading Scripture in the original languages. He clearly considered Scripture to be an infallible, totally reliable guide for Christian belief.

John Wesley called himself Homo Unius Libri - A man of one Book. In his Journal for May 14, 1765, he writes: "In 1730 I began to be Homo Unius Libri, to study comparatively no book but the Bible." Wesley possessed a passionate love for scripture and presented a theology of scripture that affirmed its divine inspiration. "All scripture is inspired of God," said Wesley. Wesley never doubted the trustworthiness of scripture. His affirmation of the inspiration and authority of scripture resulted in him saying: "I allow no other rule, whether of faith or practice, than the Holy Scriptures."

Wesley received the Bible as the written word of God and regarded it as the supreme court of appeal in all matters of faith and conduct. The strategic importance of the Scripture in Wesley's theology may be measured from this assertion: "All Scripture is given by the inspiration of God, and herein distinguished from the Jews, Turks, and Infidels. We believe the written word of God to be the only and sufficient rule both of Christian faith and practice." He expressed his high esteem for Scripture in a letter to a friend, this way: "If by Catholic principles, you mean any other than scriptural, they weigh nothing with me. I allow no other rule, whether of faith or practice, than the Holy Scriptures."
1.1.2 	Reason

Wesley used reason most often in defending doctrinal beliefs. He referred to reason as "this Precious gift of God" and pointed out that Christ and the Apostles never failed to prove every doctrine that was taught by Scripture and reason. Though he believed that reason was a legitimate and necessary aid, he agreed it was limited in helping us understand all the issues of life and in understanding and evaluating all Scripture. For Wesley the proper use of reason clearly depended upon recognition of the parameters of God's definitive revelation in Scripture and made claims such as; "I am ready to give up every opinion which I cannot by calm, clear reason defend." The role of reason was also very important to Wesley. In his "An Earnest Appear, he affirms: "We join with you . . .in desiring a religion founded on reason, and every way agreeable thereto. This is the very religion we preach; a religion evidently founded on, and every way agreeable to, eternal reason, to the essential nature of things. Its foundation stands on the nature of God and the nature of man, together with their mutual relations."
1.1.3 	Tradition

Tradition is the history of that continuing grace in which and by which all Christians live, which is God's self-giving love in Jesus Christ. Therefore, tradition is not the story of any particular tradition. In this deeper sense of tradition, all Christians share a common history. Within that history, Christian tradition precedes Scripture, and yet Scripture comes to be the focal expression of the tradition.

Wesley affirmed the teachings and examples of the Early Church and the Anglican doctrines as important for Christian belief and life. He often quoted from the Anglican Articles of Faith, the Homilies and the Book of Common Prayer. For Wesley, the tradition of the Early Church was an important criterion in determining matters of doctrine. Wesley stressed that for a doctrine to be right it must be the same as from the beginning based on Scripture. In his sermon "On Sin in Believers", Wesley's respect for tradition of the Church is highlighted. He insisted that no doctrine can be right, unless it is the very same which was from the beginning and based on Scriptures. Wesley's appeal to the full scope of tradition in church history indicated his recognition of the guidance of the Holy Spirit in the Church following Apostolic times. While he does not hesitate to point out that the Church councils not only "may err", but have "erred", he is prepared to cast well- established tradition slightly aside.

The perspective of Wesley's view is stated in his "A Short History of Methodism", where he contends that; "It is the Methodists' one desire and design to be downright Bible Christians; taking the Bible, as interpreted by the primitive Church and our own, for their whole and sole rule." The use of our own here by Wesley means the Church of England.

Wesleyan theology believes that Scripture remains the norm by which all traditions are judged, and that the story of the church is a reflection of tradition, which points to the continuing activity of God's Spirit transforming human life.
1.1.4 	Experience

Throughout his works, Wesley emphasized the need for "plain, practical and experimental religion." Wesley believed that "experience is sufficient to confirm a doctrine which is grounded on Scripture." Thus Wesley was of the view that one's experience cannot be outside that which Scripture as the source of authority in religions judged as right or acceptable.

The use of religious experience in theological construction is one of Wesley's contributions to doctrinal judgement. Wesley believed that individuals have a personal assurance of God's acceptance and the firmest ground for such assurance was an inward sensation of God's love. His appeal to experience in relation to doctrine was only to confirm what Scripture proclaimed. Since Scripture did not explicitly answer the issue of instant or gradual sanctification Wesley used experience as his primary criterion to settling it. The claim proved true in his life and the lives of his people over time.

Experience proves in our lives the truths revealed in Scripture and shown over the years by tradition. Ghristian experience gives new eyes to see the living truth in Scripture and confirms the biblical message for time. The type of experience that Wesley valued for doctrinal decisions was the wisdom acquired through living, not the spiritual sensations one felt at the moment.

In conclusion therefore, Wesleyan theologians believe that in every theological reflection, the resources of tradition, experience, and reason are closely linked to the study of Scripture but do not displace Scripture as the primary source for faith and practice. These four sources, each making distinctive contributions working together guide our quest for a vital and appropriate Christian witness to the world.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: I. THE BASIS OF WESLEY'S THEOLOGICAL THINKING
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THE BASIS OF WESLEY'S THEOLOGICAL THINKING — The Wesleyan Quadrilateral (syllabus ¶4153)

blocks.text: Wesley's doctrine of man is based on both the Western and Eastern Christian traditions. Both traditions held that humanity was created in God's image. Wesley's understanding of human nature can be classified under three main themes: (a) Humanity as God's gracious creation (b) Humanity as fallen and (c) Humanity as freshly restored.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: II. THEOLOGY OF MAN
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THEOLOGY OF MAN — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶4193)

blocks.text: According to Wesley it was the free grace of God that formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into him a living soul. Wesley stressed that the state of man before the Fall was complete perfection. He pointed out that man is a complex being composed of both body and spirit. Throughout his writings, Wesley maintained that God created humanity not as a simple creature but as a complex one, as one composed of both body and spirit. In an early sermon manuscript, "The Image of God," for instance, he elaborates: But we should observe, first, that man even at his creation was a compound of matter and spirit; and that it was ordained by the original law that during this vital union neither part of the compound should act at all but together with its companion; that the dependence on each other should be inviolably maintained.
1.1.1 	The Body

Wesley claimed that the human body is composed of four elements, namely, dust, water, air and fire all duly proportioned and mixed together. He also affirms that the body is suitably described as "a little portion of earth," basing his argument on the Genesis account of creation where God formed man out of the dust of the earth. In one instance Wesley wrote: "The body is not the man; that man is not only a house of clay, but an immortal spirit; a spirit made in the image of God, an incorruptible picture of the God of glory; a spirit that is of infinitely more value than the whole earth; of more value than the sun, 
moon, and stars put together; yea, than the whole material creation".
1.1.2 	The Soul

Wesley believed that man is not only a body, he is also a soul. He maintained that the body cannot be separated from the soul in the state of existence. However, the death of the body will not involve the death of the soul. The soul will continue to exist when the body dies. Wesley also identified the soul or the spirit of man with the image of God. Wesley discussed man created in the image of God under three images: the natural, political and moral images of God.

i) 	The Natural Image: Wesley pointed out that man was created in the natural image of God because he had a spirit that has been endued with understanding, will and liberty. He wrote in his sermon: "The Lord God . . .created man in his own image - in his own natural image. . . that is, a spirit, as God is a spirit: endued with understanding, which, if not the essence, seems to be the most essential property of a spirit. He was endued also with a will, with various affections . . .that he might love, desire, and delight in that which is good; otherwise his understanding had been to no purpose. He was likewise endued with liberty, a power of choosing what was good, and refusing what was not so. Without this both the will and understanding would have been utterly useless".

ii) 	The Political Image: Wesley observes that in creation, man was given dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, over the livestock, over all the earth and over all the creatures that move along the ground; with this in view Wesley saw man as God's vice-regent upon earth, the prince and governor of this lower world. This means that even though God is the supreme Ruler of the earth, He has graciously allowed humanity to share in this rule and exercise authority over the lower creation. Thus for Wesley, God does not rule in isolation, but rules through His appointed vice-regents.

(Explanatory Note: A regent is a person who rules a country only for a limited period, because the king or queen is absent or too young or too ill etc. Human beings are vice-regents and not regents, because God has not left his creation in our hands to rule absolutely. We are his agents responsible to him the supreme ruler).

iii) 	The Moral Image: Using Ephesians 4:24 as his guide, Wesley stressed that man was made in the image of God; holy as God who created him is holy, merciful as the author of all is merciful, perfect as his Father in heaven is perfect. As God is love, so man dwelling in love dwells in God and God in him. He was accordingly pure, as God is pure from every spot of sin. He knew not evil in any kind or degree, but was inwardly and outwardly sinless and undefiled. For Wesley, the moral image was the principal image.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: II. THEOLOGY OF MAN
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THEOLOGY OF MAN — Humanity as God's Gracious Creation (syllabus ¶4196)

blocks.text: How did man created in the image of God and lacking nothing then fall? Wesley answered this question by looking at the role played by Lucifer, the fallen angel. He sees Lucifer's role in terms of pride. He noted: "Lucifer . . .of the first, if not the first archangel, . . .was self-tempted to think too highly of himself. He freely yielded to the temptation and gave way first to pride, them to self-will. However, Wesley distinguished the fall of Lucifer from that of humanity. For him, humanity yielded to the temptation, to the lure of an active, external power of evil, while Lucifer fell in the face of an entirely good creation. The Devil was self-tempted. Wesley maintained that Adam fell, first as a result of unbelief, a lack of trust in God. Eve, Wesley said, believed a lie: she gave more credit to the word of the Devil than to the Word of God. In his comments on Hebrews 3:12, Wesley wrote: "Unbelief is the parent of all evil, and the very essence of unbelief lies in departing from God, as the living God - the fountain of all our life, holiness, and happiness". For Wesley, then, the nature of human sin is not pride, as is sometimes mistakenly supposed, but unbelief, the perversion of a relationship between God and humanity. A lack of faith in God, then, the desire to be independent, is the true foundation for the subsequent evils of pride and self-will. Out of alienation and unbelief, pride and self-will inevitably flow; out of alienation and unbelief every other evil disposition emerges.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: II. THEOLOGY OF MAN
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THEOLOGY OF MAN — Humanity as Fallen (syllabus ¶4211)

blocks.text: According to Wesley the fall of humanity had a number of unfavourable effects. Adam and Eve experienced both physical and spiritual effects of their sin. Prior to the Fall, humanity had freely received its life from the Creator; now with the relationship broken, death held sway. Sin brought not only physical death but also pain, sickness and a whole train of uneasy as well as unholy passions and tempers.

According to Wesley in the fall of humanity, Adam brought pain, labour and sorrow on himself and all his posterity; together with death, not only temporal, but spiritual and eternal. Wesley noted that humanity as God's gracious creation can relate with God, with other humans, with lower animals and with oneself. He pointed out that true humanity is where all these relationships are properly expressed. The Fall deprived man of all these relationships. Deprived of his relationship with God, man's faculties became inevitably debilitated and morally depraved. The result was that man's understanding of God was darkened; his will seized by wrong tempers and his liberty was lost.

In the teaching of Wesley while the natural and political images were polluted or lost in part, the moral image was totally lost. Having lost the moral image of God, Adam sunk partly into the image of the Devil, in pride, malice and in other evil dispositions and partly into the image of the brute, having fallen under the power of brutal passions and degrading appetites.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: II. THEOLOGY OF MAN
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THEOLOGY OF MAN — The Consequences of the fall (syllabus ¶4214)

blocks.text: The doctrine of original sin came about as the church reflected on the writings of Saint  Augustine as to how the fall of Adam and Eve affected the rest of humanity. Thus it was an attempt to find out the physical and spiritual effects of the fall on humanity. Original sin is inherited and as to how original sin is transferred from Adam and Eve to the rest of humanity Wesley cited passages like Genesis 3:1ff, Psalm 5:5 and Romans 5:12-21.

From Genesis 3:1 and following, Wesley elaborates on the Adamic inheritance and draws a contrast between the image of Adam and the image of God. Wesley explains that Adam begat a son in his own likeness which is different from the image of God in which Adam was created. From the Romans passage Wesley states that as by the disobedience of one man, many, that is, all men, were constituted sinners. This then indicates that none are exempted from this sinful legacy, that all people, infants included are despoiled in that they suffered the very same consequences of sin, as did their progenitors, namely, suffering and death. According to Wesley, God does not look upon infants as innocent, but as involved in the guilt of Adam's sin, otherwise death, the punishment denounced against that sin, could not be inflicted upon them.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: II. THEOLOGY OF MAN
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THEOLOGY OF MAN — Original Sin (syllabus ¶4221)

blocks.text: The spiritual legacy that Adam bequeathed to humanity according to Wesley is that men and women are all gone out of the way of truth and holiness, there is none righteous, no, not one. Again citing from the Prophet Isaiah he said, "The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint. From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness". Also drawing from the first Epistle of John, Wesley pointed out that first, men and women are born into the world as atheists. He claimed: "We have by nature no knowledge of God, no acquaintance with Him. Having no knowledge, we have no love of God. Alienated from the knowledge and love of God, men and women immediately engage in a species of idolatry by worshipping themselves as the centre of meaning in life". He stressed: "We worship ourselves, when we pay that honour to ourselves which is due to God only".

Second, atheism and idolatry result in pride; they result in the self-glorification whereby men and women either think of themselves more highly than they ought to think, or glory in something which they have received as though they had not received it.
Thirdly, the Adamic inheritance entails self-will. Pride is not the only sort of idolatry which we are all by nature guilty of, Satan has stamped his own image on our heart in self-will also.

The fourth consequence of original sin is love of the world. This, Wesley developed under three components: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye and the pride of life. Thus unbelief, pride, self-will and love of the world are the inheritance that Adam and Eve bequeathed to humanity.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: II. THEOLOGY OF MAN
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THEOLOGY OF MAN — The Consequences of Original Sin (syllabus ¶4226)

blocks.text: Wesley used the term prevenient grace to mean that grace which goes before any human action for salvation. The beginning of the work of salvation in any human being is God's prevenient grace. It acts before any individual has any thought of turning to the truths of the Christian faith. The import of prevenient grace is that the initiative of salvation is with God from the beginning, before the individual ever takes a step, God is there. It may also be called antecedent grace. In this doctrine God's grace always pre-vents (comes before) and makes possible human response. In the opinion of Wesley any person, however apparently ignorant and abandoned, is under the influence of prevenient grace. God comes to humanity first. That is the significance of prevenient grace. God seeks us before we ever seek God.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: III. PREVENIENT  GRACE
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — PREVENIENT  GRACE — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶4236)

blocks.text: According to Wesley, prevenient grace is available to all. He emphasized "Free Grace" saying: The grace or love of God, whence cometh our salvation, is free in all. It is free in all to whom it is given. It does not depend on any power or merit in man; no, not in any degree, neither in whole, nor in part. God's prevenient grace is with us from birth, preparing us for new life in Christ. This grace anticipates and prepares men and women for the coming of saving grace. It implies some "tendency toward life; some degree of salvation; the beginning of a deliverance from a blind, unfeeling heart."

The Free in all grace refers to prevenient grace, which does not wait for the call. We do not have to ask for it, or even desire it. It is simply there. It does not in anyway depend on the good works or righteousness of the receiver; not on anything the individual has done, or anything he is.

In the teaching of Wesley, it is God who acts first in prevenient grace, and gives humanity the power to respond. It does not dictate the response of any individual. While always holding that the very power by which persons turn to God comes from God as a gift, Wesley also maintained free choice: that all are free to choose and, in order to be saved, must playa part by choosing salvation. Though prevenient grace inspires and enables men and women to respond to God it does not force them. In other words Wesley understood that we can resist grace.

For Wesley to say that grace is free for all means it is available to everyone as opposed to the Calvinistic teaching of predestination. The grace of God is not available for a selected few, but all; therefore the outcasts, sinners, the marginalised and the sick, could be renewed by the grace of God. It was this emphasis on prevenient grace, which was the key factor that held together Wesley's teaching on social ethics. This understanding of the doctrine of prevenient grace in Wesleyan theology is relevant to the unbeliever: It places him in a position of responsibility for his actions and renders him susceptible to an appeal that would have remained meaningless without the effort of the prevenient grace of God.

Wesley sometimes understood and explained conscience of man in terms of prevenient grace. Everyone according to Wesley; "feels more or less uneasy when he acts contrary to the light of his own grace, but because he does not use the grace which he hath."

According to John Wesley, prevenient grace gives us a sense of God but is in no sense the totality of God's grace. Prevenient grace only serves to stir us to repentance, which Wesley calls the porch of religion. The entrance to the life of faith is repentance, and it is prevenient grace that leads to repentance. The Christian life cannot begin without a person's acknowledgement of sin. Repentance or conviction of sin always precedes faith. Prevenient grace makes this recognition of the fallen state possible.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: III. PREVENIENT  GRACE
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — PREVENIENT  GRACE — Characteristics of Prevenient Grace (syllabus ¶4239)

chapters.title: JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST

blocks.text: John Wesley regarded salvation through faith as the fundamental doctrine of the church. He began his famous sermon on salvation by faith by spelling out what faith is not. It is not the faith of a heathen who merely believes that some kind of God exists. Nor is it the faith of a devil that believes and fears a just punishment. In the opinion of Wesley true faith is something that has to do with the mind. It is rational, an assent or acceptance of ideas in the mind.

Faith is a disposition of the heart. The proper object of faith is Jesus Christ, who has acted mightily for our salvation. Salvation is made possible by the grace of God given freely to all who have faith in Christ. Wesley noted, salvation is possible clearly because of the grace of God and, therefore, not something for which we can claim credit. He pointed out: "of  yourself cometh neither your faith nor your salvation, it is the gift of God, the free underserved gift".

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: IV. JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST — Introduction (syllabus ¶4254)

blocks.text: Again like faith, Wesley answered this question by first dealing with what justification is not. It is not doing things that are just and righteous, although just and good works are the immediate fruits of justification. Also, justification is not God clearing us from the accusations of Satan. In addition, justification is not the clearing us from the accusation brought against us by the law.

What then is justification? According to Wesley, justification is pardon, the forgiveness of 
sins. It is the act of God the Father, whereby, for the sake of the propitiation (sacrifice) made by the blood of his Son, he showed forth his righteousness by the remission (forgiveness) of the sins that are past. The past sins of the sinner, "in thought, word and deed, are covered, and shall not be remembered or mentioned against him", any more than if they had not been. God will not inflict on that sinner what he deserved to suffer, because the Son of his love hath suffered for him. Wesley wrote that justification involves a deliverance from guilt and punishment by the atonement of Christ actually applied to the soul of the sinner now believing on him and a deliverance from the power of sin through Christ. Thus he who is justified or saved by faith is indeed born again. He is born again of the spirit unto a new life. Wesley did not separate justification from regeneration. He observed: "in order of time, either justification or new birth is before the other, in the moment we are justified by the grace of God, through the redemption that is in Jesus, we are also born of the spirit".

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: IV. JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST — What is Justification? (syllabus ¶4258)

blocks.text: Wesley pointed out that God justified the ungodly of every kind and every degree. It is wrong to expect a person to be holy before he is justified. It is not a saint but a sinner that is forgiven. God does not justify the godly, but the ungodly. It is not those who are already holy but the unholy. Those that are saved from the power and guilt of sin are sinners of every kind and of every degree. Wesley stressed that no sinner is too sinful to be disqualified from God's forgiveness. It is not only those who are condemned by God but also those who are guilty by their own conscience. He pointed out that none of our good works is good to justify us before God. Therefore a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. He stressed that the justifying faith requires a sure trust and confidence that Christ died for our sins; that he loved us and gave himself for us. Thus for Wesley, justification comes by faith alone. However, Wesley points out that to speak of justification by faith alone is not to reject the pursuit of holiness and good works as essential components of justification. Wesley states that the faith, which leads to justification, must be productive of all good works and all holiness. This means faith in a "belief in" and not a head belief. It is a total commitment of oneself to God, who first gave himself to us. It is important to note that to be justified, a person has to take a personal decision to accept God's offer of salvation for all. Thus justification has two dimensions, God's grace and man's responsibility. God justifies by His grace, but for God's grace to be effective, man must respond to God of his own free will. Wesley warns, good works cannot save, but they are the inevitable fruit of saving faith.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: IV. JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST — Who are Justified? (syllabus ¶4263)

blocks.text: From the above it can be said that the first result of justification is the joy in our faith. Wesley came to see that, whereas prior to 1738 he had the "faith of a servant" after that time he had the "faith of a son." Another result of justification is the freedom to live as a free person - not perfect, but accepted and forgiven by a gracious God. Other results of justification are love, works, and generosity, personal and social holiness.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: IV. JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST — Results of Justification (syllabus ¶4266)

blocks.text: Wesley draws the difference between justification and sanctification. He wrote: "By justification we are saved from the guilt of sin and restored to the favour of God. By sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin and restored to the image of God. All experience, as well as Scripture, show this salvation to be both instantaneous and gradual. It begins the moment we are justified by the holy, humble, gentle, patient, love of God for man. It gradually increases from that moment as a grain of mustard-seed, which at first, is the least of all seeds but afterwards puts forth large branches and becomes a great tree, till, in another instant, the heart is cleansed from all sin and filled with pure love to God and man. But even that love increases more and more, till we grow up in all things into Him that is our Head till we attain the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ".

This means for Wesley, sanctification is the process of growth into the image of God. God has not only established a relationship with the individual who turns to him, but a process of transformation has begun in his life. Sanctification begins the moment a person is justified. This sanctification is the inner renewal of a believer by the Holy Spirit. It is the process where a believer begins to live a holy life. For Wesley the rise of Methodism was the concern for holy living. The inner work of the Holy Spirit in man is what Wesley described as holy living which comes by faith in Christ. It is this holy living which Wesley called Christian Perfection.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: IV. JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST — Sanctification (syllabus ¶4271)

blocks.text: Wesley regarded love as the basis for all deeds that might in the strictest sense be called good. He discovered that it was faith alone that opened the way by which love for God and neighbour filled the heart and become the motivating force for one's actions. He saw faith and love belonging inseparably together; it is the love of God poured out in the heart that produced love for God and neighbour.

Wesley pointed out that anyone who was renewed by God's love and given the gift of faith could not resist sharing the love he had received. Love for one's neighbour was characterized not only by its selflessness, but also by its absolute refusal to judge the person to whom it is given. Out of the relationship with God defined by love grew unlimited love for all humanity, even in the face of a neighbour harbouring hatred. In the context of Wesley's theological ethics, it is an unacceptable idea that national or religious or philosophical differences make a person unworthy of love. He said every person deserved love because he or she was loved by God.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: IV. JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST — Love of God and Neighbour (syllabus ¶4276)

blocks.text: The aim of Wesley's preaching was two-fold: Firstly, to help individuals lead a meaningful life through the renewal that comes through God's grace in justification and sanctification. Secondly, to guide such individuals into activity suited to transform the whole of society from within. People who found faith in God must experience moral transformation in their lives. Wesley described these changes in the following terms: "The drunkard commenced sober and moderate; the whoremonger abstained from adultery and fornication; the unjust from oppression and wrong. He that had been accustomed to curse and swear for many years, now swore no more. The sluggard began to work with his hands, that he might eat his own bread. The miser learned to deal his bread to the hungry and cover the naked with a garment. Indeed, the whole form of their life was changed: they had left off doing evil and learned to do well".

The Wesleyan ethics meant that one showed charity must be sensitive to the social status 
of those helped. There must be solidarity (oneness) with those who receive aid. Aid should 
be accompanied by internal and external attitude of solidarity with the poor, not the kind 
of charity that looks down on the poor who is helped and humiliates them. This solidarity implied refraining from any sort of prejudice and a readiness to forgo many personal comforts of life for the sake of others.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: IV. JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST — The Renewal of the Individual (syllabus ¶4281)

blocks.text: The doctrine of Christian perfection was so dear to Wesley that he said failure to preach Christian perfection in the Methodist societies would have negative consequences: It would cause believers to grow dead and cold; membership to fall and the work of God not to prosper. Wesley argued that the doctrine is based on Scripture as it is written: "Ye shall therefore be perfect as our Father who is in heaven is perfect".

On January 1, 1733, Wesley preached at St. Mary's Church, Oxford, and said Christian perfection is what is termed holiness in the scriptures and it implies being cleansed from sin, and from all filthiness both of flesh and spirit, the result of which is being endued with those virtues which were in Christ Jesus and the being so renewed in our mind as to be perfect as our Father in heaven is perfect.

John Wesley defines Christian perfection as pure love in the heart and life of man. He argued: "This is the sum of Christian perfection loving God and loving our neighbour; these contain the whole of Christian perfection". Wesley used several terms to describe Christian perfection. These included: Second Blessing, Entire Sanctification, Full Sanctification and Full Salvation. He states that the heart of the perfect Christian is lifted up to God at all times and in all places. He prays without ceasing. Whether he lies down or rises up, God is in all his thoughts, he walks with God continually; He loves every man as his own soul. He loves his enemies and the enemies of God.

Thus Christian perfection is the freedom to obey the two great commandments that Jesus spoke about; "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and love your neighbour as yourself' (Matt. 22:37-39). Christian perfection is giving God all our heart, devoting not a part, but all our soul, body and substance to God. It is the circumcision of the heart from all filthiness, all inward as well as outward pollution.

Christian perfection is love replacing sin, love conquering' every vile passion and temper. Love has purified the heart from envy, malice, wrath and every unkind temper. It is the heart that has put on bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness and longsuffering. A tree is known by its fruits; for as he loves God, so he keeps His commandments not only some, or most of them, but ALL from the least to the greatest. He is not content to keep the whole law and offend in one point, but has in all points a conscience void of offence towards God and towards man. Whatever God has enjoined he 
does. Loving God with all his heart, he serves Him with all his strength. He cannot speak evil of his neighbour anymore than he can lie either to God or man. He cannot utter an unkind word of anyone, for love keeps the door of his lips.

He believed Methodism must have a passion for holiness and that this emphasis on holiness was a peculiar heritage given to Methodists in trust for the Church. In 1790, a year before he died, he stressed that Christian perfection is the grand deposit, which God has lodged with the people called Methodists and that He appeared to have raised us up mainly to propagate the message of Christian perfection.

Wesley's teaching on Christian perfection was opposed by people like George Whitefield who claimed that there is no such perfection on earth. In 1740 Wesley met with Dr. Edmund Gibson, then Bishop of London at Whitehall who urged Wesley to publish his doctrine on Christian perfection to the whole world. Wesley thus came out with what Christian perfection was and what it was not.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: V. CHRISTIAN PERFECTION
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHRISTIAN PERFECTION — Introduction (syllabus ¶4291)

topics.title: What Christian Perfection is NOT according to John Wesley

blocks.text: Wesley published his understanding of this doctrine in 1766 in his treatise entitled, "A plain Account of Christian Perfection." Wesley stated that Christian perfection does not mean Christians are perfectly perfect. He gave the negative and positive meaning of Christian Perfection. As this doctrine was most often misunderstood by his critics, the Moravians, Calvinists, and others, Wesley took great care in this treatise to state in what sense Christians are not and can never hope to be perfect in this world.

Christians are not perfect in knowledge. They are not free from ignorance; or from mistake. Wesley states: We are no more to expect any living man to be infallible than to be omniscient. They are not free from infirmities such as weakness or slowness or heaviness of imagination. The perfect Christian is not wholly free from temptation for the servant is not above his Master. Neither in this sense is there any absolute perfection on earth.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: V. CHRISTIAN PERFECTION
reference.topic: 1.1 What Christian Perfection is NOT according to John Wesley
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHRISTIAN PERFECTION — What Christian Perfection is NOT according to John Wesley (syllabus ¶4307)

topics.title: What is Christian Perfection according to John Wesley?

blocks.text: When Wesley addresses in what sense Christians are perfect in his Plain Account of Christian Perfection, he immediately points out that he is "not speaking of babes in Christ, but adult Christians." "But even babes in Christ," he quickly adds, "are so far perfect as not to commit sin." Wesley asserts that the graces of mature Christians, those who are "strong in the Lord" exceed those of babes in Christ in at least two respects. Wesley pointed out that those who are perfect have the following characteristics:

First, they are free from evil thoughts. If the heart is no longer evil, Wesley reasons, then thoughts involving ill will, lust, envy, or the like will no longer be present in the heart. "But it is only of grown Christians it can be affirmed, they are in such a sense perfect, as, to be freed from evil thoughts." Wesley distinguishes between two classes of thoughts: those that wander from God, and those that wander "from the particular point we have in hand," the one evil, the other not.

Second, those perfected in love are now free from evil tempers. "By perfection," Wesley wrote to his brother Charles Wesley in 1767, "I mean the humble, gentle, patient love of God and man ruling all the tempers, words, and actions, the whole heart by the whole life."
In his treatise on Christian perfection, Wesley elaborates further what he means by this doctrine:
Christian perfection is the giving God all our heart
It is devoting, not a part, but all of our soul, body, and substance to God.
It is having the mind which was in Christ, and thus enabling us to walk as Christ walked
It is the circumcision of the heart from all filthiness, all inward as well as outward pollution.
It is a renewal of the heart in the whole image of God, the full likeness of Him that created it.
It is loving God with all our heart, and our neighbor as ourselves

Sanctification, then, is love replacing sin, love conquering every vile passion and temper. The creature, once steeped in sin, now reflects the goodness of the Creator in a remarkable way. There is nothing higher than this, nothing greater than the love of God reigning in the  soul without a rival.

Wesley concluded that he never contended for absolute and infallible perfection or for sinless perfection since that is not scriptural. He never spoke of a perfection that perfectly fulfils the whole law, and so needs not the merit of Christ.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: V. CHRISTIAN PERFECTION
reference.topic: 1.2 What is Christian Perfection according to John Wesley?
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHRISTIAN PERFECTION — What is Christian Perfection according to John Wesley? (syllabus ¶4312)

blocks.text: Even though Wesley agreed there was no sinless perfection, he still thought entire sanctification could take place. He maintained that the heart must be purified in love, freed of sin before it enters the eternal presence of the Lord. Wesley stressed that entire sanctification is instantaneous but it is preceded by and followed by gradual work. He pointed out that from the moment we are justified, there may be a gradual sanctification, a growing in grace, a daily advance in the knowledge and love of God. He however believed this gift of grace is not usually received until just prior to death. He wrote: "We grant that many of those who have died in the faith, yea, the greater part of those we have known, were not perfected in love till a little before their death". Thus Wesley insisted entire sanctification is instantaneous but just before one's death.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: V. CHRISTIAN PERFECTION
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHRISTIAN PERFECTION — Can Christian Perfection be Achieved? (syllabus ¶4332)

blocks.text: Charles Wesley was born in Epworth on 18th December 1707. He was the youngest of the three male children to survive to adulthood. He had a less robust constitution than John Wesley. Charles Wesley had the same Epworth training from their mother Susanna Wesley, as John. At the age of five he started formal education and learnt the rules of numbers, scriptures and the catechisms of the Church of England.
1.1.1 	Charles Wesley at Westminster and Oxford

At about eight, Charles went to Westminster School in 1716. By virtue of his connection he was elected a student/scholar of Christ Church, Oxford in 1726. He was much influenced in his outlook by his elder brother Samuel Wesley. Charles continued his education at Christ Church from Westminster in 1727. Originally he did not show any major concern for religion. By 1729, having been influenced by his elder brother he became so disappointed with the loose religious life on campus that he proposed to set up a group for reform and asked John Wesley's advice about the system to adopt.

In Oxford, he gathered round him a devotional group of like-minded students to study Scripture and partake of the Sacrament. It was called the Holy Club. While reflecting on his life in his old age he wrote to Dr. Chandler in 1785 about his own turn to seriousness in 1729, "I went to the weekly sacrament and persuaded two or three young students to accompany me, and to observe the method of study prescribed by the statutes of the University. This gained me the harmless nickname of Methodist. In half a year, my brother left his curacy at Epworth and came to our assistance. We then proceeded regularly in our studies and in doing what good we could to the bodies and souls of men." Once launched on his evangelical career, Charles was as active as John in preaching and in all the other activities of the Holy Club.
1.1.2 	Charles Wesley in Georgia

Charles and John Wesley agreed to go out to the new colony of Georgia: John as pastor to the first settlers and the possibility of becoming a missionary to the Indians. Charles worked as secretary to the Governor of the colony - James Oglethorpe. Charles was persuaded to be ordained so that he could share in John's pastoral duties. Like his brother John the encounter with the Moravians on board the ship and also Georgia greatly influenced his spiritual journey to holiness. Unfortunately, Charles felt homesick and found the duties as Oglethorpe's secretary tiresome. His work on the colony was full of abuses. He later found himself out of favour with Oglethorpe himself. He fell sick, became disillusioned and disheartened. For less than fourteen months after his arrival in Georgia, Charles went back to England.
1.1.3 	Charles Wesley's Spiritual Experience

Charles was still searching for spiritual holiness when John arrived back in England early in 1738. In the weeks that followed a new influence came into their lives in the person of Peter Bohler. On 24th February 1738 Bohler visited Charles during one of his periods of intense pain and weakness, and prayed at his bedside. According to Charles Wesley, Peter began to ask some searching questions. "He asked me, 'Do you hope to be saved?' 'Yes.' 'For what reason do you hope it?' 'Because I have used my best endeavours to serve God'. He shook his head and said no more." Charles was still diligently seeking reassurance in the wrong direction. Two months later he was still arguing against the idea of "instantaneous conversion" which he had been introduced to by Peter Bohler. On 25th April when Peter Bohler had left for America he wrote: "We fell into a dispute whether conversion was gradual or instantaneous. My brother was very shocking; mentioned some late instances of gross sinners believing in a moment. I was much offended at his un-edifying discourse. Mrs. Delamotte left us abruptly. I stayed and insisted a man need not know when first he had faith. His obstinacy in favouring the contrary opinion drove me at last out of the room." Charles Wesley had his spiritual conversion on 21st May 1738 after reading through Luther's commentary on the Book of Galatians.

After his conversion he played a full part in the open air preaching and struggles with the Calvinists and Moravians through his composition of hymns. He worked closely with his brother John Wesley and thus they became the leaders of the Methodist Movement. Sometimes they were together but more often they succeeded one another in the path of their travels. Charles Wesley (though has been seen to stand in the shadow of his brother John Wesley) is known to be the first who tried to implement the communal attempt at "holy living": at Oxford in 1729. Charles, too, was the first to have a personal experience of conversion - John's came three days later. More than these, it would appear that the hymns of Charles Wesley have had much greater influence on the identity and sense of community experienced by the Methodists than for example the Sermons of Wesley which often are quoted as the official doctrinal documents of the Methodists.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VI. CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY — Brief Life History: Charles Wesley 1707 - 1788 (syllabus ¶4360)

blocks.text: Charles Wesley will always be remembered first and foremost for the hymns he wrote. He was unquestionably one of the most prolific hymn-writers of all time, whether we count the number he wrote as five, or six, or even ten thousand. But far more important is the quality and range of his hymns, and the extent to which they have enriched the worship not only of Methodist congregations, but of Christians of all denominations.

Peter Bohler is said to have told Charles, "Had I a thousand tongues, I would praise Him with them all." To mark the anniversary of his evangelical conversion, Charles turned these words into a hymn which included the lines:

0 for a thousand tongues to sing 
My great redeemers praise,
The glories of my God and King,
The triumphs of his grace! (MHB 1)

For over two centuries this hymn stands as number one in a succession of Methodist Hymn Books and it has always been near the top of the charts on both sides of the Atlantic. It catches the note of joyful and triumphant praise that is so characteristic of the Wesley hymns. To know the forgiving love of God in our hearts and to experience its transforming power in our lives is to "anticipate our heaven below and own that love is heaven". The original hymn carries the title "For the Anniversary Day of One's Conversion." This is an indicator of the central meaning of the moment of conversion within the Methodist renewal movement. Charles may have been expressing gratitude for his own conversion but at the same tune he was providing the members of the movement with a tool for the expression of their individual and corporate fundamental experience of conversion.

At the very heart of the Wesley's experience and of the "Methodist gospel" is the conviction that God's love is universal - "so wide it never passed by one, or it had passed by me" (MHB 77). In the 18th century this needed to be proclaimed at least as much as it does today. Some of the early Methodists, such as George Whitefield, were Calvinists, believing that only a minority of people, "the elect" were destined to be saved. These Calvinists believed and taught that from all eternity God had chosen some for salvation, but condemned others to hell-fire. Yet Calvinists did not believe in a cruel or unjust God, but one who of his own free will and out of his great mercy chooses to save some, even though they, like the rest of mankind, are too sinful ever to deserve it.

This teaching generated a great controversy between the Calvinist Methodists and the Arminian Methodists. Against what the Arminians called this "horrible decree" Charles Wesley was never tired of asserting that God's love, the love shown to humanity in Christ, is for everyone:
O for a trumpet voice

On allthe world to call, 
To bid their hearts rejoice 
In Him who died for all!
For all, my Lord was crucified,
For all, for all, my Saviour died. 	(MHB 114)
Another hymn expresses this unrestricted love of God to all humanity in a line this way: "God's love is immense, unfathomed, and unconfined." (MHB 75)

This proclamation of God's saving and transforming love for even the most sinful of his children was the heart of the message proclaimed by the Wesley brothers. They insisted from the beginning that in one sense there was no such thing as "Methodist gospel". It was simply the old-age gospel of Christianity, neglected or misunderstood, but now rediscovered, in John Wesley's words: "Methodism is the old religion, the religion of the Bible, the religion of the primitive church, the religion of the Church of England. This old religion is 'no other than love, the love of God and of all mankind'."

Nevertheless, Methodism has always had its own special emphases, expressed both in John Wesley's preaching and in his brother's hymns. One of these is the doctrine of "Christian assurance" - the belief not only that everyone can be saved, but that they can know they are saved. This may sound dangerously over-confident and arrogant unless we understand that the Christian's trust is not in himself, but in God's "sufficient, sovereign, saving grace". The Methodist hymn numbered 371, a hymn written by Charles shortly after his conversion strikes exactly the right note of assurance tempered with gratitude and wonder, especially in its triumphant climax:

And clothed in righteousness divine, 
Bold I approach the eternal throne
And claim the crown, through Christ, my own. 	(MHB 371)

Another great Methodist emphasis was on the quest for holiness - that "perfect love" which the Wesleys recognized as the goal of Christian living. The first Methodists believed that Christian conversion is no more than a first step along that road. In hymn after hymn Charles expressed his longing to be "perfected in love": to have a "flame of sacred love" burning "with inextinguishable blaze" to the glory of God on the "mean altar" of his heart:
Jesus, confirm my heart's desire
To work, and speak, and think for thee; Still let me guard the holy fire,
And still stir up thy gifts in me -
Ready for all thy perfect will,
My acts offaith and love repeat,
Till death thy endless mercies seal
And make the sacrifice complete. 	(MHB 386)

How far short of this goal we may fall, Charles Wesley insists that we ought not to be satisfied with anything less than what he calls "heaven begun below". Wesley's hymns, then, are full of Christian teaching and give us plenty to think about as we sing them. We will note four other characteristic features of them.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VI. CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY — Charles Wesley and Methodist Hymnology (syllabus ¶4376)

topics.title: The Use of the Bible in the Methodist Hymns

blocks.text: In the year 1729, John Wesley wrote, "I began not only to read but to study the Bible." The result of this devotion is to be seen in every page that he wrote. The two brothers must have had a profound, exact, and extensive acquaintance with the Bible. Indeed there can hardly be a single paragraph anywhere in the Bible that is not somewhere reflected in the writings of the Wesleys. The hymns in many cases are a mere mosaic of Biblical passages or extracts. Here is a stanza where there is a distinct quotation in every line.

Behold the servant of the Lord! 
I wait Thy guiding eye to feel,

To hear and keep Thy every word, 
To prove and do Thy perfect will, 
joyful from my own works to cease,
Glad to fulfil all righteousness. (MHB 572:1)
These six lines recall the following six passages in the Authorised Version:
Line 1	 And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord (Luke 1:38)
Line 2 I will guide thee with Mine eye (Ps. 32:8)
Line 3 If a man love Me he will keep My words (John 14:23)
Line 4 That ye may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God             (Rom. 12:2)

Line 5: For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God 
did from His (Heb. 4: 10)
Line 6: To fulfill all righteousness (Matt. 3:15)

In 1762 Charles published a collection of Short Hymns on Select Passages of the Holy Scriptures, a kind of devotional commentary in verse. In this collection we see that the Bible underpins all the hymns of Charles Wesley. Take, for example, the first verse of MHB 386 quoted below:
On the mean altar of my heart!

In these four short lines there are quotations or echoes of at least five scriptural texts: (in order) John 3:31; 1 Kings 18:38; Luke 12:49; 1 Chronicles 21:26 (picked up again in the fourth line) and Leviticus 9:24. It is an interesting and fruitful study to look up these passages and note how Charles Wesley has used them; and this can be done with almost any hymn that he wrote. All his hymns are steeped in both the language and the ideas of the Bible.

Some of his great hymns are based on particular biblical stories, such as that of how Elijah 
on Mount Horeb heard God speaking to him in the stillness that followed a great storm 
(1 Kgs. 19). Wesley treats this as an allegory of our communion with God and the result is 
a meditation on the work of the Holy Spirit in our hearts (MHB 465).

Another, generally thought to be his greatest hymn, is based on Genesis 32:21-32. Jacob, 
on his journey home, wrestles all night with a mysterious figure who turns out to be God. 
Wesley turns this into an account of the soul agonizing in prayer until it wins through to a 
confident trust in God's forgiving love - an experience familiar to many of the early 
Methodist converts:

Speak, or thou never hence shalt move, 
And tell me if thy name is Love.

'Tis Love! 'Tis Love! Thou diedst for me! 
I hear thy whisper in my heart;

The morning breaks, the shadows flee, 
Pure, universal love thou art;
To me, to an thy mercies move:
Thy nature and thy name is Love. 	(MHB 339)

To an age haunted by belief in predestination and the dread of hell-fire, the struggle was a Every real one indeed, and so was its consummation. Isaac Watts, the other outstanding hymn-writer of the 18th century, declared that this single poem, Wrestling Jacob, was worth all the verses he himself had written.

reference.chapter: VI. CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY
reference.topic: 2.2 The Use of the Bible in the Methodist Hymns
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY — The Use of the Bible in the Methodist Hymns (syllabus ¶4421)

topics.title: The Hymns and the Great Festivals of the Church

blocks.text:
Hymns written for use during the major festivals of the Christian year were not common in 
Wesley's time. John Wesley's most important hymn-book, A Collection of Hymns for Use of 
the People Called Methodists, published in 1780, contained no section devoted to them. But 
here, too, Charles made a permanent contribution to Christian worship. There are few 
churches of any denomination which do not celebrate Christmas with "Hark, the herald 
angel sing" or Easter with "Christ the Lord is risen today". For Ascension tide we have "Hail the day that sees him rise" (MHB 221) and for Whit Sunday an expression an expression of renewed confidence in:

Away with our fears, 
Our troubles and tears:
The Spirit is come,
The witness of Jesus returned to His home.	 (MHB 278)

Notto mention a wealth of hymns in the form of prayers to the Holy Spirit. Wesley's firm hold on Christian doctrine is nowhere clearer than in his hymns for Christmas. Among the traditional carols and 19th century hymns we sing at that season, his hymns stand out by their lack of sentimentality and their clear understanding of the doctrine of the Incarnation - God become man. Again and again they express the sense of wonder at the paradox of "our God, contracted to a span, incomprehensibly made man". (MHB 142)
He laid his glory by,

He wrapped him in our clay; 
Unseen by human eye,

The latent Godhead lay; 
Infant of days he here became,
And bore the mild Immanuel's name.

This was one of his Hymns for Nativity of our Lord, published in 1744. Nowhere is the mystery of the Incarnation more fully or more tellingly expressed, unless it is in another from the same collection:
See the eternal Son of God
A mortal son of man
Dwelling in an earthly clod

Whom heaven cannot contain! 
Stand amazed, ye heavens, at this! 
See the Lord of earth and skies; 
Humbled to the dust he is,
And in a manger lies. 		(MHB 134)

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VI. CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY
reference.topic: 2.3 The Hymns and the Great Festivals of the Church
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY — The Hymns and the Great Festivals of the Church (syllabus ¶4457)

topics.title: The Sacraments in the Methodist Hymns

blocks.text:
We need to remind ourselves sometimes that Methodism began as a sacramental as well as 
evangelical movement. At a time when the Church of England neglected the Lord's Supper 
and most parish churches had only three or four celebrations a year, the Wesley's put great emphasis on it as a means of grace. They encouraged their followers to receive the 
Communion regularly and as frequently as possible, hence the number of Methodists 
flocking to church for the sacrament sometimes embarrassed the parish clergy.  Charles Wesley's Hymns on the Lord's Supper, based on an article by a high church divine, Dr. Daniel Brevint, expressed the Wesley's high doctrine of the Sacrament as a celebration of Christ's sacrificial love for mankind. For him the Lord's Supper was so much more than a mere act of remembrance that he could even speak of Christ's "real presence" in the Sacrament:
We need not now go up to heaven,

To bring the long-sought Saviour down; 
Thou art to all already given,
Thou dost ev'n now thy banquet crown:
To every faithful soul appear,
And show thy real presence here! 		(MHB 771)

It must be noted however, that the "real" did not mean "physical" or imply that the 
elements of bread and wine were changed in some way. Any change that might take place 
was in the relationship between the worshipper and God. The Wesleys knew from 
experience that the sacrament was indeed a "means of grace"; for the penitent sinner it 
might even be the means by which he was converted and found peace with God:

Come thou everlasting spirit, 
Bring to every thankful mind 
All the Saviour's dying merit 
All his sufferings for mankind. 
True recorder of his passion. 
Now the living faith impart, 
Now reveal his great salvation, 
Preach his gospel to our heart.	 (MHB 765)

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VI. CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY
reference.topic: 2.4 The Sacraments in the Methodist Hymns
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY — The Sacraments in the Methodist Hymns (syllabus ¶4479)

blocks.text:
Charles Wesley wrote hymns for all occasions and moods. No small portion of his poetry is 
dedicated to nonreligious themes. He wrote love poetry, commented on political issues and 
events of the day, from earthquake in Lisbon to the loss of the thirteen North American 
colonies. It was however, his religious hymns and poems that would have the greatest 
impact.

He followed our Lord's injunction to rejoice with those who rejoice and mourn with those 
who mourn. He loved to vary his rhythms and match them to his many themes. No other 
hymn-writer comes near him in this mastery of his art. The 1780 hymn-book contains 
sections for believers rejoicing, fighting, praying, watching, working, suffering, "groaning 
for full redemption", "brought to the birth", saved and interceding for the world.

Joy was a mark of early Methodism in an age that shrank from unrestrained expressions of 
emotion. It breaks through in hymn after hymn and prompted Charles to use rhythms that 
skip off the tongue:

My God I am thine; 
What a comfort divine,

What a blessing to know that Jesus is mine! 
In the heavenly lamb
Thrice happy I am,
And my heart it doth dance at the sound of his name. 	(MHB406)

In Methodist hymnology Christian joy is more than a passing mood. It is rooted in the certainty that, as St. Paul says, nothing can separate us from God's love - not even "tribulation or distress, persecution, famine, nakedness or peril or sword". There were times when our Methodist forebears had to put this to the test. Charles Wesley was caught  up in the terrible mob violence directed against the Methodists in Wednesbury in 1743. Four years later he found himself in the midst of similar violence at Dcvizes, where the mob tore off the roof of the house in which he was preaching to get their hands on him. When it was over, he and his companions "joined in hearty praise to their Deliverer" by singing a hymn he had written for the persecuted Methodists at Wednesbury:

Worship, and thanks, and blessing, 
And strength ascribe to Jesus! 
Jesus alone
Defends his own,
When earth and hell oppress us. . .
Omnipotent Redeemer,
Our ransomed souls adore thee:

Our Saviour thou, 
We find it now,
And give thee all the glory.
In thee rejoice,
The God of our salvation. 	(MHB 412)

The traditional view that Charles' chief contribution to Methodism was in his hymns is 
correct. As a preacher he was, as one would expect, impassioned and dramatic. John 
Wesley succinctly pointed out the difference between the two brothers in these words. "In 
connexion I beat you; but in strong, pointed sentences you beat me". The development of 
this gift of music in Charles Wesley and how he exercised it and the impact on the life of the 
church may be summarized as follows:

He was involved in poetry, or verse writing like many of his contemporaries at 
Oxford. His first piece of religious verse/poetry dates from 1728.

He must have heard the Moravians singing on board the ship Simmonds and in 
Georgia, but it seems his own gift of music was released by his conversion, as in the 
"Conversion Hymn" MHB 361.

He could readily express his hopes, fears and thoughts on all manner of things in 
verse.

Charles Wesley thought his hymns educated his readers as well as released their 
emotions in worship. He did not only write on the favourite themes of conversion, 
holiness and heaven, he could also capture a major theological fact in a verse, such 
as; "Our God contracted to a span incomprehensibly made man."

Much of the language of the hymns reveals a mind so steeped in the Bible as to use its language without conscious quotation. Like his brother, Charles often seemed to be reliving the life and mind of the apostolic age and reviving that apparently remote and lost experience for his own day. In their journey from conviction of sin through conversion to perfection, the early Methodists were taught and led as much through hymns as through sermons and Wesley's pamphlets. From them too, they absorbed a measure of theology and even of culture.
