reference.chapter: VI. CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY — Charles Wesley's Infinite Variety (syllabus ¶4492)

blocks.text:
Charles Wesley's approach to marriage was less complicated and much happier than his brother. He first met Sally Gwynne during a visit to Wales in August 1747. She was nearly 21, about 19 years younger than him. John Wesley married them in August 1748. The marriage was happy and harmonious despite the strain of itinerancy and family tragedies. In 1754 Sally was permanently disfigured by small pox, her first child died of it, and other deaths were to follow. In some Methodist eyes, the fate of his surviving sons, Charles and Samuel seem tragic. The children were talented musicians and in the next generation, Samuel Sebastian Wesley was an outstanding composer of church music. Charles tried to educate his children on Susanna's method. He was certainly concerned that they should be good Christians, but also took pride in their musical talents and was keen to enable them to 
cultivate their gift.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VI. CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY — Charles Wesley's Marriage (syllabus ¶4532)

blocks.text: Charles moved from his Bristol settlement and settled in London after 1771 and did not go out again. He arranged a series of subscription concerts at their home in Marylebone. He died peacefully in his home on 29th March 1788 and buried on 5th April. As one of his preachers put it he had no disorder but old age.

With all the attention given to the hymns of Charles Wesley as his primary and preferred 
medium of expression, it must not be forgotten that he also experienced great success as a preacher, even though very few of his sermons remain. His activities as a preacher were intensive during the early 1740's when the Methodist Movement began to form and spread through massive gatherings and preaching missions in the open air. In the 1750's Charles began to withdraw from this form of evangelism and committed his energies to the Methodist societies in Bristol and London.

Poetry remained his preferred form of expression until the end of his life. Just shortly 
before his death he dictated the following lines:
In age and feebleness extreme,
Who shall a helpless worm redeem?

Jesus! My only hope Thou art, 
Strength of my failing flesh and heart; 
Oh! Could I catch one smile from Thee, 
And drop into eternity!

John was travelling when he heard the death of his brother. His response to the news was to preach on the text: "I must work the work of Him that sent me, for the night cometh wherein no man can work." Nor did he for one moment consider cutting short his tour while there mwas work to be done. But two weeks later at Bolton, he found himself giving out the hymn about "Wrestling Jacob". When he came to the lines, "My company before is gone, and I am left alone with thee" his sense of loss overwhelmed him. He burst into tears, sat down in the pulpit and buried his face in his hands.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VI. CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — CHARLES WESLEY AND METHODIST HYMNOLOGY — His Death (syllabus ¶4535)

blocks.text:
The Wesleyan Revival was first and foremost a religious revival which stressed personal religious experience. However, from the beginning of this Movement the implication of repentance for social reform was given serious attention. Wesley had noted that Christianity is essentially a social religion and to turn it into a solitary religion is indeed to destroy it. Again he noted. "The Gospel of Christ knows no religion but social, no holiness but social holiness". Though the basic task of the Wesleyan Revival was evangelism yet Wesley was able to raise the consciousness of his nation to a host of concerns and brought relief and basic reform to a lot of poor people. Through evangelism he was able to correct many social abuses. Wesley stressed on the positive ideal of planting holiness in the hearts 
of men and women. His reform efforts also had a positive thrust due to his concern for a genuine love of one's neighbour. The Wesleyan Revival showed much social responsibility for certain categories of people. We will now turn our attention to these groups. Let's for example look at his attitude towards the poor.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VII. JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶4550)

blocks.text: He gave away much of his income to help the poor. He risked his life to make sure the poor had something to eat. Even when he was over eighty years he spent days in the streets of London from morning till evening ankle-deep in melting snow raising money to clothe those that needed it most.

Poverty for Wesley was the misuse of community resource, the use of property with little or no social consideration. This grew out of his theological understanding of God as owner and human beings as stewards. According to Wesley the irresponsible use of luxuries by the wealthy was the cause of much of the deprivation in society.

Occasionally, he called for government action to relieve scarcity and hardship for the poor. A cotemporary writer summed Wesley's attitude towards the poor as follows: "When the poor gathered in huge numbers to hear Wesley preach, the ruling classes said he was threatening the social order. Indeed he was, not because he had a political message, but just because he treated the lower classes as human".

At Oxford Wesley had attended medical lectures in preparation for his journey to Georgia as a missionary. Wesley was not only concerned with providing alms for the poor but also to set forth the genuinely Christian duty to eliminate their wretchedness. Many poor people were not able to secure medicine or the aid of a physician. To this extent, Wesley himself dispensed medicine and treated simple illness. He was able to freely aid some hundreds of people most of whom did not belong to any of the Methodist societies.

From his own savings Wesley provided the basic capital of a loan fund from which the poor 
could take interest-free loans up to three months. The loan amount was first limited to 
twenty shillings, but later raised to five pounds. Within one year more than 250 persons 
had been provided with loans, thus saving them from money lenders who demanded 
exorbitant interest. According to Wesley, true Christianity consists not in a formal, lifeless 
religion such as he observed so often in his time, but in the love of God and of all mankind. 
Wesley demanded the highest respect for all mankind from his followers. For example, the 
steward's rules contain the following: "If you cannot relieve, do not grieve the poor. Give 
them soft words if nothing else. Let them be glad to come, even though they should go

empty away. Put yourself in the place of every poor man, and deal with him just as you 
would God would deal with you". Methodism as a movement communicated to its 
followers a previously unknown sense of self - worth. It gave a new orientation to their 
existence and thus laid the ground work for an otherwise inconceivable social life.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VII. JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS — John Wesley and the Poor (syllabus ¶4553)

topics.title: John Wesley and the Use of Money

blocks.text:
Wesley formulated three simple rules to guide his followers on handling worldly goods. 
These were: "Gain all you can, Save all you can and Give all you can". Wesley cited two 
reasons for this rule. The first was, most Christians did not know how to rightly deal with 
money, and no one gave them instruction. Secondly, he thought the improper use of a 
valuable good like money entrusted to human beings by God could have far-reaching 
consequences for both Christians and their neighbours.

The first rule, gain all you can, was generally a challenge to earn as much money as possible, however, through honest means. The second rule, save all you can, exhorted the Methodist to save money in private treasuries or Bank of England saving accounts and to refrain from all unnecessary spending. Wesley indicated that money was neither good nor evil. In the hands of God's children it becomes nourishment for the hungry, drink for the thirsty and clothing for the naked. All that money could achieve, good or evil, depended on how people used it. The first two rules for dealing with money were only justified through the third rule, give all you can. Wesley drew a boundary between what a person needed to keep and needed to give away. Anyone whose income exceeded the necessities of life and personal obligations should give the excess to meet the needs of others. All those who observed the first two and not the third however, are twofold more than children of hell than ever they were before.

Wesley argued that those who impiously, unjustly and cruelly withheld from others what 
God had entrusted to them for giving aid must be blamed for the needs of others. Wesley 
saw God as the true owner of all things in heaven and on earth. Humans are stewards and 
God has provided instructions for the use of what He has given. Those who love money 
cannot love God or their neighbour. As wealth has increased in the history of the church 
the mind of Christ has diminished in the same measure: it is only the observance of the 
third rule, which sets forth the social obligations of possessions that can convert an 
increasing income into a blessing. Thus those whose pure intent is to give as much as they 
can are serving God, their neighbours and their own salvation.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VII. JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS
reference.topic: 1.2 John Wesley and the Use of Money
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS — John Wesley and the Use of Money (syllabus ¶4565)

blocks.text:
The Trans-Atlantic slave trade was started by the Portuguese and England joined the trade 
in the latter part of 1550 and became the leading exporter of slaves from Africa to the American market. The profit accruing from the slave trade was so huge that the king of 
England, Cabinet and Parliament did not oppose it. Even the Church of England (the 
Anglican Church) tolerated it without objection. In 1727, Edmund Gibson, the Bishop of 
London, rejected the call on slave owners to free slaves who had become Christians. Some 
Anglican Christians who freed their converted slaves were reprimanded by Bishop Gibson 
who appealed to the New Testament as a guarantee for keeping: slaves (1 Cor. 7:25, 
Colossians 3), saying Scripture does not contain any fundamental protest against slavery.

In 1774 Wesley published his thoughts upon slavery in which he criticized the slave trade. 
He contradicted the widely held view that Blacks were not authentic human beings and 
contended that the value of a person resides first and foremost in the individual soul, 
created by God for eternal life. He argued that Blacks as well as Whites posses such a soul. 
Wesley wrote on the cruelties of capturing, transporting and selling slaves, as well as the 
inhuman treatment by their owners which reduced them to a status hardly preferable to 
beasts of burden. Wesley held the view that both slave owners and those responsible for 
unjust legislation must expect God's punishment for their misdeeds. He rejected the 
economic necessity of slavery and maintained that any wealth derived from human 
bondage was an affront to God. He wrote: "Better no trade than trade produced by villainy. 
It is far better to have no wealth than to gain wealth at the expense of virtue. Better is 
honest poverty than all the riches brought by the tears, sweat and blood of our fellow 
creatures".

Wesley supported other anti-slavery leaders like Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson and 
William Wilberforce in their campaign against the slave trade. Methodist Conferences in 
America and England submitted petitions to Parliament calling for the prohibition of 
slavery. Wesley saw this as a truly Christian plan. In the twilight of his life Wesley and 
William Wilberforce met for the first time on February 24, 1789, where they had important 
discussions concerning the abolition of slavery. Wesley wrote in his Journal, "Mr. 
Wilberforce called upon me, and we had an agreeable and useful conversation. What a 
blessing is it to Mr. Pitt to have such a friend as this!"

It is on record that the last letter, written from his deathbed, which epitomised his strong 
and unabated resolve in the campaign against slavery, was addressed to Wilberforce. 
Wesley encouraged him to persist against the opponents of abolition and to continue in 
earnest as the Athanasius contra mundum, (Athanasius against the world). He wrote:

"Unless God has raised you up for this very thing, you will be worn out by the opposition of 
men and devils. But if God be for you, who can be against you? Go on in the name of God 
and in the power of His might till even American slavery (the vilest that ever saw the sun) 
shall vanish away before it that execrable villainy, which is the scandal of religion, of 
England and of human nature."

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VII. JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS — Slavery (syllabus ¶4572)

blocks.text:
Before his Aldersgate experience, John Wesley was involved in some noteworthy activities 
to assist prisoners. After the experience, from 1739, Wesley intensified his services in the 
London and Bristol prisons. He held conversations with individual prisoners, particularly 
with those sentenced to death, praying with them to bear their grievous fate and to view it 
as an occasion for God's leading them to repentance and eternal salvation. Many prisoners 
were moved by Wesley's sermons and accepted the Christian faith thus giving them the 
power to relieve them of the fear of death.

Wesley's work in the prisons was resisted by prison authorities and pastors. He was refused permission to converse with some who had been condemned to death even though the prisoners had requested for that. In Bristol his daily worship service was limited to a sermon per week. His sermons focused on God's limitless love for all humanity.

Wesley secured a lot of the Methodists to care for prisoners. They visited the prisoners to read the Bible and pray with them. They submitted petitions to the authorities on their behalf, comforted and encouraged them and accompanied condemned prisoners to the scaffold avoiding the hooting of crowds eager for a spectacle. Money was collected in the Methodists' worship service to buy them clothing, food and mattresses.

Wesley testified to the results that a single sermon brought to the Bristol penal institution: "the entire building was cleaned, drunkenness and prostitution were eliminated, disputes were settled on the basis of testimony from those involved rather than through brawls, and the observance of Sunday and regular services of worship became a part of the routine order."

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: VII. JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS — Wesley's Concern for Prisoners (syllabus ¶4583)

blocks.text:
Second only to Wesley's stand against the slave trade was his crusade against the brewing, 
sale and use of liquor (alcohol). He opposed the liquor trade on social, humanitarian and 
religious grounds. For Wesley, liquor which was consumed generously and without 
restraint robbed the poor and the needy the grain that could be used to feed them. It took 
away money needed for other purposes, destroyed the mind and body and was a sin 
against God. For these reasons, Wesley urged Methodists not to manufacture, sell or drink 
liquor. The General Rule of Methodists forbade drunkenness, buying or selling spirituous 
liquor or drinking them.

reference.chapter: VII. JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — JOHN WESLEY'S SOCIAL ETHICS — Wesley's Teaching on Liquor (syllabus ¶4592)

blocks.text: The Arminian and Calvanist Controversy

John Calvin was one of the great leaders of the Reformation. He led his reformation in the Swiss city of Geneva. In his teaching he highlighted on predestination and argued that God was just, even in the situation where he saved the elect and damned the reprobate (reprobate = a person of bad character and habits). He noted: "the soul of the reprobate in hell should rejoice that he has been selected to that destiny".

This doctrine was challenged by Koornheert, a layman from Holland in 1589. The church 
commissioned a young priest Jacobus Arminius (1560-1609) to answer the charges of 
Koornheert. From his studies, Arminius concluded that personal salvation is always by 
faith not by decrees as contained in the teaching of Calvin. The debate on these two 
positions held by Calvin and Armininus continued in the church to the time of the 
Wesleyan Revival. Wesley and some of his followers belonged to the Arminian group, while his friend George Whitefield and his group were Calvinists. It is said that Wesley and 
Whitefield had certain things in common - methods, enthusiasm and experiences - but 
differed on the doctrine of Predestination.

The teaching on predestination and reprobate, exalts the absolute sovereignty of God and 
claims that God in his wisdom, which is impossible to understand, has ordained salvation on those whom he has selected. Arminianism on the other hand argued that it is the will of God to save all persons. The crux of the argument was whether atonement was limited or universal. The understanding of Wesley and Whitefield on the fact that the call to evangelize was greater than their differences kept their followers from attacking one another.

Wesley, however, was not to remain silent on the issue forever. In 1740 he preached his sermon titled Free Grace which was a direct attack on predestination. He denied the Calvinist view and all that was associated with it - "irresistible grace, limited atonement, perseverance of the saints and unconditional election". Whitefield responded in a letter and attacked Wesley for holding the view that sinless perfection was possible in this life. He wrote: "What a fond of conceit is it to cry up perfection and yet cry down the doctrine of final perseverance". From 1741 onwards Wesley and Whitefield began attacking each other in correspondence. Whitefield accused Wesley of falling into the heresy of universal redemption; while Wesley bluntly told Whitefield; your God is my devil."

The conflict brought a division in the English Revival with George Whitefield leading the Calvinist Methodists connexion under the patronage of Lady Huntingdon. Two of Wesley's preachers, John Cennick and John Humphrey, joined the Calvinists. Later conflict entered into what was referred to as Pamphlets of War. Numerous pamphlets were written by both camps to attack each other. The Wesley group settled to the writing of hymns. The hymns of universal redemption drove out the doctrine of election and reprobation.

reference.chapter: VIII. THE  CONTROVERSIES
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — THE  CONTROVERSIES — Introduction (syllabus ¶4598)

topics.title: Wesley and the Church of England (Anglican)

blocks.text: John Wesley was ordained deacon in the Anglican Church by the Bishop of Oxford, John Potter on September 19, 1725. When he began preaching faith as the basis of salvation, the Anglicans began putting him out of their chapels. The Anglican belief was that one was saved at the time of baptism, infant or otherwise and subsequent experience of faith was simply redundant. Wesley drew the distinction between his sermons and those preached in the Church of England. He pointed out the differences between his message and those clergymen faithful to the Church of England as follows:

"First, they speak of justification, either as the same thing with sanctification or as something consequent upon it. I believe justification to be wholly distinct from sanctification and necessarily antecedent to it.

"Secondly, they speak of our own holiness, or good works, as the cause of our justification, or that for the sake of which, or on account of which, we are justified before God. I believe neither our own holiness nor good works are any part of our justification. The death and righteousness of Christ are the whole and sole cause of our justification and it is, on account of which, we are justified before God.

"Thirdly they speak of good works as condition of justification, necessarily previous to it. I believe no good work can be previous to justification, or a condition for it, but that we are justified by faith alone, faith without works, faith including no good works."

In spite of the above differences Wesley did not separate from the Church of England. At 
the first Methodist Conference in 1744 the issue of the relationship to the Church of 
England arose and the Conference decided to maintain unity with the Church of England. It 
also expressed its willingness to remain obedient to the authorities of the Church unless 
this obedience would compromise their obedience to God in matters of faith and mission. 
They declared that they believe and taught the doctrines of the Church of England and that 
they would obey the bishops and observe the canons whenever this was possible with a 
safe conscience. In 1752 John Wesley, Charles Wesley and some of the Methodist preachers 
signed an agreement committing their loyalty to the Church of England.

The 1755 Conference revisited the matter as there was pressure from some quarters to 
separate. The Conference resolved not to separate as it was in no way expedient. The 
desire to stay in the Church was continued and the 1756 Conference was closed by a 
solemn declaration of their purpose never to separate from the Church of England. In 1758 
Wesley declared his reasons not to separate from the Church of England. He said whether 
it was lawful or not, it was by no means expedient to separate from the established church. 
Wesley believed that normally God seeks to revive his church from within and that schism 
is only necessary when the desperate situation arises if the true witnesses are thrust out. 
He saw schism as tragic, for the mission of the church was closely associated with her 
spirit of unity and division destroys that spirit.
Charles Wesley was strongly against separation so at the 1763 Conference he warned:
Let all our preachers go to Church
Let all our people go constantly
Receive the sacraments at every opportunity
Warn against niceness in hearing a great and prevailing evil
Warn them likewise against despising the prayers of the Church
Against calling our society a church, or the Church
Against calling our preachers ministers, our houses meeting-houses
Call them plain preaching - houses.

In August 1780 Wesley asked Bishop Lowth of London to ordain some of the Methodist 
preachers to minister in America but he refused. Therefore in September 1784 Wesley 
ordained Dr. Thomas Coke as superintendent and Richard Whatcoat and Thomas Vasey as 
Elders for America. Also in 1785 he ordained John Pawson, Thomas Hanby and Joseph 
Taylor to minister in Scotland. Wesley told the 1786 conference that those ordinations 
were not separations from the Church of England or the Church of Scotland. From 1785 to 
1788 Wesley ordained more preachers for the mission fields in Antigua, Newfoundland, 
Nova Scotia, and the West Indies. In 1788 he ordained Alexander Mather as superintendent 
for England and followed it up in 1789 with the ordination of Henry Moore and Thomas 
Rankin also for England. Still Wesley did not regard these ordinations as separation and 
urged the Methodists to attend the Church of England for communion. However, 
Methodism was not accepted in England as a society within the Church of England.

blocks.text:
Episcopal Leadership of the church is the system whereby the church is led by bishops. In 
1990 the Kumasi District Synod started the discussions that would move the Methodist 
Church Ghana towards Episcopal Leadership. That same year the Chairman of the District, 
Rt. Rev'd Samuel Asante Antwi submitted a proposal to the Methodist Conference meeting 
at Koforidua. The Kumasi Synod requested Conference to adopt district autonomy with 
Episcopal Leadership involving a threefold ministry of bishops, elders and deacons.

The 1991 Conference directed District Synods to discuss the Episcopal system and submit 
their reports to the 1992 Conference. The 1992 Conference discussed the system but 
rejected the idea because there were not enough reports on it from the districts. Winneba, 
Sekondi and Northern Ghana districts did not submit any report on it. Cape Coast and Akim 
Oda were not in favour. Koforidua and Tarkwa were in favour but pointed out that the 
Church's structures be maintained. Accra was in favour but asked for adequate 
preparation. It was only Kumasi and Sunyani who were fully in favour of the system. In 
1992 the Kumasi District implemented the idea of a separated Chairman as a move 
towards the Episcopal system. Kumasi was followed by the Sunyani District. The 1995 
Conference revisited the proposal and directed the 1996 Synods to do more discussions on 
it. The 1996 Conference at Winneba directed districts to give more education on the 
system to members of the Church.

reference.subject: Methodist Studies
reference.chapter: IX. EPISCOPAL  LEADERSHIP IN GHANA METHODISM
reference.citation: Methodist Studies — EPISCOPAL  LEADERSHIP IN GHANA METHODISM — Introduction (syllabus ¶4636)

blocks.text:
The process of adopting the Episcopal system was intensified when Rt. Rev Samuel Asante 
Antwi became President of the Methodist Church Conference in 1997. The thirty-eighth 
Methodist Church Ghana Annual Conference held at the Wesley Methodist Church, 
Koforidua, from 18 to 25 August, 1999 adopted the Episcopal Leadership for the Methodist 
Church Ghana. The Episcopal leadership system as it operates in Ghana Methodism is a 
Biblical Pattern of Episcopacy unlike the Roman Catholic type which is Monarchical. 
Following the adoption, Conference mandated the General Purposes Council (GPC) to make 
the transitional arrangements to the Episcopal Leadership in Ghana Methodism.

blocks.text:

blocks.text: Human beings are social animals. We live in communities that may be part of larger social groups called Societies. In other words, we are unique and individual persons who live in this world with other persons. Such a personal being is never an isolated being, for we find our primary experience to be that of living in relation with one another sharing a whole set of values, perceptions, ideas and emotions. Being born into and living with our family, race and nation is a fact of our human existence.

A Society therefore is a group of people who conceive of themselves as distinct from other groups and who are connected together through communication ties, common customs and traditions, and institutions such as politics, law and economics. What makes human Societies different from groups of other social animals is that the members of human Societies share a sense of common identity that grows out of their shared culture.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: I. THE CHURCH AND THE SOCIETY
reference.citation: Church and Society — THE CHURCH AND THE SOCIETY — INTRODUCTION: THE SOCIETY (syllabus ¶4704)

topics.title: Why do Humans Live in Societies?

blocks.text: The following four reasons may be given:

People abhor solitude and crave companionship. We spontaneously seek others 
and enjoy their company, whereas loneliness sets up a veritable hunger in the soul.

ii) 	We cannot take care of ourselves alone. The child must be reared by the parents for many years. Without the family no children grow up, and living in the family implies cooperation right from the beginning of each one's life.

iii) 	The gift of language fits us to communicate with one another, to discuss projects of common interest, to agree on means and ends for cooperative effort. Thus the 
ability of speech indicates that we are meant to live a social life.
iv) 	Intellectual and moral development requires constant communication of ideas and values among people, an exchange possible only in a Society.

Society is therefore essential to humans. Aristotle is right in saying that; "the life of 
solitude is fit only for a beast or a god".

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: I. THE CHURCH AND THE SOCIETY
reference.topic: 1.1 Why do Humans Live in Societies?
reference.citation: Church and Society — THE CHURCH AND THE SOCIETY — Why do Humans Live in Societies? (syllabus ¶4710)

blocks.text:
There can be no existing Society without members. Only rational and free beings 
can form a Society, since it is a union based on agreement about goals.
ii) 	The members must be united in a stable or enduring way.
iii) 	The members must cooperate or work together for the attainment of some end.

This end will be some common good that all the members will share in that no 
member could accomplish singly.

iv) 	Society is held together by bonds, moral bonds of means and ends. Either the 
members bind themselves by contract, pledge or agreement or the bonds are 
imposed upon them by some law, natural or positive. It is this moral bond that distinguishes a Society from a crowd, which makes the individuals committed 
members, and obliges them to their commitment.
To guide the cooperative effort to the common good, Society must be equipped with that moral power called authority. Authority is the right to determine the means and direct the members in their use.

Hence, Society may be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good. Society is not a physical thing. The only thing physical about Society is the members and their action.

reference.chapter: I. THE CHURCH AND THE SOCIETY

blocks.text:
It is said that a friend of John Wesley once told him; 'Sir, you wish to serve God and go to heaven? Remember that you cannot serve him alone". You must therefore find 
companions or make them; the Bible knows nothing about solitary religion".

These words of the unknown friend of John Wesley emphasize a vital fact that a person 
cannot become a Christian by faith in Jesus Christ, without at the same time becoming a 
member of the people of God along with all his or her fellow believers and sharing in the life of the Church. Jesus did not come to save individuals in isolation from one another, but to found a new community of people who would build one another up in the faith and evangelize the world.

Jesus used the phrase, the "Kingdom of God" (Mark 1:14 f) more than any other. By this 
phrase he meant both the sovereign, and saving action of God, revealed in his own 
ministry.

The purpose of God is to establish a people who would own God as King through Jesus 
Christ. This people are the Church. The Church, of course is not the same thing as the 
Kingdom of God. The Church means the people of God. The Church is first of all a 
responding community, a people whose task it is to discern the action of God in the world and to join his work. The action of God occurs through what theologians have sometime called "historical events", but what might better be termed "social change".

This means that the Church must respond constantly to social change. A Church whose life is defined by and shaped by what God is now doing in the world cannot be imprisoned. All forms of injustices in the society should be addressed by the church. The fact is the church, serving as the prophet of God, should be seen as performing her role as the Prophets of old such as Amos, Micah, Jeremiah, etc. did.

As Jesus rightly put it "you are the salt of the world" and "again you are the light of the 
world". These statements by Jesus mean that the Church is the conscience of Society. The teaching of the Church should be enough to influence the Society for the better. As the light of the world, the Church serving as the light of the Society should dispel all "darkness" of the Society. By "darkness" of Society, we mean to say all things that are evil and therefore cannot be done in the open should disappear as the teachings of the Church are seen in the lives of the very people that are to proclaim the message.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: I. THE CHURCH AND THE SOCIETY
reference.citation: Church and Society — THE CHURCH AND THE SOCIETY — The Church as a Society (syllabus ¶4732)

blocks.text: 1.4.1 The Church

The Church is not an institution. It is a people. The Bible calls it Laos theou, thus "people of God". It is a people whose institutions should help them to participate in God's action in the world: the liberation of man to freedom and responsibility.
The Church must be life a "confirmed gambler" as Harvey Cox puts it.
The business of Christ to the world the business of the Church. This business of Christ is that which he himself spelt out in Luke 4:18, 19:
i) 	To proclaim release to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind,
ii) 	To set liberty those who are oppressed,
iii) 	To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.
1.4.2 The church and the Society

The Church is in the Society though it is not of it. It is to address the issues that bother on the current political world, the current economic problems, high infant mortality rate, and the abuse of fundamental human rights. Other areas that the Church should concern itself with are the problem of hunger, intra and intertribal conflicts in most pars of the world, inadequate housing, and poverty. The contamination of water bodies, pollution of the atmosphere and the fast depletion of the natural forest are some of the areas that the Church which is in the Society is to address. Other areas in which the church should be seen as the voice of the voiceless are in human right abuses, corruption, both in government and society.

Christians are part of the secular Society. We live in it and we are dependent on it, and it is in a real sense part of us. Christians cannot live in a vacuum. No man can exist or function as a Christian, any more than he can function as a human being, independently of the Society which has molded him. Christians think and act as twenty-first century humans. Christians are bound up in one bundle of life with the whole twenty-first century Social system, relying on the support of its institutions, making use of its technical expertise and involved in the tension and contradictions of movements still very imperfectly understood.

The Church is part of the world "outside" the Church and the world "outside" is within our hearts and mind. The Gospel's statement is "For God so loved the world" not only good and religiously minded people, "that he gave his only begotten son." God's love embraces all humankind, and where men and women are there the Church must be, trying to help them to make the most out of life, to overcome their frustrations and despairs, seeking to understand their moral predicaments in the light of Christian insight and experience.

There is a great deal of wickedness in the world, but "Secular" does not in itself mean 
"wicked". God does not stop his work when humans stop watching it nor withdraw his 
Presence when humans are no longer aware of it. The Christian would be spiritually blind who failed to se what a vast amount of good there is in the secular civilization of our time despite its apparent loss of belief in God.

If God is what the Bible says he is, then the welfare of human Society is a concern to him. All who are honestly working for that end - whether or not they call themselves believers - may therefore be truly said to be serving God, and indeed to be on the side of Jesus Christ - he that is not against us is for us (Luke 9:49-50).

It is now within man's ability to abolish poverty, virtually eliminating disease if it so 
wishes. What is not within his power is to control the hatreds and fears and lust within 
his/her own heart.
The Church is to remind the Society of two things:

First, that he or she has a real experience of God, some actual contact with him, through the "Secular" gifts which he/she takes for granted; and secondly, that he is in the gravest 
danger of destroying himself and his world together if he/she ignores or defies the law of God and God's transforming grace through the gift of Jesus Christ.

topics.title: INTRODUCTION: THE NATURE OF HUMAN RIGHTS

blocks.text:
We are used to thinking about human rights in terms of freedom from specific abuses or 
restrictions especially by governments. The American Bill of Rights for example, prohibits (except in extreme cases) the government abridging your right to exercise your religion or free speech, from discriminating against citizens based on race and other demographic traits, from being imprisoned without trial, and from a variety of other abuses. There is, however, a more comprehensive concept of rights. This broader view holds that peoples and groups, not only have the right not to be specifically abused, but they also have rights to a quality of life that at a minimum, does not detract from their human dignity. One scholar suggests that the most fruitful way to think about human rights is to begin with the idea that "ultimately they are supposed to serve basic human needs" (Galting, 1994)
According to Galting (1994), the basic human needs which generate corresponding rights are:

Survival needs - to avoid violence: This is the right to be free from individual and 
collective violence.

Well being needs - to avoid misery: The right to adequate nutrition and water; to movement, sleep, sex and other biological wants, to protection from diseases, and 
adverse climatological and environmental impacts.

Identity needs - to avoid alienation: The right to self expression; to realize your 
potential, to establish and maintain emotional bonds with others; to preserve 
cultural heritage and association; to contribute through work and other activity; 
and to receive information about and maintain contact with nature, the global 
humanity and other aspects of the biosphere.

Freedom needs - to avoid repression: The right to receive and express opinions, to 
assemble with others, to have a common policy; and to choose from a wide range in matters as jobs, spouse, where to live and life style.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: II. HUMAN RIGHTS
reference.topic: 1.0 INTRODUCTION: THE NATURE OF HUMAN RIGHTS
reference.citation: Church and Society — HUMAN RIGHTS — INTRODUCTION: THE NATURE OF HUMAN RIGHTS (syllabus ¶4774)

blocks.text:
Before we look at the Biblical basis for human rights, let us take a look at some secular 
basis and some significant developments in the modern understanding of human rights. 
There is an ancient debate about the basis of human rights. One school, the universalists, believe that human rights are derived from one or another theological or ideological doctrine or from natural rights. This concept holds that the fact of being human carries with it certain rights that cannot be violated or cannot be violated in extremes. Universalists therefore believe that there is a single, prevailing set of standards of moral behaviour on which human rights are based.

The other school of thought, the positivists, argue that rights are the product of culture. 
Positivists therefore contend that in a world of diverse cultures, no single standard of 
human right exists or is likely to exist short of the world becoming completely homogenized culturally.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: II. HUMAN RIGHTS
reference.citation: Church and Society — HUMAN RIGHTS — The Basis of Human Rights (syllabus ¶4787)

topics.title: Developments in Modern Understanding of Human Rights

blocks.text: Human beings have doubtlessly thought about themselves and their identity, their duties and their rights, from the beginning when they decided to live in societies. Plato and Aristotle fought with the notion of freedom and justice, while Thomas Aquinas and other medieval theologians, discussed them in their writings. The following historical development may be noted:

Human right advocates in Britain claim look back gratefully to the Magna Carta 
which King John was induced to sign in 1215. Among its provisions were the 
guarantees of freedom for the Church and of fair trial by one's peers.

b) Another, milestone in British history was the Bill of Rights (1688-1689), which 
made the Crown subject to Parliament.

ii)	The American Declaration of Independence (1776), drafted by Thomas Jefferson, 
affirmed as "self evident" that all men are created equal "and that they are endowed by their creator with certain inalienable rights" especially the right to life, liberty and pursuit of happiness.

iii) 	Similar language was used in France's Declaration of The Rights of Man and of 
Citizens, which was promulgated by its National Assembly in 1789. It speaks of 
man's "natural, and inalienable rights" or "the natural inalienable and sacred rights of man"

iv) 	In 1941 President Roosevelt gave his famous "State of the union" address, in which he looked forward to the emergence of "a world founded upon the following 
essential freedoms: (a) freedom of every person to worship God in his own way; (b) freedom from want; and (c) freedom from fear - after each of which he added the words "everywhere in the world".

The United Nations Organization was established in 1945, and the preamble to its 
charter reads: "we the people of the United Nations" are determined "to reaffirm 
faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person, 
the equal rights of men and women and of nations large and small. .. ". Article 55 
says that the United Nations shall promote "Universal respect for, and observance
of human rights and fundamental freedoms for, all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion.

Universal Declaration of Human Rights: The United Nations established the Human Rights Commission, under the chairmanship of President Roosevelt's widow, Eleanor. It was tasked with the preparation of a Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the first element in the international Bill of Rights which it had been commissioned to produce. Its preamble affirms that "recognition of the inherent dignity, of the equal and inalienable rights, of all members of the human family, is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world". Article 1 deals with dignity and rights. Article 2 adds that "everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in the declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, poverty, birth or other status."

The first part of the declaration covers political and civil rights, and the second part 
economic social and cultural rights. It was adopted by the UN General Assembly in Paris 
on 10th December 1948, though not all nations ratified it. In 1966 the two international 
covenants (one on economic, social and cultural rights and the other on civil and political rights) were published. And in 1973 the Helsinki Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe was held, whose final Act (1975) included a section on "The Respect of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms". In 1976 the two International Covenants came into effect, and so the long dreamed-of International Bill of Human Rights became a reality.

reference.citation: Church and Society — HUMAN RIGHTS — Developments in Modern Understanding of Human Rights (syllabus ¶4792)

topics.title: The Biblical Basis of Human Rights

blocks.text: According to John Stott we need to ask some basic questions including the following if we are to grasp the basis of human rights:
i. 	How is it that human beings have any rights?
ii. 	Whence did they acquire them?

iii. 	Have Christians anything distinctive to contribute to the debate and action about 
human rights?

John Stott begins his answer to these questions by stating that, "The origin of human rights is creation. Man has never "acquired" them. Nor has any government or other authority conferred them. We have had them from the beginning. We received them with our life from our Maker. They are inherent in our creation. They have been bestowed on us by our Creator." "Fundamental, therefore, to human rights is the question of what it means to be human", he adds.

According to John Stott, the Biblical basis of human rights hinges on three words - 
"dignity", "equality" and "responsibility".
1.3.1 	Human Dignity
This is based on Gen. 1:27-28 which deals with God's purpose for our creation, and three issues stand out:

Our relationship to God - "God created man in his own image". Human beings have 
dignity because we are God-like beings crated by God's will in his image. The divine image includes those rational, moral and spiritual qualities which separate us from the animals and relates us to God.

Our relationship to one another - "male and female he created them." John Stott 
writes; "The God who made humankind is himself a social being, one God 
comprising three eternally distinct modes of personhood - the Trinity. This God 
said 'Let us make man in our image' and added; 'it is not good for the man to be 
alone'." It is then clear that sexuality is God's creation, marriage is his institution, 
and human companionship is his purpose. Therefore anyone who abuses these, 
abuses God, because the basis of all these relationships are derived from Him.

Our relationship to the earth and its creatures - "fill the earth and subdue it" "God 
has given us dominion, with instructions to subdue and cultivate the fruitful earth and rule its creatures. So then, all those human rights we call the right to work and the right to rest, the right to share in the earth's resources, the right to food, clothing, shelter, the right to life and health and to their preservation, together with freedom from poverty, hunger and disease" find their basis in this injunction given by God our Creator. It may therefore be summarized that, "all human rights are based on the right to be human and so to enjoy the dignity of having been created in God's image and of possessing in consequence unique relationships to God himself, to our fellow human beings and to the material world."

In addition to this dignity derived from our createdness, Christians can also talk 
about the surpassing dignity derived from our Creator redeeming or recreating us, through the incarnation and atonement of his Son.
1.3.2 	Human Equality

"The tragedy is that human rights have not always meant equal rights", so writes John 
Stott. "The good gifts of the Creator are spoiled by human selfishness. The rights God gave to all human beings equally, easily degenerate into my rights on which I insist, irrespective of the rights of theirs or of the common good. So the history of the world has been the story of conflict between my rights and yours, between the good of each and the good of all, between the individual and the community." The God we worship shows "no partiality," therefore in our attitude to other people, we must show no partiality or give special deference to some because they are rich, famous or influential.

Moses told Israel; "The Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the 
mighty, the terrible God, who shows no partiality and accepts no bribes ... " Therefore 
Israelite judges were to show no partiality either, but rather justice "to the small and to the great alike" (Deut. 10:17-18, cf. 16:18-20). All human rights violations contradict the 
equality we enjoy by creation. "He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker" (Prov. 14:31).
1.3.3 	Human Responsibility

The last word derived from our createdness is "responsibility". Whenever human rights 
are emphasized to the exclusion of human responsibility, we miss the Biblical pattern. 
What we often hear is one person asserting his or her rights against another person and 
this often leads to conflict. It seems also to encourage selfishness.

Discussions on human rights often overlook the fact that human beings have duties and 
responsibilities as well as rights.

The Bible calls us to defend other people's rights, but when it addresses us, it emphasizes our responsibilities, not our rights. The Bible emphasizes that our responsibility is to secure the other person's rights and we must forgo our own rights in order to do so.

Jesus Christ is the supreme model of this renunciation of rights as we are told in 
Philippians 2:6-7. Throughout his life he was a victim of human rights abuses and yet he 
declined to defend or demand his rights, in order that by his self-sacrifice, he might serve us, Paul therefore encourages us thus, "Let this mind be in you which was in Christ Jesus."

Paul practiced what he preached. He had rights as an apostle (the right to marry, the right to receive financial support), but he renounced them for the sake of the Gospel, in order to become everybody's slave and to serve their rights (1 Cor. 9)

The Bible enjoins Christians in several places to forgo their rights. Talking about settling 
disputes, it asks: "Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?" (I Cor. 6:7)

reference.chapter: II. HUMAN RIGHTS
reference.topic: 1.3 The Biblical Basis of Human Rights
reference.citation: Church and Society — HUMAN RIGHTS — The Biblical Basis of Human Rights (syllabus ¶4810)

blocks.text:
John Stott concludes, by addressing the Christian community or the local church which 
must set an example of God's rule as follows:
"The Church should be the one community, in the world,
in which human dignity and equality are invariably recognized and people's responsibility for one another is accepted;
in which the rights of others are sought and never violated, while our own are often renounced;
in which there is no partiality, favoritism or discrimination;
in which the poor and the weak are defended, and human beings are free to be human as God made them and meant them to be."

blocks.text: Increasing awareness of the need for mass participation in politics is compelling political scientists to pursue more inclusive definitions of the term politics. A classical definition of politics is, "An activity by which some persons conduct the public business." This definition is narrow since it excludes the activities of the masses whose actions could influence the public business. Dr. Kwame Afari Gyan wrote in 1991 that "The term politics refers to the activities, ranging from persuasion to force, which the parties to a political situation may undertake in the desire to get their preferred course of action to prevail" (Understanding Politics, Asempa publishers, 1991, p, 15).

While Afari Gyan's definition is more inclusive than the classical, it still needs some improvement since it excludes beliefs in the form of ideas, ideologies or philosophies about the way people are governed or should be governed such as aristocracy, socialism, and democracy. So a still better definition would be one that accommodates the beliefs, prayers, voting, lobbying, advocacy, civil disobedience and mass demonstrations as well as other actions by groups or the masses aimed at influencing the way that they are governed as a people. Politics then could mean the beliefs and practices in a society that tend to influence the way it is governed.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: III. POLITICS
reference.citation: Church and Society — POLITICS — INTRODUCTION: WHAT IS POLITICS? (syllabus ¶4856)

blocks.text: Throughout the church's history, from the time of Christ up to the present day the church has been struggling with how best to define its relationship with the secular state. Should the church dominate and control the state? Or, should there be a total separation between them? Or, is it possible to define some common grounds where they could come together to pursue the common good of the people and in what should they operate separately?

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: III. POLITICS
reference.citation: Church and Society — POLITICS — Church and State Relations (syllabus ¶4861)

blocks.text: Democracy is by far the most politically friendly of all political ideologies of the state as far as the Church is concerned. As beautifully expressed by Abraham Lincoln "democracy is the government by the people, for the people and of the people". Being a "government by the people" means it is not imposed by anyone but chosen by the people themselves through elections under the guidance of a self-chosen constitution. Being "for the people" means it ensures that the goods and services as well as the protection offered by the state are, as much as possible, fairly distributed to the benefit of all. Finally being" of the people" means it ensures that all sections of the populace: men, women racial or ethnic/tribal minorities, rich or poor, are given equal opportunities to compete for political positions/administrative positions in the government.

Also it is far better than all its alternatives especially, communism and other dictatorships since it ensures the type of constitution and government most conducive to the freedom and mission of the Church. For example, democratic constitutions as we have in Ghana now adopt the U.N Declaration of Fundamental Human Rights which include the right to freedom of worship, freedom of expression, and protection from discrimination on the ground of religion or sex. Like the church, democracy is not perfect. Just as the Church needs democracy for the smooth operation of her mission, democracy also needs the church to overcome some of her weaknesses or to minimize their impact on society. In the next sections some of the inherent weakness of the system and how the church could be of help are discussed.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: III. POLITICS
reference.citation: Church and Society — POLITICS — Democracy and the Church (syllabus ¶4864)

blocks.text: For its many inherent weakness, Winston Churchill once remarked, "Democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others". In other words, although democracy is not perfect, it is better than any other form of government known to man.
1.3.1 	The Tyranny of Democracy

This refers to the tendency of politicians in a democracy to look out for the interest of the majority while neglecting the interest or abusing the rights of the minority. This could be very dangerous where the majority happens to be a particular racial, ethnic, religious or ideological orientation.
Suggestion: The church can help ensure that the government is fair to all its constituents and that minority rights and interests are protected as much as possible.
1.3.2 	The Fallacy of Democracy

This fallacy is committed whenever one tries to defend "The Tyranny of the Majority" by arguing that the practice is right since democracy by definition, is the rule of the majority. It is clearly a conceptual blunder, for a majority rule does not and should not imply minority suffering. Democracy must promote freedom and justice for all, majority or minority especially where there are vulnerable religious, ethnic, religious or ideological orientations.

Suggestion: The Church can help expose this conceptual error about democracy and 
ensure that the government is non-discriminatory but fair to all citizens irrespective of 
one's political affiliation, race, ethnicity, age or sex. This is supported by Paul's statement in Gal. 3:28 "So there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles, between men and women; you are all one in union with Christ Jesus."
1.3.3 	The Disease of Democracy

Socialist critics of democracy have often taunted democracy for being sick of an incurable disease. This they claim, is the disease of frequently electing representatives to parliament/congress or other political offices who make wonderful promises to help their constituents and fail and only attempt at helping the people when they need to seek re- election amidst a tough competition.

Suggestion: Let the church educate her members and others on this selfish tendency and study political candidates very well before voting for them. The church should also train and encourage non-selfish or altruistic matured Christians who are qualified in other respects to stand as candidates for offices.
1.3.4 	Red Tapeism

Another weakness of democracy is Red Tapeism which is the tendency to complicate and unduly delay administrative and legal procedures so much that in the end those at the receiving end feel frustrated and unsatisfied or that justice has been denied them. In order to circumvent such undue delays, those in need of the relevant services may be tempted to bribe their way out. But that breeds more corruption in the society. Worse still, others feel that justice will never be achieved though the courts and may take the law into their own hands and resort to the use of arms.

Suggestions: The church can advise their members and others in administration to 
minimize delays and work as if they are working for God instead of working on lotto in the offices and protecting themselves from dismissals by appealing to employee rights and trade union conventions etc.

In the case of court delays, the church should organize some experienced church leaders, superannuated clergy, lawyers and retired judges and magistrates etc. into "Christian Family Arbitration Centres" for conflict resolution to help settle cases out of court. This would be a great contribution in the government's attempt at finding alternatives to court arbitration and for decongesting the overburdened legal system.
1.3.5 	Catalyst for Ethnic Conflicts

Democracy uninhibited, is a fountain-head that ideally ensures the free flow of freedom 
and justice for all. Recent history in eastern Europe and Africa as well as other emerging democracies however have clearly indicated a high correlation between democratization and the spread of ethnic conflicts.

The observed correlation cannot however, be dismissed as a mere coincidence since there is the natural tendency for previously oppressed and exploited ethnic groups to seize the opportunity afforded by the prevailing wind of change with its emphasis on respect for freedom and human rights, in particular "the Right To Self Determination," to separate themselves from their former oppressors in their quest for freedom and justice.

Suggestions: Churches in conflict-prone areas must be part of the "early warning system" and keep security agents informed about any attempts at separation or civil wars. At the same time the church must educate members and non-members as well on the dangers of ethnic conflicts, preach against it, and courisel the people concerned against such destabilizing moves.
1.3.6 	The Problem of Vagueness

The terminologies that constitute the tenets (i.e basic beliefs and values) of democracy are inherently vague and sometimes intolerably ambiguous. As a result, it is often difficult to determine when they have been achieved or not. These terms include, freedom, justice, equality, democracy, peace and unity etc. So while one group might be thinking that sufficient peace, freedom and justice etc, have been attained under a given circumstance, others might think otherwise and intensify the struggle towards their attainment. The questions raised include e.g. Is Ghana truly free? Is there true peace and democracy in our country?

Suggestion: The Church can help sensitize the people on the problems of vagueness an 
ambiguities inherent in the use of these terms especially within the context of conflict 
resolution or prevention and how they could be easily manipulated by political 
adventurers and opposition parties.
1.3.7 	Vulnerability to Military Coups

The history of post-colonial Africa and most of the Third World countries which began the process of democratization some 30 or 40 years ago shows that democracies in these regions are particularly vulnerable to military coups. Africa alone has witnessed about 50 coups and without exception, a common major cause cited in all of them is corruption. Consequently, it appears that as long as corruption prevails in these democracies no one can guarantee that there will be no more military take-overs and that the emerging or re- emerging democracies could be sustained. The case of Nigeria and Sierra Leone where power has been snatched away from democratically elected leaders are good examples of the renewal of this trend.

Suggestion: The church through her military chaplains, guest preachers to the barracks, 
and the mass media should help the military and all others to realize that corruption is 
part of human nature and cannot be removed by military coups. They should be helped to appreciate the checks and balances in democracies which could be further strengthened through education and legislation and the opportunity of citizens to use their voting powers to remove corrupt politicians and statesmen through the ballot box without bloodshed or violence.

In addition to praying for the state and supplementing the government's efforts through the establishment of more schools, vocational and technical institutes, as well as agricultural research centres etc., the churches could help sustain democracy by taking some of the actions suggested as solutions to the various problems of democracy.

Government, whether acting on behalf of a people or otherwise, is the result of politics. 
Politics is often considered such a corrupt and debasing profession that no self-respecting person would consider entering it. But politics is also a feature common to all human society. It is an activity that "arises from accepting the fact of the simultaneous existence of different groups, hence different interests and different traditions within a territory ruled". We have to participate in politics because we need it.

A distinguished political scientist Harold Laswell, defined politics as a process of 
determining "who gets what, when and how". David Easton, also defined politics as lithe authoritative allocation of values". Politics is therefore, a common feature of daily human existence that occurs wherever and whenever decisions are made about "who shall get what, when and how".

reference.citation: Church and Society — POLITICS — Sustaining Democracy: The Church's Role (syllabus ¶4868)

topics.title: Politics as the Making of Common Decisions

blocks.text: Any group of people must often make decisions that will apply to all of them, A family must decide where to live, what sort of rules to set for children, how to balance a budget, and so on. A country must decide where to locate a stadium, how to raise revenue by taxing its citizens, how to care for the helpless, and many other things. Each of these requires the setting of some sort of common policy for the group, a single decision that affects all members of the group.

Not all human actions, of course, involve the making of a common policy for a group. A 
person's decision to build a house is not of any common national policy, although the 
country may have policies - on interest rates, the regulation of building, land use, zoning, and so on - that affect this person's decision.

Actions that contribute to the making of a common policy for a group of people constitute politics and questions about those policies and the making of those policies are political questions. A family's decision to build a house is not a political decision for the country. But it is political for the family as a group inasmuch as it involves a common policy for the family.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: III. POLITICS
reference.topic: 1.4 Politics as the Making of Common Decisions
reference.citation: Church and Society — POLITICS — Politics as the Making of Common Decisions (syllabus ¶4911)

topics.title: Politics as the Exercise of Power

blocks.text:
A second characteristic of politics is that politics always involves the exercise of power by one person or persons over another person or persons. "Power" is the ability of one 
person to cause another to do what the first wishes, by whatever means. Politics always 
involves this: one person causing others to do what that person wants by forcing or 
convincing them to do so.

The two defining characteristics of politics, then, are that (1) politics always involves the making of common decision for groups of people and (2) those decisions are made by some members of the group exercising power over other members of the group.

Politics then consists of the making of common decisions for a group through the use of 
power. Politics generally involves considering at least the broad needs of the group for 
whom policy is being made. Any act of politics may be viewed from either of two 
perspectives, either as a cooperative search for an answer to common problems or as an act by which some members of a group impose their will on other members of the group.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: III. POLITICS
reference.topic: 1.5 Politics as the Exercise of Power
reference.citation: Church and Society — POLITICS — Politics as the Exercise of Power (syllabus ¶4918)

blocks.text:
Much of this is taken from an article by the same title in the ABC Commentary, written by James B. Rantiok. He argues that the unwillingness of many Christians to participate in politics is partly rooted in a failure to distinguish between party politics and political 
participation.
"Political participation includes exercising one's rights to vote and be voted for, speaking out against any wrongdoing by those in power and holding leaders accountable for their actions."
He continues:

"While Christians tend to avoid political participation, Muslims understand its importance. Consequently, they control political power in many African States, even those where they are a minority. Unlike Christians, they do not believe in the separation of church and state because it encourages secularism."

Kantiok adds: "Jesus, too, did not separate religion and politics. In his mission statement in Luke 4:18-19 he declared that his ministry was to those suffering various forms of bondage and oppression, including economic oppression(poverty) physical oppression (disease and disabilities) political oppression (injustice and oppressive rule) and demonic oppression (various forms of occult practices).

Other Biblical examples of political participation include Joseph in Egypt, who saved many from hunger and starvation, (Gen 41); Amos, who warned the political leaders of his time against injustice; Daniel and his tree friends, and Nehemiah.

"In the New Testament, Paul refused to give up his rights as a citizen when the political 
authorities put him in prison and flogged him without giving him a proper trial (Acts 
16:37-38; 22:25)." Kantiok therefore advises: "Moral bankruptcy, corruption, poverty, disease and ignorance: all clearly call for Christian participation in politics", and concludes "African Christians need to understand that the destinies of their nations rest on their political participation."

blocks.text: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship whether at home, work, church, nation, etc. When people come together regularly, especially when it involves issues of personal significance, differences emerge.
When conflict occurs between people (individually or in groups), they often become angry, hurt, bitter or defensive. Sometimes the conflict ends the relationship or seriously damages it.

We need to recognize that while conflict is inevitable in relationships, it can have either 
constructive or destructive results. Sometimes, conflicts measure the health of an organization. In groups where nothing happens important enough to make people fight, they have a greater chance of dying than groups were dissensions occur.

Conflicts also spotlight problems that require attention. Conflicts do not only arise between people. We also experience conflict within ourselves, when we go through an inward personal struggle or restlessness of the soul.

Conflicts may force clarification of issues and challenge leaders to question the status quo and search for better solutions. For example, good handling of the conflict between the Greeks and the Jews in the Early Church in Jerusalem resulted in the rapid growth of the Church. (Acts 6:1-7).

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: IV. CONFLICT MANAGEMENT
reference.citation: Church and Society — CONFLICT MANAGEMENT — INTRODUCTION (syllabus ¶4942)

blocks.text: There are both positive and negative effects of conflict.
1.1.1 Positive Effects
i)	Long-standing problems surface and are dealt with.
ii) 	It helps clarify people's viewpoints.
iii) 	The tension created heightens interest and stimulates creative thinking.
iv) 	It produces better ideas and forces people to search for new approaches.
v) 	People feel challenged and receive the opportunity to test their abilities.
1.1.2 Negative Effects
i) 	A climate of suspicion and distrust develops.
ii) 	It reduces contact between people and some stop communicating with each other.

iii) 	Parties that need to cooperate and work together pursue their own self-interests 
which result in resistance (active or passive) instead of teamwork.
iv) 	It leaves some to feel defeated, embarrassed and demoralized.
v) 	Some people leave organizations they belong to.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: IV. CONFLICT MANAGEMENT
reference.citation: Church and Society — CONFLICT MANAGEMENT — Effects of Conflict (syllabus ¶4954)

blocks.text: Six common causes of conflict may be identified:
Differences in perception: No two individuals perceive things in the same way, and this often leads to misunderstanding, confusion and conflict.

ii. 	Differences in Priority or Values: Values are deeply held beliefs. Conflicts often 
develop when people with different value systems try to work together. Value 
conflicts arise over differences in religious, moral, ideological, or philosophical outlooks. When conflict concerns values, people have difficulty in changing their stand.

iii.	Differences in Expectations or Role Pressures: Conflicts often arise over different expectations when they are not fulfilled. For example, you may hear two people with different expectations saying; "I wanted you to. . ." And the other responding, "I expected you to. . ."

iv.	Divergent Goals: Consider this problem: Yaw Nkrumah and Kwadwo Nsiah work 
for the same organization, but in different departments. Yaw wants to help the company make more profit by improving the quality of their products. Kwadwo wants to see the company make more profits by decreasing costs. This leads to competition among the managers for available resources. Lack of team effort can develop into enormous conflict situations.

v.	Self-Esteem or Status Threat: Yaw Nkrumah may have a good idea, but Kwadwo Nsiah's Self-esteem depends on his having all the good ideas. But Kwadwo is the boss and bosses know best. In such a situation status and authority become sources of anger and frustration.

vi. 	Personality Clashes: Troublesome individuals have hostile natures and arepredisposed toward conflict. People with strong needs to bully, use their jobs to express hostility. Often, individuals with low self-esteem overcompensate by being belligerent or hostile toward other people.

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: IV. CONFLICT MANAGEMENT
reference.citation: Church and Society — CONFLICT MANAGEMENT — Sources of Conflict (syllabus ¶4971)

blocks.text: In his article by the same tile in ABC Commentary, Tokunboh Adeyemo gives the following steps in conflict management and resolution.
He writes: "When we manage a conflict, we simply organize, regulate and take charge of it in order to make it serve a good cause. . ."
He further states that:
"In resolving any conflict, there are three key questions to ask:
What are we agreeing or disagreeing about?
Why are we agreeing or disagreeing?
How can we get past this and move forward?"
He proposes the following five principles which must guide us in resolving conflicts:

Honest Communication - Silence and isolation deepen misunderstanding, which fuels conflict. In Genesis 13:1-18, Abraham did not gloss over the potential for quarrels between his herdsmen and those of Lot. He discussed it openly with Lot and developed an appropriate strategy to deal with it.

ii) 	Getting beneath surface issues and unseen motives - Often the apparent cause of a conflict is not the real issue. Instead the conflict is rooted in people's underlying motives and beliefs, which they may not have clearly identified. In Genesis 26:19- 31, the real problem between the people of Gerar and Isaac went beyond water.

iii) 	Negotiation - The best way to find peace is through a process of give and take in which neither party to the conflict insists on being the winner. The story of 1 Kings 12 show the disastrous consequence of Rehoboarn's unwillingness to negotiate.

iv) 	External intervention - The parties involved in a conflict may be so caught up in it that they have difficulty talking to one another and reaching any agreement. In such a case the assistance of a neutral person such as a marriage counselor or an 
organization like the United Nations may be sought. In Acts 15:1-2, we have the 
story of Paul and Barnabas and their opponents taking their case to the apostles in Jerusalem.

Divine Intervention - There is a spiritual dimension to conflicts. Thus in resolving conflicts we need to seek Divine assistance or intervention. The Council at Jerusalem resolved the crisis that would have permanently divided the church into Jews and Gentiles (Acts 15:23-29).

reference.subject: Church and Society
reference.chapter: IV. CONFLICT MANAGEMENT
reference.citation: Church and Society — CONFLICT MANAGEMENT — Conflict Management (syllabus ¶4986)

blocks.text:
In Matt. 18:15-17, Jesus gave the steps that must be taken to resolve conflicts between 
believers:
Approach the other party directly, but privately, seeking honest communication.
Seek external help in the form of two or three witnesses who can help uncover the real sources of the disagreement.

If all these steps fail, we are to take the conflict to a larger body, the churc, for its 
mediation.
If the conflict persists, the root of the problem must be identified as a sinful attitude and the party who refuses to work for reconciliation must be treated as an unbeliever.
